News.title: Shocking X-ray shows knife lodged in man’s neck after he miraculously SURVIVES being stabbed ‘by wife’
News.content:
BLADE OF GORY Shocking X-ray shows knife lodged in man’s neck after he miraculously SURVIVES being stabbed ‘by wife’







Next

A HORRIFYING X-ray shows a knife buried deep in a man’s neck after he miraculously survived a savage stabbing allegedly carried out by his wife.

Alessandro José de Oliveira, 48, cheated death when the blade narrowly missed a major artery by less than half an inch.



The terrifying attack left the Brazilian man with a fractured jaw after the knife sliced through the side of his neck and emerged near his mouth.

But incredibly, the blade missed his carotid artery – a vital blood vessel responsible for carrying blood from the heart to the brain.



Alessandro was rushed to hospital following the bloody ordeal in Machado, southeastern Brazil, in the early hours of November 14.

His 45-year-old wife was arrested on suspicion of carrying out the attack after allegedly giving cops conflicting accounts of what happened.

Surgeons faced a delicate operation to remove the embedded blade without inflicting further damage to his neck.

Trauma surgeon Rommel Carneiro, who helped perform the life-saving procedure at Alzira Velano Hospital, revealed just how close Alessandro came to death.

He said: “Luckily, it passed almost a centimeter past the most important vessels. It didn’t reach the carotid artery.

“We were able to control the bleeding and perform the surgery in time.”



The medic explained that the biggest challenge was extracting the knife without causing another potentially fatal injury.

He said: “The main goal of the surgery was to remove the knife without causing further injury. And we achieved that. I believe that was the most important aspect of the case.”

Despite the gruesome wound, Alessandro pulled through the operation and spent two days in intensive care.

He was finally discharged on Thursday, November 19, and is now recovering at home following his astonishing escape.

But doctors are continuing to monitor him for potentially dangerous infections caused by the knife wound.



Rommel said: “We are monitoring for possible infections because it is a knife wound, which is dirty.

“Thank God, everything went well. I thank the entire team and the hospital for the facilities.”

The surgeon later celebrated his patient’s remarkable survival on social media, describing his recovery as “a true rebirth”.

Meanwhile, cops are investigating the circumstances surrounding the brutal stabbing.

Military Police said Alessandro’s wife was detained following the incident but allegedly gave contradictory statements when questioned.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

She was reportedly unable to explain how her husband suffered the horrific injury.

Brazil’s Civil Police have been contacted for further information about the case.

News.title: Dog almost ripped my face off in savage attack outside my home – everything turned dark & I thought I was dead
News.content:
SAVAGE ATTACK Dog almost ripped my face off in savage attack outside my home – everything turned dark & I thought I was dead







Next

A MUM’S face was nearly ripped off during a savage dog mauling outside her home.

Grim photos show the extent of Jenni Cross’s bloody injuries, which almost left her blind.



Jenni, 66, was walking three Labradors on her smalling holding land when the horror unfolded around 10am on December 28 last year.

The dogs had suddenly begun fighting each other, and when Jenni attempted to step in she was knocked to the ground.



One Lab then struck, sinking its teeth into her face and hand.

She told The Sun: “Me grabbing hold, she just reacted and came at me, and took me to the ground.

“Her face and my face were level and she snapped. But it was an accident, a reaction rather than an attack. A bad day at the office.”

Despite the damage, Jenni said the incident lasted seconds.

She recalled how her vision disappeared as she temporarily went blind in her right eye.

Jenni, from Colwall, Herefordshire, went on to say: “There was a point I thought I would die, when I saw the blackness I never thought I would see again.”



Despite her failing vision, the mum-of-one managed to stagger home across the fields before collapsing in the kitchen.

“I was thinking I just had a bang on the head, I was in shock,” she added.

Rather than her own safety, she was desperately trying to get home to call the vet to help the injured dogs.



Her son, who was home for Christmas, found his mum lying on her back by the AGA oven and feared she was dead.

In a panic, he called 999 and described Jenni’s injuries to paramedics.

Jenni said: “I remember thinking that I just need to get back and help the dogs. I was in a state of shock.”

She described her son as “absolutely terrified”, adding: “He was so shocked that all he could say to the ambulance was ‘just please get here’.

“The vet helped describe my injuries so they knew how serious it was.”



Paramedics arrived within minutes and alerted Midlands Air Ambulance, which luckily had a visiting eye specialist in its ranks.

On arrival, however, the medics couldn’t get a stretcher into the house due to the shape of the kitchen and Jenni had to be wheeled out on a chair.

She explained: “They quickly recognised that the swelling on my right eye could cause permanent blindness, and they actually operated on me in the helicopter.”



Jenni’s eye had bulged forward and was sitting outside of the socket due to a blood clot.

Midlands Air Ambulance Charity plea JENNI spoke out as Midlands Air Ambulance Charity launched its first manifesto at a reception attended by many Midlands MPs in the House of Commons. As well as celebrating 35 years of operation, the manifesto sets out the charity’s vision for the future, including calls for the Government to fund the £400,000 a year Midlands Air Ambulance Charity will pay in NHS 999 specialist enhanced care dispatch charges from 2027 and the more than £120,000 a year it spends on medicines and medical consumables. The £520,000 a year saved will help Midlands Air Ambulance Charity fund more doctors on its callout missions. The charity can currently afford to put a doctor on three out of five of its callout missions (three helicopters in the day and two rapid-response cars at night). It wants to make it five from five in future. Funding from the Government to cover NHS dispatch and medical consumable costs will go towards this. Jenni said: “It was so incredible that Dr Oli was on shift that day, a doctor that trains others in the operation that he performed on me, quite literally in the field. “He saved my sight. If it wasn’t for him, I would be blind in my right eye. “I can’t thank Midlands Air Ambulance Charity enough. “My story underlines the need for Midlands Air Ambulance Charity to have a doctor on every one of its callout missions. In my case, having a doctor on board saved my sight.”

Inside the air ambulance medic Dr Oliver Bevan cut through an outer eye ligament to release the blood and restore her vision.

He explained the swelling stops the blood supply from getting to the nerve behind the eye.

“If that doesn’t get blood for a prolonged period of time, the nerve dies and you become blind,” he added.

Jenni was flown to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham where doctors found she had fractured her cheekbone and nose, and had suffered a severe wound to her left hand.



She said: “Without the air ambulance, I would have been blind by the time I reached the hospital.”

The mum added: “I call them my earth angels.”

Her injuries have since largely healed, but unfortunately her dog had to be put down shortly after the attack.

Despite her horror ordeal, Jenni doesn’t pin blame on either dog and rather puts it down to a freak incident of animal nature.

She said: “I think when I tell most people that I was attacked by a dog they think it’s an XL Bully dog, a German Shepherd or a Rottweiler.



“But it wasn’t – this was between two well behaved Labradors that had been around each other peacefully in the past.

“It is just like human road rage, the littlest thing can set off anger, we think our pets are predictable but that’s not always the case.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I just couldn’t think of anything but to intervene when they started to fight – the first thing I wanted to do was make sure they were okay before me.

“I am just glad the air ambulance managed to get to me before my injuries got worse.”

News.title: Fury in ‘most beautiful village’ as tourists turn it into ‘Disney theme park’ – picnicking on lawns & barging into homes
News.content:
FINAL STRAW Fury in ‘most beautiful village’ as tourists turn it into ‘Disney theme park’ – picnicking on lawns & barging into homes







Next

FURIOUS locals in “the most beautiful village in England” have had enough of nosy tourists peeking in their homes and are packing their bags.

Fed-up residents of the picturesque Cotswolds village of Bibury claim they have been overrun by tourists constantly taking pictures of their beautiful homes.



Brian Scardale and his wife Jill, who have lived in the quaint fairy-tale paradise for almost 20 years, have fled their 15th century weaver’s cottage to “finally have some peace”.

Last year, the stunned Scardales returned to their cottage in Arlington Row to find a Japanese family sitting in their living room tucking into a picnic.



Like many in the low-crime town, they had left their front door open when they went to run an errand.

At the time, 83-year-old Brian told us: “I did not know this at the time, but evidently it is customary in Japan that if you leave your front door open, it’s seen as an invitation for others to enter and enjoy your hospitality.



“I couldn’t believe my eyes when I walked through the front door and saw them all sat there stuffing their faces.”

He said luckily they all saw the funny side, but Brian added: “I know I’m not the only person around here that this has happened to.

“A neighbour had a group eating a picnic in her back garden while she was out.

“Quite a few people here have now got so fed up with these intrusions that they now put notices up in Japanese and Chinese informing foreign visitors they are not allowed onto – or into – their properties, even if the front door is open.”



Close friends Phil and Wendy Challinor – who are also considering moving – confirmed the pair had upped and left their stunning property.

Retired project manager Phil, 78, told us: “The Scardales had simply had enough.

“The picnic incident was bad enough but the final straw was the continual pressing of cameras against their downstairs windows for shots of the inside, as well as the famous frontage of the house.



“They had lost all privacy. At least now they’ll finally have some peace and quiet, they said.”

He added that the level of tourism in Bibury is “intolerable”, and traffic has become an “absolute nightmare” for locals who “can’t leave” their house on weekends.

The 78-year-old said: “We have a population of just 500 people, but some days we have as many as 10,000 tourists visiting us.

“The place has simply become too popular as a result of social media and everyone wants to come here, but this is a small village with narrow roads and bridges that simply cannot cope with so many tourists at one time.

“I blame social media for this exponential rise in visitor numbers here. It has just gone crazy.



“We also get a heck of a lot of influencers coming here to advertise brands.

“Last week we had some of them setting up a table and chairs in a shallow part of the river and they sat there in bikinis drinking champagne while having their photographs taken.

Phil said the high volume of traffic clogging up the roads has also caused problems for emergency service vehicles.



He claims a local resident suffered a stroke and needed an ambulance urgently to take him to hospital – but the vehicle got stuck in traffic and allegedly took over an hour to arrive.

“Luckily he survived, but in that time he could easily have died,” Phil said.

When The Sun visited the Gloucestershire hamlet, we caught up with tourists seduced by its old-worldly charm.

Chemist Steven Dearman, 31, from Colchester in Essex, was taking in the former weavers’ cottages with his fiancee, auditor June, also 31, from Thailand.

She had heard about Bibury while in Thailand and was desperate to visit the village.



She said: “I heard about Bibury on social media and told Steven that the next time I came to England I wanted him to bring me here.

“It is so beautiful and romantic.

“It’s even better than it looked on social media. I absolutely love it here.

“We’re getting married next year and I’m seriously thinking about this as a venue for us.



“But unfortunately this visit is just a day trip. I’d love to stay longer.”

South Korean visitors Jang and Kang, both in their early 30s, were visiting Bibury with 50 other tourists and a guide.

Kang told us: “Bibury is absolutely wonderful. We’ve only got an hour or so here and that is simply not enough time to take it all in.

“I love the architecture and the water meadow. We have nothing like this back home.”

Another tourist, Anna, a retired admin worker from Hong Kong, was busy taking photographs of the row of cottages, but stopped to tell us: “To be honest, there are too many tourists here.



“I’ve had a great time in Bibury but it would have been a lot better if there were fewer visitors.

“Everywhere you look, there are tourists and I can understand why the locals might be feeling a bit overwhelmed. I probably won’t come back.”

Litter collector John, 52, told The Sun the influx of tourists means a lot of extra work.

He said: “They are a bloody nuisance. I spend the whole day picking their rubbish out of the river and the side of the roads.

“You wouldn’t believe the kind of stuff they throw in there.



“I’ve already fished out three nappies this morning – and a pair of gloves. Everything you can think of gets thrown away and I’m the idiot who has to pick it up. I wish they would use the bins.”

Cllr Tony Dale, cabinet member for leisure, culture and visitor experience, said: “We really feel for residents who are experiencing unacceptable behaviour from some visitors.

“Entering private homes, obstructing roads or causing disruption to daily life is simply not acceptable, and we understand why local people are frustrated.

“We are working closely with fellow ward councillors, local residents, Bibury Parish Council, Gloucestershire County Council, the police and other partners to understand these concerns and identify practical solutions.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We want people to be able to enjoy visiting the area responsibly, while ensuring it remains a great place for residents to live.



“That is why we will continue to work collaboratively with all the relevant organisations to explore measures that can help manage visitor pressures and ensure the voices of local people are at the heart of any decisions.”

News.title: Cops probing ‘execution’ of cab driver found bound to his steering wheel 30 years ago arrest man in his 60s
News.content:
'MURDER' RIDDLE Cops probing ‘execution’ of cab driver found bound to his steering wheel 30 years ago arrest man in his 60s







Next

A MAN in his 60s has been arrested in connection with the 1994 execution of a taxi driver.

Ethsham “Shami” Ul-Haq Ghafoor, 26, was shot dead in his taxi in Nottingham on Tuesday November 22, more than thirty years ago.



A milkman found Shami him with his hands tied and bound to the steering wheel at 4.30am near Lambley Lane Playing Fields in Gedling, Nottingham.

Shami’s daughter was born without a dad, and his mum died without getting justice for her eldest son as cops failed to identify his killer.



Several people were arrested at the time of Shami’s murder, but no one has ever been convicted with the weapon used to shoot the cabbie never being recovered.

In 2024 Nottinghamshire Police reopened its investigation into the cold blooded killing, using new forensic tech to take a fresh look at a number of items from the crime scene.

Cops believe the answer to Shami’s murder lies within Nottingham’s Asian community.

Well-known taxi driver Shami had been working around east Nottingham on the night he was killed.



He was last seen at 2.40am in Carlton Square with three Asian men in his black and white Ford Sierra.

Now, more than three decades after the killing police have made a breakthrough.

A man was taken into custody in connection with the murder on Monday November 16.

Officers arrested the man in the Broxtowe area of Nottingham and he has since been released on bail as investigations continue.

As the investigation into the cold case continues Deputy Chief Constable Rob Griffin said investigators remain just as determined to ensure justice is served for Shami’s family.



The force has urged anyone with information, no matter how small, to come forward.

Independent charity Crimestoppers has previously offered a reward of up to £50,000 for information leading to a conviction.

Speaking on behalf of the family, his sister Aisha Ghafoor said: “Shami never got to meet his daughter or his grandchildren.

“His killer or killers remain free, while our family has spent more than 30 years living with the devastation they left behind.

“They took his life. They took his children’s father. They took away every chance for his grandchildren to know his voice, feel his embrace or make a single memory with him.



“His daughter has lived her whole life without meeting her dad. His son was robbed of the years they should have shared. No words can put that right. No passing of time can give those years back.

“Shami was at the heart of our family gatherings. Now, every generation of our family lives with his absence.

“What haunts us is knowing that whoever murdered him has remained free all these years. The thought that they could still be walking the streets of Nottingham.

“No family should have to suffer what we have suffered.

“More than 30 years have passed. We are still waiting for someone to tell the truth.



“If you know or witnessed something, please understand what your silence means to us who loved him.

“It means another year without answers, another appeal, another day wondering whether we will ever know who took Shami from us.

“Perhaps you were frightened or you felt loyalty to someone. Perhaps you convinced yourself that what you knew was too small to matter.

“Whatever held you back then, please look at what our family is still living with now.

“You do not need to have every answer. Tell the police what you know. Let them decide whether it could help.



“If you cannot give your name, speak anonymously to Crimestoppers.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We are asking for something no family should have to beg for: the truth and justice for Shami.

“We are asking for information about the murder of Shami, Ethsham Ghafoor someone we love dearly.”

News.title: Man in his 40s dies after being electrocuted while hanging up Christmas lights at major UK shopping centre
News.content:
FESTIVE TRAGEDY Man in his 40s dies after being electrocuted while hanging up Christmas lights at major UK shopping centre







Next

A MAN has died after he was reportedly electrocuted while hanging up Christmas lights at a major UK shopping centre.

The man – believed to be in his 40s – was seriously injured at Brent Cross Shopping Centre in North London in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

Emergency services descended on the scene in Hendon just before 5am and the man was rushed to a major trauma centre.



But despite the best efforts of medical staff, he tragically died in hospital the following day.



Brent Cross Shopping Centre was closed after the “health and safety” incident took place.

The major outlet previously said the horror unfolded while contractors were carrying out Christmas installation works, reports Daily Mail.

It is believed the incident does not relate to the 25ft Christmas tree found on the ground floor.



A Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: “Police were called by the London Ambulance Service at 5.11am on Wednesday, November 18 to reports that a man had been seriously injured while carrying out work at a shopping centre in Prince Charles Drive, NW4.

“Officers attended and a man in his 40s was taken to hospital.

“Sadly, despite the best efforts of medical professionals, the man died in hospital on Thursday, November 19. His next of kin have been informed.

“Detectives have launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death and enquiries are ongoing.



“The Health and Safety Executive and Barnet Council’s Health and Environmental Safety Team have been kept informed.”

A spokesperson for Brent Cross Shopping Centre said: “We are deeply saddened by the passing of a contractor who was undertaking overnight works earlier this week.

“Our thoughts and sincere condolences are with their family, friends and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.

“Following checks and consultation with the relevant authorities, the centre reopened on Thursday.”

David Pinto-Duschinsky, Labour MP for Hendon, posted a statement to social media following the man’s death.



He said: “I’ve just seen the incredibly sad news that the man who was electrocuted at Brent Cross has died.

“My heart and my deepest condolences go out to his family and friends. May his memory be a blessing.”

The incident came just before Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales, as staff were preparing for one of the busiest seasons of the year for the business.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Brent Cross Shopping Centre – which opened its doors in 1976 and is this year celebrating its 50th anniversary – features over 120 stores and restaurants.

The Sun has contacted Barnet Council for comment.

News.title: Moment military helicopters open fire on FBI’s most wanted cartel kingpin ‘El Chapo Isidro’ before dramatic capture
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment Mexican military helicopters open fire on the FBI’s most wanted cartel kingpin in a dramatic capture operation.

Footage shows a rapid barrage of bullets raining down from the choppers as they fly low over Guasave city in Sinaloa on Friday night.



Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” was captured and arrested with the help of the US, Mexico’s defence ministry said.

Intelligence from Donald Trump’s administration helped authorities capture him, the Mexican government said in a report early Saturday.



The operation was conducted by “elite military forces” using “stealth and surprise” to reach their target, the ministry added.

The sting sparked violent clashes with armed militants that sent fans fleeing from a nearby baseball game in terror.

Separate footage shows baseball fans at the Kuroda Park stadium scrambling from the stands as gunfire cracks through the air.

Shouts of “get down!” and “duck” can be heard in the terrifying clip as people frantically clambered over barriers.



An official broadcast showed players from Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams fleeing the field mid-game.

Authorities “came under attack with gunfire and explosives”, the ministry said.

Vehicles were set ablaze by cartel members who set up roadblocks in several areas near the arrest site, local media reported.

A local resident said private hospitals came under siege by armed individuals as shops and petrol stations were torched.

“Just metres away from where I was, a convoy of heavily armed civilians passed by, firing shots”, he told CNN.



Sinaloa’s state government issued a statement late Friday warning people to stay off the roads.

Authorities from the Interagency Group had been deployed to restore order, it said.

Meza Flores, who led the Guasave-based cartel Los Mazatlecos, was one of the top ten targets of Mexican authorities and the FBI.



He had strongholds in Guasave, Los Mochis, and several settlements in the mountainous area, including Badiraguato.

An FBI wanted poster offered £3.8million ($5m) for information leading to his arrest.

He is accused of possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, meth, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the US, the FBI said.

The US Treasury previously said the Meza-Florez cartel was involved in “an extremely violent turf war”.

In recent years, his influence had grown amid a conflict between two other major factions of the cartel — the Guzmán and Zambada families.



Their members, the sons of drug lords Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán and Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, have been waging a war against each other for nearly two years.

The violence erupted after El Chapo and El Mayo were arrested and hauled behind bars in US prisons.

Earlier this year, sources close to the Security Cabinet told El País that he was exporting more drugs than the other groups.

The crime boss was previously indicted for drug trafficking violations and possession of a firearm in 2019, and in 2012 for drug trafficking charges.

ROAD CHAOS Serious crash shuts motorway near major UK airport as drivers warned to avoid area amid reports of ‘huge fire’







Next

A SERIOUS crash has shut a motorway near to a major UK airport with drivers warned to avoid the area.

The M42 in the West Midlands is closed northbound between Junction 5a at Birmingham Airport and Junction 6.



National Highways said the closure comes after a “serious collision” as motorists report seeing a “huge fire” while stuck in standstill traffic.

Emergency services – including cops, paramedics and the fire service – have descended on the scene.



A National Highways spokesperson said: “West Midlands Police will be carrying out collision investigation works, which are expected to take several hours.

“Once the investigation is complete, vehicle recovery and debris clearance will be required before the carriageway can reopen.”



“National Highways Traffic Officers are on scene assisting with traffic management,” they added.

Drivers have been urged to plan ahead and allow for extra journey time with three miles of congestion on approach.

Diversion Route National Highways has suggested using the following diversion route. Exit the M42 at J5A, and at the roundabout take the 1st exit on to the A4545

Travel on the A4545

At the large roundabout, take the 4th exit on to the A45

At Bickenhill Interchange, take the 2nd exit to rejoin the M42 northbound at J6

A spokesperson for West Midlands Police said: “We are currently at the scene of a serious collision on the #M42 between Junction 5A and Junction 6.

“If possible, please avoid the area and plan an alternative route.



“We will provide further updates in due course.”

The Sun has contacted West Midlands Ambulance Service and West Midlands Fire Service for comment.

News.title: Catherine talks openly about how cancer changed her in documentary on BBC
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.

The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."

It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day.

"It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William.

"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.

News.title: 'We're not meant to carry life's challenges alone', Catherine says in first clip
News.content:
The Princess of Wales' cancer journey is set to be depicted in a new BBC documentary "Heal" that will air next weekend.

It follows Catherine announcing in January 2025 that she was in remission after having revealed her diagnosis less than a year prior.

She has since spoken openly about her illness and treatment although has never disclosed publicly what type of cancer she faced.

The new documentary will include footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," she says.

News.title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
News.content:
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".

He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".

"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.

She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the Â£17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the issue of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".

He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take Â£500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".

He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway."

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.

She told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals."

News.title: Who will be Robert Pattinson's 'Bond girl' - and does the role need to change?
News.content:
Belluci's inclusion in Spectre as a "Bond woman" aged 50 was widely praised for spotlighting a different type of sex appeal (even though she was only four years older than Daniel Craig in real life).

We've also had other powerful women in Bond, such as Michelle Yeoh's Colonel Wai Lin and Lashana Lynch's MI6 agent Nomi, who also made history as the first black female 007.

Rather than fitting the traditional Bond girl mould, both of them were competent women who could give Bond a run for his money.

"We've moved away from the role being someone with a silly name and for Bond to pat on their bottom," says film critic Ivan-Zadeh. "It's moving in the right direction".

Many people say, however, there is still further to go.

Having more female Bond villains, as well as love interests, could be one way to make it more equal, suggests Rose. "That's what I'd want to see."

"They can be romantic interests, villains, spies, allies or even the person who ultimately outsmarts Bond. There's room for all of those roles,â agrees showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

Another way the roles could evolve is by bringing in "a queer or sexually fluid Bond woman," suggests Ivan-Zadeh. "Someone whose desires donât simply revolve around Bond. That would create some genuinely interesting chemistry.â

Others are hoping to see more diverse actresses cast from film markets such as China, India or Nigeria.

âThere have been a number of women of colour in the past, but I'd like to see more," says Be Manzini, writer and filmmaker.

"I'd like to see an Indian Bond girl," agrees Chapman. "Aishwarya Rai was touted for the follow up to Die Another Day but never got there."

More broadly, there is an appetite to see Bond girls have their own lives.

âFor me, it's about giving these women proper storylines,â says Onafuye. "They should have their own motivations and their own ambitions.â

None of this is to say we should do away with the traditional Bond glamour.

"No-one wants to see Bond girls slumping around in their PJs," says Ivan-Zadeh.

But the important distinction is that "being sexy shouldn't be the only thing a female character has to offer,â says Onafuye.

âTo those arguing that it's fine for Bond's women just to be sexy and hot, I'd say there's nothing sexier or hotter than a woman (or man) with a brain and a wit,â adds entertainment journalist Caroline Frost.

News.title: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
News.content:
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

News.title: These dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
News.content:
The livestream begins.

A man â bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses â walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."

"Purebreds," says the woman filming.

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

News.title: How Phoebe Bridgers banning phones at concerts sparked a wave of fan artwork
News.content:
Phoebe Bridgers has drawn in fans over the years with her raw, vulnerable lyrics and indie sound that can make even the messiest emotions feel less lonely.

The US artist's third album Lost Weekend, released this summer after a six-year wait, delves into falling in and out of love, grappling with change and the confusing feelings that come with grief.

On her tour of the Grammy-nominated record, Bridgers has introduced a no-phone policy - a move that's had an unexpected side effect.

Instead of taking photos and videos of the shows, some are creating artwork as a reminder of the gigs.

Massive Bridgers fan Olivia MacDonald, from Massachusetts, attended the singer's show in Boston last month.

She was initially "shocked" by the no-phone rule, as employed by artists including Bob Dylan and Jack White, but became a convert.

Without the distraction of phones, she says, fans chatted, danced and sang along with each other.

"Once I got to the concert, I realised this is such a unique way to connect and bring everybody together," she says.

News.title: 'I was exhausted': Two days in the shoes of a tradwife
News.content:
Dressed in an unfamiliar long skirt, Poppy Jay is standing in a chicken coop faced with an angry cockerel as she checks for eggs.

As a director and writer, Jay is normally behind the camera, but today she's in front of it, trying out life as a tradwife.

The Tradwife - short for traditional wife - movement sees women embracing traditional gender roles in the home, such as cooking, cleaning and child rearing, while submitting to their bread-winning husbands.

While tradwives say they are bringing back old-fashioned family values, the movement has faced controversy. Its critics say tradwives fuel inequality and diminish women's empowerment by reinforcing archetypal gender roles.

For three days, Evangelical Christians Molly and Aaron Edwards welcomed Jay, a proud feminist, into their Yorkshire home to show her their lifestyle for the BBC One documentary Young, British and Tradwife.

On two of the days, the couple - who have seven children - allowed Jay to take on the homely duties that are usually Molly's responsibility, so Jay could try out the tradwife life.

"I was exhausted," Jay exclaimed when she spoke to BBC News.

During her stay, she helped Molly cook, home school the children, tend to the garden and brave the chicken coop.

She was given a book called The Gift of Womanhood to study the night before and asked to wear a dress.

"What struck me was how hard Molly works - like any mum of seven," Jay said. "She is a devoted mother, she cooks and cleans, she's doing endless loads of washing. She's barely got a moment to herself and I felt like I was getting in the way."

News.title: Staff gagging clauses lifted ahead of probe into culture at data watchdog
News.content:
Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) signed by staff at the UK's information watchdog will be lifted to allow them to speak out about its culture, the government has confirmed.

Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.

It follows the departure of the watchdog's boss five months ago amid allegations of sexually inappropriate behaviour.

A government spokesperson confirmed that NDAs, known as "gagging clauses", would not be enforced by the Information Commission, saying the regulator "will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the review".

The government "will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly", they added.

The Information Commission is one of the UK's most high-profile regulators charged with the crucial task of regulating AI, data protection and Freedom of Information requests.

It recently won a court battle with TikTok after it fined the social media platform Â£12.7m for misusing children's data, and has penalised bodies including the Ministry of Defence after an email blunder exposed the details of interpreters fleeing Afghanistan.

But it has been without permanent leadership since Information Commissioner John Edwards resigned earlier this year.

It came after an independent investigation found a "case to answer" over reports of alleged inappropriate behaviour towards staff including claims of sexual harassment.

The Information Commission said the investigation found Edwards' behaviour "fell short of the conduct expected from a public official".

In a resignation statement posted on his LinkedIn page in June, Edwards said he disagreed with how the investigation had been carried out but accepted his position had "become untenable".

The statement continued: "I have accepted that there have been occasions where I exercised poor judgement and made attempts at humour that were inappropriate and caused offence."

Freedom of Information requests have found that since the start of Edwards' tenure in 2022 to the present, 16 current and former employees have signed non-disclosure or confidentiality clauses costing more than Â£354,000.

Nine of those , externalincluded a "non-derogatory clause" which legally prevents employees from making negative comments publicly.

While this is a small proportion of the more than 1,000 staff employed by the commissioner, government advice stipulates that public bodies should only use confidentiality clauses "when necessary" and that they should "not seek to stifle or discourage staff from raising concerns".

Since 2025, new laws also mean they cannot be used to silence employees subjected to harassment or abuse.

After Edwards' departure, the government announced a review, external into the Commission's culture and governance, with the then-Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology Liz Kendall telling a committee of MPs she was "absolutely appalled at what the independent investigator found - sexual harassment and bullying".

Five months later, the investigation has not begun.

In recent weeks, the two major civil service unions, the PCS and FDA, have pushed for an external examination of the events leading up to Edwards' resignation in meetings with government officials.

The unions have also asked for those who signed non-disclosure agreements with the ICO to be released from them so they can contribute to the review.

The PCS union says other concerns had previously been raised with them about Edwards, including a bullying complaint, which was investigated at the time.

An internal staff survey, published in August and released under FOI, external points towards wider issues at the Commission, with 14% of all employees reporting they had either personally experienced bullying, harassment and discrimination.

Multiple current and former employees have also told the BBC of experiencing or witnessing incidents of bullying or harassment.

PCS General Secretary Fran Heathcote said the union's members at the Commission "have been failed for too long by a toxic leadership culture that has allowed bullying and harassment to persist, leaving many staff fearful of speaking out".

Heathcote said she welcomed the "positive engagement" the union had received in recent weeks from the Commission and officials at the Department for Culture Media and Sport (DCMS), which oversees it.

But she added: "For the review to command the confidence of staff, it must be genuinely independent, robust in its approach, and prepared to identify where accountability lies."

Conservative MP Caroline Dinenage, who chairs the DCMS select committee, said the Commission "needed a firm new direction" after the departure of its former boss.

"Instead, a leadership vacuum has compounded what went before at a rudderless organisation where it seems the worst behaviours in the workplace are not being challenged," she added.

She said it was "vital" the government brought in "someone who can set a new tone and is dedicated to changing attitudes and protecting staff" to head up the Commission.

A spokesperson for the Information Commission said its commitment to an independent review reflected its "ongoing commitment to listening and learning from the events of the past year and those leading up to it".

"Our new Board, appointed this summer, has been working exceptionally hard to provide fresh leadership, ushering in a new governance structure and a new strategy," they added.

"It is committed to listening carefully to the review's findings and recommendations, and building on the positive work on our culture already taking place across the organisation."

News.title: Man charged with attempted murder after Bradford councillor stabbed
News.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with attempted murder after a Bradford councillor was seriously injured in a stabbing.

Councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:00 GMT on Thursday on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to nearby Manse Street, according to West Yorkshire Police.

Arfan Ali, 32, of Thornbury Avenue, is also charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place. At Leeds Magistrates' Court earlier, he was remanded into custody until he appears at Bradford Crown Court on 21 December.

Councillor Ali remains in hospital in a serious but stable condition, police said.

Councillor Ali is a Your Bradford Independent Group representative for Bradford Moor ward and was first elected in May.

He works as a community development manager at charity The Leap, and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.

Speaking after Thursday's incident, his family thanked police, paramedics and members of the public who "courageously provided first aid and assistance at the scene" and asked people to "keep him and his family in your duas [prayers]".

News.title: Serious crash closes M42 near Birmingham Airport
News.content:
Motorists have been warned the M42 near Birmingham Airport could remain closed for several hours after a serious crash involving a vehicle fire.

National Highways said the northbound carriageway was shut between junction 5A and junction six following the crash, with police, fire and ambulance services attending.

Drivers caught in standstill traffic described seeing a "huge fire" after the crash, while West Midlands Police urged motorists to avoid the area.

Investigation work was expected to take several hours, National Highways said, after which recovery of the vehicle and clearance of debris would need to be completed before the road could reopen.

Drivers travelling through the area were urged to plan ahead and allow extra time for their journeys.

The cause of the crash and whether anyone is injured has not yet been confirmed.

There are currently four lanes closed, and traffic is expected to clear at around 17:45 GMT, National Highways added.

News.title: Bad Girls star Helen Fraser dies aged 84
News.content:
British television, theatre and film star Helen Fraser, who was perhaps best known for her role in the hit prison drama Bad Girls, has died.

The actress, who also appeared in episodes of Coronation Street and The Royle Family, reportedly died on 10 November at Yaxley House Care Home, in Eye, Suffolk. She was 84.

Born in Oldham, Lancashire, she had lived in Wickham Skeith, in Suffolk, with her late husband Peter Handford.

From 2004 until 2019, she was also an ambassador for East Anglia's Children's Hospices (EACH). The charity said it was "deeply saddened" by her death and would "remember her with enormous fondness and gratitude".

"Helen was very special to us and a wonderful ambassador, supporter and friend who worked tirelessly to champion our cause," a spokesperson said.

"Whether fundraising, attending events, opening our shops or rallying our volunteers, Helen brought incredible warmth, empathy and joy.

"She had a wonderful way with people and made a lasting impression on all those fortunate enough to spend time in her company."

The actress first trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before making her breakthrough in the 1963 film Billy Liar.

But it was her role as the tough prison officer Sylvia Hollamby in the long-running ITV show Bad Girls that made her a household name among British audiences.

Fraser appeared in more than 90 episodes across all eight series, from 1999 to 2006, and later reprised the role in the West End stage version of Bad Girls: The Musical.

Fraser's funeral will be held at West Suffolk Crematorium on 4 December at 13:30 GMT, according to a death notice published by the East Anglian Daily Times, external.

Attendees are asked to make donations in her honour to East Anglia's Children's Hospices charity.

"We feel truly honoured that EACH will benefit from donations made in her memory at her funeral," the charity's spokesperson added.
