News.title: Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips
News.content:
Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of Â£1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.

The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services.

The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.

Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations".

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches".

They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events".

Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit.

In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity Â£1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork.

They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers.

Girlguiding would also be subject to the levy.

In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity.

"But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors."

News.title: Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm
News.content:
A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."

Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.

According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.

They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."

To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.

For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.

Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.

After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.

"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"

Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.

News.title: PM to meet pub bombings families in new year
News.content:
The prime minister is to meet the families of people killed in the 1974 Birmingham pub bombings as they continue to call for a public inquiry.

MP Liam Byrne and Richard Parker, the West Midlands mayor, met Downing Street officials this week to press for a date for families to put their case to Andy Burnham.

Burnham has now confirmed in a letter to Byrne that he will meet the families in Birmingham early in the new year.

Saturday marks the 52nd anniversary of the atrocity when two bombs exploded in the Mulberry Bush and Tavern in the Town pubs in the city centre, killing 21 people and injuring 220. No-one has been convicted over the murders.

Six men were convicted of the murders but their convictions were overturned in 1991.

"The families are asking for something very simple: they want to know who murdered their loved ones, they want to know why nobody has been brought to justice and they want a process they can trust to establish the truth," said Byrne, MP for Hodge Hill and Solihull North.

"It is time to answer the question that has haunted our city for half a century: who bombed Birmingham?"

Parker said that although the meeting was "one step forward", it would not undo "decades of hurt".

News.title: Plans unveiled for one of UK's biggest solar farms
News.content:
Plans have been unveiled to build one of the biggest solar farms in the UK across a huge slice of Essex's Dengie Peninsula.

Low Carbon wants to install panels across 4,200 acres (1,700 hectares) of sprawling countryside between Burnham-on-Crouch and Bradwell-on-Sea.

The developer said the site could generate 1GW of power - enough to supply 250,000 homes, or every house between Basildon and Shoeburyness.

However, critics have questioned how the project will impact wildlife and local roads during construction.

The scheme has been deemed a nationally significant infrastructure project, which means the government has the final say on whether it will go ahead.

Simon Morgan, the Conservative leader of Maldon District Council, said it had emerged "out of the blue".

"It was a complete shock when we saw the extent of the area that's being planned," he told the BBC.

"It's almost, in my view, one-third of the land in the Dengie Peninsula, which is quite an extensive amount of land to be put under solar panels."

News.title: Israeli strike kills three in car distributing aid in Gaza, witnesses say
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An Israeli strike killed three Palestinians in a vehicle carrying papers and food for ⁠the World Central Kitchen charity in Gaza City on Saturday, Gaza's health ministry and witnesses said.

World Central Kitchen, an aid organisation that distributes food in the Gaza Strip, said, however, that the vehicle was not affiliated with it.

The Israeli military said several militants had been targeted in the area without providing further ⁠details. It did not immediately respond to questions ​on ⁠why it had hit a vehicle that appeared to be distributing aid.

A witness said the vehicle appeared to be carrying packaged foodstuffs, and that papers inside ⁠carried World Central Kitchen's logo.

"It was just about to stop to distribute the food ​and drink to ⁠children when it was hit ‌by a missile," said Abu Zein Al-Daya, who witnessed the strike.

Afterwards, meals of cooked rice were scattered around the vehicle, which was partially covered in the blood of the victims of ‌the attack.

open image in gallery Mourners carry the body of Khaled Naem during a joint funeral for him, Mustafa Refa’i and Ahmad al-Sawafiri in Gaza City, Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026. The three men were killed in an Israeli airstrike. (AP Photo/Yousef Al Zanoun) ( AP )

The Israeli military killed ‌seven World Central Kitchen workers in a 2024 strike, including citizens of Australia, Britain and Poland.

At the time, the military said there had been "serious errors and breaches of procedure" but in 2026 it said it had found no ⁠basis on which to open criminal investigations into the incident.

Israel briefly launched a ground operation in Gaza earlier this week and killed six people in a strike on a hospital that it said was targeting a commander for the Palestinian militant group Hamas.

open image in gallery Palestinian children look at the remains of a van that was transporting food rations to displaced people after it was targeted by the Israeli army, killing three people, in Al-Sina'a Street in the Tel Al-Hawa area, west of Gaza City on November 21, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

An October 2025 US-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory but has not stopped Israeli attacks on Gaza or secured Hamas' disarmament.

At least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since then, ‌according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies.

Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of ​Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, with ‌Hamas controlling a sliver of territory along ⁠Gaza's coast.

Israel's more than two-year-long assault on Gaza has killed tens of thousands, ⁠caused a hunger crisis, internally displaced Gaza's entire population and led to assessments of genocide from scholars and a United ‌Nations inquiry.

Israel says its ​actions are self-defence after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 ‌people and took more than 250 hostages ​in an October 2023 attack on Israel.

News.title: England summon spirit of World Cup winners in remarkable All Blacks thrashing
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The last England side to conquer the All Blacks in back-to-back meetings went on to rule the world and on the evidence of this fantastical, fanciful afternoon, Steve Borthwick’s men may yet have hope of emulating them. Twickenham has known a few remarkable rugby days but seldom anything quite like this; not even in 2012, when England ran riot, has this mighty New Zealand team been reduced to rubble quite so spectacularly.

It was an English performance of the heady halcyon days, summoning the spirit of 2003 with a World Cup winner setting the tone. Perhaps we should have known what was to come when Lewis Moody strode out to join Maro Itoje’s men to stare down the haka – the former captain wore white again in a show of unity as he faces a battle beyond rugby; it proved a spell-binding start to a quite extraordinary afternoon.

open image in gallery England thrashed the All Blacks by a record margin ( Reuters )

So much for an All Blacks backlash, a charged-up riposte to a day of infamy in Cardiff. New Zealand were simply not allowed to have their say – shut down, shut out and shut up. The final margin of English victory was a record 25 points; it could quite conceivably have been more. Yes, England had beaten their visitors this time last year but that was a side ebbing away under the doomed premiership of Scott Robertson – this felt different. A tough last Test on Nations Championship finals weekend still must be negotiated but this surely catapults England into World Cup contenders.

One wondered what England could conjure to match the spell-binding Welsh wall of red that met the Haka a week ago; the arrival of Moody to join Maro Itoje and his men provided an emotional answer. The former England captain had presented the current crop with their shirts on match eve, while their boots bore the slogan “Front Up to MND” in the week that Moody unveiled his latest charity campaign. The 48-year-old somehow held it together as he stared down the traditional pre-match Maori challenge – the same was not true of many inside Twickenham.

open image in gallery Lewis Moody joined England for a spell-binding pre-match display ( Getty )

Those customised boots were soon flashing into action. England had started fast against Japan and Australia and continued that theme, registering inside four minutes. It was Fin Smith who found the space behind the New Zealand defence with a delectable grubber, and Henry Slade on hand to gobble it up – having thought his international career might be over last November, the 13 is relishing his renewed centrality.

It proved the precursor to another opening half-hour of almost complete English dominance. Itoje and Borthwick had been clear in the week that they were unlikely to have as much control as had been enjoyed across the last two Saturdays, but it proved a false hypothesis. Defensively, the hosts flew up into the faces of a flustered All Blacks; in attack, there was punch and panache. Where a couple of missed opportunities may in the past have incited panic, it was England who seemed to reset more quickly each time – to eventually draw joy.

open image in gallery Henry Slade gave England a flying start ( Reuters )

Slade again was at the heart of it, gliding between would-be tacklers before dinking a kick over the last defender. Jordie Barrett just about hauled him back but New Zealand could not quell Jack van Poortvliet two phases later, the No 9 up like a salmon over dark deep water to the line. When Ben Earl burst away brilliantly from the base of an increasingly effective scrum, England were in dreamland.

England had enjoyed three quarters of the possession and territory; this was as comprehensive a half as any side had produced against any All Blacks side. An irrepressible Earl was everywhere, often with Ollie Chessum or Alex Coles as a clattering comrade. Fin Smith patrolled and picked his passes perfectly; one missed punt to the corner the only blot on a copy-book as white as the shirt in which he had started.

open image in gallery New Zealand were reduced to rubble by England ( Getty )

Where was the New Zealand response that had been promised? Their first entry into England’s 22 did not arrive until the 38th minute but the All Blacks did at least purloin points, Ethan de Groot ploughing a fierce furrow around a ruck.

Could it last? Everything seemed to be breaking England’s way. Beauden Barrett threw what must be pretty close to the worst pass of a Test career now 150 caps long, while even charged down box kicks settled in home hands. Chessum, totemic once again, soon became a fourth try-scorer.

The hosts were not, though, thinking about Nations Championship bonus points. A vintage score from the eldest Barrett brother from deep in New Zealand territory served as a reminder that they could not drop their guard, but the intensity seldom looked like dropping. Five of the six forward replacements arrived in unison, with only Henry Pollock withheld; Marcus Smith was an early arrival, too, with namesake Fin hobbling on a dodgy calf.

open image in gallery England ran riot at Twickenham ( Getty )

They did not relent. Seb Atkinson pumped a first of victory after the newly-arrived Smith slipped him a cute pass, a disbelieving smile broadening as he went. When a penalty arrived in the final moments, Itoje made an almost taunting point to the posts – why not, one would suppose, extend that record margin of victory on a day where that distinction was deserved.

News.title: England v New Zealand LIVE: Brilliant England make statement with All Blacks domination
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Lewis Moody faces haka as England take on All Blacks

England thrashed New Zealand by a record margin in a remarkable performance at Twickenham to establish themselves as World Cup contenders.

The hosts ran rampant on their way to a 37-12 victory, beating the All Blacks in back-to-back meetings for just the second time in their history. New Zealand had promised a response following a shock defeat to Wales but were not allowed to find their flow, with England on top in just about every facet in a complete team performance.

Maro Itoje’s men had been inspired by the presence of Lewis Moody, a 2003 World Cup winner, who joined the squad to stare down the haka ahead of kick off. The English players wore personalised boots in support of the former captain’s battle against motor neurone disease, and produced a performance of which Moody could be most proud.

Follow all of the latest from the crunch clash with our live blog below:

News.title: Scotland score 11 tries in rout of Japan
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Darcy Graham and Liam McConnell inspired much-changed Scotland to a comfortable 11-try 67-5 Nations Championship victory over meek Japan.

Wing Graham moved on to the 41-try mark for his country with a hat-trick as he stepped six clear of Duhan van der Merwe at the top of the national team’s all-time scoring charts.

Back-rower McConnell also enjoyed a day to remember as the 22-year-old back-rower broke his Scotland duck with a treble of his own.

Ollie Smith helped himself to a double while Kyle Rowe, Jamie Dobie and Rory Hutchinson also crossed as the Scots completed their pool-stage fixtures with a fourth win from six matches ahead of their trip to London for finals weekend.

News.title: England hammer New Zealand in Nations Championship
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

England fired a warning to their rivals ahead of next year’s World Cup by crushing New Zealand 37-12 in a stunning victory inspired by former captain Lewis Moody.

To roars of appreciation at Allianz Stadium, Moody joined England’s V-formation response to the haka – and then watched from the stands as the All Blacks were torn apart.

The presence of Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease last year, visibly lifted Maro Itoje’s men to set the scene for a five-try rout that registered back-to-back wins against New Zealand for the first time since 2002 and 2003.

It also clinched a fifth consecutive Test victory, providing thrilling validation of their post-Six Nations resurgence with the 2027 World Cup final just a year away.

Man of the match Ben Earl, Ollie Chessum and Itoje were at the forefront of England’s forward dominance, which continued when the bench arrived to step up the assault on the All Blacks line.

News.title: Specially bred mosquitoes help fend off dengue in ‘exciting’ study as Florida grapples with outbreak
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A specially bred mosquito appears to offer strong protection against dengue and chikungunya, according to a new study, as cases of mosquito-borne illnesses spike in Florida.

The major study of more than 5,700 children in Brazil, one of the world's dengue hot spots, offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit viruses can be a viable new strategy instead of relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten.

Dr Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team, said children in neighborhoods populated by Wolbachia-carrying insects showed about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections compared with similar neighborhoods.

open image in gallery Scientists bred mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

The effect was sustained even during Brazil's severe 2024 dengue outbreak, she said. The findings were reported at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.

Florida grapples with large outbreak

The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s.

Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa.

Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy. Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia.

How Wolbachia strategy works

The bacteria are harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Wolbachia dramatically reduce the mosquitoes' ability to transmit certain viruses.

Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects, males and females, into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population.

Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses.

But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus.

“This is really exciting,” said Dr David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn't involved with the Brazilian study.

He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places.

News.title: Enzo Maresca finds the key to Elliot Anderson’s brilliance but Man City still flounder
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A £116m transfer fee would automatically place anyone under the spotlight. Of late, it has appeared that Elliot Anderson has assumed a prominence anyway, and not always in ways he would have wished. A first return to Nottingham Forest was notable for the challenge he lost to Xavier Schlager that led to Liam Delap galloping clear to score. A meeting with Spain’s World Cup winners was curtailed by a red card for fouling Lamine Yamal; naively, really, given it brought the dual punishments of a dismissal and a penalty.

So if it is safe to say Manchester City needed Anderson’s equaliser against Fulham, it feels equally true that he did. “Nice moment for him, nice moment for us,” said Enzo Maresca. City were facing up to the prospect of a fourth straight league defeat. Anderson’s first top-flight goal since an extraordinarily expensive move averted that.

It offered an illustration of his considerable qualities – and, his mishap at the City Ground notwithstanding, Anderson has been one of City’s finest players in their decidedly mixed season – as well as an idea of how best to deploy them. “We used him today for the first time since the season started as an attacking midfielder,” Maresca explained.

A problem for much of this season is that Anderson has seemed to be playing centre midfield on his own which, even for a player who commanded a nine-figure fee, posed certain difficulties when he was outnumbered. It had felt all the more needless when City’s midfield rebuild came at a record cost.

With Enzo Fernandez reduced to a cameo, his wanderlust taking him to the bench, and Ayyoub Bouaddi starting, Anderson had a partner. “Ayyoub and Elliot were both really good,” said Maresca. It was not a one-stop solution to bring City solidity: they still conceded, for the 18th occasion in their last nine games, and looked too open. “We need to find a way to keep clean sheets,” Maresca admitted.

But Bouaddi’s presence helped liberate Anderson and there were two moments to demonstrate what he can do when unleashed in the final third. The first was his leveller, a crisp, clean volley from the edge of the box, almost as impressive technically as his strike at the Etihad Stadium for Forest last season. “Fantastic goal,” said Maresca.

open image in gallery Elliot Anderson equalised for Man City after falling behind to Fulham in the first half ( Reuters )

It came after Fulham had cleared a corner so arguably Anderson would have been in the same position if Fernandez was not on the pitch. Not when he almost got a winner, though: eight yards out, angling a shot just wide after linking up with Erling Haaland, following the kind of box-crashing run that players like Ilkay Gundogan and Kevin De Bruyne have made when used as No 8s by City. They have instead tended to be Fernandez’s remit this season.

And if Fernandez is the conundrum, rather than Anderson, there is nevertheless the case that a double act really brings the best out of him. Until his early exit, he excelled alongside Declan Rice in a duo in Madrid. “It has been an interesting week,” said Anderson, which rather underplayed it.

A problem for Maresca is that, even when identifying a way of using Anderson, City still floundered. This was another incoherent display as the longest winning streak between two clubs in English football came to an end. “We knew we lost the last 20 times we played Manchester City but I told [the players] we would have the chance to beat them if we play with courage, with character,” said Alvaro Arbeloa.

open image in gallery Fulham earned their first point against City since 2011 to signify progress under Alvaro Arbeloa ( Getty )

Fulham’s first point against City since 2011 was a sign of the progress under the Spaniard, following draws against Liverpool and Manchester United. Arbeloa knocked City out of the Champions League last season when with Real Madrid. He showed his prowess with lesser players as Fulham pressed man-for-man, played a variant of 4-2-2-2 and deservedly led.

The instigator was Oscar Bobb, sold by City in January, with a driving run on the right. Rodrigo Muniz’s first touch took him past Abdukodir Khusanov. His second was placed in the top corner. The striker celebrated by putting the ball up his shirt to mark his wife’s pregnancy. Muniz admitted he struggled last season when she had a miscarriage. It is too trite to say he looked a player reborn, but he gave Fulham a threat.

The opposing No 9 thought he had levelled. A disputed decision ensured otherwise, referee Thomas Bramall ruling Haaland had kicked the ball out of Bernd Leno’s hands when he bundled it over the line. “I had the ball in my hands,” the goalkeeper said. “I had the feeling I controlled the ball and Haaland crashed into me and slid into me.” City disagreed. “From my point of view it is quite clear that it is not a foul,” said Maresca. He said Haaland concurred, but the City top scorer may wish he had met Iliman Ndiaye’s cross with a better finish at the first time of asking.

open image in gallery Erling Haaland was left frustrated after seeing his equaliser disallowed ( PA Wire )

It was not the only example of wastefulness. Haaland blazed over when released by Foden. Only three of City’s 15 shots were on target. They could have lost it. After recent errors, there was a redemptive element to Gianluigi Donnarumma’s saves from Bobb and Muniz. City’s winless streak nevertheless continued. “We don’t like this kind of moments in terms of four games in a row,” said Maresca. For Anderson, though, a different game brought a different status, as scorer and saviour.

News.title: Inflation, economic growth and the mood of US consumers in focus this week
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Inflation has become the current that runs through almost all corners of the U.S. economy and there will be more on that front this week.

A key report on inflation will headline a holiday-shortened week, along with a look at the latest gauge of consumer confidence. High prices on everything from groceries to gasoline are changing consumer behavior and there is pressure on policy makers to act. The data on prices arrives ahead of the next meeting of rate-setters at the Federal Reserve, the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season, as well as Thanksgiving, which may be uncomfortably expensive this year given rising prices for food.

Here’s a look at some of the key reports coming in the week ahead.

US consumer confidence is being tested

Business group The Conference Board on Tuesday will release its consumer confidence survey for November. Economists expect it to show that confidence remains low as inflation puts more pressure on budgets. Overall, consumer confidence is down sharply from two years ago.

The wide-ranging and unpredictable U.S. trade war with much of the world prompted price increases and made planning ahead difficult for both consumers and businesses. The U.S. war with Iran that started in 2026 fueled inflation throughout the year by curtailing the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz and raising energy prices. Higher prices for oil and gasoline boosted shipping costs for a wide range of goods.

The high cost of energy, goods and services has been notably referenced by write-in responses to the monthly consumer confidence surveys.

Inflation data could tip balance toward higher borrowing costs

A inflation update is expected to provide more details on what most Americans know — things have become expensive. The U.S. will release the October personal consumption expenditures report, or PCE, on Wednesday. The data carries a lot of weight because it is the preferred measure of inflation used by the Federal Reserve, which is attempting to bring inflation down to its target rate of 2%.

Inflation has been rising at a sharp rate since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran early this year fueling a surge in energy prices. Higher gasoline prices have eaten up a bigger portion of household budgets. Higher costs for shipping and warehousing goods because of soaring diesel prices are leaching into the broader economy.

The Fed's main tool in fighting inflation is raising interest rates and that makes something else more expensive — borrowing money. The central bank is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate at its next meeting to cool down the economy. It's a tough balancing act because the Fed's other mandate is maximum employment. Higher rates can make employers less likely to hire.

The US economy is motoring along

The U.S. Department of Commerce on Wednesday will release an update on the nation's economic growth during the third quarter. The first read showed gross domestic product grew at 3.4% during the third quarter. GDP is a measure of the nation's output of goods and services.

The economy has proven resilient despite inflation. Economic growth accelerated from the 2.2% increase in the second quarter. Much of that growth has been driven by an AI investment boom, but that is a sector that has been rattled in recent weeks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled more than 8% last week, with particularly sharp declines to end the week.

Low-hire, low-fire employment in the US

The latest weekly update on unemployment claims, which are a proxy for layoffs, will be released Wednesday in a scheduling shift ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. Economists watch this weekly report closely because it can provide signals about where the job market is headed.

Claims have remained at historically low levels amid a broader jobs market that has remained a strong point in an economy pressured by rising inflation. Layoffs remain modest by historic standards.

News.title: England lose to ‘Australia B team’ in thriller
News.content:
England’s white-ball tour of Australia continues as a five-match T20 series between kicks off in Melbourne at the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground, with the sandpapergate saga rumbling on. The first part of the tour went England’s way, as they came from 1-0 down to win the ODI series 2-1, following wins in Adelaide and Hobart. All of that action on the field has taken place whilst there has been plenty of “he said, she said” as some, like Cameron Bancroft, David Warner and Usman Khawaja say that everyone knew about the use of sandpaper whilst Pat Cummins has categorically denied that.

The last time these sides met in a T20 series back in September 2024, the three-match series ended in a 1-1 draw, with the final match abandoned. England won the last series played down under in October 2022, claiming a 2-0 series victory. Therefore, England are unbeaten in their past three bilateral mens’s T20I series against Australia. England are currently top of the ICC T20 rankings, with Australia third.

England were last in T20 action back in September, when they beat Sri Lanka 3-0. They have won all but two completed T20Is in 2026, with their last defeat coming in the World Cup semi-finals against India in March. They have decided to rest a number of the seamers who played in the ODI series including Jofra Archer and Gus Atkinson, whilst Josh Tongue is out injured. With those seamers absent, it will likely present opportunities for Henry Crocombe and Eddie Jack. Jacob Bethell remains out with a knee injury that he is still struggling with whilst Jos Buttler continues to recover from an hamstring injury.

Australia bombed out of the T20 World Cup in the group stages earlier this year, the first time that has happened since 2009. They did though win their most recent T20 series, beating Bangladesh 3-0 in June. Australia’s fast-bowling trio of Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood have all been rested for England’s white-ball tour, something that was planned long before the 2018 sandpapergate was reignited. Not only are that trio not involved but the likes of Nathan Ellis and Xavier Bartlett will also not play, therefore it will be a relatively inexperienced bowling attack for the hosts.

They will give a debut to wicketkeeper Sam Harper, who was named player of the tournament in the most recent edition of the Big Bash with the Melbourne Stars, with Josh Inglis being rested ahead of Australia’s upcoming busy Test schedule. Inglis is not the only player to sit out this series having played in the ODIs, with the likes of Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green and Cooper Connolly also not participating.

Play from the MCG gets under way from 8.15am GMT.

News.title: Anthropic plunges as Wall Street suffers AI sell-off
News.content:
Anthropic’s share price slump triggered a sharp sell-off on Wall Street with tech stocks closing down more than 5pc.

More than $163bn was wiped off the value of the AI giant on Friday, just a day after it touched a $2tn valuation on its stock market debut.

The decline prompted a wider flight from AI shares, with the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 down 5.6pc. It means the index has now erased all its gains year to date.

The S&P 500 fell 3.7pc at close, putting it on course for its worst week since Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffs last year, and into correction territory.

Anthropic has endured a hugely volatile introduction to public markets, surging as much as 39pc on the Nasdaq on Thursday, before closing the day 17pc higher.

However, it fell by as much as 14pc to $83.16 on Friday, just above where it started trading on Thursday.

It started the day at $97, less than 24 hours after it hit a high of $115.

The latest sell-off has fuelled fears that the company’s record-breaking float, which raised $87bn, is not enough to dispel lingering concerns over the AI bubble.

It comes after a series of threats to the investment boom.

That includes anti-data centre Democrats taking control of Congress, the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and tighter export controls on chips to China.

The Philadelphia semiconductor index, a grouping of the major US chip companies, dropped by as much as 9pc on Friday.

AI-linked companies dragged the Nasdaq lower, with the likes of semiconductor maker ARM losing 14pc.

CoreWeave also weighed on the Nasdaq, with its shares down 12pc.

European shares were also on track for their worst week since March amid investor concern over an AI bubble.

In a day of volatile swings on Wall Street, Nvidia also slipped behind Google parent Alphabet to become the fourth-most valuable US company.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “It’s been another hectic and negative week and one where even positive news is struggling to help the market stabilise.”

Pressure on stocks also rose after Donald Trump on Friday threatened to ban technology companies from building data centres outside of the US.

In a White House press conference, Mr Trump warned there would be “tremendous penalties” on US companies that tried to build data centres in foreign countries.

He said: “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen.”

He added: “We’re going to fight very hard for the data centres because we’re not going to let China [overtake us].”

The ban threat will raise questions for AI developers who are spending hundreds of billions of pounds building data facilities in the UK, Europe and across Asia.

It is not clear whether Mr Trump’s ban would apply to all data centre developers or just the most advanced facilities.

The sell-off came as Anthropic’s approach to copyright was slammed by news publishers, who said the company lacks “a basic moral compass”.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, attacked the company for its policy on journalism.

Anthropic told investors it could not guarantee it would adhere to measures that prevented journalism from being used to train AI models.

The Claude maker said it took steps to abide by paywalls but that this “may not always be successful”.

News.title: New case of bird flu confirmed in US dairy farm worker
News.content:
Another person in the US has contracted H5N1, bringing the number of confirmed cases in the country this year to four.

The patient, whose identity has not been released, works on a dairy farm in the US state of Oregon, local health officials confirmed on Thursday.

Their symptoms are reportedly mild, and they do not require hospitalisation.

All four of the H5N1 cases recorded in the US this year – one of whom died – have been in dairy workers who have had close contact with sick cattle.

The virus, which experts have long warned could trigger the next human pandemic, has become endemic in US dairy cattle after ‘jumping’ from birds to cows in late 2023.

Since then, it has been detected on nearly 1,000 dairy farms across dozens of states.

The US has reported 74 human cases of bird flu since 2024, nearly all of which have been from close contact with poultry or cows.

Earlier this month, United Farm Workers (UFW), a union which represents thousands of workers across the US, released a statement on X that said many farmers were experiencing symptoms of H5N1 and were not being tested for the virus.

They said the workers’ symptoms ranged from “very mild to very severe” and that surveillance on farms had been poor.

News.title: Violence and mistrust hamper Ebola response
News.content:
Six months after the deadly Bundibugyo Ebola virus flared in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the outbreak is far from under control.

Scores of new cases of the deadly haemorrhagic fever are being recorded every day and half of those diagnosed go on to die.

The official toll of 11,000 cases and more than 5,400 deaths is likely to be a vast underestimate and the outbreak is more than halfway to becoming the largest ever recorded.

Beyond the bare figures, aid agencies and emergency responders are also increasingly warning about the chaos, disorganisation and violence hampering the response.

Among the most worrying markers is that with 400 to 500 new cases reported every week, some two-thirds of deaths are occurring outside Ebola treatment centres.

Epidemiologists warn that figure is a sure sign cases are spreading undetected and that the tracking and quarantining of suspected patients is not working.

The outbreak has become like a deadly game of whack-a-mole, with new hotspots emerging just as responders manage to gain control over some of the early epicentres.

“Progress in some places is not control of the outbreak as a whole,” Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization (WHO), warned this week.

News.title: Anthropic achieves $2tn valuation as shares soar
News.content:
Anthropic has surged to a $2tn (£1.5tn) valuation as the Claude-maker defied a tech sell-off with a record-breaking float.

Shares in the Silicon Valley AI lab soared as high as $111.50 in opening trading on the Nasdaq exchange in New York on Thursday. The stock traded up around a third on its initial price of $83, before falling back to $97 per share at close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 closed 2.3pc lower, with investors cashing-in on the excitement, analysts say.

Dow Jones ended the session 2.2pc lower, while the S&P 500 closed down 2pc.

The AI lab raised a record $107bn in the stock market listing, smashing a previous $86bn record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June.

Many investors had been concerned about the backdrop to the blockbuster listing after a Chinese spying scandal engulfed US chip giant Nvidia and Jensen Huang, its former chief executive.

Nvidia is a major investor in Anthropic, but it has suffered a $900bn share price wide-out since Mr Huang admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an alleged Chinese spy earlier this month.

The US midterm elections, meanwhile, wiped trillions of dollars from the stock market earlier this month over concerns about a Democrat-led crackdown on AI companies and data centres.

Anthropic is likely to emerge as a bellwether for the wider AI industry. The AI giant plans to spend more than $1tn on technology infrastructure to power its digital chatbot and its pursuit of superintelligence, which its founders claim could lead to unprecedented growth and an “age of miracles”.

The float also sees Anthropic leap ahead of its main rival, ChatGPT-developer OpenAI, which is plotting its own trillion-dollar float next year.

The deal cements the status of Anthropic’s seven founders, including chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela, and British policy boss Jack Clark, as multi-billionaires.

The seven were worth around $19bn at the initial float price, which valued Anthropic at $1.4tn late on Wednesday, but could be worth as much as $26bn based on its latest valuation.

It also catapults Mr Clark, a 37-year-old former journalist from Brighton, into the ranks of the richest Britons.

Anthropic was founded just six years ago with a promise that it would pursue superintelligent AI while focusing on safety. It was launched after Mr Amodei quit OpenAI amid a bitter split over its approach to safety with founder Sam Altman.

The company’s founders have been deeply concerned about the potential risks of AI, including that an uncontrollable future AI system could spell disaster for humanity.

Mr Amodei said on Thursday that AI carried “real risks” but that the company would be “obsessed with safety”.

Anthropic launched its Claude AI as a helpful chatbot in 2023, but it has since found widespread use among businesses for coding or acting as an AI “agent”, a kind of digital co-worker.

The company reported revenues from its AI tool of around $33bn in the first nine months of the year, although it lost $104bn.

The deal also mints nearly all of Anthropic’s staff as millionaires. Private market data company Hill estimated that, at its initial float price, some 5,100 out of its 5,300 staff would become overnight millionaires. Some 580 will have fortunes of more than $100m.

It will provide a stunning return for many of Anthropic’s early investors, who include Ashton Kutcher, the actor, and Jaan Tallinn, the founder of Skype.

XTX Ventures, a fund launched by British billionaire trader Alex Gerko, is also set for significant gains after a $10m investment in Anthropic three years ago.

Dan Ives, a technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, said after trading began that the deal would help “restore some investor confidence” that the “AI revolution” is not waning.

However, Joe Maher, an analyst at Capital Economics, warned the deal may not be enough to “save the AI trade” as stocks fell on Thursday.

Elsewhere, a short-seller report targeting AMD, a chip company led by Lisa Hsu, the cousin of Nvidia chief Mr Huang, prompted an 8pc share price fall. The report claimed AMD had deeper ties to China than widely believed.

An AMD spokesman said the report “misrepresents” its business practices.

As the float got underway, there were protests outside the Nasdaq exchange, with several anti-AI demonstrators arrested.

In recent months, Anthropic’s own researchers have warned of the risk of an AI disaster that could destroy humanity. One suggested the risk was as high as 10pc.

The protests in New York called for a “a freeze to reckless AI development and destruction”.

News.title: Genocide verdict puts Netanyahu on notice
News.content:
The finding by the world’s top court that the military junta in Myanmar is guilty of genocide will send a shiver through Israel’s legal and military establishment.

No case is directly transferable from one country to another: each is judged on its own merits.

But the legal precedents set in the case against Myanmar are certain to shape the allegations of genocide against Israel over its actions in Gaza following the massacre by Hamas on Oct 7, 2023.

Perhaps it was the Court’s forensic and coldly logical presentation of the 191-page historic judgment, but as it was read out over the course of almost three hours in a hushed courtroom in The Hague, it was impossible not to see parallels.

Unlike other war crimes and crimes against humanity, the crime of genocide hinges on being able to establish “genocidal intent”.

Without it there can be crimes of mass killing, rape and even widespread ethnic cleansing. But there can be no finding of genocide unless those directing the violence “intentionally” planned to destroy a group “in whole or in part”.

Moreover, genocidal motivation must be found to be the “single” reasonable explanation for a defendant state’s actions.

Lawyers in Israel – like most international lawyers – have long stressed how high that bar is, with some believing it was insurmountable without a written document of the “final solution” type filed away by the Nazis.

But Thursday’s judgment by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) blows that assumption out of the water.

News.title: Myanmar guilty of genocide, International Court of Justice rules
News.content:
Myanmar’s military junta has been found guilty of committing genocide in a ruling that could have implications for Israel and its war on Gaza.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, the UN’s highest court, said Myanmar had systematically attempted to destroy the Muslim minority Rohingya population. It is the first time in its 81-year history that the ICJ has found a state guilty of genocide.

The 2017 attacks led to one of the largest movements of people in modern history, with hundreds of thousands fleeing violence across the border to Bangladesh. The court said the attacks constituted more than an attempt to contain unrest in the region through military means.

The judges said: “The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations.”

The judges ruled by nine votes to six that it had been genocide.

Sports.title: McKinney earns England Test call up for South Africa series
Sports.content:
England have added Ben McKinney to their Test squad touring South Africa next month, with the uncapped Durham opener serving as a replacement for the injured Jacob Bethell.

McKinney, a 6ft 7in left-handed batter, has become a regular in the England Lions set-up and underlined his growing reputation on this month's tour of St Kitts, hitting 145 against West Indies A.

He will provide competition and cover for England's top order that includes county colleague Emilio Gay.

Image: Jacob Bethell was released from the touring squad of South Africa due to an ongoing knee issue

Bethell underwent a second bout of knee surgery on Thursday after being ruled out of the series due to an ongoing issue that also required an operation in the summer.

The 23-year-old had linked up with England's white-ball squad in Australia earlier this month, only for his anticipated comeback to be cut short by a flare-up of his knee injury.

England's the three-Test series in South Africa gets under way in Johannesburg on December 17.

Jacks an injury doubt for rest of white-ball series in Australia

Meanwhile, England's white-ball side could be scrambling to find a captain by the end of their Australia tour after Will Jacks suffered a bloody finger injury in the closing moments of their series-opening T20I loss in Melbourne on Saturday.

Image: England's Will Jacks reacts after injuring his finger in the first T20 against Australia

Jacks hade to leave the field in the penultimate over of the three-wicket defeat with blood streaming from his right hand following a painful attempted caught-and-bowled off Ben Dwarshuis.

Jacks had been set to captain England for the first time in the fifth and final T20 in Canberra, with regular white-ball skipper Harry Brook having brought forward his departure ahead of next month's Test tour of South Africa.

"I don't know [how bad it is],-he obviously came off with a lot of blood but I couldn't quite see what happened," Brook said of Jacks' funger after Saturday's loss at the MCG.

"Hopefully he is alright because he has been such a valuable player for us in the last two years. It would be sad to see him go home early.

"I've not even thought about that one [the captaincy] yet, that's a decision we'll have to discuss but I don't have an answer yet."

Sports.title: Man City end losing streak but held at home by Fulham
Sports.content:
Man City ended their losing streak but were still held to a 1-1 draw at home to Fulham at the Etihad Stadium.

Elliot Anderson volleyed City level early in the second half after Erling Haaland had seen a first-half equaliser controversially ruled out. But Alvaro Arbeloa's Fulham were well worth a point, Rodrigo Muniz's fine opener setting the tone for an enterprising display.

There was frustration among the City players and supporters when Haaland looked to have bundled in the equaliser soon after Muniz's goal but referee Thomas Bramall ruled that the Norwegian striker had fouled Bernd Leno and the VAR did not overrule him.

Image: Erling Haaland scores a goal that was disallowed for a foul on Bernd Leno

The ambition of Fulham's approach merited some fortune. They were aggressive out of possession and confident enough to play when they had the ball - which was plenty. Former City man Oscar Bobb should have doubled the advantage before the interval.

Enzo Maresca had responded to the defeat away to Nottingham Forest, in which City's vulnerability on transition was a striking feature of the game, by bringing in Ayyoub Bouaddi for Enzo Fernandez. But Fulham had little problem playing through them.

The response eventually came through Anderson. It was not just his spectacular volley through a crowd of bodies. He was racing through on goal as City chased a winner, going close with a left-footed effort that drifted just wide of the post, driving his team on.

Image: Manchester City's Elliot Anderson celebrates after scoring the equaliser

City still needed Gianluigi Donnarumma at the other end, saving from Muniz and Calvin Bassey, whose presence in the box following a breakaway summed up Fulham's intent. They did more than hold on, and David Affengruber continually bested a below-par Haaland.

The draw extends improving Fulham's unbeaten run to five matches and does at least end City's three-game losing streak under Maresca. But the Italian coach continues to have problems to solve on this evidence. They remain third, below Brighton in second.

Sports.title: Norwich hit back to beat Cardiff
Sports.content:
Norwich came from behind to beat Cardiff 2-1 and make it five straight Championship victories - after losing their previous five.

The Canaries went behind just after the break when Yousef Salech got on the end of a free-kick from deep but the visitors were quickly back on level terms as Paris Maghoma scored for the fourth game running.

And it did not take them long to score what proved to be the winner, with Mathias Kvistgaarden tapping home on 68 minutes after his penalty had been kept out by Nathan Trott.

Cardiff performed gamely all afternoon but were unable to get the equaliser their gutsy performance probably deserved.

Both sides knocked the ball around neatly in an evenly-contested first half, with the visitors creating the better chances.

Image: Paris Maghoma of Norwich City celebrates scoring his team's first goal

With just three minutes on the clock home keeper Dan Grimshaw did well to tip a beautifully-struck Rubin Colwill free-kick over while the Cardiff skipper went even closer midway through the half. This time a move that ran the length of the pitch ended with the big midfielder clipping the crossbar with an effort from just outside the 'D'.

Norwich launched plenty of promising attacks of their own, but they generally lacked any penetration and Andre Brooks' close-range effort into the side netting on 25 minutes was the closest they came to breaking the deadlock in the opening period.

Cardiff took a little over two minutes to get their noses in front after the break as Alex Robertson's inswinging free-kick to the back post was missed by home defence and Salech was on hand to stroke the ball into the bottom corner for his ninth goal of the season.

Norwich responded well and should have been back on level terms on the hour mark when Anthony Musuba bore down on goal from the left only to screw his shot horribly wide.

But the home faithful did not have to wait long for an equaliser. On 62 minutes the visitors unwisely left Maghoma with some space on the edge of the area and the in-form midfielder curled a delightful shot beyond the reach of Trott and into the far corner.

The momentum was now very much with the Canaries and they completed a swift turnaround by going ahead from the spot in the 68th minute. Ronan Kpakio was penalised for bring down Brooks as he made his way to the byline and although Trott saved Kvistgaarden's penalty, the Danish striker had no problem converting the rebound to make it 2-1.

Salech had a header rightly ruled out for offside as Cardiff sought a response while at the other end substitutes Lucien Mahovo and Jovon Makama were both inches away from stretching Norwich's lead.

Cardiff top scorer Jack Moylan was foiled by a good stop from Grimshaw late on as the home side notched up another win.

Sports.title: Australia complete record T20I chase at MCG to edge England in thriller
Sports.content:
Australia pulled off a record T20I run chase of 188 at the MCG to beat England by three wickets with a ball to spare in a thrilling series opener in Melbourne on Saturday.

England captain Harry Brook had tonked 68 off just 25 balls - hitting six sixes - as England posted 187-9, though his side wasted a dominant position of 119-4 at the halfway point of their innings by adding only 68 from the last 10 overs.

Image: Harry Brook's quickfire 65 saw England recover from the loss of two early wickets

Nikhil Chaudhary, who had helped drag Australia back into the contest with the ball - the hosts having dropped six chances - then top-scored with a magnificent 68 off 38 with the bat.

He was dismissed with 20 still required off the final two overs, Australia seven down, but Jack Edwards (25no off 11) struck a couple of crucial sixes in a clutch cameo before finishing the job with a boundary.

Image: England trail 1-0 in the five-match T20I series despite Harry Brook's fine innings

Score summary - Australia vs England, first T20I, Melbourne England 187-9 in 20 overs (inserted at toss): Harry Brook (65 off 28 balls), Tom Banton (39 off 22), Jordan Cox (27 off 20); Nikhil Chaudhary (2-21), Jack Edwards (2-27) Australia 191-7 in 19.5 overs (target 188): Nikhil Chaudhary (66 off 38 balls), Mitch Marsh (37 off 32), Sam Harper (32 off 15), Jack Edwards (25no off 11); Will Jacks (2-29)

After being inserted by the hosts, England's innings had got off to the worst possible start as Phil Salt picked out mid-off first ball, while Aneurin Donald (10) - put down two deliveries prior - perished soon after.

But Brook, dropped on 2 and 3, made Australia pay for their profligacy as he smoked three sixes in a row in taking Riley Meredith's fourth over for 24, the touring captain romping to a 20-ball fifty.

He and Tom Banton (39 off 22) - shelled twice, taking Australia's tally to five inside seven overs - put on 107 for the third wicket, with Adam Zampa also taking some tap as his opening over went for 20.

Image: Tom Banton made 39 before he was impressively caught by Lachlan Shaw

Chaudhary ignites Australia fightback

Both were gone in the space of six deliveries though, Chaudhary's wrist spin accounting for Brook, caught behind, and Banton gone to a sensational diving catch in the deep by debutant Lachlan Shaw.

England stumbled their way to a rather underwhelming score thereafter, despite the best efforts of Jordan Cox (27 off 20) and Sam Curran (21 off 20), the visitors falling short of the 200-run target they'll have surely been eyeing.

That said, it was still a record T20I chase at the MCG for Australia to reel in, and their assignment was made all the tougher when Liam Dawson (1-30) struck in the opening over - Jake Fraser-McGurk (1) bowled when charging the left-arm spinner, deceived in the flight.

Image: England's Liam Dawson celebrates the wicket of Jake Fraser-McGurk in the opening over of Australia's reply

Mitch Marsh hammered Henry Crocombe's first ball in T20 international cricket for six over deep backward square for quite the introduction, but the young quick responded well to remove fellow debutant Sam Harper (32 off 15) for his first wicket in his second over.

Harper had provided some impetus to the Australian innings, Jamie Overton's opening over plundered for 21 runs, and Chaudhary maintained that momentum, with useful support from his captain Marsh (37 off 32) and Tim David (20 off 13).

David failed to cash in a huge slice of luck when the bails failed to dislodge as he inside-edged one back onto his stumps, as he departed a ball later to the returning Adil Rashid (1-30).

It prompted a rather sizeable Australian wobble, with three wickets tumbling for 13 runs in little more than an over, and when Chaudhary finally fell - caught in the deep - it looked like England might be in the ascendency, only for Edwards to have other ideas.

Brook not sure how bad Jacks injury is

Image: England's Will Jacks reacts after injuring his finger in the first T20 against Australia

In other worrying news for England, Will Jacks left the field late on, splitting the webbing on his hand as Ben Dwarshuis drilled a ball back at him in the penultimate over.

He is due to captain the team in the fifth and final T20I of the series as Brook departs for the Test tour of South Africa.

Speaking afterwards Brook said: "I don't know [how bad Jacks' injury is]. He obviously came off with a lot of blood but I couldn't quite see what happened.

"Hopefully he is alright because he has been such a valuable player for us in the last two years. It would be sad to see him go home early.

"I've not even thought about [the captaincy] yet. That's a decision we'll have to discuss but I don't have an answer yet."

Sam Curran, Tom Banton and Phil Salt could be captaincy contenders for a squad already missing Jacob Bethell (knee).

Hampshire's former Scotland seamer Scott Currie has been called up for the final T20I in Canberra.

Chaudhary enjoyed 'chirp' with England

Player of the Match, Nikhil Chaudhary:

Image: Chaudhary scored 66 off 38 balls in Australia's successful chase

"I was just trying to hit the wickets at the start and got the big wicket of Harry [Brook]. I wanted to bowl that five, six-metre length. That was my goal.

"With the bat, you knew it was going to be a big game and that there was going to some chirp. I just had to stay stable and play my game.

"Hopefully I did that and won the game for the team, which was great. There is nothing better than playing at the MCG and winning."

Brook: England were 10 runs short

England captain Harry Brook:

"It was a very entertaining game, going down to the last couple of balls. It's what the fans want to see and everybody watching at home.

"We were probably 10 runs short of what we needed on that surface. If we get those, we probably end up winning the game."

'I was worried when we dropped Brook twice!'

Australia captain Mitch Marsh:

"I was worried when we dropped the best batter in the world [Brook] a couple of times. Most of the time you don't deserve to win.

"But outside a few tough chances, I thought the energy and speed was great to watch. They are all good kids.

"It has been a pretty crazy 12 days but right there is the future of the Australian cricket side with all these young guys. Hopefully we can get back to enjoying that.

"They are a great bunch. I want them to not care about making mistakes and enjoy the environment. Hopefully a win like that shows them they belong."

Sports.title: Southampton see off Derby to return to winning ways
Sports.content:
Cyle Larin returned to action with a bang as Southampton extended their unbeaten run at home in the Championship to 18 games with a 2-0 victory over second-bottom Derby.

Larin turned in his eighth goal of the season but his first since 12 September - after a four-game drought and a hamstring problem.

Divin Mubama added a second in stoppage time as Saints shrugged off worries of failing against lower-placed sides - having dropped points against Watford, Preston, Wrexham, Lincoln and Bolton already this season.

Despite Tonda Eckert signing a new contract and Saints' incredible home form, St Mary's felt subdued on and off the pitch for much of the early kick-off.

The visitors, languishing in the relegation zone came in with a well-drilled defensive gameplan, and the hosts - without injured stars Leo Scienza, Caspar Jander and James Bree - struggled to break through.

Image: Cyle Larin of Southampton celebrates after opening the scoring

Southampton's possession advantage did not translate to chances, as their only first-half shot on target saw Finn Azaz fashion a crafty flick at the near post.

They also struck the crossbar in a rare moment of quality, as Azaz dropped a ball into the six-yard box as Larin saw his stretched volley bounce back off the goal frame.

But it was the visitors that ended the half with more fluidity and had a trio of good efforts.

The lively Mohammed Fuseini flashed a snapshot across the face of goal. Carlton Morris looped a bouncing ball and forced Daniel Peretz into an acrobatic save, before Shane Duffy poked the resulting corner over.

The second half began in a similar manner with Saints struggling to unlock the defence, while the Rams' Fuseini tested Peretz at the other end.

Then, early in the second half, Southampton finally found some joy.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cyle Larin finishes off a slick Southampton move to open the scoring against Derby County in the Championship.

The ground was lifted when Azaz pirouetted in the box and lashed a shot at Jacob Widell Zetterstrom, before James Ward-Prowse's follow-up was blocked.

And that energy brought the opener, as Azaz, Ryan Manning and Samuel Edozie neatly played the ball around before Azaz's low cross was bundled in by Larin in the 57th minute.

The Canadian had missed the last four matches, and was a welcome return after attacking struggles at West Brom and Preston.

Azaz almost followed it up by getting on the scoresheet himself, but he scuffed straight at Zetterstrom from the edge of the area.

Ward-Prowse had a shot deflected over and had the ball in the net, pinging in from the half-way line when the whistle had already gone for an offside as the home team attempted to put the game to bed.

With Zetterstrom up for a corner in the fifth minute of added time, Man City loanee Mubama ran the length of the pitch on the counter to make it 2-0 - celebrating long before slotting home.

Sports.title: QPR battle to victory at 10-man Millwall
Sports.content:
Nicolas Madsen's scruffy winner gave Queens Park Rangers their first away victory since August as they defeated Millwall 1-0 at The Den.

The result against their London rivals ensured the Hoops will end the weekend inside the play-off places in the Sky Bet Championship after they played the majority of the contest against 10 men following Zak Sturge's 15th-minute red card.

Despite a commendable defensive performance with depleted numbers, this was a third straight defeat for Millwall whose campaign continues to stutter.

Millwall began brightly, with their captain Jake Cooper nodding Camiel Neghli's cross into the path of Kyrell Lisbie - whose shot from an acute angle was saved by QPR goalkeeper Pierce Charles.

Ilias Chair tried to catch out Millwall's keeper, the returning Lukas Jensen, by trying his luck from just inside the Lions' half, with his audacious effort dipping wide.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Sky Bet Championship match between Millwall and Queens Park Rangers.

Then came a big blow for the home side when Sturge was shown a straight red card for tripping Paul Smyth just outside the area as the last defender.

Smyth was then involved in an altercation on the touchline in the 24th minute that led to Millwall boss Alex Neil being shown a yellow card as the temperature in this London derby simmered.

Just when it looked as though the Lions would hold out until half-time, QPR took the lead in first-half stoppage time as Jensen first saved from Chair before Madsen's follow-up crossed the line despite Caleb Taylor's attempted heroics.

Millwall had goalkeeping coach Dean Thornton sent from the dugout in the aftermath and, short on numbers on the pitch, it looked a long way back for them in the second half.

The Hoops brought on Japanese midfielder Koki Saito at the break and he almost struck within six minutes of the restart when his shot from outside the box was pushed behind by Jensen.

Chair then curled a shot from the edge of the area narrowly wide and at this point it looked just a matter of time until the dominant visitors would score again.

But they were having a hard time of making all their possession count, with Richard Kone having a shot comfortably saved by Jensen as the match ticked towards the final 15 minutes.

QPR sub Karamoko Dembele had a good chance to make the game safe but his effort from Glen Kamara's cut-back went wide.

Jake Clarke-Salter was then narrowly off target from 25 yards in the 90th minute for the Hoops, for whom one goal proved to be enough.

Sports.title: Elliot Anderson ends Manchester City’s losing run but boos greet Fulham draw
Sports.content:
Manchester City are living in Premier League purgatory, without a win in four but at least ended their three-game losing run against Fulham. As they await the fate of their much-publicised appeal after being found guilty of financial breaches, their form has slumped as further evidenced by a passive draw.

Arguments will be made over Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal but City did not deserve anything more. The Norwegian uncharacteristically missed a number of fine chances as Rodrigo Muniz took advantage of City’s porous defence, who had to rely on Elliot Anderson to get anything out of the fixture.

City approached the game with the same subdued nature of the crowd, as is customary for a Saturday lunchtime kick-off. For a team amid a poor run of domestic form, they offered little in the way of dynamism from the off. A couple of half-chances were brushed off by Fulham, who were allowed to ease themselves into the game.

Confusion between defence and midfield has repeatedly caused problems for City under Enzo Maresca, who witnessed Marc Guéhi going over the halfway line to press a throw-in deep inside the Fulham half. When the visitors won the first header, the centre-back was out of position and everything was far too simple from then on. The former City winger Oscar Bobb shimmied and Muniz curled into the top corner from the edge of the box, before an emotional celebration in honour of his pregnant wife, who previously suffered a miscarriage.

View image in fullscreen Rodrigo Muniz opens the scoring for Fulham during the first half. Photograph: Phil Oldham/Shutterstock

It was a day where the team needed to inspire the crowd and City finally discovered intent midway through the first-half. Iliman Ndiaye’s dangerous cross found Haaland at the back post but he could not finish at the first time of asking, allowing Bernd Leno to get his hands to the ball but whether the German had it under control is another matter. Haaland jabbed at the goalkeeper, nudging the ball through his grasp but the referee signalled for a foul and the video assistant referee (VAR) did not intervene. No one connected to City felt it was a correct decision, with Thomas Bramall offering the benefit of the doubt to Leno.

City lacked a cutting edge; Phil Foden, given the nod over Rayan Cherki at No 10, had chances to feed Haaland in good positions but twice the execution of the pass ensured there was no change. At the third time of asking, the pair connected, only for Haaland to balloon a shot from close range, and under little pressure, into the stands. Every Haaland finish was a whimsical version of what you would nornally expect, miscuing a straightforward chance from a Nico O’Reilly cross, too. It felt like one of those days.

City continued to find it difficult as David Affengruber and Calvin Bassey put in fine performances at centre-back, reading every strand of danger and snuffing it out. To find a way back into the match, City needed to increase the tempo and find some aggression which had been sorely absent from their play, something Anderson belatedly provided by violently volleying a cleared corner into the bottom corner from 18 yards.

View image in fullscreen Erling Haaland challenges for the ball but Bernd Leno was deemed to have it under control so the goal was disallowed. Photograph: Dave Thompson/AP

Anderson is becoming Maresca’s most trusted player, preferred to Enzo Fernández to provide the thrust alongside Ayyoub Bouaddi. In a team lacking energy, the England international is a catalyst in what is a difficult period for an underperforming team. He latched on to a Haaland flick-on but could not stay on his feet and the pair combined for a second time but Anderson’s quick feet and cute finish concluded with the ball slipping an inch wide.

With the tide turning, City’s flaws were there for all to see as Fulham won the ball and within a blink of an eye Muniz was through on goal thanks to the lack of resistance in blue. Gianluigi Donnarumma was the last – and sturdiest – line of defence, repeating the feat against Bassey soon after. These were the best opportunities of the second half, as City were unable to create a meaningful chance on another worrying afternoon, which concluded with further jeers.

Sports.title: Championship roundup: Southampton get Larin lift as Norwich win five in a row
Sports.content:
Cyle Larin returned to action with a bang as Southampton extended their unbeaten run at home in the Championship to 18 games with a 2-0 victory over second-bottom Derby.

Larin turned in his eighth goal of the season but his first since 12 September – after a four-game drought and a hamstring problem. Divin Mubama added a second in stoppage time as Saints shrugged off worries of failing against lower-placed sides – having dropped points against Watford, Preston, Wrexham, Lincoln and Bolton already this season.

But for their four-point deduction for Spygate, the result would have taken Southampton top for at least a couple of hours. Derby would wind up bottom if Preston pulled off an unlikely win at West Ham.

Norwich came from behind to beat Cardiff 2-1 and make it five straight Championship victories – after losing their previous five. The Canaries went behind just after the break when Yousef Salech got on the end of a free-kick from deep but the visitors were quickly back on level terms as Paris Maghoma scored for the fourth game running.

View image in fullscreen Mathias Kvistgaarden celebrates scoring the second goal for Norwich City against Cardiff. Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images

Mathias Kvistgaarden then tapped home in the 68th minute after his penalty had been kept out by Nathan Trott. Ronan Kpakio had been penalised for bringing down Andre Brooks. Cardiff performed gamely all afternoon but were unable to get the equaliser their gutsy performance probably deserved.

Quick Guide League One roundup: Bromley stun Reading Show Playoff chasing Reading suffered a shock 1-0 home defeat to basement side Bromley at the SCL Stadium. Reading dominated a hugely one-sided first half but were denied by a succession of fine saves from Shamal George. The Ravens then went in front in the 58th minute when the substitute Victor Adeboyejo slotted home on a rare Bromley attack, and they stubbornly held on for a valuable win. Wigan picked up their first away win of the campaign with a 2-1 comeback victory against managerless Blackpool at Bloomfield Road. The Seasiders managed to break the deadlock with three minutes of the first half when Zac Ashworth reacted quickest to poke home the rebound after Joe Whitworth palmed Albie Morgan’s free-kick into his path. However, their lead would last less than two minutes as Jensen Weir jinked through three Blackpool players before laying it on a plate for Jon Mellish, who tapped in a side-footed finish at the far post. The Latics then took the lead just after the hour mark through another of their defenders when Finley Burns reacted quickest to nod in from close range after Morgan Fox headed a Fraser Murray corner across the six-yard box. PA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Nicolas Madsen’s scruffy winner gave Queens Park Rangers their first away victory since August as they defeated Millwall 1-0 at the Den. The result against their London rivals ensured the Hoops will end the weekend inside the playoff places after they played the majority of the contest against 10 men following Zak Sturge’s 15th-minute red card. Sturge was shown a straight red card for tripping Paul Smyth just outside the area as the last defender.

View image in fullscreen Nicolas Madsen is congratulated by teammates after scoring their the winner at Millwall. Photograph: Ian Tuttle/Shutterstock

QPR took the lead in first-half stoppage time as Lukas Jensen first saved from Ilias Chair before Madsen’s follow-up crossed the line despite Caleb Taylor’s attempted heroics. Despite a commendable defensive performance with depleted numbers, this was a third straight defeat for Millwall whose campaign continues to stutter.

Quick Guide League Two roundup: McCleary rescues Gillingham in thriller Show Garath McCleary came off the bench to rescue a point for Gillingham in an end-to-end 3-3 draw against Crewe at Priestfield. In a game of three penalties, McCleary headed home with just seconds left to play when it appeared Calum Agius, also a sub, had netted the winner for Crewe. Ronan Hale had cancelled out Conor McManus’s early own goal, netting two first-half spot-kicks, only to see the sub Charlie McNeill convert a penalty for the visitors, before Agius put the Railwaymen in front with a tidy finish. Aaron Lewis scored twice as Newport piled the pressure on Ian Holloway with a 2-0 win against Swindon at Rodney Parade. It was a 10th defeat in the last 15 games in all competitions for the visitors. The first goal came in the sixth minute as Lewis reacted quickest when Kion Etete’s shot was blocked and he poked in the loose ball with his studs from close range. The second, 12 minutes later, started with a Cameron Norman free-kick into the area, which was headed back across goal. Lewis was again in the right place and, after his first effort was blocked, he fired in at the second attempt. PA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Later kick-offs include Birmingham, the leaders, at Stoke, Middlesbrough in second at home to Bristol City and third-placed Wolves hosting Charlton.

Sports.title: Liverpool keeper Keating holds leaders Chelsea at bay in scoreless WSL draw
Sports.content:
Khiara Keating’s resilient performance in goal denied Chelsea, the Women’s Super League leaders, and earned Liverpool a point. After hard-fought 1-0 wins against Manchester City last Saturday and Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday night, Chelsea drew a blank.

Against Gareth Taylor’s side, Chelsea’s lack of cutting edge was clear a week after beating City to go top. The calf injury picked up by Melvine Malard against City, the absence of Lauren James, who has a thigh injury, and the form of Aggie Beever-Jones, who scored her first WSL goal in more than a year in the 6-0 defeat of Charlton, have left Chelsea’s attack short.

Despite almost 70% possession and 47 touches in the box to Liverpool’s 12, Sonia Bompastor’s side amassed only 19 shots to Liverpool’s 13 and seven on target to their opponents’ four. Although the Blues remain unbeaten in the WSL, their third draw in five games in all competitions means City can leapfrog them at the top if they beat Tottenham on Sunday.

Liverpool had chances, particularly in the first half, but were hanging on after the break and Keating helped them to a fourth clean sheet, a tally bettered only by Bompastor’s side.

“It was a bit stressful; we don’t want to sit back but in games like this you have ‌to ride it out,” Keating told Sky Sports. “A clean sheet is ​always on our minds every game. We knew the mission. It was such a close game, it could have gone either way.”

The January transfer window will give the Blues an opportunity to strengthen their attack, but with three games before the winter break they need to step up in the final third, starting with their tricky fixture against London City Lionesses on 12 December after the international break.
