World.title: Diallo present as Africa football boss Motsepe reiterates Infantino support
World.content:
African football supremo Patrice Motsepe has said that all 54 members of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) support Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election as FIFA president.

Motsepe made the declaration on Saturday in Abuja, where CAF is holding its ordinary general assembly and at which one of Infantino’s two rivals, French football chief Philippe Diallo, is present.

Former Japan Football Association president Kozo Tashima is the other candidate.

The trio will learn whether they have been successful on March 18 next year in Rabat – the winning candidate must obtain a majority of the 211 associations.

CAF’s support for Infantino comes hours after another of his steadfast supporters, South American football’s governing body CONMEBOL, gave him their “unanimous” backing.

CAF has been consistently behind Infantino – who is seeking a fourth and final term – even after the furore he stirred up in July with his short-lived FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Morocco is cohosting the 2030 World Cup.

“Gianni, you have our support on behalf of the 54 nations in Africa to be our candidate,” Motsepe said.

“I have a report from all 54 member associations in Africa to say that we are unanimously supporting Gianni.”

Infantino has faced multiple calls to step down and lost the backing of European football’s governing body UEFA, while CONCACAF has also been strident in its criticism of the 56-year-old Swiss lawyer.

Motsepe, though, has been a vocal supporter, and Infantino said such loyalty was reciprocal.



“You will always find, in me and in FIFA, a trusted partner,” Infantino told the assembly, announcing cash inflow of $25m to each member of CAF, starting January 2027 for development projects.

On Wednesday, UEFA Vice President Laura McAllister told the AFP news agency that Diallo, a 63-year-old lawyer whose Senegalese-born father boxed for France at the 1960 Olympics in Rome, should not be seen as solely a European candidate.

“He is a Francophone, which is an important asset in lots of CAF countries,” she said.

McAllister, who in 2023 became the first woman to be elected a vice president of UEFA, noted that confederations do not vote as a bloc.

“There is a soft space which Philippe can exploit and convince some federations within each confederation to support a reform agenda,” the 61-year-old said.

“There is a lot of discomfort around the behaviour of Gianni Infantino and a desire to challenge the concentration of power in his hands.

“This applies everywhere in world football. This is not about Europe; the same rules apply globally.”

World.title: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
World.content:
British maritime agency reports two incidents near Oman, while Iran says a tanker caught fire due to naval mine.

Share Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping on social media

British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.

The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.

Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.

Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.

No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.

Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.

In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.

The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.

A ‘pattern’

Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.



Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.

“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”

If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.

Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.

He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.

The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.

The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

World.title: Man City claw back 1-1 draw with Fulham to end three-game losing streak
World.content:
Rodrigo Muniz set Fulham on the way but Elliot Anderson volley earns Manchester City a valuable Premier League point.

Manchester City avoided the ignominy of a fourth-straight defeat as Elliot Anderson’s strike kept an unsettled Etihad Stadium at bay in a 1-1 draw with Fulham in the Premier League.

Rodrigo Muniz opened the scoring in the 16th minute for the away side, who had only won two of their opening 10 league games to start the day just two points and three places above the relegation zone.

Anderson’s driven volley from the edge of the box in the 57th minute handed City their first point in the league since they opened their campaign with seven consecutive wins.

The midfielder, who had netted his first City goal since arriving from Nottingham Forest, nearly added a second with a burst into the box, but dragged his effort across the face.

City, who sit five points off top spot, had lost to Brighton, RB Leipzig and Forest in their previous games.

Holders and league leaders Arsenal play their game in hand over City at Newcastle later on Saturday.

City held one of the longest winning streaks in English football history with 20 straight victories over Fulham dating back to 2012.

That run is now over, but City’s run of poor results is not.

Boos from the home support greeted the final whistle, with City’s winless run in the league extending to four games — a stretch that has come soon after the club was found guilty of large-scale financial rule-breaking that leaves its future shrouded in uncertainty.

The display was far from convincing for City, with Erling Haaland guilty of wasting two great chances in the first half — and having one goal ruled out in contentious circumstances.



After having a close-range effort saved by Bernd Leno, Haaland followed up and bundled the ball out of the Fulham goalkeeper’s possession and into the net on the goal line.

It was judged that Haaland kicked the ball out of Leno’s hands, with the Premier League saying Leno was deemed to be “in control of the ball”.

World.title: Could Iran reverse its stated policy of a civil-only nuclear programme?
World.content:
Iran’s FM Araghchi says there is ‘major strategic debate’ about the future of Iran’s nuclear doctrine.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the country’s stockpile of enriched uranium will be used according to its needs, “however they are defined”, as he spoke about possible changes to Iran’s longstanding nuclear doctrine.

Araghchi’s comments during an interview with Iranian media on Saturday have increased speculation that Iran may be moving away from its policy of limiting its nuclear programme to civilian purposes amid its conflict with the United States.

The future of Iran’s nuclear programme has become a major sticking point in efforts to end the war, with Washington insisting that it must have guarantees that Iran will never develop a nuclear weapon before it will agree to a full ceasefire.

So, is Iran’s nuclear policy changing, and what could that mean for the conflict?

What is Iran’s official nuclear policy?

Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes only, such as for electricity generation, medical research and agriculture.

This policy has been underlined by a decades-old religious decree, or fatwa, issued by the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, banning the development of nuclear weapons.

However, Iran has also insisted it has the right to enrich uranium for these purposes under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), which it joined in 1970. It has called this right “non-negotiable”.

What have Araghchi and other officials said?

In an interview with Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency on Saturday, Araghchi reiterated that Iran’s stockpile of enriched material would remain inside the country.



The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated in 2025 – before Israel launched strikes on Iran in June that year – that Iran had about 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched to about 60 percent. This is short of the 90 percent required for making nuclear weapons, but is the level at which it becomes much quicker to reach 90 percent. It is also far beyond the roughly 3 percent needed for power generation.

This material, Araghchi said during his interview, would “be used according to our needs however those needs are defined”.

Araghchi also made reference to an ongoing debate among lawmakers and officials in Iran about altering its nuclear doctrine, and said people on both sides of that debate have “strong arguments”.

“This is a major strategic debate, and there is nothing wrong with examining it seriously because it directly concerns national interests and security,” Araghchi said, adding that those in favour of reform argue Iran’s current approach of no nuclear weapons has “failed to protect” the country’s nuclear facilities, which have come under attack from US and Israeli forces both last year and this year.

However, Araghchi acknowledged that any official change to the policy would have “far-reaching consequences”.

“For now, our doctrine has not changed, and our official position remains the same,” he said.

Other Iranian officials have also spoken about a potential review of the country’s nuclear doctrine. Earlier this month, security chief Mohsen Rezaei said “there is a discussion on whether we want to continue to follow the previous nuclear doctrine in the event of a new war breaking out”, though he also stressed that Tehran has not yet made any change.

On November 12, Iran’s Assembly of Experts, the body that appoints the supreme leader, said reviewing “the country’s defence doctrine and establishing the necessary deterrence have become unavoidable necessities”.

Ali Fathollah-Nejad, a German-Iranian political scientist who directs the Center for Middle East and Global Order (CMEG), told Al Jazeera the move by the Assembly of Experts “appears to mark the first time a governing institution has endorsed this position”.

Why do the US and Israel think Iran is developing nuclear weapons?

Besides being a signatory to the NPT in 1970, Iran also initially complied with a nuclear agreement it struck with the US and other global powers in 2015 – the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), which required it to limit uranium enrichment to very low levels and undergo inspections.



But after Washington pulled out of the deal in 2018 under the first administration of US President Donald Trump, Tehran eventually went back to intensifying its nuclear programme and abandoned restrictions imposed by the deal.

In June 2025, the IAEA’s board of governors declared Iran was no longer complying with its commitment to international nuclear safeguards. Tehran rejected that report and accused the IAEA of giving a pretext for US and Israeli attacks targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, including Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, just days later during the 12-day war.

In March of this year, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said at least 200kg (440lbs) of Iran’s enriched material was believed to have survived the US-Israeli attacks and was likely buried underground in or near the Isfahan nuclear facility site.

Grossi has since said the agency cannot verify the amount or location of Iran’s enriched material due to a lack of access.

The IAEA has called Iran’s enrichment level “a matter of serious concern”, while the US has pointed to it as evidence that Iran is pursuing nuclear weapons despite its official policy.

“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel?” US Vice President JD Vance said in an interview with the Reuters news agency last month. “And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue.”

President Trump has repeatedly stated that Iran must never be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon.

Officials in Israel, which is widely believed to have its own undeclared nuclear weapons, have also long accused Iran of pursuing nuclear weapons.

“The Iranian regime, which seeks to destroy Israel, is once again working to revive its nuclear programme,” said Israel’s now-caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an address last week. “We must remove this existential threat once and for all.”

Will Iran officially reverse its no-nuclear-weapons policy?

That remains to be seen, but it is “within the realm of possibility”, Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.

He said the US-Israeli war launched against Iran in February this year “has significantly changed all the calculations in Tehran”, with more open discussion about whether to renew the late ayatollah’s ban on nuclear weapons now taking place.

“What used to be a fringe opinion, leaving the NPT and potentially going for a nuclear weapon, is now something that’s within the realm of possibility – even though all the major players are still warning against it,” said Parsi. “It’s not a decision but an indication that deterrence is being rethought in light of the war.”

Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera that a “broadly rational defensive reason” for potentially shifting Iran’s nuclear policy is emerging within the country, though adding that such a shift would be legally and ethically problematic.



“If you look at the sort of traditional nuclear logic, it says that nuclear weapons play a very strong defensive role in deterring the actions of another state,” Mabon told Al Jazeera. “That would be very sound logic for the Iranians in light of what’s happened.”

“This, of course, is something that’s deeply problematic,” said Mabon. “It goes against the terms of the NPT, it goes against the spirit of the NPT, so it would necessitate withdrawal from that.”

CMEG director Fathollah-Nejad said that there are serious divisions within Iran’s government over the direction of its nuclear programme.

Hardline lawmakers and religious leaders view Iran’s nuclear and missile assets as “indispensable” to “regime security and deterrence”, while a separate camp that includes former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif argues against the development of nuclear arms, saying it would “almost inevitably” trigger further attacks by the US and Israel, said Fathollah-Nejad.

For now, he added, Iran “plays with the ambiguity” of its nuclear policy.

What does this mean for US-Iran negotiations?

Fathollah-Nejad said a shift in Iran’s nuclear doctrine would directly counter the US’s “single most important goal” in the conflict: to secure nuclear concessions from Tehran.

The US has insisted Iran must make nuclear commitments at the outset of any negotiations, while Iran wants its own seven stated conditions met, including lifting the blockade, restoring access to its frozen assets and ending hostilities on all fronts, before even beginning discussions about its nuclear programme.

Mabon said a change in Iran’s nuclear policy “would have a dramatic impact on how the Americans and the Israelis read the next phase of this conflict”, with the Israelis likely believing it necessitates a “return to violence”.

“That’s where some of the other dangers start to come in,” Mabon added. “The shift in Iran’s doctrine, even if it’s meant intentionally as a defensive shift, can easily be read in offensive terms.”

“I think it’s a very, very dangerous moment,” he said.

World.title: Jerusalem Daily: Gaza faces deadly strikes and health crisis
World.content:
NewsFeed Jerusalem Daily: Gaza faces deadly strikes and health crisis

Israeli strikes kill at least three Palestinians in Gaza, where displaced families face worsening conditions. An Israeli settler calls for settlements to be built in Gaza. And in the occupied West Bank, raids and attacks continue, while Netanyahu faces a political challenge over plans to form a new government. Al Jazeera’s Reem Takieddine has more.

World.title: Chaudhary helps Australia beat England in T20 shake-off of scandal-hit run
World.content:
Australia beat England by three wickets with only one ball to spare as Nikhil Chaudhary’s 66 leads the charge in Melbourne.

Nikhil Chaudhary blasted 66 and a late cameo from Jack Edwards helped Australia edge past England by three wickets with a ball to spare in the opening T20 International of the series.

Chaudhary’s 38-ball knock was crucial, but it was Edwards’ late flurry that got the job done, with the fast-bowler hitting an unbeaten 25 off 11 as they chased down a victory target of 188 on Saturday.

It ensured they took a 1-0 lead in the five-match series and temporarily lifted some of the clouds hanging over Australian cricket. Four of the country’s previous five matches have resulted in defeats, including a 2-1 One-Day International home series defeat by England.

The win also came on the day that Cricket Australia backed Pat Cummins to stay on as Test captain, despite continued allegations that he and the rest of the 2018 team were aware of the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball during their tour of South Africa.

England captain Harry Brook’s quickfire 65 had guided the visitors to 187-9 – the highest T20I score at the Melbourne Cricket Ground – but Australia’s response had already begun prior to the chase when their bowlers restricted the end of the tourists’ innings that had looked set to comfortably pass 200.

“Right, there is the future of the Australian cricket side with those young guys in it,” said Australia captain Mitchell Marsh.

“They’re a great bunch. Hopefully a win like that gives them a lot of confidence that they all belong.”

The run chase started badly for Australia with opener Jake Fraser-McGurk falling to just his third ball, undone by the spin of Liam Dawson.



Australia got going when debutant Sam Harper came in and took 20 off Jamie Overton’s first over.

But the 29-year-old swung the bat once too often and departed for 32 off 15 balls, earning new England fast-bowler Henry Crocombe a first T20 wicket.

They were 86-2 at the halfway mark, and when Dawson took a stunning catch to remove Marsh for 37, Australia’s hopes appeared to rest with Tim David.

But the big-hitter struggled to get going and was out for 20, leaving Chaudhary, in only his fourth T20 for Australia, in charge.

He departed chasing another boundary, only for Edwards to step up.

They needed 11 of the last over from Sam Curran, and when Edwards smacked a six off the first delivery, they were on their way to the win.

“Very entertaining to go down to the last couple of balls,” said Brook. “We were probably 10 runs short of what we needed on that surface.”

Earlier, England lost opener Phil Salt to the first ball and they were 13-2 in the third over after Aneurin Donald was also removed cheaply for 10.

But Brook went to town, smacking three straight sixes from paceman Riley Meredith.

He reached 50 off 20 deliveries before his fiery knock ended when he got a faint outside edge off Chaudhary to wicketkeeper Harper.

Tom Banton was put down on 11, among six dropped catches by Australia, but his luck ran out on 39 when another debutant, Lachlan Shaw, held on to a difficult chance.

The wickets kept tumbling with Curran caught out on 21 and Will Jacks out lbw for three, with Jordan Cox hitting 27 to keep the scoreboard moving.

World.title: Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?
World.content:
Mathematicians say the claimed proof, made with Claude, could be historic, but it may take weeks to understand it.

A mathematician from the tech giant Anthropic claims to have proven one of the world’s most famous – and most elusive – maths problems with the help of AI.

Levent Alpoge wrote on his website on Friday: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”

If his claim holds up, the proof he says he has would settle a question that has defeated mathematicians for 167 years. Independent experts are now trying to verify it, but so far no human has read through the entire argument.

Here is what we know.

What is the Riemann hypothesis?

First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics.

Prime numbers are whole numbers which can be divided only by one and themselves, such as 2, 3, 5 and 7. They appear to be scattered along the number line with no obvious pattern but the Riemann hypothesis proposes that their overall distribution actually follows a deep, hidden order – just one that humans have yet to identify.

“The Riemann hypothesis is the most famous and important unsolved problem in mathematics,” Abhishek Saha, professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.

“The patterns of the primes are encoded in a mathematical object called the Riemann zeta function, introduced by Bernhard Riemann in 1859.”

It is one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1m award.



What has the Anthropic mathematician claimed?

Alpoge, a member of the company’s technical staff, made the announcement on Friday in a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said the proof he has found covers the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which extends the original conjecture to a broader family of mathematical functions.

He did not publish a conventional paper. Alpoge released the argument in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks reasoning step by step. He was open about how much of the work was Claude’s, writing that “Claude far outpaced me near the finish line”.

Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said nobody yet understands what the proof actually shows.

“At the minute, we don’t even know why the theorem is true,” he told Al Jazeera. “It’s 17 million lines of Lean code, and this might correspond to tens of thousands of pages of mathematics. We don’t even yet know how much of this mathematics is new ideas, how much of it is just sort of standard stuff the machine just had to develop.

“At the minute, the proof is just millions of lines of gobbledygook written in a strange programming language,” he said. “And right now, as we speak, there’s people all over the world who are translating parts of this programming language back into English.”

He expects answers to come fairly soon, however. “Experience shows you that you give the humans the Lean code, and within a week or two, they have a much better understanding of what’s actually going on in this code,” he said.

Why is the Riemann hypothesis so important?

“The implications of this hypothesis extend across large parts of mathematics, and hundreds of other mathematical results have been proved assuming this hypothesis is true,” Saha said. “A proof would settle a question that has occupied some of the greatest mathematical minds for over 160 years.”

Buzzard said the result also matters beyond pure mathematics, including for internet security.

“We know there are some algorithms that we run where they’re very quick, but we don’t actually know for sure if they work,” he said. “They seem to work, and we know that if the generalised Riemann hypothesis is true, then they do work.”

He said cryptographers had long worked on the assumption that the Riemann hypothesis is true. “In practice, people do tend to assume that the Riemann hypothesis is true because it’s a viable hypothesis to assume, because there’s so much evidence that it’s true,” he said. “But we can sleep slightly safer in our beds at night because it is true.”



Buzzard said the result stands out among recent AI breakthroughs in mathematics. He compared it with the Navier-Stokes problem, another Millennium Prize problem, which OpenAI said an unreleased AI model had solved in September. “That one doesn’t really have any applications at all,” he said, calling it “just of theoretical interest”. “Whereas the Riemann hypothesis has applications to neighbouring fields.

“It’s a very hard problem, but it’s definitely not the hardest problem in mathematics,” he said, pointing to even stronger versions such as the “extended Riemann hypothesis and the grand Riemann hypothesis”.

“The Riemann hypothesis is just, in some sense, at the foot of a mountain,” he said. “We’re beginning our trek up the mountain with this theorem.”

Why has it remained so elusive for so long?

“The problem is relatively simple to state, but extraordinarily difficult to prove,” Saha said. “Mathematicians have developed vast amounts of sophisticated theory in their attempts to solve it, but none of the techniques developed over the past 167 years has been sufficient. The direct methods have all been tried, and none of them come close to resolving it.

“Until very recently, most mathematicians, myself included, believed that a proof would require substantial new mathematical theories, perhaps developed over the next few decades.”

He said the claimed proof had overturned his expectations. “My own intuition was that we were still several years away from a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. This claimed proof, if correct, shatters my model of reality,” he said.

“If difficult problems are like valuable mineral reserves buried miles underground, you first need to build the infrastructure to reach them. What this proof seems to have done is something completely different. It takes an incredibly complicated tour through the infrastructure built to reach a hundred other mineral reserves, situated far from the original destination, and somehow creates a wormhole to that destination.”

Buzzard said it is still too early to know what humans had been missing. “There is a chance that there were no ideas that the humans were missing. There is a chance that all of the ingredients were there, that nobody had just been smart enough to put everything together,” he said. “There is a chance that there’s a thousand pages of new ideas, very deep new theories.”

“Right now, we honestly can’t tell you, because nobody understands the proof of it. That will change. In a matter of weeks, that will change.”

What role is AI playing in solving major mathematical problems?

The past year has been one of AI-driven advances in mathematics. An earlier AI-assisted result showed that at least 67.25 percent of a particular set of mathematical values follow the pattern predicted by the Riemann hypothesis. The new claim, if correct, would extend this to all of them.

“AI is creating a revolution in mathematics,” Saha said. “It is helping us solve problems previously thought out of reach and, in doing so, it will undoubtedly lead to the creation of new mathematics. However, this also means that the way mathematicians have traditionally conducted research will no longer be how it is done in the future.



“Asking the right questions, creating new research directions, writing good expositions, and acting as an effective director or conductor for AI will become increasingly important, while technical brilliance in constructing proofs may become less so.”

He argued that the credit should go to Alpoge. “Much of the press is referring to this as a proof by Claude. I think they should instead credit the person involved: Levent Alpoge,” he said. “Others with similar access to frontier AI models and computing resources were not able to come up with a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.

“This proof shows that a brilliant mathematician can direct and orchestrate AI in ways that allow them to prove theorems others cannot. The honour of proving RH, if the proof holds up, belongs largely to him. He should get a Fields Medal for this.” The Fields Medal is a prestigious mathematics prize awarded every four years by the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) to mathematicians under age 40.

Do we even need humans to do maths any more?

Buzzard rejected fears that AI has made human mathematicians redundant. “The rumours that maths is dead have been greatly exaggerated,” he said. “What’s actually happening is that mathematics has a very exciting and powerful brand new tool.”

“Mathematics is infinitely big. You can’t solve all of it,” he said. He compared AI with the telescope. “Historically, astronomers were just staring at the sky, right? And then the telescope was invented, and all of a sudden we can see everything much, much more clearly.

“The AI doesn’t have taste, not yet anyway. You tell it what to do, and it does it,” he said. “We’ve basically got our own telescope.”

Buzzard said AI was “beginning to democratise” mathematics, although for now the breakthroughs are concentrated in a few firms. “Currently, it is the tech companies with access to the new internal models who are doing the best breakthroughs right now, but this will change as more powerful models become available to the public and the tech companies lose interest.”

He said some of the unease among mathematicians is about loss. “They are grieving because the field is changing rapidly, and with change comes loss. We will do mathematics in new ways going forward, and some people will miss the old ways,” he said.

“The other reason people are upset is that it has hurt a lot of people’s egos. Humans were the best at mathematics, and the best humans would prove theorems, and the theorems would be named after them.”

World.title: Rescue efforts under way as drones hit Russian ship off Finland coast
World.content:
Two drones attack a cargo ship that Finnish authorities say has links to Russia’s armed forces.

Share Rescue efforts under way as drones hit Russian ship off Finland coast on social media

Rescue efforts are under way in the Gulf of Finland after a Russian cargo ship was hit by drones close to Russia’s maritime border.

The ship, the Sparta II, is on fire and has now drifted into Finnish territorial waters, authorities say.

Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with the vessel sustaining damage, and dispatched Finnish Border Guard units to the scene.

A photograph taken by a Border Guard patrol plane shows flames and thick smoke coming from the rear of the ship.

The attack happened west of Gogland Island on Saturday morning, with Finland temporarily instating air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.

Finland’s Border Guard said the vessel is known to have links to the Russian armed forces.

According to the Border Guard, the crew of the Sparta II have not been forced to abandon ship, and there has been no environmental damage so far from the drone attack, while the vessel is in the open sea off the southern coastal town of Loviisa.

“The Border Guard is preparing to evacuate people and assist in firefighting operations,” Finnish authorities said.

It is not clear who was behind the attack, but Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X that “war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity. The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”



Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, said the damage had yet to be fully assessed.

“Three nautical miles from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max.

Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.

The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members. It connects Russia’s former capital of Saint Petersburg with its Kaliningrad enclave by sea.

Finland’s Ministry of Defence said air and sea traffic restrictions had been put in place as a precaution in case further drones needed to be intercepted, adding that Finland had notified its allies of the incident.

Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.

Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki said it had raised concerns with Kyiv about striking in the area afterwards.

World.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

World.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
World.content:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

World.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
World.content:
Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.

For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.

The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.

The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.

Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."

But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.

He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas, external.

The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.

Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.

World.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
World.content:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC contacted the FBI for comment.

This comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.

It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.

In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .

Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.

The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

World.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
World.content:
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.

Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.

Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.

World.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
World.content:
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

All were told they could never serve in the police again.

The case became a cause cÃ©lÃ¨bre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

The case was heard by a panel of five judges.

The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

World.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
World.content:
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.

Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attachÃ© will now be expelled.

Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".

Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.

"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."

The rapper's real name is Albert Vasiliev.

PET said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.

PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.

Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.

Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars LÃ¸kke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.

Russia's defence attachÃ© must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Copenhagen was already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians could still get a Schengen visa in another country and travel to Denmark.

Copenhagen wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

World.title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
World.content:
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.

One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.

Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.

Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.

Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".

"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."

Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.

They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.

They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.

The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

World.title: Umuahia Renewal: Abia to create new access road to link Okpara Square to Bende Road
World.content:
In line with Governor Alex Otti’s directive, the Abia State Government is creating a new access road to link Okpara Square to Bende Road.

With this, motorists and other road users will no longer need to pass through Library Avenue, FMC and Umudike junctions before accessing Bende Road.

With this development, traffic will also be drastically reduced around the FMC and Umudike junctions.

Ferdinand Ekeoma, the special adviser on media and publicity to Governor Otti, disclosed this in a statement issued on Saturday.

The project is being driven by the Umuahia Capital Development Authority (UCDA), under its General Manager, Kingsley Agomuo, in line with the governor’s directive for the transformation of the capital city.

The route is a link road from Bende Road Junction by Post Office Tower, through the railway crossing, to the First Bank / Akanu Ibiam Road (Goodshed) axis, linking Okpara Square to Bende Road.

On 26 August, the Abia State Government signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Nigerian Railway Corporation to construct the access road across the railway corridor.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The road is part of a comprehensive plan to integrate the Umuahia railway station and bus terminal into a major transportation hub, and to give the state capital a facelift.

The state government will also reconstruct the abandoned road linking First Bank to the Keystone, Sterling and FCMB bank areas, giving motorists an alternative, shorter route without passing through the Government House axis.

Governor Otti directed the UCDA to relocate the existing police station within the railway corridor to a temporary space and to come up with the design of a new railway station with a police station, to be shared with the NRC.

“Never again will Abia be mocked in the comity of states for underdevelopment,” Mr Ekeoma said in the statement.

“We are not there yet, but the vision and determination to get to our destination remain alive.”

World.title: EFCC arraigns man for alleged N7.8m land fraud
World.content:
The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) has arraigned one Sani Ahmed before Justice Dorcas Agishi of the Federal High Court in Jos, Plateau State.

Mr Ahmed was arraigned by the Gombe Zonal Directorate of the EFCC on 19 November on a two-count charge of obtaining by false pretence.

Count one of the charge reads: That you Sani Ahmed and Nasiru Labaran ( at large) sometimes in 2025 at Jos, Plateau State within the jurisdiction of this honourable court did agree to commit an offence to wit: obtaining money from one Mr. Umar Abdullahi by false Pretence via your bank Account nos:0010633291 domiciled with Taj Bank and 3210446768 domiciled with First Bank of Nigeria and thereby committed an offence contrary to Section 8(a) and punishable under Section 1(3) of the Advance Fee Fraud( and other Fraud Related Offences ) Act 2006.

Count two reads: That you Sani Ahmed sometimes between May and June 2025 at Jos, Plateau State within the jurisdiction of this honourable court did fraudulently obtained the total sum of N7,850,000 from Mr.Umar Abdullahi via your bank Account numbers: 0010633291 domiciled with Taj bank and 3210446768 domiciled with First Bank of Nigeria under the pretence that the said sum was for investment into land in Abuja, purportedly owned by your boss Nasiru Labaran (currently at large), which you knew to be false thereby committed an offence contrary to Section 1(1)(a) and punishable under Section 1(3) of the Advance Fee Fraud( and Other Related Offences) Act 2006.

ALSO READ : EFCC returns recovered N125 million to Lagos land fraud victim

He pleaded not guilty to the charges when they were read to him, prompting the prosecution counsel. M.D.Aliyu, to ask the court for a trial date and to remand the defendant in a Correctional Centre.

However, counsel to the defendant, PN Washpam, moved a motion for bail, urging the court to use its discretion and grant the bail request.

Justice Agishi, having listened to both counsel, adjourned the case to 3 December 3 for hearing of bail application and ordered that the defendant be remanded at Jos Correctional Centre, Plateau State.

World.title: A gathering for peace that began with a funeral
World.content:
Sheikh Yahaya Masussuka was supposed to begin a 20-minute address at Muhammadu Dikko Stadium in Katsina at 11.50 a.m. on Saturday, 31 October.

His name was still on the printed programme. So was the Peace Ambassador title he was scheduled to receive.

Five days earlier, gunmen had killed him outside his residence in Dutsin-Ma.

The people he invited turned up anyway.

Among them were Christian leaders, Muslim scholars who disagreed with some of his teachings, former Sports Minister Solomon Dalung and followers who had travelled to Katsina for his burial.

Whenever Masussuka’s name was mentioned, sections of the crowd responded with loud cheers and words of praise. Participants remained under the sun as the programme continued.

They had come to pray for peace, security and violence-free elections in Nigeria. The man who brought them together was no longer alive to address them.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The gathering brought together religious figures who had disagreed over Masussuka’s teachings. Their appeals for tolerance and justice came five days after his killing, with police yet to publicly identify the attackers or announce investigative findings. The event also reflected its organisers’ wider concern about peaceful coexistence ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 elections.

From the burial ground to the stadium

On Friday, 30 October, large crowds of mourners converged on the area around Muhammadu Dikko Central Mosque, near the Emir of Katsina’s palace, for Mr Masussuka’s funeral.

When PREMIUM TIMES visited, mourners filled the space outside the mosque and occupied the roads extending past the palace into surrounding streets.

The funeral took place four days after Masussuka was killed in Dutsin-Ma. The Federal Teaching Hospital, Katsina, had confirmed to PREMIUM TIMES on 29 October that his remains had been embalmed but that no post-mortem examination had been conducted at that point.

As his remains were taken to Abatuwa Cemetery for burial, mourners chanted in Hausa words meaning, “Masussuka is not dead, his virtues are still alive; shame on his enemies.”

Cries of “Allahu Akbar” (God is greatest) rang through the procession. Some mourners wept openly, while others reached towards the ambulance carrying his remains.

Islamic scholars, traditional leaders and followers who had travelled from outside Katsina joined the mourning. Some later proceeded to Muhammadu Dikko Stadium, where prayers and religious ministrations continued through Friday night.

The formal Unity Assembly for Peace followed on Saturday. The programme, prepared before the assassination, listed representatives of different Muslim traditions and Christian denominations. Its stated purpose was to promote national unity, peace, security and violence-free elections.

For Apostle Golu Jan Silas, a Christian cleric from Barkin Ladi in Plateau State, the funeral marked a personal first.

“Yesterday, I entered a mosque for the first time,” he told participants.

Mr Silas recalled a 2025 visit by Masussuka to his predominantly Christian community in Plateau State, where he said the Islamic cleric preached peaceful coexistence and distributed gifts.

“They killed him, but his messages are alive,” the apostle said.

Gunfire outside his home

On Monday, 26 October, Masussuka and his associate, Suleiman Abubakar, went on a condolence visit following a death in the family. Later that evening, Mr Abubakar returned to drive the cleric to his studio.

Mr Abubakar said he arrived after 8.30 p.m. and unlocked the car for Mr Masussuka.

“I pressed the button to unlock the car so he could open the door and enter. Suddenly, I heard gunfire.”

He took cover in an unfinished building as the shooting continued. Mr Masussuka and his companion, Adamu Abubakar, were shot. They were taken to Dutsin-Ma General Hospital, where they were pronounced dead.

The Katsina State Police Command announced an investigation, saying two armed men on a motorcycle carried out the shooting. President Bola Tinubu and Governor Dikko Radda condemned the killing and called for those responsible to be brought to justice.

Ansaru claimed responsibility in a video obtained by PREMIUM TIMES and repeated the claim in another video reported on 3 November. Neither video independently establishes the identity of the attackers, and the police have not publicly confirmed the group’s involvement.

Mr Masussuka had complained of threats. Mr Abubakar said such statements were reported to the authorities whenever the cleric’s circle became aware of them.

“Whenever we hear any statement that poses a threat, we go and inform the authorities. We don’t remain silent,” he said.

“We don’t suspect anyone. Even if someone says they will do something, that does not mean they actually did it.”

The available reporting does not establish what action investigators took over the earlier threats, whether a post-mortem was subsequently performed or what forensic evidence, if any, has been obtained.

The dispute over his teachings

Mr Masussuka emphasised the Qur’an in his preaching and questioned certain Hadith narrations.

His associates said he rejected narrations he considered inconsistent with the Qur’an, disrespectful to the Prophet Muhammad or supportive of extremism.

His teachings drew criticism, including allegations that he rejected Hadith altogether. His associates disputed that characterisation, saying he questioned particular narrations rather than every tradition attributed to the Prophet.

In November 2025, the Katsina State Government intervened after receiving complaints that his teachings contravened Islamic principles. It also acknowledged a separate complaint from the cleric, who alleged that people he identified as members of Jama’atu Izalatil Bid’ah Wa Iqamatus Sunnah (JIBWIS) had insulted him and threatened to attack him.

According to a statement by the Secretary to the State Government, Abdullahi Faskari, both sides were invited for discussions before the Katsina Emirate Council. Governor Radda subsequently directed Mr Masussuka to prepare to defend his teachings before a committee of Islamic scholars. PREMIUM TIMES has not established whether the committee met.

The disagreement continued into 2026. In a legal notice dated 15 June, lawyers for JIBWIS’s Katsina branch demanded that he withdraw statements they considered offensive to prominent Hadith collections and Islamic scholars, apologise and remove specified recordings.

They warned that legal action could follow if he failed to comply within 14 days. The notice did not threaten physical violence.

Mr Masussuka later responded in a video, offering to withdraw provocative remarks if his critics did the same.

No evidence has established a link between the religious dispute and his killing.

Those who disagreed still came

At Muhammadu Dikko Stadium, those differences were acknowledged openly.

Sheikh Nuru Khalid acknowledged that he had disagreed with Mr Masussuka’s interpretations.

“I disagreed with Malam Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka on certain perspectives of his, but I loved him for the sake of peace,” he said.

The official programme identified Mr Khalid under the Ahlussunnah JIBWIS tradition. He called for those responsible for the killing to be brought to justice and warned against retaliation.

Mannir Koza, another Islamic scholar, said he had opposed demands for Masussuka’s arrest over his preaching. He also said he had personally appealed to Governor Radda to allow the cleric to continue teaching while other scholars challenged his interpretations through debate.

“Let him preach, let us preach, and let the arguments be examined,” he said, recalling his appeal.

PREMIUM TIMES could not independently confirm the reported conversation with the governor.

“We can disagree with someone in our understanding, but we must live in peace,” Dr Koza told the gathering.

Other speakers returned to the need for religious tolerance. Sheikh Ibrahim Lamido of Kaduna drew on Qur’anic teachings about the creation of different peoples and communities. He asked whether God had made a mistake by creating people with different identities.

“No!” the crowd answered.

Sheikh Yaqub Yahya Katsina criticised the description of Christians as pagans, noting that Islamic teaching recognised them as People of the Book. He also urged Muslims from different schools of thought to tolerate one another and leave ultimate religious judgement to God.

Abubakar Surumbay, speaking for the religious circle of Sheikh Dahiru Bauchi, said Muslims and Christians needed to coexist for Nigeria to prosper.

The Emir of Katsina, Abdulmumini Kabir Usman, was represented by the Sarkin Fadan Katsina, Abdulƙadir Isma’ila Damale, who conveyed condolences and support for peaceful coexistence as Nigeria approached the 2027 elections.

Former Sports Minister Solomon Dalung described Masussuka as his confidant, friend and brother. He said the organisers originally intended to hold the gathering in Jos, Plateau State, but moved it to Katsina because of insecurity.

Mr Dalung said Mr Masussuka had faced insults and accusations of unbelief because of his teachings, but that he had never heard the cleric respond with similar hostility.

“Whatever wrong has been done to you, forgive them,” he urged the cleric’s followers.

Imam Abdurrashid Kano, also known as Abdurrashid Ghana, addressed participants on Mr Masussuka’s behalf. The printed programme identified him as Rasheed Kano, while he was introduced at the gathering as vice-chairman of the Qur’anic Believers Harmony for Peace Initiative.

Mr Abdurrashid said Mr Masussuka had invited representatives of different Muslim traditions, including Tijaniyya and Qadiriyya adherents, Shiites, Qur’an-centred Muslims and Sunni scholars, alongside Christian religious leaders.

“Where did you get the authority to force someone to follow your interpretation, or kill them if they refuse?” he asked.

He urged followers to remain calm while the authorities investigated.

“No violence, no insults, no abusive language,” he said. “Let us give the authorities the opportunity to do their duty.”

The honour, and the man chosen to succeed him

Mr Masussuka was scheduled to receive a Peace Ambassador title at the gathering. Following his death, Ambassador Zaharaddin Sani Amy, chairman of the Northern Peace Foundation, led a ceremony to affirm the honour posthumously.

The cleric’s eldest son, Yusuf Masussuka, was designated to receive the certificate on behalf of his father and the family.

Mr Amy recalled that the foundation had organised a programme in Kebbi State around the same period in 2025, sponsored by Mr Masussuka. He appealed for support for the cleric’s family and announced a further certificate recognising his lifetime contributions to peace. The foundation also named Abdurrashid a Peace Ambassador to represent it.

A separate announcement concerned the leadership of Mr Masussuka’s own initiative. Aliyu Yusuf, chairman of the Qur’anic Believers Harmony for Peace Initiative, named Mr Abdurrashid as Mr Masussuka’s successor in leadership and religious instruction, under Sheikh Muhammad Dan Gungun of Kaduna.

“Today, Sheikh Imam Rashid Ghana stands in the position of Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka,” Mr Yusuf declared.

Mr Masussuka’s name remained on the programme as host.

The organisers had reserved 20 minutes for his address, beginning at 11.50 a.m.

He never lived to deliver it.

World.title: COP31: Nigerian, global groups accuse presidencies of risking ‘disappointing’ climate deal
World.content:
A coalition of 100 civil society organisations, including three Nigerian groups, has accused the COP31 presidencies of failing to demonstrate the leadership needed to secure an ambitious climate agreement, warning that the summit could become one of the most disappointing in the history of global climate negotiations.

In an open letter dated 20 November and addressed to COP31 President Murat Kurum and President of Negotiations Chris Bowen, the organisations said the draft outcome of the conference risked undermining efforts to tackle the climate crisis, particularly by excluding explicit commitments on transitioning away from fossil fuels.

The Nigerian organisations listed among the signatories are Environmental Rights Action, Health of Mother Earth Foundation (HOMEF) and Parents for Future Nigeria.

The coalition said the joint leadership of Türkiye and Australia failed to provide sufficient direction during negotiations, allowing disagreements over climate finance, adaptation and the transition away from fossil fuels to weaken the expected outcome.

The letter was issued as negotiations in Antalya extended beyond their scheduled 20 November conclusion, with countries still struggling to reach consensus on key elements of the final agreement.

Disagreement over fossil fuels, finance

A major concern raised by the organisations is the removal of explicit references to fossil fuels from the revised draft cover decision.

An earlier version of the text contained two formulations on transitioning away from fossil fuels, including language calling for accelerated action to phase them out. However, the references were removed in the subsequent draft released on 19 November.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The revised text retained provisions promoting carbon capture and carbon dioxide removal technologies, prompting concerns among environmental groups that the agreement could create room for continued fossil fuel production rather than prioritising emissions reductions.

The signatories described the draft as a gift to the fossil fuel industry, arguing that coal, oil and gas, the major drivers of the climate crisis, were no longer adequately addressed.

They also criticised the treatment of the proposed global electrification target, which seeks to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035.

Although the target remains in the revised text, the organisations argued that it must be explicitly linked to renewable energy and the transition away from fossil fuels.

Without such safeguards, they warned, increased electricity consumption could still be powered by fossil fuels, leaving countries dependent on the energy sources responsible for worsening global warming.

The groups also questioned the prominence given to carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), calling for the removal of a quantified target for the technology from the draft agreement.

Developing countries face climate finance uncertainty

Beyond energy commitments, the organisations expressed concern over the weakening of provisions on climate finance, particularly funding for adaptation in developing countries.

The earlier draft included a proposed target of at least $120 billion annually in adaptation finance. However, the figure was removed from the revised text, leaving uncertainty over how the commitment to increase adaptation funding would be delivered.

The coalition accused developed countries of arriving at the negotiations without new financial commitments, arguing that the failure to provide adequate funding would leave vulnerable communities exposed to worsening climate impacts.

It called for an accountability mechanism for public climate finance obligations, including a delivery plan for the proposed $120 billion adaptation funding target.

The organisations also urged the presidencies to restore provisions recognising the distinct and collective rights of Indigenous Peoples, including their right to self-determination, free, prior and informed consent, and secure land tenure.

They further called for the final agreement to acknowledge the International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion on states’ obligations in addressing climate change, alongside a relevant United Nations General Assembly resolution.

Pressure mounts on COP31 leadership

The letter adds to mounting criticism of the negotiations, particularly following the removal of fossil fuel language from the draft agreement.

The disagreement reflects a wider divide between countries pushing for stronger commitments to move away from fossil fuels and those concerned about the economic and financial implications of such a transition.

The COP31 presidencies have defended the revised text, arguing that the negotiations must focus on securing an agreement that countries can collectively support rather than repeatedly restating existing commitments.

READ ALSO: COP31 climate talks spill into overtime as nations quarrel over fossil fuels

However, the signatories said the presidencies must use their remaining time to restore stronger provisions on climate finance, electrification, Indigenous rights and the transition away from fossil fuels.

They also urged Türkiye and Australia to work with Brazil’s COP30 presidency and Ethiopia, which will host COP32, to advance the roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels through a presidency-led dialogue outside the formal consensus process.

The organisations warned that without decisive action, Ethiopia could inherit unresolved disagreements and the responsibility of advancing commitments that COP31 had failed to secure.

The letter concluded by reminding the two presidencies that they had voluntarily taken on the responsibility of leading the negotiations and still had an opportunity to prevent the summit from ending without meaningful progress.

World.title: Akwa Ibom teenagers lured into online sextortion traps, official reveals
World.content:
Akwa Ibom State has recorded 340 cases of gender-based violence (GBV) in 2026, including 129 cases of threats to life and physical assault, 87 incidents of spousal battery and 56 rape cases.

The figures, disclosed by the Secretary of the Akwa Ibom State Gender-Based Violence Management Committee, Emem Ette, highlight the continuing challenge of preventing abuse despite years of government interventions, public campaigns and promises to prosecute perpetrators.

Ms Ette, a lawyer, presented the figures on Monday during a courtesy visit by members of the committee to the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Akwa Ibom State Council, at the Press Centre in Uyo. The visit was live-streamed on Facebook.

The breakdown shows that threats to life and physical assault account for 37.9 per cent of the reported cases, while spousal battery represents 25.6 per cent and rape accounts for 16.5 per cent.

Other reported incidents include 25 cases of child abandonment (7.4 per cent), 24 cases of emotional abuse (7.1 per cent), 12 cases of forceful ejection from homes (3.5 per cent) and seven cases of harmful widowhood practices (2.1 per cent).

A persistent pattern of abuse

The latest figures come against the background of earlier reports of widespread abuse in the state.

In November 2023, PREMIUM TIMES reported that Akwa Ibom recorded 321 GBV cases between January and 24 November that year, including 120 rape cases and 170 incidents of spousal battery.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The 2026 figure of 340 represents a 5.9 per cent increase over the 321 recorded in 2023.

The figures also show that rape remains a significant concern, although the 2026 report lists 56 cases compared with 120 reported in 2023.

In February 2025, Helen Obareki, coordinator of the Office of the First Lady, warned that the government would go after the perpetrators of GBV. At the time, Ms Ette disclosed that the committee had handled more than 1,410 GBV cases, predominantly involving intimate partner abuse.

These figures suggest that the problem extends beyond isolated incidents and requires sustained prevention, reporting mechanisms and effective prosecution.

Sextortion emerges as another concern

Ms Ette identified technology-facilitated abuse, particularly sextortion involving teenage girls, as an emerging threat.

She said some victims, mostly between 13 and 19 years old, were allegedly lured into sexual activities before their intimate photographs and videos were used to blackmail them for money.

She attributed the reluctance of some victims to report abuse to stigma, victim-blaming, fear of retaliation, and financial dependence.

She also identified domestic and intimate partner violence, sexual harassment, exploitation, child marriage, female genital mutilation, harmful traditional practices and economic abuse among the forms of GBV requiring attention.

According to her, abuse thrives where society normalises violence, silences survivors and protects perpetrators through social acceptance.

She illustrated the problem with an account of a man who allegedly killed his wife, after which their children reportedly pleaded for their father’s release because their mother was already dead.

“When a crime is committed, it is not a crime against the person but against society and the state, and the state must exercise its powers to ensure that perpetrators are made accountable,” she said.

She urged the media to challenge interventions by influential individuals and community leaders seeking to secure the release of alleged perpetrators.

“NUJ should help us spread the news that Akwa Ibom has zero tolerance for people coming to beg for perpetrators.”

Support services and prevention efforts

The committee secretary said the state had established a 66-bed GBV shelter where survivors, including women and children displaced by abuse, could stay for up to three months.

She also identified sexual assault referral services at the General Hospital, Ikot Ekpene, Heartland Alliance Hospital, Uyo, and Agape Centre, Eket, covering the state’s three senatorial districts.

The committee, she said, had trained more than 350 people through its skills acquisition programme, including 15 participants who completed training the previous week.

It has also formed a coalition of more than 560 members, including over 80 non-governmental organisations, to support its interventions.

For the 2026 16 Days of Activism Against GBV, scheduled for 25 November to 10 December, 46 NGOs have submitted activities for implementation across the state.

“A three-day awareness fair will also be held at the Idongesit Nkanga Secretariat in Uyo, where survivors and skills acquisition beneficiaries will display their products alongside other vendors to protect their identities and prevent stigmatisation.”

Beyond campaigns and arrests

The committee’s engagement with the NUJ aimed at securing media collaboration for the global campaign.

Ms Ette said the committee comprised representatives of nine ministries, including information, health, education, and women affairs, alongside the police, NGOs and community leaders.

She said media participation was essential because public attitudes towards abuse were influenced by what people read, hear and see.
