World.title: South Africa: Former Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka Dies
World.content:
Cape Town — Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa's first woman deputy president and a former United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at 71, the South African government announced on Friday.

Acting President Paul Mashatile conveyed condolences on behalf of President Cyril Ramaphosa, who is in the U.S., and said further details would be shared in consultation with the family.

A former anti-apartheid activist and member of parliament (MP), Mlambo-Ngcuka was deputy president from 2005 to 2008. She also served as minister of minerals and energy and as deputy minister of trade and industry.

She was in the first generation of MPs in South Africa's democratic Parliament, and sat in the Constitutional Assembly, which helped draft the country's democratic Constitution. Her time as deputy president was under President Thabo Mbeki.



She later took on a prominent international role as UN Under-Secretary-General and Executive Director of UN Women, serving from August 2013 to August 2021.

"I have lost a sister and a comrade, and the world has lost a fearless feminist leader. Phumzile never let us forget that AIDS is not only a health crisis. It is a crisis of inequality, and the women and girls who carry its heaviest burden must be at the centre of the response. She brought the courage of a freedom fighter to the UNAIDS family. In South Africa, she brought government and communities together around a shared plan to respond to HIV. We will honour her by finishing the fight she gave so much of her life to: ending AIDS, and ending the injustices that drive it. Rest in power, dearest Sister Phumzile," said Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS.

Ramaphosa called her death a sad day for the country, and described her as a leader whose contribution went well beyond her years in government. The University of Johannesburg, where she had been chancellor since 2022, said her death was an immeasurable loss. The ANC called her a distinguished leader of the movement and a dedicated servant of the people. Parliament also paid tribute to her contribution to democracy, social justice and women's rights.

She is survived by her husband, Bulelani Ngcuka, and their five children.

World.title: Africa: WGS Dialogue for Latin America and the Caribbean Explores Stronger Cooperation in Shaping the Future
World.content:
10 heads of state and government and international organisations

His Excellency Luis Abinader, President of the Dominican Republic, expressed his country's appreciation for the commitment of His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of the UAE, and His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai, to investing in a long-term strategic relationship with the Dominican Republic. He reaffirmed his country's commitment to strengthening these relations and taking them to new heights.

He noted that hosting the World Governments Summit Dialogue for Latin America and the Caribbean reflects the two countries' shared vision and commitment to providing a platform that brings together governments, business leaders, international organisations and experts to open a new chapter in relations and intensify joint efforts to shape the future.

The President of the Dominican Republic said: "His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum put forward an idea that deserves to guide this Dialogue: what is the 'currency' of the future? Is it water? Artificial intelligence? Energy? His Highness offered an answer that carries a profound lesson: trust is the currency of the future."

His remarks came at the opening of the World Governments Summit Dialogue for Latin America and the Caribbean, held in Cap Cana, Dominican Republic, with the participation of 10 leaders of states, governments, and regional and international organisations, more than 70 speakers, representatives of over 30 countries, and 120 private-sector companies. Participants exchanged perspectives on the future of partnerships and international cooperation across 35 dialogue sessions and 15 leadership meetings. The programme covered six themes: geoeconomics and strategic investment; tourism, culture and experience economies; international cooperation and regional integration; foresight for the future of governments; logistics and global connectivity; and human capital and the future of work.

His Excellency Luis Abinader said: "We gather today with a shared conviction that the future is shaped by the decisions we make and the relationships we sustain. Last year, when we hosted this Dialogue, we affirmed the Dominican Republic's readiness to serve as a trusted bridge connecting Latin America and the Caribbean with the Middle East."

He added: "The Dominican Republic is committed to this initiative because it has succeeded in consolidating political, social and economic stability, and seeks to turn these achievements into new opportunities for its people. We also believe in dialogue as a means of strengthening relations and deepening connections. We look forward to building on these strengths to forge closer partnerships with the UAE, supported by a committed government, a private sector ready to invest, and organisations capable of sustaining and deepening dialogue and translating it into tangible results."

He explained that his country sees the future of relations between Latin America and the Caribbean and the Middle East in broader cooperation between businesses, stronger investment flows, knowledge exchange and deeper ties between communities. He noted that the UAE's experience demonstrates what can be achieved through long-term vision and hard work, stressing that its expertise in logistics, connectivity, tourism and innovation offers significant opportunities for cooperation.

His Excellency Luis Abinader said: "The importance of the World Governments Summit lies in its ability to bring together people who can learn from one another and work together. One government's experience can help improve services in another country. The Dominican Republic invests in this platform because it believes in the strength of these connections and is committed to this partnership for the long term."

Mohammed Al Gergawi: UAE leadership embraces a comprehensive vision for international cooperation

His Excellency Mohammad Abdullah Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs and Chairman of the World Governments Summit, affirmed that, under the guidance of its wise leadership, the UAE embraces a comprehensive vision for international cooperation, based on partnerships to shape the future, improve quality of life and ensure a better tomorrow for future generations.

World Governments Summit His Excellency Mohammad Abdullah Al Gergawi

His Excellency said that, since its launch last year, the World Governments Summit Dialogue for Latin America and the Caribbean has demonstrated the importance of making the future a shared goal for governments, organisations and businesses around the world. It has also highlighted the need to strengthen efforts to shape that future through dialogue, the exchange of knowledge and expertise, and broader cooperation, supporting governments and communities in their pursuit of a better future.

He added that the partnership linking the UAE and the World Governments Summit with the Government of the Dominican Republic reflects a shared understanding of future challenges and opportunities. It builds on a common commitment to creating and strengthening an ecosystem of new opportunities through cooperation and partnerships, advancing efforts to shape the future of vital sectors and taking cooperation to new heights. His Excellency noted that the true value of the Dialogue is measured by the pathways it opens for government action and the development challenges it helps address. He stressed that the ambition is for working teams to sustain their efforts throughout the year, with each edition providing a foundation for the next, accumulating knowledge and giving cooperation a deeper and more lasting impact.

Strong participation by leaders from the UAE, Latin America and the Caribbean

His Excellency Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan bin Mubarak Al Nahyan, Minister of State, headed the UAE delegation participating in the Dialogue. Heads of state and government and officials from Panama, Guyana, The Bahamas, the British Virgin Islands, Ecuador, El Salvador, Jamaica, Uruguay and Haiti also took part.

The programme also featured participation by the Organization of American States, UN Tourism, the Association of Caribbean States, the International Finance Corporation, and CAF – Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean.

Noura Al Kaabi: Dialogue reflects the UAE's approach to building bridges and strengthening global ties

In a keynote address, Her Excellency Noura bint Mohammed Al Kaabi, Minister of State, affirmed that the Dialogue reflects the UAE's approach to engaging with the world, based on building bridges, strengthening meaningful connections and sustaining them. She noted that this approach has guided the development of relations with countries across Latin America and the Caribbean, founded on trust, credibility and mutual respect, and strengthened through practical cooperation that delivers tangible results.

Her Excellency said that the two regions are meeting at a time when their partnerships matter more than ever, as supply chains are being reshaped and new trade routes are emerging. She highlighted four key areas for stronger cooperation: trade and investment, climate action, digital transformation and people-to-people connections.

She added: "Partnerships are not built through a single visit; they are strengthened through repeated visits, continuous follow-up and tangible results. Oceans may separate our regions, but our ambitions are shared. The UAE stands fully ready to open new horizons with you and work together to shape the future we all aspire to."

World Governments Summit: cooperation in shaping the future

In a keynote address during the Dialogue, Mohamed Yousuf Al Sharhan, Managing Director of the World Governments Summit Organization, explored the major questions about the future raised by the rapid development of artificial intelligence and its implications for work, the economy, society and governments. He emphasised the need to accelerate progress to keep pace with, and anticipate, future changes, including technological, demographic and environmental challenges.

Al Sharhan discussed the World Governments Summit ' s role in bringing together leaders from different sectors in a unified effort to address questions about the future, particularly the role of governments in anticipating change, strengthening readiness and building institutions capable of rapid adaptation, experimentation, learning and effective decision-making. He noted that the Summit embraces a vision of government that empowers people, equips them with skills and expertise, develops solutions to overcome challenges and strengthens collaboration across sectors. He stressed that, in an interconnected world, the ability to cooperate becomes a key enabler of government, and that the Dialogue for Latin America and the Caribbean embodies this vision.

World Governments Summit Luis Abinader delivering a sppech during the event

Presidential dialogue explores the new geography of opportunity

As part of the programme, His Excellency Luis Abinader, President of the Dominican Republic, and His Excellency José Raúl Mulino, President of the Republic of Panama, participated in a presidential dialogue entitled " Governments and the New Geography of Opportunity " . The discussion explored the role of technology, trade and investment in opening new economic corridors and strengthening the region ' s competitiveness.

During the session, His Excellency Luis Abinader discussed investment and growth in the Dominican Republic's tourism sector, saying: "We expect to welcome more than 12 million visitors, and there is still considerable room for further growth. We have expanded significantly in cruise tourism and intend to open a sixth cruise pier in Samaná. We are also developing sports tourism in Punta Cana."

His Excellency José Raúl Mulino highlighted Panama's progress in attracting investment and strengthening regional ties. He said: "Panama has decades of experience in free zones and is now launching an expansion project worth approximately US$400 million. We are also moving forward with airport concessions to support tourism development in the Farallón beach area in central Panama."

The future of tourism and culture

A panel discussion entitled " The Role of Governments in Shaping the Future of New Tourism Destinations " explored how governments can bring together connectivity, innovation and natural assets to create competitive tourism destinations and experiences. Participants included the Honourable Dr Natalio D. Wheatley, Premier of the British Virgin Islands; Her Excellency Shaikha Al Nowais, Secretary-General of UN Tourism; His Excellency Harris Whitbeck, Director-General of the Guatemalan Tourism Institute; and Elena Martínez, Co-Founder of SOS Biotech.

In a session entitled " Can Culture Become a Nation ' s Most Important Export? " , Garfield Kerr, CEO of speciality coffee company Mokha 1450, explored how linking a national crop such as coffee to a distinctive cultural identity can create new global economic opportunities.

Proactive government

A session entitled " Government Proactivity in Responding to Emergencies " examined the role of foresight, technology and partnerships in helping governments prepare for emergencies and strengthen readiness. Speakers included Simon de Montfort Walker, Executive Vice President of Industry Applications at Oracle, and Dr Saleh Fares Al Ali, former President of the International Federation for Emergency Medicine.

In a session entitled " Can Champions Win Twice? " , former American football player Frank Renaud; former baseball players Julian Infante and José Nicolás; former professional basketball player Gary Forbes; and New York Rise player Nicole Mendes explored the role of governments in enabling accomplished athletes to take on new roles and build future opportunities in other fields.

In a session entitled " The Next National Advantage: Rapid Learning " , global investor and entrepreneur Dr Faustino shared his vision for the role of governments in developing lifelong learning and turning it into a national advantage that strengthens the future readiness of individuals and institutions.

Zero bureaucracy

His Excellency Hisham Amiri, Deputy Chief of Government Services in the UAE Government, outlined the UAE ' s experience in eliminating bureaucracy during a discussion entitled " What a Zero-Bureaucracy Government Looks Like " .

Dev Torakhia, Founder of AI Tech, and Lasha Tabidze, Chief Operating Officer of VEON, discussed the significant potential and opportunities offered by artificial intelligence, and how to harness them to shape the future, in a session on AI ' s role in creating future opportunities.

World Governments Summit Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan and the President of the Dominican Republic attending the event

In a session entitled " When Governments Speak " , Edgar Rodríguez, Head of Public Policy for Latin America at TikTok; Ahmad Fayed, Co-Founder of Dose of Society; journalist and content creator Jeannette Reyes; and Fernanda Ramos, content creator at BioPlus, discussed how storytelling and trusted voices can strengthen communication between governments and people and encourage community participation in shaping the future.

New economic horizons

A session entitled " AI, Investment and New Economic Horizons " explored how artificial intelligence, connectivity and investment are shaping the future of the economy. Speakers included the Honourable Philip Davis, Prime Minister of the Commonwealth of The Bahamas; His Excellency José Ramón Icaza, Minister for Canal Affairs of the Republic of Panama; His Excellency Senator Jonathan Reid, Minister of Innovation, Industry, Science and Technology of Barbados; Her Excellency Noemí Espinoza Madrid, Secretary-General of the Association of Caribbean States; Sufyan Al Issa, Global Head of Business Development and Client Relationship Management at the International Finance Corporation; Juan Sabater, Partner and Co-President of Valor Equity Partners; Alonso Aznar, Founder and CEO of Zaria Capital; and René Grullón Finet, CEO of Grupo Popular.

A session entitled " 10 Trends Redefining the Governments of the Future " explored the major shifts set to reshape government leadership, services and opportunities over the next decade. Speakers included Juan José Daboub, Chairman of the HUGE Business and Investment Council; Jason Marczak, Vice President and Senior Director of the Atlantic Council ' s Adrienne Arsht Latin America Center; and Dr Carlos Díaz-Rosillo, Founding Director of the Adam Smith Center for Economic Freedom.

The future of aviation

A session entitled " The Future of Aviation " explored the future relationship between governments and airlines, examining how they can develop frameworks for cooperation and harness technology, infrastructure and investment to shape aviation ' s future and strengthen economic competitiveness. Speakers included Adrian Neuhauser, CEO of Abra Group; Juan José Salmón, CEO of Lima Airport Partners; and Arturo Barreira, CEO of Airbus in Latin America.

Her Excellency María José Pinto, Acting President of the Republic of Ecuador, and the Honourable Brigadier (Ret'd) Mark Phillips, Prime Minister of the Co-operative Republic of Guyana, participated in a session entitled "The Transformation of National Wealth". They discussed how governments can turn natural resources into diversified economic wealth and build higher-value industries to ensure prosperity for future generations.

The economy and communities

In a session entitled " What Does the Economy Mean for Communities? " , internationally renowned Emmy Award-winning artist Aloe Blacc discussed ways governments can translate economic growth into opportunities that improve communities ' quality of life.

In a dialogue entitled " More Than Just an Island " , the Honourable Dr Natalio D. Wheatley, Premier of the British Virgin Islands, and the Honourable Philip Davis, Prime Minister of the Commonwealth of The Bahamas, discussed how island states can build on their potential to strengthen resilience, create economic opportunities and increase their global impact.

In a session entitled "The Future of Governments", His Excellency José Ignacio Paliza, Minister of the Presidency of the Dominican Republic, discussed how national ambition, institutional integration and public-private cooperation can translate a future vision into measurable action.

A session entitled " How Technology Brings Islands Closer " explored the impact of emerging aviation and maritime technologies on connecting islands with the world and improving access to services, markets and economic opportunities. Adam Triolo, Vice President of Commercial Business Development at REGENT, spoke during the session.

World Governments Summit Noura Al Kaabi delivering her speech during the event

Regional cooperation

A dialogue entitled " Regional Cooperation and the Communities of Tomorrow " explored the role of partnerships, innovation and human potential in shaping the future of communities. Participants included His Excellency Everly Paul Chet Greene, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Immigration of Antigua and Barbuda; His Excellency Mohammad Alhawi, Undersecretary of the UAE Ministry of Investment; Can Cotterdom, President for Latin America and Canada at Philip Morris International; Sami Al Mufleh, CEO and Founder of Hills Advertising; Murad Osmann, Founder of FollowMeTo; Mikkel Thomassen Olesen, Founder and CEO of Runway Sports Group; and Luis Felipe de Oliveira, CEO of Exactly Consulting and Services.

A session entitled " New Investment Frontiers and Government Readiness " examined how governments can anticipate capital flows, attract investment and position their economies for growth. Participants included Jorge Subero, CEO of Cap Cana; Juan Carlos Sadala, Chief Planning and Projects Officer at DP World; Tim Kingston, Chairman and Head of Investment Banking for Latin America at Goldman Sachs; and Eduardo Coello, Regional President for Latin America and the Caribbean at Visa.

In a session entitled "Rethinking Government: Sustaining Reform", His Excellency Félix Ulloa, Vice President of the Republic of El Salvador, shared his perspectives on sustaining government reform across successive administrations and governments.

The future of the Global South

The dialogue sessions concluded with " New Bridges, New Influence: The Future of the Next Global South " , featuring Her Excellency Noura bint Mohammed Al Kaabi, Minister of State; His Excellency Víctor Bisonó, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic; and His Excellency Everly Paul Chet Greene, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Immigration of Antigua and Barbuda. The discussion explored the potential of Global South countries and their influence on the future of international relations and trade.

UN Tourism explores the role of air connectivity in strengthening competitiveness

As part of the World Governments Summit Dialogue for Latin America and the Caribbean, a high-level UN Tourism dialogue entitled " Air Connectivity in the Americas: A Key to Competitiveness and Regional Integration " explored how aviation policies and incentives can improve connectivity between markets and strengthen tourism competitiveness.

Five Majlis discussions explore government innovation and economic priorities

Five Majlis discussions, inspired by Emirati traditions of dialogue, addressed key topics including government innovation; global connectivity and economic competitiveness; talent, skills and the future workforce; national resources and future prosperity; and artificial intelligence and future horizons.

The discussions explored how international government experiences can inform improvements in services and institutional readiness; how transport, trade and digital connectivity can strengthen economic competitiveness; how to build the human capabilities needed for emerging industries; how to harness strategic resources for sustainable prosperity; and how to develop national AI capabilities and promote innovation founded on trust and accountability.

The Majlis moderators included Abeer Tahlak, Director of the Mohammed Bin Rashid Centre for Government Innovation; Tim Kingston, Chairman and Head of Investment Banking for Latin America at Goldman Sachs; Steven Bertoni of Forbes; Athan Stephanopoulos, Senior Adviser at Antenna Group; and Jason Marczak, Vice President and Senior Director of the Atlantic Council's Adrienne Arsht Latin America Center.

The 2025 World Governments Summit Dialogue for Latin America and the Caribbean brought together representatives from 22 countries, 29 speakers, and 59 companies and institutions. It also saw the World Governments Summit Organization and the Government of the Dominican Republic sign a memorandum of understanding to develop joint initiatives and establish a sustainable platform for cooperation between the UAE, Latin America and the Caribbean.

World.title: Africa: Africa's Solar Boom Shifts From Mega-Projects to Small-Scale Systems - IEA
World.content:
Nigeria, alongside Algeria, Kenya and Senegal, added more than one gigawatt of solar capacity each in 2025, highlighting the growing adoption of solar energy across African economies

Africa's solar energy boom is increasingly driven by small-scale installations as imports of photovoltaic (PV) equipment surge. Countries, including Nigeria, are expanding solar deployment to address persistent electricity shortages, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said.

The World Energy Outlook report, published by the IEA on Thursday, said solar PV imports to Africa have increased since 2017, with most of the increase coming from China, where imports have grown 28-fold.

The surge has contributed to an eightfold increase in installed solar capacity across the continent, reflecting growing adoption of solar energy as an alternative to conventional electricity sources.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

While utility-scale solar projects dominated Africa's solar market a decade ago, smaller installations are increasingly emerging as the main driver of growth, reflecting a shift toward decentralised energy systems as households, businesses, and industries seek alternatives to unreliable electricity supply.

Nigeria, alongside Algeria, Kenya and Senegal, added more than one gigawatt of solar capacity each in 2025, highlighting the growing adoption of solar energy across African economies.

The shift comes as solar imports continue to expand, with trade data indicating that Africa imported approximately 26 gigawatts (GW) of solar PV equipment in 2025 alone, compared with reported installations of about 10 GW.

Since 2020, imports of solar PV equipment from China to Africa have reached about 60 GW, while recorded installations across the continent have amounted to less than half that volume.

The IEA said the disparity raises questions about the pace of solar deployment, the accuracy of installation data and the extent to which imported equipment is being stockpiled, re-exported or deployed in installations missing from official statistics.

According to the agency, the gap between imported and recorded installed solar capacity stood at approximately 35 GW over the past five years.

It attributed the discrepancy partly to equipment remaining in inventories for extended periods, installations not being captured in official statistics and possible structural inconsistencies in trade and deployment data.

Around 15 per cent of solar imports are also solar cells rather than finished modules, some of which could be supplying Africa's emerging solar manufacturing industry.

Although solar module production capacity across Africa remained limited in 2025, Egypt and Ethiopia have since emerged as leading producers, while several other countries, including Nigeria, are pursuing ambitious plans to expand domestic manufacturing.

The rapid adoption of solar technology highlights the growing pressure climate activists are placing on world leaders at the ongoing climate talks in Turkey to phase out fossil fuels and transition to renewable energy equitably and justly.

Nigeria's emerging solar market

In recent years, households and businesses across Nigeria have increasingly adopted solar systems as an alternative energy source amid unreliable electricity supply and rising energy costs.

Repeated grid collapses, ageing infrastructure, metering gaps, gas supply shortages, mounting debts and estimated billing have undermined electricity delivery across the country, despite decades of investment in the sector.

The removal of the petrol subsidy in 2023 by President Bola Tinubu's administration further intensified the cost-of-living crisis, as petrol prices rose sharply, increasing the cost of running generators for households and businesses.

These pressures, alongside persistent electricity shortages, have strengthened the appeal of solar energy as consumers seek more reliable and affordable alternatives to grid electricity and petrol- and diesel-powered generators.

Nigeria's growing solar market reflects increasing efforts to reduce dependence on the national grid, particularly among households, businesses and industries grappling with unreliable electricity supply and rising energy costs.

The growing availability of imported solar panels and related equipment has helped expand access to alternative energy systems, while the country continues to explore opportunities to strengthen local manufacturing and supply chains.

The expansion of small-scale solar systems is also reshaping Africa's energy landscape, shifting growth beyond large utility-scale projects to distributed installations that serve consumers directly.

A decade ago, solar PV deployment was largely concentrated in utility-scale projects in relatively mature markets such as Egypt and South Africa.

Today, the market is increasingly driven by smaller installations, with Algeria, Kenya, Nigeria and Senegal each recording more than 1 GW in solar capacity additions in 2025.

The report noted that South Africa remains a major contributor to the continent's solar expansion, accounting for more than one-third of total capacity additions over the period examined.

As Nigeria's adoption of solar energy systems continues to grow amid unreliable electricity supply and rising petrol and diesel prices, energy experts have called for increased local manufacturing, affordable financing and stronger regulation to unlock the sector's economic potential.

Solar expansion outpaces official records

Despite the rapid growth in imports, questions remain about how much solar equipment is actually being deployed across Africa and how accurately governments capture the expansion in their energy statistics.

The IEA said newly developed tools combining satellite imagery and remote sensing have provided fresh evidence that a significant share of imported solar equipment is being deployed in utility-scale and distributed installations missing from official records.

Close 

Across Africa, the analysis identified more than 50 per cent more utility-scale solar capacity than governments had officially recorded.

However, even after accounting for the underreported installations detected through satellite imagery, the additional capacity remains insufficient to explain the volume of solar equipment imported, leaving a gap of nearly 30 GW.

The discrepancy suggests that Africa's solar market may be expanding faster than conventional energy statistics can capture, although the extent of equipment stockpiling, re-exportation and unrecorded deployment remains uncertain.

Outlook

In the IEA's Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), Africa's installed solar capacity is projected to increase sixfold over the next decade, signalling further expansion of the continent's solar market.

The growth is expected to build on an increasingly diverse range of projects, from utility-scale installations and industrial energy systems to smaller distributed solar systems serving households and businesses.

Beyond large-scale solar farms, the accelerating adoption of smaller systems could reshape how Africans access electricity, particularly in countries where grid reliability, affordability and access remain major challenges.

For Nigeria, the trend offers opportunities to expand energy access, reduce reliance on diesel-powered generation, strengthen domestic solar manufacturing, and accelerate the transition to a more reliable electricity supply.

World.title: Sudan: West Kordofan - Intensified Conflict and Deadly Oil Pollution
World.content:
For nearly a decade, civil society groups in the oil-rich areas of West Kordofan State have raised environmental and health concerns linked to the oil sector, where local communities say industrial chemicals and petroleum residues, including oil leakages, have triggered an ongoing health crisis.

The current conflict between the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has compounded the problem further, especially now that it is flaring up in West Kordofan State, these local groups told Ayin.

Since the war began, oil extraction facilities have been in the crosshairs of the warring parties. The destruction of pipelines, poor infrastructure maintenance, and lack of environmental oversight, local residents told Ayin, have only made conditions worse. "We have observed a severe deterioration in the situation since the war began," says one local civil society actor who has been documenting it. The source requested anonymity for security reasons. "There is no maintenance, and, in addition, there has been deliberate destruction, theft, and--in many areas--explosions at the oil wells," the source added. The civil society source, along with industry experts and aid workers, describe how weak safeguards in the oil extraction industries in West Kordofan used prior to the outbreak of the war in April 2023 have all but disappeared.

Oil pollution in wartime

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

From late October, the fight over oil-rich West Kordofan has intensified between the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). On November 5, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and allied groups launched a multi-pronged offensive from El-Obeid, marking their return to West Kordofan State after more than a year. Advancing southwest, the SAF coalition successfully recaptured the administrative hub of Al-Khuwai and its surrounding villages by November 13, ending an RSF occupation that had been in place since May 2025. The SAF and its allies are now continuing their westward push toward Al-Morkib and El-Nuhud, directly threatening major RSF strongholds in the region.

Despite the SAF's recent territorial gains in the northeastern section of the state, the RSF continue to control an estimated 85% to 90% of West Kordofan, including major strongholds and oil hubs like Al-Fula, Abu Zabad, Babanusa, Al-Muglad, and the Heglig complex. Earlier this month, the RSF announced plans to revive oil extraction operations in three sites within the state, potentially aggravating the pollution problem further. The RSF have dispatched a technical delegation to inspect the Neem, Defra and Kanar oilfields as part of preparations to restore production, according to local news reports.

According to one local civil society organisation, the areas of concern are the residential areas near the Heglig oil field, specifically the Al-Barzaya and Al-Zurga areas. "While the entire region is a source of deep concern for us, these areas (near the Heglig oil fields) are particularly worrying due to their high volume of oil flows, combined with the destruction of oil wells and pipelines," the civil society actor said.

Deteriorating health

According to the local civil society organisation, which continues to document and confirm cases of oil explosions at wells and ruptured pipelines, there is a correlation between oil pollution and deteriorating public health. "There has been a sharp rise in cases of foetal deformity; (we) have consistently noted that women from oil-producing regions have a high rate of giving birth to children with deformities," the civil society actor said. The same source told Ayin there are growing cases of infertility and forms of cancer that may also be linked to the pollution. The ongoing insecurity, however, has prevented the organisation from conducting definitive tests to see if there are direct links between the pollution and illness. "Often, these health issues are only diagnosed once individuals leave the oil-producing regions," the same source said. "We frequently hear that someone who went elsewhere to see a doctor has been diagnosed with cancer."

In other cases, residents have attempted to seal off damaged oil wells or repair ruptured pipelines and get injured in the process. "It is particularly concerning that the parties to the conflict - who should be responsible for these areas and their maintenance - show a lack of interest and focus on the matter."

A decade-long complaint

A local humanitarian worker told Ayin that local groups began investigating suspected environmental damage since 2016, focusing on problems associated with oil extraction and processing. During the rule of former president Omar al-Bashir, senior officials received their complaints, but the groups struggled to secure government support. The humanitarian actor attributed this difficulty partly to the influence of former oil minister Awad al-Jaz and the close relationship between the oil sector and the security institutions of the former regime.

Following the 2019 revolution, local activists protested outside the Ministry of Oil in July of the same year. The then oil minister, Adel Ali Ibrahim, received representatives of the communities, who called for an environmental assessment of the consequences of oil production. According to the source, the activists questioned whether Chinese oil companies operating in the region were adequately adhering to quality and environmental protection standards. A committee was formed and field surveys took place in 17 oil-processing sites, including Sharaf, Helaid and Baleela, the same source added.

The committee documented cases of congenital abnormalities, skin conditions, eye irritation among children, sexual health problems among men and infertility - all symptoms with suspected links to local oil production. The humanitarian actor said they identified more than 20 children with physical or congenital abnormalities and also reported cases of paralysis, blindness and eye inflammation.

The accounts raised serious questions about environmental exposure and public health in oil-producing areas but did not identify a direct correlation to the oil operations taking place. Testing that link would require medical examinations, environmental sampling and epidemiological evidence.

The oil industry's view

Industry insiders describe a different picture. An environmental quality-control expert with previous experience working at Sudanese oil refineries said the sector has an established system for environmental monitoring, reporting and remediation, although implementation varies between companies. The expert said oil operators are expected to monitor emissions against predetermined limits, report incidents to the relevant ministry and take corrective action when measurements exceed permitted thresholds. The Ministry of Oil's health, safety and environment department also conducts inspections, although these may be infrequent, the expert said.

The existence of monitoring procedures, however, does not establish that environmental standards are consistently met or that communities' complaints have been adequately addressed. Assessing how effectively the system operates would require access to monitoring results, inspection records, incident reports and remediation assessments.

The expert also warned against attributing miscarriages, infertility or cancer to oil operations without specialist evidence, arguing that unsupported claims could weaken the credibility of legitimate environmental concerns.

Mohamed Ibrahim, an oil supply chain and operations management expert who spoke to Ayin, identified the wording of Sudan's petroleum agreements as one area requiring closer scrutiny. He argues that environmental provisions in contracts are often too general and depend heavily on existing national legislation rather than setting out sufficiently detailed operational requirements.

"One of the problems with contracts in Sudan is that environmental provisions are drafted in very general terms and rely on Sudan's environmental laws and terminology," Ibrahim said. "This raises questions about whether petroleum agreements clearly define companies' environmental obligations."

Close 

Wastewater and gas flaring

Oil extraction produces more than crude petroleum. Depending on the field and extraction process, operations can also generate associated gas and contaminated water, both of which require appropriate treatment or disposal.

Ibrahim identified the handling of produced water - toxic, underground water brought to the surface during oil extraction - as a major environmental challenge. If dumped into the open, such toxic wastewater devastates local agriculture, poisons groundwater, and acts as the primary driver for public health crises linked to the oil industry.

Gas management presents a separate problem, Ibrahim said. In some countries, associated gas is routinely burnt through flaring, while others with strict regulations require operators to explore alternatives. Where flaring is permitted, its environmental effects depend in part on operating conditions, emissions and the controls in place.

"Gas flaring must also be governed by specific studies and measurements, because excessive flaring causes environmental pollution. Measurements should be conducted by an independent third party to ensure transparency and provide reliable information," he said.

Evidence and transparency

For residents of West Kordofan, the central issue remains whether oil production is being conducted in a way that protects their health, livelihoods and surrounding environment. Imagery and footage shared with Ayin provide visual evidence of oil leaks in parts of West Kordofan, but the extent of contamination, its origins and its potential effects on nearby populations require further investigation.

Nearly a decade after local groups began raising concerns, these complaints remain unheeded and will only increase as signs of conflict-induced damage to oil fields in West Kordofan take place.

World.title: Sudan: In War-Torn Sudan, Mothers Worry About Empty Plates and Lost Childhoods
World.content:
The World Food Programme can't "outfeed conflict," says WFP's chief Luke J. Lindberg on his first official visit to Sudan, where years of conflict and aid cuts risk deepening one of the world's biggest hunger crises.

Samia has the dreams of any Sudanese mother. To see her five children educated. To put three square meals on the table. To go back to her old life of farming before war tore it apart.

Today, her new normal is a sandy displacement camp in the south-central Sudanese city of Kosti. Home is a white tent affixed with rickety poles. Now the family's main breadwinner, the 37-year-old mother tries to put food on her children's table by working in the local market.



"Some days, when work is good, I can give them a good meal," Samia told World Food Programme (WFP) Executive Director Luke J. Lindberg, during his recent visit to Goz El Salam displacement camp where she now lives. (For their protection, WFP does not use last names of war-displaced people.) "When work is not good, I make kisra (a fermented flatbread) for breakfast, and for lunch maybe lentils."

"We are doing our part to make sure we're delivering, and it's time for world leaders to step up and do their part and end this war." - Luke J. Lindberg, WFP Executive Director

As Sudan wraps up another year of brutal conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions, many like Samia are simply fighting to stay alive. Across Sudan, more than 19.5 million people face acute hunger. More than 4 million women and children are acutely malnourished.

And at a time when the war risks deepening one of the world's biggest hunger crises, humanitarian aid is shrinking for lack of funds. That includes WFP assistance that in August fed 4 million people. Since then, we have been forced to cut nearly a million people from our food and nutrition support.

But vanishing assistance is only part of the problem.

"The World Food Programme can't outfeed the conflict," Lindberg said during his visit to Sudan earlier this month-- his first field mission since becoming WFP chief. "We are doing our part to make sure we're delivering, and it's time for world leaders to step up and do their part and end this war."

Fleeing war, finding hunger

WFP is delivering in places like Goz El Salam, where lines of cloth tents are pitched in a sea of sand. More than 28,000 displaced people now shelter here, many having fled fighting in the central Kordofan region and Darfur to the west.

Workers unload bags of WFP sorghum, vegetable oil and pulses from trucks ahead of distributions for the camp's most vulnerable residents. For Samia and her family, it will be their first WFP support - and, as funds run short, it's uncertain how long it will last.

"I hope the World Food Programme can continue providing assistance, so we can feed our children and keep them in school," she says. "So they can have a better future."

Samia and her five children arrived at Goz El Salam in April, after fleeing heavy fighting in her South Kordofan hometown of Dilling. Her husband stayed behind with other family members.

"There is nobody supporting us financially," Samia says. She and her children rely on what little she earns at the market. Times have become so lean, she adds, that her oldest son works there as well, pushing goods with a wheelbarrow.

"I do not want him to work with me," Samia says, hoping someday "he can stay in school and continue studying with his siblings."

A mother's wish for her children: food, peace and school

Across the dusty Goz El Salam camp there are many stories of hardship. Another mother of five, Noor, spent months running from war with her family. Like Samia, she, too, hails from the Kordofan region.

Her face creased with worry, Noor describes how she buried her husband after he was killed in the fighting. How a charity gave her the funds to cross into South Sudan, where she and her family found refuge for a few months and sold tea for a living. How they finally earned enough to return to Sudan - and the relative safety of Goz El Salam.

Like many, Noor's family now depends on WFP food assistance to live. And like for many, it is not enough.

Close 

"In the morning I give them tea with milk. Otherwise, they go to school two or three times a week with nothing in their stomachs." - Noor, a displaced mother who lives at Sudan's Goz El Salam displacement camp

"In the morning I give them tea with milk," Noor says of her three youngest children who go to one of the camp's schools taught by volunteers. "Otherwise, they go to school two or three times a week with nothing in their stomachs."

For her part, Samia still hopes to go back home to Dilling. Back to farming and peace. "We farmed many things," she recalls of the distant days without hunger.

"My children had enough food and drink, and they were in school," she adds. "They did not lack anything."

WFP's food and nutrition support in Sudan is made possible thanks to donors including the African Development Bank, Austria, Canada, Croatia, the Czech Republic, the European Union, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Kuwait, Lithuania, Monaco, Norway, Private Donors, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Nations, the United States of America and the World Bank.

World.title: Africa: TrustAfrica Announces New Board Leadership as It Prepares to Enter Its Third Decade
World.content:
Dr. Abdoulie Janneh was elected Chair of the Board of Directors of TrustAfrica.

press release

TrustAfrica has announced a significant transition in the leadership and composition of its Board of Trustees, following the 43rd meeting of the Board, held in Dakar, Senegal, on 9–10 November 2026.

After eight years of distinguished service as Chair of the Board of Trustees, Ms Coumba Toure has stepped down from the position she had held since October 2018. Her tenure spanned a defining period in TrustAfrica’s evolution, including navigating the turbulent years of the COVID-19 pandemic, significantly expanding the organisation’s programme portfolio, strengthening its institutional systems and resource base, and deepening partnerships with regional institutions and leading Pan-African civic and philanthropic networks.

During this period, TrustAfrica expanded and strengthened a number of flagship initiatives, including the African Philanthropy Conference, co-organised with the Centre on African Philanthropy and Social Investment (CAPSI) at Wits University and several other Pan-African networks; the African Social Movements Baraza; the Harambee-Ubuntu Pan-African and Feminist Philanthropies Initiative, jointly led by TrustAfrica and Urgent Action Fund-Africa; the reimagining of governance and democracy work under the West Africa Democracy Fund; the Africa Youth Panel and NextGen Initiative; and the Global Africa Reparations Caravan.

These advances have strengthened TrustAfrica’s ability to fulfil its mandate of reinforcing African agency in addressing the continent’s most pressing challenges, deepening solidarity, and advancing people-centred transformative change across Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Board elected Dr Abdoulie Janneh as its new Chair. A respected African statesman and development leader, Dr Janneh previously served as Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA) and as Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations. His extensive experience in African development, governance and international cooperation will help guide TrustAfrica as it enters its third decade.

TrustAfrica also welcomed three distinguished leaders to its Board of Trustees:

Dr Hippolyte Fofack, former Chief Economist and Director of Research and International Cooperation at the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank). He currently holds the inaugural SDSN Parker Fellowship at Columbia University in New York, is a Distinguished Fellow at the Global Federation of Competitiveness Councils (GFCC), and serves as a Research Associate at Harvard University’s Center for African Studies.

Dr Adeyemi Dipeolu, former Economic Affairs Adviser to the President of Nigeria. He is an Adjunct Professor at the Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance at the University of Cape Town, a Fellow of the Development Leadership Dialogue Institute at SOAS University of London, and a member of the AfCFTA Trade and Industrial Policy Advisory Council.

Ms Ainka Sanders Jackson, founding Executive Director of the Selma Center for Nonviolence, Truth and Reconciliation in Selma, Alabama, USA, and Co-Executive Director of the Selma Bridge Crossing Jubilee, one of the largest annual civil rights commemorations in the United States. An inaugural Obama USA Leader, she has contributed to national and international conversations on racial and economic equity, nonviolence, democracy and social justice.

The addition of these three leaders brings to TrustAfrica’s Board a wealth of experience spanning African economic transformation, public policy, development, racial and economic justice, civil rights and international cooperation. Their appointment reinforces TrustAfrica’s commitment to harnessing the knowledge, expertise and resources of Global Africa, encompassing the continent and its diaspora, as well as friends of Africa around the world, to advance the continental transformation agenda and contribute to building the Africa we want.

The Board also confirmed 1–2 April 2027 as the new dates for TrustAfrica’s 20th Anniversary Conference in Abuja, Nigeria.

Under the theme “Sustaining African Agency, Building the Future We Want,” the high-level 20th Anniversary Conference will bring together TrustAfrica’s partners, current and former leaders, civil society actors, intellectuals, policymakers, philanthropists and friends from across Africa and other regions of the world. The conference will provide an important opportunity to reflect on two decades of work, celebrate the communities and partnerships that have shaped TrustAfrica’s journey, and collectively consider the challenges and possibilities facing Africa in the decades ahead.

As TrustAfrica marks twenty years of work and prepares for its next chapter, we express our profound appreciation to all our partners and supporters, and to all those who, over the past two decades, have served as Board or staff members.

We extend our sincere gratitude to Ms Coumba Toure for her dedicated leadership and eight years of service as Chair of the Board. Her contribution has been invaluable to the institution and to our collective efforts to strengthen African agency and advance a more equitable and just continent.

Close 

We warmly welcome Dr Abdoulie Janneh as Chair of the Board, alongside Dr Hippolyte Fofack, Dr Adeyemi Dipeolu and Ms Ainka Sanders Jackson as new Trustees. Their experience, leadership and commitment will enrich TrustAfrica’s work as the organisation enters its third decade.

We look forward to bringing together our partners, friends and wider community in Abuja on 1–2 April 2027 for TrustAfrica’s 20th Anniversary Conference, an important moment to celebrate what we have built together, reflect on our shared journey, and collectively imagine the future we want.

Dr Ebrima Sall

Executive Director

TrustAfrica

Dakar, Senegal

About TrustAfrica: TrustAfrica is an independent African foundation headquartered in Dakar, Senegal. For two decades, the organisation has worked to strengthen African agency and advance equitable development through grantmaking, knowledge production, convening, advocacy, and support for movements, institutions and networks working for social, economic and political transformation across the continent.

World.title: Africa: Presidents And Government Leaders Discuss Strengthening Strategic Partnerships And Expanding Cooperation With The UAE
World.content:
press release

The Leaders’ Meeting, held as part of the World Governments Summit Dialogue for Latin America and the Caribbean, explored ways to strengthen the strategic partnership between the UAE and countries across the region and expand economic and investment cooperation. Discussions focused on translating shared opportunities into projects and partnerships that advance development priorities and mutual interests.

Held in Cap Cana, Dominican Republic, as part of the Dialogue taking place on 20 and 21 November, the meeting provided a platform for direct dialogue among government leaders on prospects for cooperation between the two regions. Discussions focused on creating an attractive investment environment, facilitating trade and developing long-term partnerships that deliver sustainable economic and development value.

The meeting was attended by His Excellency Luis Abinader, President of the Dominican Republic; His Excellency Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan, Minister of State and Head of the UAE delegation; His Excellency José Raúl Mulino, President of the Republic of Panama; Her Excellency María José Pinto, Acting President of the Republic of Ecuador; the Honourable Philip Davis, Prime Minister of the Commonwealth of The Bahamas; the Honourable Brigadier Mark Phillips, Prime Minister of the Co-operative Republic of Guyana; and the Honourable Dr. Natalio Wheatley, Premier of the British Virgin Islands.

Also attending were His Excellency Víctor Bisonó, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic, and Her Excellency Noemí Espinoza, Secretary General of the Association of Caribbean States. The discussion was moderated by Mohamed Yousef Al Sharhan, Managing Director of the World Governments Summit Organization, with participating leaders sharing their perspectives on relations and prospects for cooperation.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Abinader: Committed to sustaining dialogue and translating its outcomes into tangible results

In his opening address to the Dialogue, His Excellency President Luis Abinader outlined the Dominican Republic’s ambition to strengthen its role as a bridge connecting Latin America and the Caribbean with the Middle East. He stressed the importance of sustaining joint efforts beyond the Dialogue and measuring its impact through the results it delivers for businesses, young people, communities and government services.

His Excellency said: “We are committed to organising this Dialogue every year and working throughout the year to ensure it delivers tangible results.” He added that his vision for the future of relations between the two regions centres on expanding business cooperation, strengthening two-way investment flows, creating new opportunities for young people to exchange knowledge and expertise, and deepening ties between communities.

He identified logistics, free zones, trade, hospitality and tourism as key areas for expanding cooperation, citing the partnership with DP World and the Caucedo Port development project as examples of projects that modernise infrastructure, stimulate economic activity and create jobs.

He also expressed his aspiration to establish a direct Emirates flight between Dubai and the Dominican Republic, in cooperation with the relevant authorities and the airline, and to work towards creating the conditions needed to achieve this.

Shakhboot bin Nahyan: Moving from dialogue to projects and impactful partnerships

His Excellency Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan conveyed the greetings of His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of the UAE, and His Highness’s emphasis on strengthening the strategic partnership between the UAE and the countries of Latin America and the Caribbean.

His Excellency highlighted the considerable potential underpinning relations between the two regions, offering promising opportunities to diversify markets, strengthen economic connectivity and expand cooperation.

His Excellency said: “We believe the next phase requires us to move from dialogue to action, from identifying opportunities to implementing projects, and from bilateral cooperation to building broader partnerships that connect our two regions.”

He added: “We therefore look forward to the World Governments Summit Dialogue in Latin America and the Caribbean identifying clear shared priorities, tasking our relevant teams with following them up, and translating them into initiatives and partnerships with tangible economic and development impact.”

His Excellency highlighted the role of Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements in opening new markets, facilitating trade and investment, and enabling businesses to benefit from opportunities in both directions. He cited DP World’s expansion of Caucedo Port and its associated free zone as an example of partnerships that strengthen connections between markets in Latin America and the Caribbean and the Gulf, Asia and Africa.

His Excellency Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan highlighted promising opportunities to deepen cooperation in renewable energy, food security, technology, infrastructure and water security. He pointed to the 2026 United Nations Water Conference, which the UAE is co-hosting with the Republic of Senegal, as an opportunity to develop practical partnerships and projects that strengthen water security and the sustainability of water resources.

José Raúl Mulino: Building a sustainable future requires responsible decisions

His Excellency José Raúl Mulino, President of the Republic of Panama, said that building a sustainable future requires responsible decisions that look beyond short-term gains and strengthen the foundations of growth for future generations.

He explained that Panama is working to strengthen its public finances, modernise its institutions, accelerate digital transformation and develop human capital to support innovation, enhance resilience and reinforce confidence in its economy.

He noted that his country aims to capitalise on its geographical position to become a strategic platform for trade and investment by developing an integrated ecosystem encompassing the canal, ports, logistics and energy. He reaffirmed Panama’s openness to international partnerships that enhance the competitiveness of the region’s economies and expand opportunities for development and prosperity for its people.

María José Pinto: turning resources into knowledge, productivity and wellbeing

Her Excellency María José Pinto said that transforming natural wealth into sustainable economic and development value requires responsible resource management that creates jobs, attracts investment and improves living standards.

She noted that President Daniel Noboa’s government has launched Ecuador’s Growth Agenda 2040 to diversify the economy, advance innovation and build international partnerships that provide financing, technology and knowledge, support responsible investment and preserve natural resources. She said the success of economies is measured not only by the scale of their resources, but also by the opportunities they create and the quality of life they deliver. The challenge, she stressed, is to turn resources into knowledge, innovation and productivity, ensuring that every investment builds lasting capabilities and every partnership opens broader horizons for future generations.

Philip Davis: Translating dialogue into tangible results

The Honourable Philip Davis extended his greetings to His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai, and commended the World Governments Summit Organization’s efforts in organising the Dialogue.

In his address, he stressed the need to translate the Dialogue’s outcomes into practical results, strengthen the role of international law and modernise international institutions to keep pace with global change. He called for climate finance to be directed towards the countries and communities most exposed to risk, strengthening their ability to prepare for disasters and address their consequences, protect future generations and build a safer, more stable future.

Mark Phillips: Developing new partnership mechanisms

The Honourable Mark Phillips said the Dialogue provides an opportunity to discuss issues central to advancing government performance and improving services to meet communities ’ needs. He stressed that achieving sustainable development in the region requires collective effort and a comprehensive programme of action focused on addressing climate change, strengthening food and energy security, accelerating digital transformation, and expanding trade and investment to support economic diversification and sustainable growth.

He said the Dialogue gains greater significance through closer cooperation and deeper integration, calling for new partnership mechanisms and expanded technical cooperation, knowledge exchange and engagement within and beyond the region. He highlighted the importance of using technology to build more efficient, transparent government institutions that respond to citizens’ needs, and strengthening partnerships to uphold peace, sovereignty and the rule of law, turning shared challenges into opportunities for progress and sustainable prosperity.

Close 

Mohamed Al Sharhan: building long-term partnerships and projects that improve communities’ lives

His Excellency Mohamed Al Sharhan said the World Governments Summit Dialogue in Latin America and the Caribbean enables governments to shape a shared vision for the future of cooperation between the two regions and direct partnerships towards development priorities that harness economic potential and expand opportunities for sustainable growth.

He explained that the Dialogue’s outcomes focused on strengthening long-term partnerships, aligning government visions and translating shared priorities into projects that benefit national economies and the lives of their communities.

Invitation to participating leaders

The meeting strengthened opportunities to align priorities and policies with available investment potential and consolidate the foundations of sustainable cooperation between the UAE and the countries of Latin America and the Caribbean.

His Excellency Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan renewed the invitation to participating leaders to attend the World Governments Summit, scheduled to take place in Dubai in February 2027, to continue exchanging expertise and build on the priorities addressed in the discussions.

A platform connecting regional priorities with global opportunities

The Leaders’ Meeting was held as part of the World Governments Summit Dialogue, organised by the World Governments Summit Organization in partnership with the Government of the Dominican Republic and the Center for Public Policy Analysis. The Dialogue brought together heads of state and government, more than 70 speakers, representatives from over 30 countries, and more than 120 private sector companies and institutions.

World.title: Rwanda: Women-Owned Exports Decline By 51 Percent As Finance Challenges Linger - New Report
World.content:
Rwanda needs to expand access to trade financing and support women-owned businesses to move into higher-value production as their exports decline, a new report by the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) and the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR) has recommended.

The report shows that exports by women-owned firms fell from a peak of $1.16 billion in 2021 to $563 million in 2024, a decline of about 51 per cent, highlighting challenges in sustaining their participation in international markets.

ALSO READ: Govt launches centre to boost financing for women-led businesses

To address the trend, the report proposes expanding trade financing to at least 50 per cent of women-led firms in the medium term, alongside support for value addition, manufacturing and access to regional and international markets.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The report, examined women's participation in trade between 2004 and 2024, covering employment, entrepreneurship, financial inclusion, informal cross-border trade and export performance.

ALSO READ: Why women-owned businesses struggle to cross EAC borders

It identified access to credit as one of the major constraints facing women-owned businesses.

In 2024, only eight per cent of female loan applicants secured financing, compared with 13 per cent of men, despite significant progress in women's access to mobile financial services.

It recommends introducing export credit guarantees specifically for women-owned businesses to ease collateral requirements and establishing a dedicated financing window for female traders under the Economic Recovery Fund.

ALSO READ: Women-led businesses on higher rise in past five years - new report

It also proposes increasing the Business Development Fund's partial credit guarantee scheme from 75 per cent to 85 per cent for women-led trading firms.

Commercial banks should also allocate at least 30 per cent of their trade finance portfolios to women-owned exporters by 2027, according to the report.

Beyond financing, the report recommends supporting women-owned businesses to move from trading raw commodities into manufacturing and processing, which could help them capture more value from their exports.

It identifies agro-processing, including coffee roasting and horticulture packaging, as well as light manufacturing such as textiles and leather goods, among the priority areas.

Proposed interventions include subsidised access to Special Economic Zones and ready-to-use factory units for women's cooperatives, as well as grants to purchase processing machinery and packaging technology.

The recommendations come as women's export performance has fluctuated considerably over the years. Their exports increased from $261 million in 2017 to $1.16 billion in 2021, before falling to $563 million in 2024.

Between 2023 and 2024 alone, exports by women-owned firms declined from $689 million to $563 million.

In manufacturing, the value of trade by women-owned businesses fell from about $278.1 million in 2023 to $265.6 million in 2024. Their trade in agriculture, forestry and fishing also declined from approximately $15.7 million to $7.6 million.

The report says strengthening export competitiveness and diversifying products are important to creating more sustainable opportunities for women-owned firms.

Simplifying cross-border trade

The report also recommends simplifying trade procedures and creating pathways for women involved in informal cross-border trade to access formal markets.

Women accounted for 61 per cent of informal cross-border traders in 2024, compared with 39 per cent for men.

The value of goods traded by women reached $84.2 million in 2024, compared with $68.1 million for men.

However, the report notes that men tend to generate higher trade values per trader, suggesting that women are more concentrated in lower-value transactions.

To address this, it proposes simplified border procedures, dedicated lanes for women traders and mobile-based pre-clearance and payment systems.

It also recommends providing market information, including prices, regulations and business opportunities, through SMS and other mobile platforms.

Other proposed measures include expanding the Simplified Trade Regime to cover more products commonly traded by women, simplifying business registration through Irembo and offering fee waivers to first-time female registrants.

The report further recommends linking women traders to formal export markets and regional value chains under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

Addressing employment and care responsibilities

Women's representation in trading firms has increased, although the report raises concerns about the quality and security of jobs.

Women accounted for 46 per cent of employees in trading firms in 2023, up from 39 per cent in 2014. They also held 45 per cent of senior management positions, compared with 38 per cent in 2017.

However, half of women employed in trading firms held temporary or seasonal contracts in 2023, up from 37 per cent in 2017. The proportion holding permanent contracts stood at 41 per cent.

Close 

The report recommends that the Ministry of Public Service and Labour and the Gender Monitoring Office introduce a biennial Gender Wage and Contract Audit in the trade sector to monitor wages, employment contracts and working conditions.

It also proposes incentives for firms that maintain high proportions of permanent employment contracts for both women and men.

Unpaid care responsibilities remain another constraint. In 2024, women spent an average of 3.9 hours per day on unpaid care work, compared with 2.5 hours for men.

Although the proportion of children under three years of age in formal care increased from 12 per cent in 2017 to 77 per cent in 2024, the report says further efforts are needed to address the unequal distribution of care responsibilities.

It also recommends training women in digital trade, e-commerce, digital payment systems and AfCFTA requirements, including rules of origin, to help them access wider markets.

To strengthen monitoring, the report proposes establishing a Gender-in-Trade Desk within NISR to produce annual gender-disaggregated trade reports in collaboration with the Ministry of Trade and Industry and the Gender Monitoring Office.

The report says implementing these measures would help women move beyond participation in trade towards greater leadership and involvement in higher-value economic activities.

World.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

World.title: FBI probes second cyberattack in months as hackers breach key crime database, sources say
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Hackers breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), three sources familiar with the matter told Fox News, marking the second cyberattack against the bureau in months.

The FBI is investigating the hack to determine the unauthorized entry point, but for now, it is unclear what information was compromised, sources said.

The NCIC database is a critical information-sharing tool for federal, state and local authorities, helping them track fugitives, monitor registered sex offenders, check whether someone has failed a gun background check, among many other things.

In an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany on Saturday morning, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack.

TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS

"I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that," Trump added.

The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. CNN first reported the hack.

In September, a group called ShinyHunters hacked into the FBI's job portal website intending to steal sensitive employment records.

The mysterious group, known for extortion plots, claimed it stole sensitive information belonging to almost every FBI agent, including names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, assignments and, in some cases, the names of family members.

FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER

Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested on Oct. 8 and faces federal extortion conspiracy charges in connection with the FBI's investigation into ShinyHunters, according to court records and law enforcement sources that spoke to Reuters.

The details of Dubrovsky's alleged crimes are unknown as the court records in relation to his case remain sealed.

FBI Director Kash Patel announced the arrest of ShinyHunters "suspected co-conspirator" on Oct. 9, a day after Dubrovsky was taken into custody.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence, and act quickly," Patel said in a statement at the time. "We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate."

In 2023, hackers infiltrated a computer network at the FBI's New York field office used in child sexual exploitation cases — a system that also stored images tied to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported.
