World.title: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
World.content:
An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain

toggle caption i Mark Felix/AFP via Getty Images

A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.

It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.

Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.

Sponsor Message

If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.

There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.

"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.

Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.

So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.

Sponsor Message

One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.

And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.

Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.

And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.

The practical and legal hurdles

Some legal scholars have observed that this agreement between states could run afoul of the compact clause in the Constitution, which says that "no state shall, without the consent of Congress … enter into any agreement or compact with another state … unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."

Norman Miller, a constitutional law professor at Willamette University, said that beyond the legal hurdles, he sees a range of practical issues with the compact.

Mostly, he said, it could upend what is a core feature of American presidential elections, which is that they are largely decentralized.

States individually decide who can vote and how they can vote. He said forcing electors from one state to vote according to the tallies in another state could create some tension.

"We would want to have a standardized, uniform set of rules regarding who gets to vote for president, how they vote, how those votes are tabulated, and to have a federal election authority doing that tabulation," he said. "I think trying to nationalize [the current system] and entrusting a national election to 51 separate election administrators would just sow discord and distrust."

Sponsor Message

But John Koza, the chairman of National Popular Vote, said if the compact works the way it is supposed to, none of that will be necessary.

"We don't need a centralized bureaucracy or a presidentially appointed commission that could be manipulated," he told NPR. "The simple fact is current state and federal law provide for the issuance of a certified vote count from each state. And all that has to be done is add them up."

But mostly, Miller said the biggest question before this effort is whether such a large reform should be done via a constitutional amendment.

Upending the Electoral College, some argue, would be a profound change to how the U.S. chooses the leader of the free world. Opponents of a national popular vote, such as Save Our States, argue that without the incentives created by the Electoral College, American politics will move more toward "toward more regional politics and would exacerbate existing divides."

Miller said even though it will be much more difficult to pull off, it would be worth going through a more fulsome process via Article 5 to get rid of the Electoral College, instead of working around it.

"This is where I think process matters," he said. "If you really want to have a national popular vote for the president and avoid all of the legal and practical difficulties, you need to do that through a constitutional amendment, because only a constitutional amendment can address the legal and practical challenges of conducting a national popular vote for the presidency."

A similar effort to pass an amendment to get rid of the Electoral College in 1969 failed, though. And very few amendments have even gotten close to passing in recent history.

Rosenstiel, the consultant to the National Popular Vote, said this is why he thinks groups like his are seeking a creative solution to something most Americans agree is a problem.

Sponsor Message

And, he said, he ultimately thinks a national popular vote will solve multiple problems at once. For one, he said, it will force presidential candidates to appeal to most of the country, as opposed to a select group of voters in battleground states.

And, importantly, he said, it would make all voters feel like their vote matters.

"We should have a system where every American citizen feels valued and is valued when they cast their vote," he said. "And there's only one reform that delivers it."

World.title: Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
World.content:
Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?

toggle caption i Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.

"There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."

Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.

Sponsor Message

The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.

But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.

The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.

Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."

Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.

"There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented," the company warned investors.

Sponsor Message

Anthropic's founders and employees just got very rich

Anthropic's corporate structure is intended to protect its mission, even as it pursues commercial success. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation (PBC), meaning its board must balance shareholder interests with its social mission.

As part of that structure, the company has installed an oversight body known as the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which has the power to appoint four of the company's seven directors. The founders effectively control the appointment of the remaining three.

The trust can, however, be dissolved. Doing so would require the approval of all seven co-founders, as well as a majority vote among shareholders with voting rights.

That arrangement could create a potential route for founders and shareholders to override the trust's influence over company decisions, legal experts interviewed for this article said.

"If there is a fight about some important safety decision, such as 'Are we satisfied that this super-advanced model is safe for users and society, or should we hold off for a couple of months to do extra tests or for whatever other safety reason?,' there's the possibility for the founders and the employees to basically ally against the trustee and neutralize their control rights," said Roberto Tallarita, an assistant professor at Harvard Law School.

The listing has also made many Anthropic employees wealthy. Each of the company's seven co-founders hold a stake in the company currently worth more than $20 billion. Its 5,300 employees hold an estimated $232 billion in combined equity. Non-founder employees were able to sell up to 10% of their holdings on the first trading day.

Those substantial financial stakes could influence how Anthropic's staff approaches decisions around safety and risk, said Tallarita.

"If they make decisions that are driven by safety considerations, but are bad for the bottom line, the stock price will react, and private investors will have reasons to exert some pressure on the company," he said.

Sponsor Message

The financial rewards could also change Anthropic's internal culture, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University.

"And now so many of these people will be multimillionaires too, which I think will just raise the temperature and egos and sense of stakes," Kreps said.

In his comments on Thursday, Amodei addressed these concerns.

"To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," he said. "Today puts the company in a stronger financial position and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing."

Commercial and competitive pressures may compete with safety

Competition between AI companies is fierce.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman described the rivalry between major AI developers as a "race dynamic in the fog of war" while speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit this week.

That dynamic is "a bad thing," Altman said. "I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted."

OpenAI also plans to go public, and filed preliminary IPO paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, shortly after Anthropic. But Altman said in September the company has delayed those plans.

In an essay the same month, Amodei discussed the need for AI companies to carefully "pace" the development of frontier models.

"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless," Amodei wrote. "We have sought a middle way: to show that it's possible to build carefully and succeed commercially, and to make safety something on which AI companies compete."

Sponsor Message

"Anthropic has done a fairly good job of investing in analysis of what its models can and can't do, and the vulnerabilities that it creates, and publishing at least some version of this analysis," Kreps said.

In April, Anthropic announced that it would restrict access to its Claude Mythos model after internal testing revealed its powerful cybersecurity capabilities. The company said Mythos could identify and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers, making it a potential tool for hackers.

On June 9, less than three months later, Anthropic introduced Fable 5, a Mythos-class model, for general use with additional safeguards to restrict certain high-risk cyber, biological and chemical capabilities. The original Mythos model remains restricted to selected partners.

"In the past, the fact that the trust and the founders were aligned helped them delay the release of Mythos for several months," said Stavros Gadinis, faculty director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Business at the University of California Berkeley's law school. "But this was at a moment when they felt they were leading the pack."

Anthropic's decision to enter the defense contracting space has raised questions about how its commercial relationships align with its stated mission, said Kreps.

In November 2024, Anthropic announced a partnership with defense contractor Palantir, whose software is used in military intelligence and targeting operations. Under the agreement, Anthropic made its Claude models available to U.S. defense and intelligence agencies through Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform.

However, Anthropic earlier this year resisted allowing the Pentagon to use its technology for autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance. Negotiations broke down in February, resulting in the U.S. government designating Anthropic a "supply chain risk to national security."

"It does seem to raise a set of concerns about partnering with Palantir, which is contracting with the Pentagon for targeting. What part of that is AI for humanity?" said Kreps. "A lot of people who work there went there because safety was the guiding light."

Sponsor Message

AI development is accelerating

Questions over Anthropic's promise to prioritize safety over commercial success are becoming more pressing as the technology itself advances. Anthropic is entering the public markets at a moment when its own research suggests the pace of AI development could be accelerating dramatically.

A November 2026 assessment by AI research nonprofit METR concluded that Anthropic's AI capabilities were improving at about twice the previous rate. Researchers estimate that a majority of this acceleration is now driven by Anthropic's use of AI tools to assist its own researchers. METR found no clear bottlenecks that might slow this progress, such as limits on data and computing power.

This could bring the company closer to a future in which increasingly capable AI systems help build even more advanced systems — a process known as autonomous recursive self-improvement. The prospect has fueled fears that Anthropic and other AI developers could lose control of their most advanced models, with potentially significant consequences for society.

"I'm scared myself, but it's very hard to imagine AI technology stopping or pausing," said Gadinis. "We are in a situation where these companies know better than anyone their models to the extent that someone understands them. So we have to work with them as a society."

A federal regulatory vacuum

Society is left relying heavily on AI company executives to make consequential decisions about the risks posed by their own products, experts interviewed for this story said.

Since there are few government safeguards in place to shape how AI companies make decisions about safety and security, the industry's power is going largely unchecked, they said.

At the federal level, the AI sector remains largely unregulated. Under the second Trump administration, the White House has prioritized a deregulatory approach, seeking to limit federal oversight in favor of allowing AI labs to innovate without being encumbered by red tape.

Sponsor Message

In June, the White House announced its AI framework, which lets developers submit their newest models to federal agencies for cybersecurity and national security evaluations before release. However, the initiative is entirely voluntary.

"I don't think the government knows enough to regulate AI," said Tallarita. "This is a conversation that we should have as a political community, and probably the most serious conversation we should have right now."

Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

World.title: Allies are buying Canadian underwater surveillance drones. Canada is 'not there yet'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada has a three-ocean, 243,000-kilometre coastline and about 20 underwater drones to help defend it.

Defence officials talked last year about the need for a short-term fix to assert Canada's sovereignty, according to an internal document obtained by CBC News.

But the Royal Canadian Navy's commander, Vice-Admiral Dan Charlebois, confirms there isn't an interim solution ready.

"We're still working very closely with industry to get there. We're just not there yet," said Charlebois in an interview with CBC News.

The navy wanted to see if Canadian underwater drones could help address surveillance gaps along the "sparsely" monitored coast until its first uncrewed underwater surveillance system is ready, the paper obtained through an access-to-information request said.

The navy's current small fleet of American underwater drones is equipped with tech built by Canadian company Kraken Robotics. But the navy uses those drones for mine hunting and testing, not surveillance.



Kraken, based in Newfoundland and Labrador, and Cellula Robotics in B.C. are viewed as world leaders in underwater drone technology and are already selling their systems to allies around the globe for surveillance. But not yet to Canada.

WATCH | Canada makes underwater drones, so why isn't it using them for surveillance?: Canada makes underwater drones, so why isn’t it using them? | Duration closed caption 6:01 Defence experts warn Canada's lagging behind on underwater surveillance and its coastline is vulnerable to threats. For The National, CBC’s Ashley Burke examines current surveillance capabilities and learns the Navy is looking for an interim solution to close the gaps.

Other countries are racing to monitor and protect critical underwater cables from potential acts of sabotage by adversaries.

A massive network of these communication cables runs along ocean floors, carrying more than 95 per cent of the world's internet traffic and trillions in financial transactions. Damage could cripple societies.

Hundreds of submarine cables run along ocean floors around the world. These fiber-optic cables have allegedly been targeted by adversaries. (Kevin Kirk/CBC)

University of Calgary defence expert Rob Huebert said Canada has "very significant vulnerabilities" because it can't fully detect when adversaries are entering Canadian waters.

Canada has long relied, Huebert said, on co-operation with the U.S. Navy as a safety net and allowed its fleets, submarines and satellites to age and deteriorate.

"The backstop that I think Canadian governments have always counted on was of course, if we were slow, if we were late on any of these surveillance capabilities off our coastline, well the Americans would take care of it," Huebert said.

He called that a "policy of hope."

The navy is undergoing its biggest peacetime fleet renewal since the Second World War. But some replacements aren't coming until the 2030s and 2040s.

Ottawa's in the initial procurement phase for a $250-million to $499-million underwater surveillance system that uses drones and sensors to detect, monitor and gather intelligence about threats. The system is expected to be used in Canadian waters, including the Arctic, and during deployments abroad.

"We expect to take delivery of some large autonomous vehicles in the early 2030s," Charlebois said. "That is just around the corner when you're talking about delivering a very advanced large-scale system."

The Royal Canadian Navy's commander, Vice-Admiral Dan Charlebois, says the navy is testing out drone technology. (Mathieu Theriault/CBC)

The government wants the system fully delivered by 2043. But it isn't clear yet if foreign companies will be able to bid on the project.

When asked about the obstacles to finding an interim solution, Charlebois said the procurement system "can be challenging," but he's seen an appetite from Ottawa to cut down on red tape.

"The products that the navy needs exist here in Canada," he said. "We just have to enable ourselves to actually procure them and procure them at pace."

Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to speed up procurement through the Defence Investment Agency. He's also vowed to massively scale up drone production.

Canada has 2,000 drones or so in its inventory, Carney said earlier this fall. But he said the country will need millions in the years to come.

WATCH | Why Canada lags in underwater drone tech: 'Not there yet': Why Canada's navy lags in underwater drone tech | Duration 2:13 Canada’s NATO allies are sounding the alarm about foreign adversaries suspected of damaging critical underwater cables. A network of the cables run along the ocean floor and are responsible for about 95 per cent of the world’s internet. The threat comes at a time when Canada's facing surveillance gaps along its coastline. One solution? Underwater drones powered by Canadian tech. The problem? Ottawa isn't buying them yet for surveillance.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the government is creating a roster of preapproved companies for sole-source contracting. The navy says this will open up "new opportunities" to work with the industry on underwater drones.

Allies using tech to monitor underwater cables

Off the coast of Halifax, Dave Shea, the executive vice-president of strategy and growth at Kraken Robotics, said one of the biggest challenges his company has faced in Canada is the pace of procurement. But he is excited the government wants to speed it up.

His company outfitted the navy's small fleet of drones with synthetic aperture sonar systems.

Those sonar systems, Shea said, scan the sea floor for objects of interest and take high-resolution images. Kraken's technology can also listen for any submarines or boats operating in the area, he said.

The Kraken Robotics underwater drone Katfish is designed to be towed by a boat. It carries a synthetic aperture sonar system that can take high-resolution images of the seabed. The Royal Danish Navy, the Polish Navy and Royal Australian Navy use this technology. (David Laughlin/CBC)

In recent years, Shea said allies have pivoted to use their technology to monitor if underwater cables or pipelines have been tampered with.

Canada could too, he said, but would need a much bigger fleet and longer-range drones because the coastline is so vast.

"There's a lot of technologies that are being built and delivered by companies like Kraken … that could be deployed directly here in Canada to help understand what's actually happening, who's in our waterways, who's in our sovereign waters and what are the risks to be able to protect Canadian capabilities," Shea said.

Orders headed to Europe, U.S., Asia

Cellula Robotics CEO Neil Manning says his company has sold its long-range drone to five NATO allies, but not Canada.

Systems are on order and will be heading to Europe, the U.S. and Asia, he said.

Cellula Robotics says its Guardian drones can carry out long-endurance missions. (Submitted by Cellula Robotics)

Cellula uses hydrogen fuel cell technology, Manning said, that's been adapted from NASA's space launches to work in the water.

The company's long-range drones can travel up to 5,000 kilometres or stay out at sea for up to 45 days, he said.

"I'm highly confident that we will see domestic spend as well," Manning said. "But at the moment we're still in that cycle of building trust with with our local governments."

'We need to get further ahead'

Charlebois is aware critical infrastructure is being challenged elsewhere in the world and said he's trying to get ahead of the problem.

"This is why we're working more closely with Canadian industry than I've seen in my 34 years in the navy because we know we need to get further ahead in this space than we are," he said.

The navy's fleet diving unit put an underwater drone in the water to practice looking for mines in 2021 off the coast of Halifax. (Master Cpl. Anthony Laviolette/Canadian Armed Forces)

Canada contributes to underwater surveillance capabilities with the U.S., Charlebois said, that deliver a "really high level" of awareness, but he wants to do more and is prioritizing sensors.

Asked why Canada is lagging behind protecting underwater infrastructure, Defence Minister David McGuinty said the government is working on it.

"I say that we're rebuilding all of our capacity underwater, on land, in the air and connected to satellites," McGuinty said. "We're building a combined layered approach to being able to understand and identify what might be coming at Canada."

The navy said it has a layered network of capabilities to protect this infrastructure, but noted the government, owners and allies are also responsible.

World.title: The pros, cons and risks of using AI as your personal assistant
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Imagine a chatbot that can not only recommend a great restaurant in your area, but can also book a reservation, put it in your calendar and email an invitation to your friends.

In recent months, that scenario has become reality, with some of the world's biggest AI developers launching digital personal assistants they say will make users' lives easier.

The companies behind these new mass market agents say they are remarkably capable, safe and easy to use.

But cybersecurity experts say the more advanced tasks come with more risk that something could go seriously wrong.

What are AI assistants, and how do they work?

Three of most well-known ones on the market — Meta's Muse, OpenAI's dots and Anthropic's Claude Duet — all debuted within weeks of each other and all have similar capabilities.

Muse can be spoken to as if it were a chatbot and instructed to send emails, book travel, make purchases and more on your behalf when connected to third-party apps like Shopify and Ticketmaster.

It can handle multiple tasks at once and continue working through them even while the app is closed.

LISTEN | Tech columnist on her experience using Muse: The Current 21:24 What could possibly go wrong with Meta's Muse? Meta's personal AI agent Muse is now one of Canada's most downloaded apps, and has attracted millions of users since it was first launched in September. It acts as a personal assistant and can help with things like paying bills and ordering food, but it relies on a lot of your personal information. We speak with the Wall Street Journal's personal tech columnist, Nicole Nguyen, who has tried the app and tells us why she finds it both incredible and terrifying at the same time.

OpenAI says users can instruct dots to do "nearly anything" by messaging or calling them through ChatGPT. They can be connected to other devices and over 4,000 apps, and even have the ability to use your laptop.

Anthropic's Claude Duet has been pitched as more of a proactive agent for work than as an assistant to take on personal errands.

The agent can take on simple administrative tasks, like scheduling meetings, and more complex projects, like creating financial reports or building web apps, according to the company's product announcement.

While Muse is free, dots and Claude Duet each require a subscription. Claude Duet isn't available in Canada yet.

How do AI personal assistants keep your personal info safe?

CBC News reached out to Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic to ask how they protect users' privacy and prevent their personal assistant agents from going beyond the scope of the tasks they're assigned, along with what advice they'd give users to prevent this from happening.

A spokesperson for Meta said Muse runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud that is designed so users' data is securely stored, referring CBC to a blog post by software engineer Tarek Sheasha outlining the safeguards built into Muse.

They also referred CBC to another blog post that says Muse checks with users before taking on sensitive actions, like sending an email or making a purchase, and shows a complete audit trail of everything the agent has done.

A spokesperson for OpenAI referred CBC to a blog post outlining its safeguards, which includes encryption for users' content and account security systems that monitor for suspicious use.

OpenAI also monitors dots as they plan and carry out actions "looking for potentially harmful behavior, such as acting outside your instructions or trying to bypass safeguards," the blog post says.

OpenAI also notes that users can give dots custom rules, such as to never send emails, and says certain actions require a user's confirmation each time, such as permanently deleting data and installing or running software from an unrecognized source.

A spokesperson for Anthropic said Claude Duet was built to enable people to stay in control of what it does, and so their information is handled with discretion.

The model never sees users' passwords, browser cookies or sign-in tokens, and Claude Duet is instructed never to share sign-in credentials, credit card and bank account numbers and government ID numbers — even if you ask, the spokesperson said.

What can go wrong?

Some users have reported getting more than they bargained for when putting these high-powered assistants to work.

A Montreal man asked Muse to handle his Facebook Marketplace transactions. But after listing a keyboard for sale, Muse gave out his home address to a stranger without his knowledge.

When the buyer showed up, Muse even told him the seller was there even though he wasn't home.

"Muse doesn't check with me, it doesn't tell me this guy has messaged and then it gives the guy my address, agrees to his price and literally tells him to come right now, that's the crazy part," Matt Robb told CBC News last month.

WATCH | Meta AI agent gives out man's address: He used Meta’s AI agent Muse for Marketplace sales. Then it set one up behind his back | Duration closed caption 2:39 Matt Robb started using Muse, Meta’s AI agent, to handle Facebook Marketplace transactions. But after listing a keyboard for sale, he got more than he bargained for. One expert advises people to really look at what they’re letting Muse access.

Asked how something like this could happen, a spokesperson for Meta pointed CBC to a social media post made by Robb about his ordeal, where he explained he had clicked "allow always" instead of "allow one time" when asking Muse to handle his Marketplace transactions on his behalf going forward.

While these agents can be innovative and exciting tools, they should be used in a limited way and given very specific instructions in order to avoid these kinds of mishaps, said Claudiu Popa, a Toronto-based certified cybersecurity professional with privacy consulting firm Datarisk Canada.

"Unless you tell them very specifically what they can and cannot do you're going to have unpredictable results," he said.

"That's the issue with all AI agents, and this issue is going to continue for the foreseeable future."

David Shipley, CEO and co-founder of Beauceron Security in Fredericton, said he hasn't let these agents get near his computer at all.

"I absolutely do not trust this technology," he said.

Shipley compared trusting them with your personal errands to a monkey's paw wish, referring to the classic horror story that serves as a cautionary tale to be careful what you wish for.

"You might wish for it to do a certain set of actions and it's going to go and do those actions, but perhaps not in the way that you intended it to do that."

Why have Canada's biggest banks blocked AI assistants?

With a client's authorization, AI agents can also connect to bank accounts and credit cards to monitor balances and transaction histories and give tips on budgeting.

But concerns over AI agents accessing sensitive information have also prompted Royal Bank, TD Bank, CIBC and Bank of Montreal to block them from directly accessing their clients' online bank accounts and other information.

The CEOs of RBC and BMO recently warned that third-party AI agents are not to be trusted with personal banking information.

WATCH | Canada's banks ban AI agents from access client accounts: Why banks are banning AI agents | Duration 1:23 As privacy fears and security concerns rise, some of Canada's biggest banks are hitting the brakes on clients using personal AI agents — with most outright banning them.

Those warnings should give people pause about using these agents entirely, given that banks "have been among the more fervent adopters of digital technology over the last 30 years," Shipley said.

But Popa said he thinks these AI personal assistants can be used in a limited way without compromising your personal information, such as for tasks like research or writing emails — not sending them — for you.

"You can't necessarily trust an outside AI agent with your private information. So sharing calendars, emails, all sorts of personal information and personal files, that is for me, it's not a line that I would let it cross."

World.title: A Canadian study pinned a baby's death on codeine passed through breast milk. 20 years on, it's been retracted
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A highly influential yet controversial Canadian study that linked a baby's death to codeine passed through breast milk — and informed global guidance on breastfeeding and pain management over the last two decades — has been pulled from a leading medical journal, which said omissions in the research amounted to "falsification."

In the latest issue of The Lancet, set for release Nov. 21, the journal announced it has retracted the 2006 paper by Gideon Koren, the once esteemed founder of the Motherisk drug testing lab at the Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) in Toronto.

The saga involving Koren's long-questioned study included years of Canadian media coverage, a sweeping New Yorker investigation last January, and a decision by The Lancet to add an "expression of concern" to the case report in February following new allegations of falsified toxicological data, authorship issues and ethical concerns.

The case focused on the deadly poisoning of an Ontario infant in 2005.

The study purported that the boy's mother was prescribed the painkiller Tylenol 3, which contains both acetaminophen and codeine — a mild opioid that gets partially metabolized into morphine inside the body — causing a deadly amount of morphine to pass to the boy through her breast milk.

Koren long insisted the case showed maternally ingested codeine can be fatal for breastfeeding infants, despite mounting questions about that likelihood from other pediatricians and toxicologists.

"This paper is the cornerstone of an entire field of pediatric pharmacology and toxicology that, honestly, should not exist," said Toronto-based internist and pharmacologist Dr. David Juurlink, a longtime critic of what he called a "botched" study on a coroner's investigation.

"This isn't just about one mischaracterized infant death. The narrative that babies can die through opioids passed through breast milk has greatly influenced postpartum pain care. It has caused women taking opioids to forgo breastfeeding, thereby depriving infants of the benefits of breastfeeding, which are numerous."

WATCH | The joint CBC/Toronto Star investigation into Motherisk hair testing: Tainted Tests: Broken Families | Duration 44:43 It seemed so perfect, so scientific - but the 'Motherisk' hair testing was deeply flawed. A joint CBC/Toronto Star investigation.

'Omitted findings' in case report

The Lancet's retraction notice said the journal had received the "outcome and conclusion" of a formal investigation from SickKids' research integrity office after referring its allegations to the Toronto hospital.

"The authorship issues and ethical concerns could not be fairly investigated as a meaningful participation of Gideon Koren was unlikely to be possible," reads the notice.

"On the allegation of omission of material toxicological data, including the infant's blood codeine and acetaminophen concentrations and the qualitative identification of codeine in the infant's stomach contents, the report concluded that this omission constitutes falsification. The omitted findings left readers without the information necessary to assess the publication's conclusion."

It's just the latest blow against Koren, who relinquished his medical licence in Ontario after a scandal-filled career that included the closure of the Motherisk lab in 2019.

The facility gained worldwide attention for using hair strands to test for drug and alcohol use in mothers — methods deemed "inadequate and unreliable" by an independent provincial review in 2015, but not before they were used in thousands of child protection cases and broke apart families across the country.

CBC News has contacted Koren for comment.

In a statement to CBC News following The Lancet's retraction notice, a spokesperson for SickKids said the facility "takes all matters of research integrity seriously."

The hospital's formal inquiry concluded material toxicological data had been omitted from the published report and determined that this "constituted falsification under SickKids' Responsible Conduct of Research Policy." The hospital declined to provide further details on the findings, due to the "confidential nature of research integrity inquiries."

The Lancet's retraction notice has been "a long time coming," Juurlink said.

"It's surprising that it took such a long time for this to happen. Not just that it took a long time, but that it took investigative journalism to cast a light on the institutional failures that kept this paper alive for 20 years."

World.title: How Canadian Survivor contestant Daniel Kilby lost most of his belongings to auction after filming the show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian Survivor contestant Daniel Kilby lost many of his personal belongings earlier this year, including a painting of a "cheetah dressed as a general," his PlayStation 5 and many household appliances, after missed payments on a storage locker while he was on the show led to them being put up for auction.

"That's where it's been annoying … I'm like, 'Oh, I want to make a sparkling water. JK, you can't,'" said the 30-year-old game designer who now lives in Halifax.

Kilby, who'd been living in London, Ont., was renting at the time, and his lease was coming up. He didn't want to pay rent while filming the 51st season of the hit reality competition, so he stored most of his belongings in a storage locker for what he says was around $100 a month and moved in with his girlfriend in Florida.

There, he could begin his Survivor training, including learning to swim and practicing fire-making.

But on his flight to Florida in February, he says he lost his wallet. So he had to get a new debit card and update his payments. The problem? There was one payment he forgot to update.

He says he realized in mid-April — the weekend before he left to film in Fiji — that he hadn't updated his payment info with the StorageMart in London. He says he tried to call the location but couldn't update his details with the person he spoke to, and he ultimately decided to leave it until after the show was filmed.

Kilby stands next to one of his prized possessions, his 'cheetah dressed as a general' painting. (Submitted by Daniel Kilby)

At the time, he says he was more focused on living his dream and getting a shot at a million dollars on Survivor.

"I also, like, low-key did not expect them to actually auction my stuff. I thought this was like a dumb mistake that I'd have to pay when I got back," said Kilby.

Arriving home

Kilby placed 11th on the season and was voted out on the eighth episode, which aired on Nov. 11. So no million-dollar prize. Instead, he returned in June to find a very different financial matter.

The first email he read upon returning to Canada was that his storage locker — and all his stuff — was going up for auction.

While he'd been away, StorageMart had tried to contact him to update his payment information and inform him he had missed at least three payments. But since he was stuck on an island at the time with no connection to the outside world, they were unable to reach him.

"My phone is blown up. I have like a hundred emails from them being like, 'Hey, you haven't paid,'" said Kilby.

Kilby reached out to the storage unit company, hoping he could get his stuff back. He says he was told he would need to cough up $2,000 and retrieve his stuff immediately to do so. It was a lot of money, plus he'd need to rent a vehicle that could hold it all.

"Plus, I'm like, a lot of my stuff sucked," said Kilby, who estimates it was probably worth about $2,000 altogether.

CBC reached out to StorageMart for information on its policies around late payments and when a unit goes up for auction but didn't receive a response before publication.

StorageMart's website says there is no grace period for late payments, and that late fees will apply if payments are late, with the specifics dictated on a customer's lease. StorageMart also has an online payment portal for customers, as well as a helpline it says is operated 24/7.

Kilby came in 11th on the latest season of Survivor, which is still airing. (Robert Voets/CBS)

So he had another idea. Now that his stuff was up for auction, he could just bid on it and hope no one else was too interested.

With his bid sitting around $400, he was feeling good that he would be reunited with his belongings. But at the last second, someone with the username "Prince C" made a bid and won the auction for $441.

"It's brutal; it's sad," said Kilby. "I thought we were just winning it, so I felt kind of dumb there. But I also felt kind of relieved because I'm like, 'OK, I don't have to go pick it up.'"

'It's a funny story'

Kilby said the possessions in the locker ranged from IKEA furniture to his collection of Pokemon cards.

He tried scouring Facebook Marketplace in London after the locker sold, hoping he would see some of his stuff pop up. He even posted on Reddit, hoping someone could point him to the buyer. There are some personal belongings he wishes he could get back.

"There's, like, some sentimental thing. So I had this, like, weird painting of a cheetah dressed as a general. I thought that was really cool," said Kilby. "My mom knit a bear that's in there. That sucks."

Plus there are all the household appliances such as a SodaStream and a blender that he's needed to replace.

The rest of the stuff? He's OK to live without. Since filming the show, Kilby and his girlfriend moved to Halifax, and he says many of the items in that locker wouldn't have made the trip.

"It's a funny story, and I'm somebody who lives my life trying to do things in a way that you get a funny story at the end," said Kilby.

"It's like, hey, the passion for Survivor made me just completely [lose my stuff]."

World.title: Elon Musk looks to break up with MAGA. To what end?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

From his first time donning a black MAGA hat and declaring himself "dark MAGA" at an October 2024 rally for Donald Trump to his multimillon-dollar splurge on Republican candidates ahead of this month's midterms, Elon Musk has certainly seemed to embrace the Make America Great Again movement.

Why does that matter? Because the Tesla and Space X CEO now appears to be distancing himself from his MAGA bonafides, saying that he never really considered himself a MAGA adherent.

"I'm not MAGA," Musk declared e arlier this week, in an interview with The New York Times.

"I'm not sure what MAGA means," he said during the newspaper's DealBook Summit. "If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties."

That may come as a surprise considering Musk made at least five appearances between 2024 and 2025 in which he associated himself with the movement, according to Mediaite, a news website.

But Musk's MAGA split appears to come at a time when association to the brand could prove to be a business and legal liability for the world's richest man.

"It's so tra nsparently convenient," said Matthew Dallek, a professor of political management and historian at the D.C.-based George Washington University, who has researched the MAGA movement.

Musk's comments follow the Republicans' disastrous showing in the U.S. midterms and the so-called Democratic blue wave that saw the party take control of the House and the Senate.

Along with MAGA-boosting appearances, Musk also spent more than $400 million U.S. on Trump-aligned Republican candidates in the midterms — the most money of any individual campaign donor.

Can Musk disassociate from MAGA?

"Now that [MAGA]'s on the losing side, all of a sudden, he's not MAGA," said Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University.

"I mean, come on. This is just laughable. This is the guy who glossed himself 'dark MAGA' and had black MAGA stuff put together ... when Trump took over. He was completely in with it."

Prof. Matthew Dallek says Elon Musk, seen speaking before Donald Trump at a campaign rally on Oct. 27, 2024, made his 'MAGA bed' and now must lie in it. (Evan Vuccu/The Associated Press)

Dallek said Musk has spent years making his "MAGA bed."

"Now he's got to lie in it, even when it's politically uncomfortable."

Musk, who also urged his followers on X to vote Republican, now says he feels "pretty foolish" for spending so much money on the midterms. He also said in his NYT interview that ideologically he is "quite moderate" and doesn't have any "extreme political views."

But Dallek said if he's really such a moderate and not part of the MAGA ranks, there were non-MAGA Republicans he could have backed during the elections.

Instead, Musk spent around $200 million US backing Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who Dallek call ed, "arguably the most MAGA of all the midterm candidates."

Musk has based himself and several of his companies in Texas, including Tesla, SpaceX ‌and a planned chipmaking venture between the two. But the state is almost all blue following the U.S. midterms.

"The government is no longer in the hands of his allies," Dallek said. "He is in a very vulnerable position. Businesses are very vulnerable."

Dallek also questioned just how "moderate" Musk is, as he's has turned X into a platform for extremist views. As well, a February 2025 NBC News report said Musk had been encouraging right-wing political movements, policies and administrations in at least 18 countries as part of a global push to slash immigration and curtail regulation of business.

"It's just transparently false when he says, 'I'm a moderate,'" Dallek said.

What's driving Musk's MAGA retreat?

One reason: The MAGA brand is at its lowest net favourability ever, said CNN’s chief data analyst Harry Enten.

"It is a brand that is failing amongst the American public," he said.

But perhaps more importantly, Musk may be trying to engender better relations with Democrats as he faces government probes and red tape.

WATCH | Alex Gibney warns of Elon Musk's 'unchecked power': Alex Gibney warns of Elon Musk's 'unchecked power' in new documentary | Duration closed caption 8:25 Filmmaker Alex Gibney discusses the making of his new four-hour documentary about Elon Musk, telling CBC’s Jackson Weaver why he sees the tech oligarch’s growing influence and ‘unchecked power’ as a serious threat.

Democrats have indicated they may want to investigate the months Musk spent in 2025 spearheading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

DOGE team activities led to widespread dismantling of foreign aid programs, as well as allegations that team members breached privacy laws by illegally accessing the sensitive data of Americans.

Musk may also face slower approvals for the billions of dollars Space X plans to invest in data centre campuses in Texas and Arizona.

"They're going to be turning their eyes toward him and his space facilities, and the environmental issues that they're causing and tax issues," Belt said. "Things that could really make life difficult for him. He doesn't want to poke the bear."

World.title: A real '3 Body Problem': Astronomers discover a nearby 'weirdo' triple-star system
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Roughly 28 light-years from Earth lies a peculiar star system called IRAS 21500+5903.

For years, astronomers had known about the two stars that orbited one another. But then, when looking for exoplanets — planets that orbit other stars — a group of astronomers made a surprising discovery: there was another star in the system. Instead of being a binary star system, this was a triple-star system.

"It's a freak thing. It was an annoying object," said Étienne Artigau, a researcher at the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx) at the University of Montreal. "It's not what we were looking for."

Their findings were released this week in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

The system contains a red dwarf, a type of star that is very common in our galaxy, and two smaller, dense white dwarfs. One is roughly 1,000 astronomical units (the distance between the sun and Earth) away from the red dwarf. The other, they found, was a mere two astronomical units away, a little similar to the distance from the sun to Mars.

The inner white dwarf orbits the red dwarf, while the outer white dwarf orbits the pair.

A quirky neighbour

What's surprising is that no one had discovered it over the decades.

"It's weird that no one found the system, but it also says that there are weird things overlooked just next to us," Artigau said. "It's like not next door, but down the road, just one block away of a stellar neighbourhood."

When a low- to medium-mass star reaches the end of its life, it first swells into a red giant before leaving behind the dense and small white dwarf. It is what will happen to our own sun in roughly five billion years.

This artist concept depicts an ultra-dense dead star, called a white dwarf, passing in front of a small red star. (NASA/JPL-Caltech)

While looking for an exoplanet in this system, the international team of astronomers — led by the University of Montreal team — used an instrument at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope in Maunakea, Hawaii, called SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou). It is used to detect exoplanets and does this by measuring tiny changes in a star's velocity, which can be caused by orbiting planets.

But the red dwarf wasn't doing what it was supposed to be doing. It was moving differently, with velocity changes of nearly 16 kilometres a second. That's a huge difference.

Initially, they thought it was a brown dwarf, a type of substellar object that has a mass of about 75 times that of Jupiter.

But that still didn't make sense.

More weirdness

The velocities were so off that they broke Artigau's code.

"At some point, we said, Okay, we should get to the end of it. Something's wrong with that object. And so I fixed the code," he said. "And then we just said, let me do the math of that brown dwarf. Okay, no, it doesn't work."

It was a real head-scratcher.

What they eventually discovered is that what was causing the perturbations was a high-mass… something. But it also couldn't be seen.

Could it be a black hole? A neutron star? A white dwarf?

The team turned to the Gemini North telescope, also on Maunakea. Using high-resolution images from its 'Alopeke instrument — a specialized high-speed camera — they found what they were looking for: a faint companion star — a white dwarf — orbiting closely around the red dwarf.

WATCH | The orbit of the Welopō'ai triple-star system:

Here's where it gets weirder.

Before becoming a white dwarf, the star would have become a red giant. As it swelled up, its orbit would have been so close to the red dwarf that the pair must have interacted with one another. Many times these types of stars envelop the red dwarf, or the two may even merge. This didn't happen.

And there was more.

The inner white dwarf should be spiralling inward toward the red dwarf. Instead, it is in a stable orbit.

It could be that the more distant white dwarf is somehow stabilizing the orbit, though they don't know yet how. That's for future research.

The image on the left shows the two components of the system: Welopō'ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and Welopō'ai B, a second white dwarf located farther away. The image on the right provides a close-up view of the inner pair and their orbital paths. (Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST, left, International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab, right. Graphical construction by Étienne Artigau & Heidi White (UdeM/IREx))

"We're saying it cannot exist," Artigau said. "Of course, it exists. It's there."

Paul Delaney, professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at York University in Toronto, believes that perhaps the more distant white dwarf was once much closer to the other pair.

"I mean, when planetary systems form now, one of the standard things is migration," he said. "I would bet that they were relatively proximate to each other and then they did engage in a bit of gravitational embracing, and the further white dwarf today was much, much closer in its heyday."

To add to the weirdness, the astronomers calculated that the system is roughly 10 billion years old, older than our own solar system of 4.6 billion years, and its stars are metal-rich. Typically, these older stars are metal-poor.

"It's tantalizing, and we just don't know if it means anything. It may just be a random draw basically of a stellar population," Artigau said.

Still searching for an exoplanet

The astronomers gave this system the Hawaiian name Welopō'ai, combining "welo" which means an inherited family trait, and "pō'ai," which means an orbit or circular path. The name therefore means "path of family traits."

The very popular book and Netflix show 3 Body Problem looks at a triple-star system and the effects it could have on a nearby planet, mainly to a civilization that has evolved on that planet.

One of the terms that is used to describe the triple-star system in the show is "chaotic," which affects the speed at which the civilization can evolve.

The issue is an age-old physics problem. Two-body systems are predictable. But add a third, and everything blows up. That's because Body A pulls on Body B and Body C. Body C in turn pulls on Body A and Body B, and because of these interactions, it changes their motions and their forces forever.

WATCH | Newton's three-body problem explained:

While researchers didn't find an exoplanet, Artigau said the search isn't over.

"It's such a weirdo system that Atanas Stefanov, one of the authors, he's applying for time to get, to look for planets around the red dwarf," he said.

Whether there is a planet there or whether an alien civilization could live on a planet in a triple-star system remains to be seen.

For Artigau, he said the fact that something new was thrown at him was very exciting.

"I like it," he said. "Little things that are just sideways in your life in research. It's fun."

World.title: Canada's sport integrity watchdog introduces rules aimed at match fixing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada’s sport integrity watchdog has created new rules aimed at discouraging competition manipulation, something its CEO describes as “a serious safety issue” for athletes.

It’s the result of growing concern around the impact of Canada legalizing single-event sports betting, according to Sport Integrity Canada CEO Jeremy Luke.

That has opened up the world of prop bets, where people can pick up their phone and gamble on everything from who will score first in an NHL game to which team in Formula 1 completes the fastest pit stops.

“What that's done is it has really increased the level of gambling that's taking place within the country and on sport,” Luke said in an interview with CBC Sports.

The risk of match fixing isn’t isolated to big-money pro leagues. According to Luke, the risk goes up in sports where athletes aren't making big salaries.

WATCH | A New Game Plan: Sports Funding 101: A New Game Plan: Sports Funding 101 | Duration closed caption 7:32 CBC Sports' Donnovan Bennett sat down with Canada's secretary of sport, Adam van Koeverden, among others, to discuss Canada's current sporting system, and how it can be rebuilt.

“They can be more subject to influence or to grooming or those types of activities,” he said. “So we want to pay particular attention not just to professional sport but to lower levels of sport where that type of manipulation can occur. That's why it's really important that in Canada we have rules and education that extends across all our national sport organizations.”

The Canadian Program to Prevent Competition Manipulation prohibits athletes, sport organization staff members, board members, officials and referees, among others, from betting on any competition in their sport, regardless of the level or format. That includes directing someone to bet on their behalf.

There are also rules aimed at discouraging people from soliciting or using inside information for betting.

It bans intentional acts that could manipulate the outcome of a game, as well as acts that manipulate part of a game. Luke cited an example of a tennis player committing an intentional double fault in the third set of a second game when people have placed bets on that particular serve.

“That's the type of behaviour that we're trying to identify, but also what we're trying to do is educate athletes in particular and officials and other participants that this is a real threat to their safety,” Luke said. “Often individuals can be coerced or groomed into doing these types of things by organized crime or other individuals who are wagering on these activities.”

The rules are rolling out slowly with an initial set of voluntary adopters, as national sport organizations (NSOs) and multi-sport organizations (MSOs) review the new program.

As sport organizations sign on, Sport Integrity Canada plans to create a public registry detailing sanctions, similar to registries that already exist for those who’ve faced sanctions related to safe sport or doping violations.

The hope is for Sport Canada to make the rules mandatory as a condition of federal funding, similar to the safe sport and anti-doping programs administered by Sport Integrity Canada, Luke said.

“In the last couple of years, [sport organizations] have been asking for these rules to come into play as well, given they see this as a risk, and their international federations in many cases see this as a risk,” Luke said. “The reception is positive. It’s just [that] it would be far better for the rules to be mandatory in order for us to get the traction needed to get everyone to comply with the rules and to get them put into place.”

'A growing threat to the sport system'

Canadian Olympic Committee CEO David Shoemaker believes there is room in Sport Canada’s new funding framework to make it mandatory for sport organizations to adopt the new rules.

“Competition manipulation is a very important thing for us to collectively address,” Shoemaker said. “We've seen how and where it can have really negative impact on participants in sport. And we certainly support it. We fund efforts to combat it. I believe I'm about to sign on Monday the new code on behalf of the Canadian Olympic Committee and certainly wouldn't be at all disappointed to see it in there.”

It also garnered support from the Canadian Paralympic Committee. Having mandatory rules tied to funding as just a starting point, CEO Karen O'Neill said.

WATCH | A New Game Plan: Paying to play: A New Game Plan: How high a price is pay to play sports? | Duration closed caption 6:52 Donnovan Bennett explores how the pay to play model is impacting the Canadian sports system.

“Obviously it has to have many other initiatives around to make it substantive or to have the kind of change we hope will occur, but the funding compliance framework is a first step,” she said.

The federal government acknowledges competition manipulation is a “growing threat to the sport system” that “contributes to unsafe sport environments at all levels.”

But it hasn’t yet committed to making the rules a condition of federal funding for sport organizations.

“The Government of Canada is proud to have committed funding for Sport Integrity Canada for the development and implementation of the Canadian Program to Prevent Competition Manipulation (CPPCM) and the program’s launch marks an important step in Canada’s work to address this emerging issue,” Bahoz Dara Aziz, a spokesperson for Secretary of State for Sport, Adam van Koeverden, wrote in a statement to CBC Sports.

“The Government of Canada will continue to monitor this issue as the CPPCM builds capacity and experience and will adjust its conditions to funded organizations to protect the integrity of sport as needed.”

Limited ability to work with law enforcement

Sport Integrity Canada initially supported the decision to remove the prohibition around single-event sports betting, seeing it as a harm reduction measure that could regulate things that were already happening on the black market.

“What didn’t follow, from our perspective, after that happened was the necessary steps to protect athletes and sport participants from this risk and to protect sport integrity more generally,” Luke said. “And that's what we've been advocating for over these years, is what goes hand-in-hand with legalization is harm reduction strategies to protect participants from these risks.”

WATCH | Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There's a push to change that: Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There’s a push to change that | Duration closed caption 2:29 Federal MPs are moving forward with a bill to restrict sports betting ads in Canada. It comes as new data shows that the number of problem gamblers is on the rise in Ontario.

The organization would also like to see the federal government sign and ratify the Macklin Convention, which lays out a framework for how countries across the world are dealing with the issues around match fixing and sports betting.

Even with the new rules around match fixing, Sport Integrity Canada is missing legislation that would open the door to sharing information with law enforcement agencies that are investigating the same cases — a major gap in a world where online gambling has been used for money laundering and funding global terrorism .

“Often this is connected to organized crime,” Luke said. “You're dealing with regulators such as the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario or others. Having the ability to share information across those platforms is essential to the work that we do and it's something that we need to continue to explore.”

World.title: A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, a healthy 24-year-old Montrealer, died suddenly in Istanbul on June 17, 2025.

A Turkish autopsy report concluded the cause of death was food poisoning.

But for her family, that doesn't add up.

A joint investigation into Deveaux-Cattino's death by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed a different poison at work and 12 similar deaths.

The recent medical school graduate had decided to celebrate by taking a trip with a few of her closest friends.

"She'd never been to Turkey," said her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. "She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country."

The group hit the tourist trail and its highlights, including the requisite balloon ride in Cappadocia.

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino had never been to Turkey before her trip in 2025, says her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. ‘She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country.’ (Radio-Caanda)

With only two days to go, Bérengère and one of her friends headed for Istanbul, a city she'd longed to visit.

Watch the full documentary, "The Invisible Killer," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

They checked into Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel and went straight out to explore. They soaked up the sights and street food, then settled down for a proper meal, a chicken casserole followed by Turkish tea and baklava.

The next morning, they woke violently ill.

Laurie recalls the final days

The details of those final days come from Laurie, the woman who travelled to Istanbul with Bérengère. What happened on that trip left her traumatized and we've agreed to protect her identity and not use her real name.

She said that within minutes of waking, Bérengère was throwing up.

"Then I started feeling unwell," Laurie said, "and suddenly we were taking turns running to the bathroom to vomit until we realized that whatever it was, it wasn't just going to pass."

They called the front desk and an ambulance took them to hospital.

‘My sister is younger than me,’ said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino, right. ‘I’d never imagined a life without her.’ (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)

'Things aren't going well'

That same day, across the ocean in Montreal, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino saw her screen light up: Laurie was FaceTiming her.

"I thought: 'This isn't normal. Something's off. This is going to be bad news,'" said Deveaux-Cattino. "She says 'Élo, we're in the hospital in Istanbul, and things aren't going well. I've been told to contact the family.'"

Deveaux-Cattino and her father, Henri Cattino, scrambled to find flights to Istanbul. While waiting for their connection in Paris, Deveaux-Cattino called the embassy.

"I said: 'Please, can you tell me if my sister has died?'" said Deveaux-Cattino. ”And she said: 'I'm very sorry, Éléonore, but your sister is dead.'"

Three days into their trip to Istanbul in November 2025, the Böcek family from Hamburg fell ill. Five days later, all four family members were dead, poisoned by phosphine gas. (@ismailsaymaz/X)

The Böcek family

The Deveaux-Cattinos repatriated Bérengère's body and asked the Quebec coroner's office to examine it. They buried their daughter and sister without confirmation of the cause of death.

As they waited for answers from Turkey, the family speculated about what else could explain Bérengère's death: Organ trafficking? Alcohol poisoning? Medical malpractice?

Then, in November, as we were investigating, a diplomatic source texted with a tip that pointed to an entirely different explanation.

"A family of four has just died in Istanbul. Watch this report."

The Böceks, a Turkish-German family from Hamburg, were visiting Istanbul. Their hotel was blocks from where Bérengère and Laurie stayed. All four fell ill and died within days of each other.

Investigators initially suspected food poisoning there, too. But within days, authorities concluded that another poison had been at work: aluminum phosphide, a highly toxic agricultural pesticide used to kill rodents and insects.

The 'bomb'

Exterminators call aluminum phosphide "the bomb." It is used in pellet form. Once the pellets are exposed to air, they release phosphine gas. Exterminators say that when placed in a sealed room, the gas kills every living, breathing thing within 72 hours. In Turkey, it's illegal to use in urban areas.

But, like all big cities, Istanbul has a bedbug problem.

WATCH | An exterminator explains treatments to kill bedbugs: Safe extermination of bedbugs | Duration 1:26 Istanbul exterminator Birkan Cihan explains the difference between legal and lethal treatments to kill bedbugs.

Exterminator Birkan Cihan said he can barely keep up with calls from desperate home and hotel owners. Some ask whether he treats bedbugs with "gas." He doesn't.

"We tell them their neighbours could die from it, and that they could, too. But they say: 'We have no choice, it's the only thing that works,'" Cihan said

The phosphine gas these pellets emit is so potent and volatile that it can spread through a building, even if the area being treated is sealed.

In the case of the Böcek family, fumigation in the neighbouring room was determined to be what killed all four of them.

Investigations by Enquête and the fifth estate have found similar cases. In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand.

In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand. (Submitted by Bélanger family)

'That doesn't make any sense'

Just before Christmas 2025, the Deveaux-Cattinos received the autopsy report from Turkey. It concluded that food poisoning caused Bérengère's death. Unconvinced, they handed the report to the Quebec coroner's office.

"The coroner here ran some tests, and she couldn't confirm that food poisoning was the cause of death because, usually, there are signs of intestinal irritation," Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said. "There were none in my sister's case."

We showed the Turkish autopsy report to another Quebec pathologist. Although not authorized to speak publicly, he also questioned the autopsy's conclusions.

"Two young, healthy women who end up in the hospital with food poisoning — OK, I'll buy that. But to die of it so quickly, without any signs of bloody diarrhea or other complications, that doesn't make any sense."

Turkish freelance journalist Ayse Adanali covered the story of the death of the Böcek family in Istanbul in 2025. (Radio-Canada)

Women and children

In Turkey, we started working with Ayse Adanali, a freelance Turkish journalist who'd covered the Böcek story.

Together, we documented nearly 30 cases of phosphine poisoning, including a dozen deaths, since 2023 in Turkey.

Some were tourists, like the two Dutch teenagers found dead by their father in their Istanbul hotel room in August 2025. But most of the victims were Turkish, like Karan Yazıcı, a three-year-old boy poisoned in Istanbul in April 2025 following a fumigation in the neighbouring apartment.

The majority of the victims are women and children. Members of the same family were often poisoned together. While some survived, others died. In most cases, food poisoning was initially blamed for making them sick.

'This is not food poisoning'

Şebnem Korur Fincancı is a human rights activist, professor emeritus and leading forensic pathologist in Turkey.

She's studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas.

Turkish forensic pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı has studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas. (Radio-Canada)

She'd never heard about Bérengère; her death had not been covered by Turkish media.

"This is not food poisoning," she said after reading the Turkish autopsy report.

"I don't think that this is food poisoning because there is no story of diarrhea, only throwing up."

She added that the timing of Bérengère's decline suggests food poisoning couldn't be the culprit.

"Rather, it is the pesticide poisoning."

Fincancı sees one undeniable detail in this report, a finding common to all victims of phosphine gas poisoning she's examined: something called metabolic acidosis, which increases the levels of acidity in the body.

"There is the metabolic acidosis, which also indicates the pesticide intoxication," she said. 'It is one of the main findings of these kinds of cases."

She believes there could be more cases of phosphine poisoning than currently reported.

"With all these misdiagnoses, we have to consider the situation."

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and her friend, Laurie, stayed at the Seven Days Hotel in Istanbul. (Radio-Canada)

150 bites

We scoured hundreds of Google and Tripadvisor reviews for the Seven Days Hotel to see if they'd had a bedbug problem around the time of Bérengère and Laurie's stay.

One stood out: A tourist claiming he'd been bitten 150 times during his stay in June 2025.

We tracked him down. He confirmed he stayed in Room 107, the room next door to where the two women stayed 10 days later.

The windows in those two rooms open onto each other.

That left one critical question: Had Room 107 been treated after his stay? And, if so, with what?

We contacted hotel manager Bahattin Demir. He remembered Bérengère and Laurie and had gone to the hospital after they'd been admitted.

We told him about the tourist in Room 107 and asked him whether extermination work in that room could have killed Bérengère.

"I don't think so, because if it was that product, I'm sure that, you know, everybody would have this problem," he said.

Inside Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel where Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and Laurie stayed. (Radio-Canada)

He said exterminators spray the rooms in the hotel monthly. He offered to contact them and find out what product they use, but then wrote back, referring us to them for more details.

The extermination company is called Wolves.

A contact called them for us. We're protecting her identity because undercover work can lead to jail time in Turkey.

Posing as an Air BnB owner in Istanbul's Fatih district, she claimed to be struggling with bedbugs.

The employee was cautious on the phone.

He didn't name the product specifically, but his detailed description is similar to how aluminum phosphide is used.

"For 72 hours, nobody goes in, the doors are locked and nothing living enters."

We called Wolves for an interview. The employee who answered the phone was not authorized to speak, but denied using aluminum phosphide.

Neither the hospital that treated Bérengère nor the Forensic Medical Centre where her autopsy was performed replied to our inquiries.

The tourism police similarly declined our interview request.

Going over notes Laurie had shared, we noticed she and Bérengère had left the window open the first night. But the next evening, to avoid being woken by the call to prayer, they closed it and turned on the air conditioning. And that was the night they got sick.

We asked pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı whether phosphine gas residue could build up in air conditioners.

"Of course," she said.

WATCH | Honouring her sister's memory: A life without her | Duration 0:52 Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants her sister, Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, to be remembered.

'Those who are gone'

The Böceks' case went to trial in June 2026. The defendants were charged with criminal negligence causing the deaths of this family of four. The ruling came down within days. The owners of the extermination company were found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in prison. The hotel owner and employees received 12 to 13 years.

While awaiting the verdict, the paternal grandfather, Yilmaz Böcek, commented that even the stiffest penalty could never bring back his children and grandchildren.

"Those who are gone never come back."

Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants Bérengère to be remembered.

"My sister is younger than me. I'd never imagined a life without her. We used to be two against the world … now I'm all alone," she said.

"But I'm stubborn. And since she can no longer speak, I'll speak for her. I'll never let her go."

In the summer of 2026, the government of Canada added a new entry to its travel advisory for Turkey, alerting travellers to "cases of poisoning linked to the use of chemical pesticides in tourist accommodations in Istanbul."

After this story first aired on Oct. 15, 2026, Turkish consular officials contacted us, confirming the investigation into Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino's death in Istanbul remains open.
