World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: Havana Takes Center Stage
World.content:
Photos by Nike and a host of Cuban artists.

Photo Feature by Nike

HAVANA TIMES – Since 2008, the Fototeca de Cuba, an institution dedicated to promoting and researching photography, has organized the event Noviembre Fotográfico (Photographic November), featuring the participation of Cuban and international photographers. It is a celebration of photography in Havana.

As part of this year’s program, the group exhibition Ambientes Urbanos (Urban Environments) has opened, curated by art historian and photographer Alain Cabrera, who conceived it as “a space for critical reflection on the city and its many dimensions, where technique serves creativity and artistic sensitivity.”

The exhibition, which opened on November 14th at the Mariano Rodriguez Art Gallery in Villa Panamericana, is also part of the annual Germán Puig Body Photography Salon, held at this gallery. It is dedicated to artist Gerardo de la Llera, a member of the Lente Artistico Collective, who also served as a curator of the exhibition.

Images of a city and its metamorphosis into a human body through its own decomposition.

I invite you to visit this photography exhibition, which will remain open to the public until January 2027.

See more photo features here on Havana Times.

World.title: Exile Destabilizes Both Those Who Leave and Those Who Stay
World.content:
Books left for me from someone leaving the country.

By Lien Estrada

HAVANA TIMES – One thing that brings me joy is that my friends remember me when they need someone to give their books to before leaving the country. Many leave for the United States. Another went to Bolivia. The latest went to Guyana. There’s the professor from the journalism school in Holguín who tells me not to be foolish, to sell all the books and use the money to buy food.

Then there’s the one who left for Bolivia, a writer and bookseller, who told me he wanted to know his books were in good hands. He believes they will remain in mine permanently, and asked me, please, not to sell them. There’s the Quaker pastor who told me to do whatever I wanted with his books. And there’s this latest friend, who left for Guyana because, as he told me, oil had been discovered there and he would surely find work. He said some of the books he left me were for selling, while others I should keep because they were very good and hard to find.

The day before leaving Cuba, he called me to come pick up some books. When he arrived in Guyana, he wrote to me on WhatsApp, asking me to go back to his house for another batch. When I got there, I discovered that he had also left me one of those white plastic wristbands bearing the word “Cambio” (Change), along with a deck of playing cards, each with the same word printed on the back. I thanked him profusely for those gifts and the books. It was a gesture that deeply moved me. As his mother handed them to me, she burst into tears.

On more than one of these occasions, everything I learned in pastoral counseling classes at the Evangelical Theological Seminary in Matanzas seems to turn to ashes. His mother told me how terribly she missed him. My friend, like most Cubans who leave the country, wasn’t going away on vacation for a few days or taking a three-month work contract. He left, and no one knows when he will return. And it’s easy to understand that it may be forever.

I hugged her and told her it was time to keep the faith and believe that everything would turn out all right. Me, someone who has to take alprazolam and sertraline three times a day just to get out of bed and manage the little I can accomplish during the day. Of course, I didn’t tell that last part to the mother of my friend who had just emigrated to Guyana and left me some books to help me get by. I kept that part to myself.

Instead, I shared with her that other side of Christian spirituality, which holds that faith the size of a mustard seed can move mountains. Because I feel indebted.

I owe a debt to every friend and family member, along with the medication I take under my psychiatrist’s guidance, all of whom have helped me keep functioning to this day. They tell me that I must help myself through my own thoughts, even when everything looks bleak, as it does to me. And for all those souls who help me stay alive, the least I can do is help someone else who crosses my path struggling to stay on their feet, often just as I struggle in the face of the reality we have been forced to endure under this dictatorship all these years.

My friend’s mother told me that was true, and that she attended church. I told her that was a good thing. She handed me the books, and I thanked her. And I couldn’t bring myself to leave without telling her that if there was anything I could do to help, she should please count on me. She thanked me for that, too.

Among the books my friend left me is one by Carlos Alberto Montaner, Las columnas de la libertad (The Columns of Freedom), published by Edhasa in Buenos Aires in 2007. I wouldn’t sell that one, not even for weeks’ worth of food and beer to go with it.

These are truly challenging times. Powerful experiences. And surviving them is the challenge.

Read more from the diary of Lien Estrada here on Havana Times.

World.title: When Christmas Is Decreed in a Country Plunged into Darkness
World.content:
En la plaza O’Leary de Caracas. – Foto: Gleybert Asencio

By Antigona Urbana

HAVANA TIMES – In almost every country in the world, Christmas has its place on the calendar. In Venezuela, however, it has become a bureaucratic procedure. Here, all it takes is a nationally televised announcement for the government to decide that it’s time for everyone to be happy.

This year, the order came on November 1; on another occasion, Christmas was decreed in October. On paper and on television, we’re already in the season of Christmas music and good wishes, but the reality on the streets is quite different. The streets are alive with protests by workers demanding Christmas bonuses, basic services, and decent wages. Meanwhile, the people in Miraflores Palace are like Shakira’s song: blind, deaf, and mute.

And we have “anecdotes” that reveal what’s really happening. On the night the Christmas decorations were switched on in Plaza O’Leary, in downtown Caracas, something happened that seemed like a cruel joke: while the lights of the official ceremony shone brightly for the cameras, the entire surrounding neighborhood of El Silencio was completely without electricity. An illuminated Nativity scene in the middle of a blackout.

That scene perfectly captures what we’re living through. There’s no point in moving December forward by decree when people in Zulia, Carabobo, Lara, and Barinas spend six or seven hours a day without electricity, enduring unbearable heat. Talking about Christmas lights in places where people can’t even turn on a fan sounds like mockery.

But beyond the lack of electricity, there is suffering that cannot be concealed with Christmas trees and decorations. This year, we’re being ordered to celebrate while a tragedy remains unresolved: the earthquake in Vargas. While those in power call for festivities, residents along the coast are still digging through the rubble, searching for loved ones and recovering bodies. You cannot order people to celebrate when families are still turning over stones in search of their missing relatives.

That’s why, during a recent conversation, a simple idea emerged, one born not of anger but of dignity. It’s not a protest with shouting or placards, but a gesture that each household can make: don’t turn on a single Christmas light this year.

Leave the Christmas tree lights off out of respect for those still searching through the rubble in Vargas. Leave them off in solidarity with those who spend sleepless nights in Maracaibo, Carabobo, Lara, and Barinas waiting for the electricity to return. Leave them off to make it clear that joy cannot be decreed, and that a country plunged into darkness cannot be fixed with a few decorations in a public square.

Read more from the diary of Antigona Urbana here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Friday, November 20, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Friday, November 20, 2026.

Senate Rejects War Powers Resolution to Limit Trump’s Attacks on Iran

Nov 20, 2026

The Senate rejected a war powers resolution on Thursday that would have directed President Trump to seek congressional approval before resuming attacks on Iran. The resolution failed on a vote of 51-48. Three Republicans voted in favor, while Pennsylvania Democratic Senator John Fetterman voted in opposition. The House approved the resolution in September. Both the House and Senate previously approved a war powers resolution back in June, but President Trump largely ignored it. Thursday’s failed vote in the Senate came after Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries suggested he would not block funding for attacks on Iran in the government funding package due by December 11. Meanwhile, a Pentagon official said Thursday the cost of the war on Iran has topped $48 billion. That figure does not include damage to U.S. bases, the cost of providing healthcare to hundreds of injured troops or the tens of billions of dollars in higher fuel costs triggered by the war.

Senate Passes Permitting Reform Bill with Support of 14 Democrats, Including Leader Chuck Schumer

Nov 20, 2026

The Senate has approved a permitting reform bill that would weaken environmental laws to speed approval of new housing, roads, energy projects and other infrastructure. While the bill would make it easier to build new transmission lines and wind and solar farms, it would also speed construction of fossil fuel power plants and new data centers, including on public lands. Meanwhile, Native leaders and advocacy groups strongly opposed the legislation, saying it would weaken tribal sovereignty and threaten cultural and sacred sites. This is Oregon Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley, who voted “no.”

Sen. Jeff Merkley: “First, it makes it a lot easier to build data centers. Did anybody notice data centers were a big issue in this most recent election? Here we come right in after the election, and we’re going to pass a bill that makes it easier to do data centers by striking down tools that states have when they decide they do not want to have a data center because it threatens key clean air or clean water issues.”

Despite those objections, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, passed on a vote of 62-33 with 14 Democrats in favor, including Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer. In a statement, Food & Water Watch said, “Sen. Schumer’s alignment with Republicans over a majority of his own Democratic caucus in voting to advance this terrible pro-polluter, pro-data center permitting bill is all the reason needed to demand that Schumer step down as leader of the Senate Democrats.” The bill now goes to the House and is expected to be voted on the week after next.

Climate Activists Condemn “Slimmed-Down” COP31 Draft Text That Makes No Reference to Fossil Fuels

Nov 20, 2026

Here at the COP31 U.N. climate summit, negotiators published a “slimmed-down” draft text on Thursday that stripped out any reference to fossil fuels, or ending their use. Instead, the document promotes carbon capture and storage, an unproven technology that critics say will never have a meaningful impact on the climate crisis. Activists at the COP are demanding more financing to help poorer countries adapt to a warming world. This is Iona Stewart of the climate action group Global Witness.

Emily Iona Stewart: “Mentions of human rights, especially human rights and environment defenders, which had previously been introduced by the Brazilians, are now being walked back in this cover decision. So that’s really worrying for us. Another thing: fossil fuels, still not in there. Where is the text on phasing out fossil fuels and having a concrete roadmap for all of the parties? We need that now. And then, finance. There’s not enough momentum on making sure that countries who have already signed up and pledged to give climate finance actually deliver on those pledges.”

Russian Attacks Kill 8 After Ukraine Bombs Bridge Connecting Russia to Occupied Crimea

Nov 20, 2026

In Ukraine, officials say eight people were killed and dozens injured overnight, as Russia launched a massive drone and missile attack. In Kyiv, Russian bombs struck three ⁠bridges over the Dnipro River. Meanwhile, in Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people.

The Russian attacks came after Ukraine bombed the Kerch Bridge, the only link between mainland Russia and Russian-annexed Crimea. Engineers say it could take years for Russia to repair the damage.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the bridge strike and warned of further action.

President Volodymyr Zelensky: “We have long been telling Russia: Enough of striking bridges, our cities and villages, Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, railways and grain ships. Enough of this war. But every time, Russia chooses a new escalation.”

Meanwhile, Poland’s military said it was investigating a suspected violation of its airspace by Russia near Poland’s border with Ukraine, after an unidentified object crash-landed this morning.

Charity Warns Record High 1 in 4 Children Now Live in Conflict Zones

Nov 20, 2026

A new report by Save the Children has found one in four children now live in conflict zones worldwide — a record high. In Africa, an unprecedented two in five children are impacted by conflict. Almost one-third of all violations against children documented last year took place in the Occupied Palestinian Territories, where Israeli attacks have killed at least 22,000 children since 2023.

11-Year-Old Palestinian Boy Dies of Wounds Amid Relentless Israeli Attacks on Gaza

Nov 20, 2026

In Gaza, 11-year-old Mansour Khader Nabhan has died of his wounds after he was bombed by an Israeli quadcopter in Jabaliya. In a separate strike, several children were wounded when an Israeli drone targeted a group of Palestinians, including some on their way to school. On Thursday, Israeli attacks left at least five Palestinians dead, including two people killed by a drone near a community kitchen serving displaced people in Gaza City.

Somali American Driver Is Assaulted After Trump Calls on Minnesotans to “Fight Back” Against Somalis

Nov 20, 2026

In Minnesota, a Somali American Uber driver is fighting for his life after he was allegedly run over multiple times with his own vehicle by a passenger who disliked his Muslim name. Mohamed Yusuf remained in critical condition Thursday with life-threatening injuries following Saturday’s attack. It follows last month’s raid on the D.C. home of Somali American Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar by federal agents. And it follows president Trump’s repeated racist attacks demonizing Somali American communities. Trump has called Somalis “garbage” and “low-IQ people” who “contribute nothing.” Just weeks ago, Trump wrote on social media, “Fight back Minnesota, fight back!”

“A Mockery of Court Orders”: Federal Judge Holds ICE in Contempt for Rearresting Immigrants

Nov 20, 2026

A Colorado federal judge has held ICE officials and the Trump administration in contempt over a practice to instantly rearrest immigrants after a court has ordered their release from ICE jail. In her ruling, U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte Sweeney wrote that ICE “made ⁠a mockery of court orders.” The ACLU has described the practice as “sham releases.” At the center of the case is the detention of Mexican immigrant Ramón Quintero Álvarez, who has lived in the U.S. for more than 30 years. Álvarez was immediately rearrested late last month shortly after his release from an Aurora ICE jail.

U.S. Appeals Court Freezes Deportation Protections for Venezuelan Immigrants

Nov 20, 2026

A federal appeals court is allowing the Trump administration to end, for now, deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan immigrants living in the U.S. This came as the Trump administration also filed an emergency appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court in its effort to end temporary protected status for an estimated 600,000 Venezuelans. Since returning to office, Trump has ended the humanitarian relief for well over a dozen countries as part of his mass deportation campaign.

Texas Death Row Prisoner Reinaldo Dennes Cries Out in Pain During Botched Execution

Nov 20, 2026

In Huntsville, Texas, a man on death row repeatedly moaned out in pain during a botched execution that took over an hour. Reinaldo Dennes remained strapped to a gurney as prison officials struggled to locate a vein to administer a lethal dose of pentobarbital. After more than an hour Thursday evening, vein lines were ultimately found in his neck and one of his feet. Seventy-year-old Dennes reportedly exclaimed that his leg felt like it was on fire. This comes just over a month after the botched execution attempt of Christa Pike in Tennessee that drew widespread condemnation. Pike survived two lethal injections and was left hospitalized in critical condition and unconscious for nearly a week. She’s now back in prison.

Florida Carries Out 20th Execution This Year, a Record Pace

Nov 20, 2026

Florida carried out a 20th execution this year, breaking its own record as the highest single-year total of executions in Florida since capital punishment was reinstated in 1976. Seventy-one-year-old Thomas Mitchell Overton was put to death by lethal injection Thursday. Florida has now carried out more than half of the nation’s 39 executions to date this year under Republican Governor Ron DeSantis. Two more are scheduled for December.

White House Taps GOP Operative and Lobbyist Eric Ueland to Lead Government Accountability Office

Nov 20, 2026

The White House has picked Eric Ueland to run the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s independent watchdog, for a 15-year term. Ueland is a longtime Republican operative who served as a Big Pharma and fossil fuel lobbyist before joining the Trump administration in 2016. Senate Republicans are skipping the bipartisan process used for every GAO head since 1980, in which top lawmakers submit a short list of candidates. Twenty-one inspectors general are urging congressional leaders to reject Ueland’s confirmation, writing, “the credibility of any oversight institution depends on two pillars: strict adherence to statutory safeguards designed to protect its independence, and leadership defined by proven, nonpartisan fidelity to objective evidence. Mr. Ueland’s nomination fails on both counts.”

Journalist Camilo Rodríquez, Who Exposed Costa Rican Politicians’ Drug Trafficking Ties, Is Murdered

Nov 20, 2026

In Costa Rica, journalist Camilo Rodríguez has been assassinated. Rodríguez gained prominence for exposing alleged links between suspected drug traffickers and Costa Rican politicians. Rodríguez had previously reported threats to his life.

This is the first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years.

World.title: How Do We Address Violence When It Comes from a Fellow Activist?
World.content:
Photo: Urci Dream/CC

If we want to transform power relations, that transformation must also take place among ourselves.

By Brisa Bucardo (Confidencial)

HAVANA TIMES – Throughout my life, I have learned to speak out against gender-based violence, political violence, abuse of power, and racist violence. My involvement with feminism has also led me to examine what I have learned and recognize how much of the machismo we challenge remains present in the ways we think and relate to one another.

However, I find it curious that when certain behaviors come from other women, something changes in the way I react. I begin looking for explanations, thinking about the violence that woman may have experienced, about the patterns we have all internalized. And sometimes, while trying to understand her, I end up not knowing how to set boundaries against what is hurting me, especially when we share the same spaces.

It is clear to me that machismo is also reproduced among women. It can appear in competition, discrediting others, controlling relationships, or the habit of turning women against one another. Recognizing its structural roots is important but understanding them does not mean overlooking these behaviors. Having experienced violence does not prevent us from perpetrating it, nor does our history of activism place us above the principles we defend.

Reflecting on this, I have come to realize that reacting to violence committed by another woman makes me feel as though I am betraying something fundamental to my own feminism. It sounds contradictory, but I am not the only one who experiences this. I know that setting boundaries should not make me feel guilty, but it does.

During my journey into forced exile, I experienced an attempted kidnapping. During that improvised escape, we trusted someone because he was an opponent of the dictatorship I was fleeing. Another person who helped me get out of that situation told me something I will never forget: “I thought that because he was an opposition activist, he was a good person.” I am not comparing that experience to situations that may arise within an organization, but I do remember what I learned then. Sharing a cause does not guarantee sharing ethical principles.

In exile, trust takes on particular importance. Many of us arrive after losing our homelands, routines, and loved ones, carrying wounds that did not begin with exile. Finding fellow women with whom we can connect helps us rebuild a sense of belonging. That is why, when trust is violated, the consequences can extend beyond a personal relationship and affect how we experience spaces we once considered our own.

There are ways of exercising power that do not require open threats. They can appear through constant interference in other people’s decisions, attempts to control relationships, or efforts to influence how people perceive one another. Sometimes an insinuation, a distorted account, or a seemingly well-intentioned expression of concern is enough to plant doubts. We do not always recognize these dynamics because we tend to look for violence in its more obvious forms.

Part of the political culture we challenge remains present in our own practices. We come from contexts where power struggles, silence, disparagement, and personal loyalties have shaped sociopolitical relationships. And sometimes we carry those same patterns into spaces that are supposed to operate horizontally. Disagreements are no longer discussed openly, competing accounts circulate in private conversations, and factions form. What seems to matter more is how many people support a position rather than what actually happened. I am not talking about organizing to denounce violence and demand justice, but about turning differences and tensions into struggles for influence.

I am particularly concerned when emotional bonds end up becoming political capital. When closeness seems to imply an obligation to support certain positions, when disagreeing or standing beside someone who is being mistreated by a person close to us is interpreted as disloyalty. We can know a fellow activist for years and still be unaware of how she treats other people. Affection should not replace our ethical judgment, nor should hearing one side of a story first prevent us from thinking for ourselves.

It is also important to recognize that we have the power to stop some of these practices, even when they come from someone we love. On one occasion, I listened to the account of someone very close to me and, rather than accepting it as the only truth, I also tried to approach the other person, without intending to take sides. Over time, as I observed certain attitudes and learned more about the situation, I realized that things were very different from how they had been described to me. The person initially portrayed as responsible for the conflict was actually being discredited and mistreated.

That experience led me to question a relationship I had valued until then, not because of a personal disagreement, but because I began to recognize behaviors I could no longer justify. It also made me think about how often, out of affection or loyalty, we may end up supporting practices that harm other women without even stopping to question them. Sometimes we also have a responsibility to break with those dynamics, even when doing so means reassessing our own relationships.

We talk a great deal about care within feminist movements, but what does it mean to care without reproducing power relations? Concern for another woman does not give us authority over her life, her relationships, or how she chooses to participate. Nor does commitment to a cause give us the right to interfere in everything. If we defend women’s autonomy, that commitment must be reflected in our everyday relationships.

In Central America, feminists have been subjected to attacks, hatred, and deeply sexist attempts to discredit us. That hostility has also influenced how we handle internal contradictions. I understand the fear that any criticism might be used to undermine our struggles. But how often have we ended up applying the saying that “dirty laundry should be washed at home”? And what happens when, even within that home, we cannot find the conditions to speak openly?

I worry that protecting an image of unity may become more important than examining our own practices. Silence should not become the price of defending a cause.

Not every disagreement constitutes violence, nor can we attribute intentions to others that we do not know. But we should not need an obvious act of aggression to question specific behaviors. Sometimes their consequences can be seen in the distrust they seek to generate, the relationships they damage, or the freedom that others feel they have lost.

When a situation involves women with whom we share affection and struggles, speaking out about what is happening can come at a cost. We wonder how others will react, what versions of events will circulate, or whether we will be able to continue participating without discomfort. Even without an explicit prohibition, we begin weighing our words and decisions. And those who listen also bear responsibility for what they repeat and the conclusions they draw.

We can care about a fellow activist while questioning her behavior, support her without endorsing everything she does, or distance ourselves without launching a campaign against her. No relationship should demand loyalties that take precedence over our principles.

And here another question arises for me. Why do we assume that every situation must end in reconciliation? Is it always necessary to sit face-to-face with someone who has hurt us to demonstrate political maturity? Some conversations make it possible to acknowledge mistakes and repair relationships, but insisting on such an encounter can be retraumatizing if a woman feels she must agree to it in order to maintain her place within a group.

After a breach of trust or an experience of violence, it is not always possible to return to normal. Some encounters create tension, conversations in which we carefully measure every word, and spaces that no longer feel comfortable. Coexistence cannot be built on an obligation to pretend that nothing happened.

I also think about the women who eventually withdraw. Some stop attending meetings, making proposals, or taking on responsibilities, not because they have stopped believing in a cause, but because staying has become exhausting. From the outside, those absences may be mistaken for a lack of interest. How many fellow activists have we lost without asking ourselves what conditions made it difficult for them to continue?

Perhaps part of my feminist learning process involves accepting this contradiction and no longer thinking that questioning a fellow activist means abandoning my convictions. I also feel the need to bring into the open issues that we often avoid discussing publicly for fear that doing so will be interpreted as a lack of unity. But what good is defending our unity if maintaining it requires us to give up questioning ourselves?

I believe we need to develop collective ways of addressing these situations without depending on personal affinities or on who holds the most influence within a group. This means listening without automatically accepting one version of events, recognizing power imbalances, setting boundaries against practices that discredit others, and creating conditions in which women can speak about what they are experiencing without fear of losing their place.

It also means understanding that not every situation can be resolved through reconciliation, and that distancing ourselves from someone should not prevent us from continuing to share a common struggle.

This is not about demanding perfect relationships or pretending that our organizations are free of contradictions. It is about accepting the political responsibility to examine them and act when we identify harmful practices.

If we want to transform power relations, that transformation must also take place among ourselves. And perhaps a more genuine way of building unity is to stop confusing it with always agreeing and instead ground it in our ability to question ourselves, acknowledge responsibility, and ensure that no fellow activist has to choose between her dignity and her political participation.

First published in Spanish by Confidencial and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Nicaragua here on Havana Times.

World.title: Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro hospitalised in Brasília with abdominal pain
World.content:
Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro hospitalised in Brasília with abdominal pain

21st Saturday, November 2026 - 06:25 UTC Full article

Jair Bolsonaro surrounded by security officers.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted to hospital in Brasília on Friday after suffering abdominal pain and distension, according to a statement from the medical centre where he remains. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, under house arrest on health grounds.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted to hospital in Brasília on Friday after suffering abdominal pain and distension, according to a statement from the medical centre where he remains. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, under house arrest on health grounds.

Doctors carried out a series of tests to determine the cause of his symptoms, the hospital said. News of his admission was first given on X by his son Carlos Bolsonaro, elected senator in October's elections, who spoke of “intense abdominal pain”.

Bolsonaro, who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2022, was convicted by the Supreme Federal Court in September 2025 and has been serving his sentence since that year. He was granted house arrest at his home in Brasília on humanitarian grounds. Since 2018, when he was stabbed in the abdomen at a campaign event, he has undergone several surgeries and been hospitalised on numerous occasions.

His eldest son, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, lost the October 25 presidential run-off to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, did not concede defeat and left Brazil via the Argentine border bound for the United States. From 2027, four members of the Bolsonaro family will hold seats in Brazil's Congress.

World.title: Trump threatens to penalise tech companies that build data centres outside the US
World.content:
Trump threatens to penalise tech companies that build data centres outside the US

21st Saturday, November 2026 - 06:22 UTC Full article

Donald Trump waves as he boards Air Force One.

US President Donald Trump on Friday threatened to penalise American technology companies that build data centres abroad, through tariffs or other levies, although he did not explain what goal he was pursuing or how he would enforce the measure, and acknowledged he had not even presented the idea to his team.

US President Donald Trump on Friday threatened to penalise American technology companies that build data centres abroad, through tariffs or other levies, although he did not explain what goal he was pursuing or how he would enforce the measure, and acknowledged he had not even presented the idea to his team.

“We are not going to allow companies to build data centres in other countries,” Trump said at a White House press conference, where he promised “tremendous punishments” for companies that try. Such a measure would likely face opposition from the companies affected and from Congress, which Democrats will control from January.

The threat comes amid heightened Washington scrutiny of data centres in third countries. The Commerce Department last week announced measures to prevent countries deemed a risk, such as China, from accessing Nvidia's most advanced chips through remote use of data centres located in other countries. The investigation centres on Megaspeed, a Singapore company that bought billions of dollars' worth of chips from Nvidia and whose former executive, Alice Huang, is suspected by Washington of spying for China.

The case led to the resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive, after it emerged that he had an extramarital relationship with her. Trump again called for his return to the helm of the company, something Nvidia has said it is not considering. Huang may have made “bad decisions”, the president said, but “he is a brilliant man. We have to protect our brilliant men, and Jensen is one of them.”

Trump was speaking to review his Thursday meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. At his bilateral meeting with Xi, the two countries agreed to hold consultations to establish safeguards and warning mechanisms for possible problems in the development of the most advanced artificial intelligence models.

The president insisted that data centres are key to winning the artificial intelligence race and pledged to “fight hard” for them, despite growing opposition among Americans. According to El País, in this month's midterm elections voters approved 40 of the 41 measures put to referendums in various states to ban or restrict their construction.

World.title: UK and EU sign their biggest deal since Brexit in Brussels
World.content:
UK and EU sign their biggest deal since Brexit in Brussels

20th Friday, November 2026 - 19:42 UTC Full article

The flags of the United Kingdom and the European Union at the European Commission headquarters in Brussels.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa signed three agreements in Brussels on Friday on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility, the largest package agreed between the two sides since Britain left the European Union, a decade after the Brexit referendum.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa signed three agreements in Brussels on Friday on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility, the largest package agreed between the two sides since Britain left the European Union, a decade after the Brexit referendum.

“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe,” said Burnham, who called the agreement “landmark”. Von der Leyen described it as “a turning point” in relations. In a joint statement, both sides committed to building an “ambitious and dynamic” relationship, according to AP. It is the second summit between the two sides since Brexit; the first, held in London in May 2025, opened the negotiations that concluded on Friday.

The first agreement creates a common sanitary and phytosanitary area that will scrap checks on trade in animal and plant products, including goods moving between Great Britain, Northern Ireland and the EU. The British government puts its impact at £5.1 billion a year, about US$6.7 billion, although it will not apply before March 1, 2028, as the UK must pass legislation to align dynamically with EU rules. The second links the two sides' emissions trading systems, exempting British companies from the EU's carbon border levy from 2028. The third creates a scheme allowing 100,000 young people from each side to live in the other's territory for up to three years to work, study or travel. Burnham pitched the package as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people”.

Open questions remain, however. According to a member-state document obtained by AFP, the 27 are making ratification conditional on the UK lowering university fees paid by European students, currently higher than those paid by Britons; two diplomats cited by the press point to a compromise. Nor was British access to the EU's industrial programme resolved, which Brussels makes conditional on London aligning its trade policy, including tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The British government acknowledged that “talks will continue in some areas”.

Burnham, in power since July, announced he will open a discussion with European partners on “options for the long-term relationship,” ranging from maintaining the status quo to a customs union or membership, and did not rule out his party including re-entry in its next election manifesto. The next general election is due in 2029.

The opposition reacted sharply. “Naive Andy Burnham has gone to Brussels and run into the hard reality I have been warning about for decades. Flexibility is a fantasy,” Reform UK leader Nigel Farage wrote on X. The Conservatives accused the prime minister of “betrayal” of Brexit.

World.title: Buenos Aires marks King Charles's birthday with a reconciliation message amid bilateral tension
World.content:
Buenos Aires marks King Charles's birthday with a reconciliation message amid bilateral tension

20th Friday, November 2026 - 14:21 UTC Full article

Guests and the Northlands school pupils' choir at the British ambassador's residence in Buenos Aires, during the reception marking King Charles's birthday.

The British Embassy in Buenos Aires celebrated King Charles III's 78th birthday on Thursday with a reception at which Ambassador David Cairns defended the strength of ties with Argentina despite “not-so-good days” and announced that in 2027 the 45th anniversary of the Falklands War will be marked together with veterans and families of the fallen from both countries.

The British Embassy in Buenos Aires celebrated King Charles III's 78th birthday on Thursday with a reception at which Ambassador David Cairns defended the strength of ties with Argentina despite “not-so-good days” and announced that in 2027 the 45th anniversary of the Falklands War will be marked together with veterans and families of the fallen from both countries.

“In international relations, as in personal relationships, there can be good days and not-so-good days,” Cairns told some 800 guests from politics, the judiciary, business, diplomacy and culture gathered at the ambassador's residence. “I am the 56th British ambassador to Argentina, and as such I will continue working to strengthen the ties between our two countries. I am convinced we will enjoy more good days than not-so-good days.”

As an example of that strength, the ambassador recalled last year's celebrations of the bicentenary of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and announced that next year the 45th anniversary of the “South Atlantic conflict” will be marked “with respect and sensitivity, working together with veterans and the families of the fallen in both countries to promote reconciliation and friendship”. Cairns also highlighted values associated with the monarch, such as diversity, inclusion and care for nature: “Countries are stronger when their societies are diverse and open.”

The celebration, held as a garden party, included the British and Argentine national anthems performed by the pupils' choir of Northlands school, performances by the Orquesta de los Barrios, a programme for young musicians from disadvantaged backgrounds, and a mural by artist Costhanzo featuring British and Argentine icons. The event was sponsored by British and Argentine companies, including Pan American Energy, BP and Standard Chartered.

The reception took place two days after Javier Milei's government rejected Princess Anne's visit to the islands as a “provocation”, and nine days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rules on Argentina's request to halt the Sea Lion oil project.

World.title: Brazil's Central Bank sells US$1 billion to curb the dollar's rise
World.content:
Brazil's Central Bank sells US$1 billion to curb the dollar's rise

20th Friday, November 2026 - 04:27 UTC Full article

A person walks past the Central Bank of Brazil headquarters in Brasília.

Brazil's Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its international reserves on Thursday in an attempt to curb the rise of the US currency, which approached 5.93 reais, amid financial market distrust of the fiscal adjustment proposed by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government. The move brought initial relief, but the dollar rose again in the afternoon.

Brazil's Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its international reserves on Thursday in an attempt to curb the rise of the US currency, which approached 5.93 reais, amid financial market distrust of the fiscal adjustment proposed by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government. The move brought initial relief, but the dollar rose again in the afternoon.

The intervention follows several days of falls on the São Paulo stock exchange and a sharp depreciation of the real, which makes imports more expensive, especially fuel, and puts pressure on inflation. Investors doubt the government's ability to control spending and stabilise public debt, which exceeds 92% of gross domestic product.

The spending containment plan, already approved by the Senate, will be voted on next week in the Chamber of Deputies. The government estimated savings of between 50 billion and 60 billion reais in 2027, between US$8.4 billion and US$10.1 billion, although the figure may change due to amendments made in Congress. One of its pillars caps growth in public spending above inflation at 2% a year, down from the current 2.5%. Part of the market considers the plan insufficient.

The adjustment has drawn criticism from the Brazilian left, particularly from sectors to the left of the Workers' Party, who fear cuts to health and education. Lula said on Thursday that “some comrades” had not understood the proposal and pledged that, as long as he is president, “there will be no reduction in the rights the Brazilian people have won”. He told the market that he too wants fiscal control, but criticised the moves of recent days: “What is really happening is that there are people trying to make money from speculation, from rumours.”

Lula, re-elected on October 25, has not announced who will be his economy minister for the term that begins on January 5, another source of uncertainty. The current minister, Dario Durigan, expressed concern about the pace of the economy in 2027, although he ruled out a recession. According to the Central Bank's latest survey of analysts, published on November 16, growth will slow from 2.3% in 2025 to 1.7% this year and 1% in 2027. The benchmark Selic interest rate stands at 13.75% a year, after the Central Bank halted a cycle of five consecutive cuts in November.

World.title: Colombia to euthanise hippos for the first time: ten animals in four months
World.content:
Colombia to euthanise hippos for the first time: ten animals in four months

20th Friday, November 2026 - 04:24 UTC Full article

A female hippo with her calf in the Magdalena River basin, Colombia.

Colombia's government will for the first time carry out chemical euthanasia on hippopotamuses, an invasive species in the country since drug lord Pablo Escobar brought the first animals to his estate in the 1980s. The Environment Ministry announced on Wednesday that ten animals in Antioquia department, located near populated areas, will be put down over the next four months.

Colombia's government will for the first time carry out chemical euthanasia on hippopotamuses, an invasive species in the country since drug lord Pablo Escobar brought the first animals to his estate in the 1980s. The Environment Ministry announced on Wednesday that ten animals in Antioquia department, located near populated areas, will be put down over the next four months.

The measure is part of the first phase of the national plan for the prevention, control and management of the hippopotamus, which also includes sterilisation, relocation and confinement, along with population monitoring, work with communities and environmental education. The pilot phase has a budget of about 500 million Colombian pesos, and the next would require more than 8 billion, funding that has yet to be confirmed. The ministry is working with experts from South Africa on techniques for capturing hippos in water, and has not ruled out moving animals to a wildlife rescue centre in India.

Among the animals selected is one that appeared in late July in the river used daily by 23 schoolchildren in Puerto Nare, and those seen a week ago in a video crossing a road at night in Puerto Triunfo. At least three people have been injured in attacks in the Magdalena Medio region, one of whom is now in a wheelchair.

“Ethically and environmentally it is the best measure. And it had to be taken sooner or later,” said David Echeverri of Cornare, the regional environmental agency that has managed the species for 15 years and has castrated 58 animals. “What we want is for it to be as soon as possible and painless,” he said. Echeverri stressed that it is a long-term plan: “We will be able to say the problem is over when the sterilised hippos die of old age and the problematic ones are gone. That is years away.”

The decision marks a turnaround for Environment Minister Fabio Arjona, who on taking office had proposed a sanctuary for the species and said that “it is cheaper to keep them than to kill them”.

Some 250 hippos live in Colombia, spread over about 2,000 square kilometres of the basin of the Magdalena River, the country's main waterway. The Humboldt Institute warns that, without control, they could reach 1,000 by 2035. Scientists warn of their impact on native species and water quality. The only previous lethal intervention was in 2009, when an animal known as Pepe was shot.

World.title: Trump, Putin and Xi hold their first three-way summit, rich in symbolism but short on announcements
World.content:
Trump, Putin and Xi hold their first three-way summit, rich in symbolism but short on announcements

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 18:38 UTC Full article

Putin, Xi and Trump arrive together for their first trilateral summit on Thursday in Shenzhen.

US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the three powers in Shenzhen on Thursday, an encounter rich in symbolism that ended with a commitment to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks but no concrete measures.

US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the three powers in Shenzhen on Thursday, an encounter rich in symbolism that ended with a commitment to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks but no concrete measures.

“We are truly making history,” Trump said during the nearly hour-and-a-half meeting, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lower the risk of those weapons being used,” he added. “Everything possible must be done to prevent a nuclear war,” Xi said, adding that “the seeds sown at today's trilateral meeting will surely take root”. Putin recalled that the three countries were “the victors of World War II” and share “responsibility for maintaining international peace and security”.

According to the declaration issued after the meeting, the three leaders committed to “engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation”, and agreed to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products. The text also states that “the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”, upholds respect for the immunity of state officials and calls for reform of the United Nations. The International Criminal Court has an outstanding arrest warrant for Putin.

The New START treaty, which limited the US and Russian nuclear arsenals, expired in February 2026. Trump has proposed replacing it with an agreement that includes China, which in turn demands that Washington and Moscow first reduce their arsenals. “We need more than diplomatic theatre and photo opportunities,” Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, told AP.

The summit marked a new step in Putin's return to the international stage. Trump, who had not met him since their Alaska summit in August 2025, called him a “friend”. “God protect us from friends like that,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk responded on X. European governments and Ukraine had feared the three leaders would discuss the country's future without Kyiv at the table.

Trump and Xi will meet again at the G20 summit on December 14 and 15 at the Trump National Doral resort in Florida. Putin has not decided whether he will attend. “I will think about it. We will see,” he said.

World.title: UK Parliament briefing details London's response to Argentina's offensive against Sea Lion
World.content:
UK Parliament briefing details London's response to Argentina's offensive against Sea Lion

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 18:35 UTC Full article

Flags of Britain's Overseas Territories fly near the Houses of Parliament in Westminster, London.

The House of Commons Library has published a research briefing setting out the response of Andy Burnham's government to Argentina's legal, economic and diplomatic offensive against the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, nine days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea decides whether to order a halt.

The House of Commons Library has published a research briefing setting out the response of Andy Burnham's government to Argentina's legal, economic and diplomatic offensive against the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, nine days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea decides whether to order a halt.

The document, prepared by researchers Patrick Butchard, John Curtis and Philip Loft, is not a government statement but an analysis intended to inform lawmakers, Infobae reported. It reviews four fronts of Argentina's offensive this year: the reaffirmation of sovereignty at the UN General Assembly, sanctions against some 60 individuals and companies linked to exploration, the revival of construction at the Ushuaia naval base, and the case before the Hamburg tribunal. “The UK government has said it will contest the legal case and introduce protections for businesses operating” in the islands, it summarises.

Those responses include the business guidance published in September by Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran, which states that the islanders “have the right to develop their natural resources as they see fit”, with the government's “full support” for companies. In October, London announced measures under its Protection of Trading Interests legislation so that British companies “can continue to make commercial decisions in accordance with UK law” despite Argentine sanctions.

The briefing devotes a section to the United States. It recalls that Donald Trump said in August his administration was reviewing its traditional neutrality on sovereignty over the islands, and that Burnham subsequently raised with him “the economic consequences of Argentina's coercive measures for the UK and the US”. Citing Argentine media, it says Washington's concern over possible sanctions on US companies may have led Buenos Aires to slow down its sovereignty defence bill.

That bill suffered a fresh setback on Wednesday: the Chamber of Deputies session called to debate it collapsed for lack of quorum, with 126 deputies present, three short of the 129 needed, after the Provincias Unidas and MID blocs refused to take their seats over objections to the articles on foreign interference and freedom of expression.

Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno defended the legal route the same day. “This arbitration focuses on the exploitation of natural resources while the underlying issue has not been decided,” he told a legal forum in Buenos Aires. “Once a drop of oil is extracted, that drop cannot be recovered.” Quirno said that, whatever the decision on November 28, “the arbitration continues”.

Sea Lion, operated by Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum about 220 kilometres north of the islands, has estimated reserves of 1.7 billion barrels and is expected to begin drilling in January 2027.

World.title: Chicano baby: The Mexican lowriders challenging gang stereotypes
World.content:
Every Sunday, a special kind of meetup takes place in downtown Mexico City: a few dozen men and women gather in oversized white shirts and baggy jeans with blue bandanas hanging from their pockets, all sporting gleaming silver lowrider bicycles.

Inspired by the Mexican-American Chicano communities of 1960s and ‘70s California, their style is often associated with cholos: a Los Angeles street culture that has long been stereotyped as synonymous with gang violence.

But that’s exactly what this group wants to challenge. They are here to represent a subculture shaped by migration and marginalization, honor its heritage and scrap the stigma of violence attached to it.

“We represent culture, that’s it,” Hiram, a member for two years, explains.

Most members in this report chose to be identified by first name only, citing privacy reasons.

“We are not violent, we are not a gang. We’re here so people can see us, see we’re not bad guys.”

Finding support and love

This wanna-not-be gang is strikingly intergenerational. There are little kids in gangster white face paint running between the bikes, veteran-looking men covered in tattoos, a mother and her teenage son — a real family, as the group’s name “Mexican Family” would have it.

“Many of us come from a dysfunctional family; we find support and love from people who aren’t blood. That was the primary purpose of creating this group,” explains el jefe, Babo, who founded the group three years ago.

The members meet every week, tinker and ride their bikes — all hand-wrought from different bicycle parts and adorned with jewels — pose with passersby and invite people to try their bikes.

Contrary to what its aesthetics would suggest, not all of them share the Chicano identity.

At its origin, Chicano was used as a derogatory term for the Mexican-American working class in the U.S. before activists in the 1960s and ‘70s reclaimed the identity as a symbol of resistance and pride.

Some members of the group are Mexican-American, others have been deported from the United States over the years, and many of the youngsters are just Mexican.

What brings them together is a shared love of lowrider bicycles and cars, as well as an appreciation for what Chicano identity symbolizes.

“It’s tradition, history, resistance,” explains a young Mexican member with no ties to the U.S., who goes by the name Estonet. “Chicano means keeping Mexican culture alive anywhere in the world.”

Tessie joined a year ago to spend time with her teenage son, a lowrider fan. She wants people to stop associating the club with gangs. The point, she says, is to “go slow and happy on a bike, no matter which one it is.”

But the stigmatization of this culture mostly comes from its association with the cholos.

Unpacking the term ‘cholo’

Cholo also began as an insult, a colonial-era slur for people of mixed Indigenous and European descent, before Mexican-American youth in Los Angeles reclaimed it as a style, taking visual influences from Chicano culture such as the lowrider bicycles and cars.

Over time, however, police discrimination and popularization through gangster films such as “Blood In Blood Out” (1993) made the term synonymous with dangerous gangs.

“For better or for worse, culture changes,” el jefe continues. “The cholo has more to do with gangs, with prison.”

Some members’ own pasts are not far removed from those associations.

Hiram, who self-deported from the United States nearly two years ago after getting into a car accident and fearing imprisonment, says most of the older members of the group used to be in gangs.

“Arriving somewhere that receives you with open arms is very hard… you don’t know the problems you had, the gangs you were in.”

Joining the group, he says, has been “like going back to the place where something was missing.”

1 of 11

A family affair

Juan, who brought his lowrider car to one of Mexican Family’s Día de Muertos parades with his teenage daughter, shares the same sentiment. “We grew up in the street, but we’re here because we don’t need the street anymore,” he says.

“Ten years ago, you could not have seen us here all together, from different barrios,” he says, alluding to the fact that many of them were members of different street gangs here in the city.

For Alvin, who grew up without papers in the U.S. and voluntarily came back to Mexico five years ago, his membership in the group is a family homage.

“My father was a cholo. I grew up watching my dad with all the bikes, these cars,” he says.

In this way, Mexican Family seems to have also become an asylum for men with troubled pasts to start anew, without forgetting the culture that raised them.

Toeing the line between bravado and vulnerability, the group could be accused of glorifying the violence attached to gang aesthetics. But perhaps what it does best is hold space for the complexity of an identity crossed by a multitude of borders, subject to poverty, marginalization and all too often, violence — and seek to redefine it as a community united by culture, pride and family.

Mathilde Hourticq is a multi-platform journalist based in Mexico City covering breaking news, subcultures, youth issues and many other things in between. Her video-journalism has appeared on the Associated Press, AFP, and Press Association.

World.title: ‘Trading Places’: A new podcast by Mexico News Daily
World.content:
The team at MND is excited to be launching a new podcast series to complement our existing “Confidently Wrong” podcast and “MND Hits the Streets” series of videos.

Cesar Martinez will be joining me as the co-host of Trading Places. Both Cesar and I have, in fact, traded places. I was born in Wisconsin and now live in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato, after having lived, studied, worked, or traveled in Mexico for over 30 years. Cesar was born in Mexico City and now lives in Los Angeles, California. Cesar has spent over 40 years living in the United States, between Texas and California.

Each episode, Cesar and I will speak about Mexico with a different person of Mexican heritage (first and second generation Mexican Americans) living in the United States. We will reflect on how the guests’ perceptions of Mexico have evolved and changed (and why) as well as their current thoughts on the country, its leadership and its future. We will explore if they are feeling more of a pull towards (or away) from Mexico, and if so, why. We will review how their children’s views on Mexico differ from their own, and how theirs differs from those of their parents. We will, of course, also discuss the evolving relationship between the United States and Mexico, and what that means for both countries.

The goal of the podcast is to encourage the nearly 40 million Mexican diaspora living in the United States to reflect on their own relationship with Mexico and hopefully inspire them — each in their own way — to build a stronger connection with the country. We believe that there is a significant opportunity for the U.S. population of Mexican descent to have an outsized impact on the economic growth and overall well being of Mexico and want to provide a platform to share inspiring case studies and stories.

Please tune in, get informed, and get inspired!

Check out the first episode of MND’s Trading Places here:

We Both Left Our Home Country—for Opposite Sides of the Border | Trading Places - Episode 1
