Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Is education the biggest challenge facing Mexico? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Let me start with why I’m writing about this, because I know education can often feel like a heavy or hopeless topic. I’m not here to lecture. I’m writing because this is as much a business issue as a social one. Mexico became the largest supplier of goods to the U.S. in 2023 and now accounts for over 18% of U.S. imports. That partnership depends on a Mexican workforce that can keep learning as technology changes, and reading and learning are foundational to that workforce. When that foundation weakens, it affects Mexican families, the companies that employ them, and the U.S. businesses and consumers who rely on them.

The U.S. and Mexico don’t face the same problem. In the U.S., student achievement is slipping from a higher level. In Mexico, the problem is structural: Too many students never build strong reading and math foundations to begin with. I also see an opportunity here. Used practically and skillfully, artificial intelligence could change what’s possible in education. For example, early studies show well-designed AI tutors can help students learn faster, and simple tools on a basic phone can reach classrooms short on teachers and resources. It’s no cure-all, but it gives us something new to work with.

I was perhaps a bit slow in recognizing the scale or seriousness of the education problem here in Mexico. Having done business in the country for over 30 years now, to be honest most of my interaction in the business world was with professionals in corporate environments — people who went to private schools and had college degrees. Of course in non-business settings I interacted with people of all walks of life and different levels of education throughout the country, but the scale of the problem didn’t really hit me until we purchased MND and I began researching more about Mexico’s educational results and the impacts its having on productivity and growth.

I have written about how Mexico’s education problem is translating into a productivity problem (which ultimately translates into an economic growth problem) here: Mexico has a labor productivity problem: Our CEO’s perspective and here: Productivity brings prosperity: Is Mexico really failing at both? A perspective from our CEO.

Mexico’s public schools have always had their challenges, but when compared against other OECD countries, the country was doing OK, and the results were slowly getting better. But this year’s recently released PISA results squashed just about any reason for optimism. Mexico’s results, compared to other OECD countries, are getting worse. Compared to its own prior years’ results, the country is losing ground in all three focus areas of testing: reading, mathematics and science. The statistic that most jumped out to me was that only half of Mexican 15-year-olds can read at a high enough level to enable further learning. I recently wrote about it here: Mexico fails the 2025 PISA evaluation: A perspective from our CEO.

To make matters worse, the workplace is quickly evolving. The old basic assembly and manufacturing jobs that lifted so many people out of poverty around the world aren’t what they used to be. Automation and robotics are doing an increasing amount of that work, forcing workers to learn new skills or be replaced and be out of work. Artificial intelligence is quickly proving to be a superpower for those who have the education to learn and apply it, and a massive potential disruptor to those who do not. Last year, I wrote a three-part series on why and how I think Mexico needs to start evolving its economy, given what is likely coming in technology disruption:

The thought of a workforce that is no longer needed for most manufacturing jobs and yet unable to learn new skills to find other types of work should scare all of us. The question is, what can be done about it? The solutions are not easy, but the team at MND is committed to helping do our part. Here are some specific examples of what we have done so far, and what is coming:

1. We had our team do a deep dive report, beyond the most recent PISA scores, to get a data-driven view on how Mexico is doing in educational attainment and results. We wanted to create and publish a data-driven baseline as a starting point on a topic that can very quickly get emotional in the absence of solid numbers. We published that report recently as part of our ongoing Mexico Well-being Series.

2. As a follow-up to the PISA results and the MND report, I recently took a trip to the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia to learn more. Why UPENN? Because they are one of the leading universities in the world in education policy, training leaders from across the world (including Mexico) on how to improve educational systems. They also have a rock-star, world-renowned professor named Dr. Sharon Ravitch who is on the leading edge of researching how AI could be an accelerator for kids (and school districts, and countries) to improve educational results. I met with Dr. Ravitch and reviewed with her my concerns about Mexico’s educational system and what I think is one of the biggest challenges holding back Mexico.

3. Dr. Ravitch was concerned about the PISA scores, inspired by our reporting, and understood the challenge facing Mexico. She has had both personal and professional connections with the country and wanted to help. So she gathered a group of Mexican and Mexican American doctoral graduates of an executive doctoral program at UPENN’s Global School of Education. The group, who hail from across the U.S., has studied issues related to education and equity. They offered to create a special series of articles for MND diagnosing the problems and suggesting a range of practical solutions, while taking into account the reality of where Mexico is today and the challenges and opportunities created by AI.

Starting this week, MND will be publishing a weekly installment on this topic. The team has worked hard to ensure that these articles are written to educate, inform and inspire action. They are not written for federal government policymakers, but rather for the rest of us who are concerned about the problem and looking for ways to contribute. They are written for locals and foreigners living in Mexico hoping to help, for the Mexican diaspora living abroad who want to make a difference, and for business and NGO leaders seeking suggestions and solutions.

4. Of course, Mexico News Daily also continues to publish articles for children on our MND Kids platform. This site is in both Spanish and English and provides students, parents and educators an easy-to-use digital tool to teach reading via real MND news stories about Mexico that have been rewritten for kids. If you haven’t checked it out yet, you can join the thousands already using the platform here: mndkids.com.

If the importance of this topic resonates with you, please follow the series each week, share it with someone who could help, and tell us how you’d like to be involved — whether as a contributor, partner, volunteer, school connection or supporter. Just put your thoughts in the comments or write to us directly at mndadmin@mexiconewsdaily.com. The more people who engage, the faster we can turn good ideas into real results for Mexican students.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: How the Vikings and 49ers are training for Mexico City’s thin air
World.content:
The San Francisco 49ers headed for the mountains. The Minnesota Vikings brought thin air indoors. Before meeting Sunday night in Mexico City, two of the NFL’s best teams have taken different routes to prepare for the altitude.

The high-scoring 49ers — No. 1 in the ESPN Power Rankings with an 8-1 record — have spent the week training at the Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs, Colorado, where the practice field sits about 7,250 feet above sea level.

Meanwhile, the Vikings — a defensive powerhouse tied for first in the NFC North at 7-2 — stayed home, using a temporary altitude chamber at their Minnesota practice facility in advance of a Saturday flight to Mexico.

The challenge awaits at Estadio Banorte, better known as Estadio Azteca, about 7,352 feet above sea level — more than 2,000 feet higher than Denver. Reduced oxygen can accelerate fatigue, making preparation another part of the matchup.

The 49ers flew directly from Dallas after their 46-40 victory over the Cowboys last Sunday, repeating the Colorado training approach they used before beating Arizona in Mexico City in 2022.

The 49ers brought cooks, strength and conditioning equipment and rehabilitation resources to Colorado Springs. Their flight to Mexico is also scheduled for Saturday.

Minnesota’s preparations have included cardio workouts in the altitude room over about five weeks, using stationary bikes and a treadmill. Nearly the entire roster has completed at least five sessions, with simulated elevations gradually increasing from 9,000 to 12,000 feet, according to the team.

The 49ers already have one international result this year supporting their approach.

For their season opener in Melbourne, the 49ers arrived a week before kickoff. The Los Angeles Rams prepared at home, treating the trip more like a routine road game, arrived later and got pummeled 27-7.

Sunday’s game in Mexico City, which will kick off locally at 7:20 p.m., ends a four-year NFL absence from Mexico. An anticipated return in 2025 fell through because of renovations ahead of the 2026 World Cup.

Sunday’s game will be Mexico City’s sixth regular-season NFL contest and San Francisco’s third. The league has committed to games there through 2028.

The last Mexico City NFL game was on Nov. 21, 2022, when the 49ers beat the Arizona Cardinals 38-10 before an announced crowd of 78,427 at Estadio Azteca.

Ticket demand for this week has been enormous, with nearly 840,000 fans registering for tickets by early October. Official prices were advertised from 2,108 pesos (US $117) to 11,656 pesos ($649), and the NFL says the roughly 87,000-seat venue is sold out.

EFE reported Friday that resale upper-level end-zone seats on StubHub were listed from US $462 to US $815, while some premium and VIP listings across resale sites reached US $21,000.

As for Sunday’s important NFC matchup, it pits the NFL’s most productive offense against its stingiest scoring defense.

San Francisco, which will be the designated home team, leads the NFL in total offense at 399.8 yards per game and ranks second in scoring at 31.2 points per game.

49ers quarterback Mark Purdy, a leading MVP candidate, has completed 70.1% of his passes for 2,369 yards, 20 touchdowns and five interceptions. He leads the league at 9 yards per pass attempt and threw for 389 yards and three touchdowns without an interception against the Cowboys.

Running back Christian McCaffrey also had a big game against Dallas, catching four passes for 161 yards and two touchdowns and rushing for 62 yards and another TD. The 49ers outgained the Cowboys 584-439 in total offense.

Minnesota allows a league-low 14 points per game and leads the NFL with 37 sacks. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ unit has surrendered just six touchdown passes in nine games and is coming off an eight-sack, four-takeaway performance in a 30-10 victory over Green Bay.

Kirk Cousins will make his second start since the Las Vegas Raiders traded him to Minnesota — and will face San Francisco for the second time in three weeks. He threw three interceptions against the 49ers in his final game with Las Vegas in Week 9.

The 49ers have been the top-selling team on NFL Shop in Mexico for five years, underscoring their popularity in the league’s largest market outside the United States. They are expected to draw a heavily partisan crowd Sunday, giving the game a home-field feel.

Kickoff is at 8:20 p.m. EST. The game will air on NBC and Peacock in the United States, TSN and CTV in Canada, and Canal 5 and ESPN in Mexico. Paid streaming options are also available.

With reports from The Sporting News, 49ers Webzone and Bleacher Report

World.title: Former Iguala mayor sentenced to 60 years for Ayotzinapa-related crimes
World.content:
A former mayor from the state of Guerrero was sentenced to 60 years in prison for his role in the infamous September 2014 Ayotzinapa case in which six people were killed and 43 students disappeared.

José Luis Abarca — along with 25 co-defendants, including the former municipal police chief — was found guilty of six counts of aggravated homicide and multiple counts of attempted murder in incidents related to the attack on the students in the town of Iguala.

Abarca, the former mayor of Iguala, is currently in a federal prison in the state of Coahuila serving 20 years for the murder of Justino Carbajal, a social activist killed in March 2013, and 92 years for the kidnapping and murder of members of the Popular Unity Peasant Movement (UPEZ) later that same year.

The 60-year sentence was handed down on Nov. 10 by a federal judge in the state of Tamaulipas after Abarca and his co-defendants were found guilty of firing upon a bus carrying members of the Los Avispones soccer team in a case of mistaken identity, among other crimes.

The horrific events of Sept. 26-27, 2014, were triggered by Abarca, his municipal police force and members of a local drug cartel, after students from the nearby Ayotzinapa Teachers College allegedly hijacked a bus in Iguala.

Police and cartel gunmen gave chase and attacked the bus carrying the soccer team as it returned to town following a match, killing the driver and a 15-year-old player. A woman in a nearby taxi was also killed.

Three Ayotzinapa students were later found dead, and investigations continue into the “disappearance” of the 43 other students. Federal authorities presented “four new lines of investigation” in the case eight weeks ago.

Abarca fled Iguala on Sept. 30 and was captured in the Mexico City borough of Iztapalapa six weeks later. He was ruled guilty as “the instigator” of the attack.

Felipe Flores Velázquez, the Iguala police chief, was arrested after two years on the run when he sneaked back to Iguala to visit his wife. Flores was convicted of being “the indirect perpetrator” of the murders.

Abarca’s lawyer objected to the ruling, saying the judge failed to take into account that the former mayor was not in charge of the local police at the time.

He argued that Abarca had earlier ceded control of the force to then-Governor Ángel Aguirre who was arrested three months ago on charges that he destroyed evidence related to the Ayotzinapa case.

With reports from El Universal, La Jornada, Infobae and El Financiero

World.title: Legislator apologizes for fumigating a Monterrey park full of migrating monarch butterflies
World.content:
Lorena de la Garza, a local legislator in the northern state of Nuevo León, has issued a public apology after members of her team conducted pest-control spraying in a public park, where monarch butterflies were resting during their migratory journey.

The incident in the state capital of Monterrey drew criticism from residents and prompted environmental authorities to intervene and investigate potential harm to the butterflies.

“My team conducted pest-control activities that should not have taken place, especially during the migration of the monarch butterfly,” Deputy De la Garza said in a message shared on her social media accounts. “It was a mistake, and I take responsibility for what happened.”

In her statement, she said that she requested the suspension of all pest control activities after becoming aware of the situation, and sought specialized advice on how to proceed.

She explained that the spraying lasted approximately five minutes and covered about 40 square meters. She said that her team did not find any dead butterflies and that following the advice of a biologist, they watered the area in an attempt to dilute the product that had been applied.

De la Garza said she “really regretted what happened” and said she would review the procedures used by her team to prevent a repeat occurrence.

The pest-control work took place on Nov. 12 at Sierra Alta Park in the southern part of Monterrey in preparation for a dengue vaccination drive. According to De la Garza, the target of the sprayed-chemical substances was dengue-carrying mosquitoes.

In response to the complaints the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa) ordered a total suspension of pest-control activities and reported that an inspection was carried out in the area to protect the monarch butterfly along its migratory route.

The imposed measures included prohibition on washing, pruning, or otherwise altering the area, and a 48-hour deadline to submit a map of where applications took place, as well as a remediation plan.

An investigation continues to determine the extent of any damage and to establish sanctions in accordance with the law.

As of Friday morning, no map identifying the areas where spraying took place or details of the remediation plan could be found publicly, nor was there any confirmation that the required documents had been submitted to Profepa.

With reports from Infobae, Periódico Correo, El Universal and El Diario MX

World.title: President Sheinbaum presides over Revolution Day parade in Mexico City
World.content:
Listen to this article

Hours after arriving home from a five-day trip to China, President Claudia Sheinbaum on Friday presided over the military-civic parade commemorating the 116th anniversary of the start of the Mexican Revolution.

At 10 a.m. local time, Sheinbaum walked across the Zócalo flanked by Defense Minister General Ricardo Trevilla and Navy Minister Admiral Raymundo Pedro Morales for a ceremonial flag-raising.

116 Aniversario de la Revolución Mexicana. Ciudad de México https://t.co/luurZLWDR4 — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) November 20, 2026

They then returned to a podium erected in front of the National Palace for a brief tribute to the military, followed by a series of speeches, culminating with the president.

Sheinbaum invoked the 1917 Constitution (a direct result of the Revolution) — describing it as the world’s most advanced charter for social justice at its time — issued a defense of democratic freedoms and expressed her administration’s rejection of elite privilege.

She also hearkened back to the violence and foreign interference that led to the turmoil of the Decena Trágica (a 10-day coup in February 1913 that ousted President Francisco Madero during the Revolution), accusing political opponents and foreign interests of attempting to weaken her administration and delegitimize the 2027 midterm elections.

During his comments, Gen. Trevilla praised Sheinbaum — Mexico’s first female commander-in-chief — reaffirmed the armed forces’ loyalty to the Constitution and civilian leadership, and claimed that the military draws its strength and social character directly from the working-class and campesino origins of the Revolution.

Following the speeches, performers in period costumes vacated the Zócalo to prepare for the parade. Before the floats appeared, actors narrated the meaning of the Revolution and its celebrations, soldaderas danced and sang corridos.

Then came the pageant floats depicting historical events such as the 1908 Creelman interview (in which President Porfirio Díaz hinted at democratic liberty after 34 years of dictatorial rule), Madero’s 1910 Plan de San Luis (a political manifesto urging an armed uprising), the 1913 Plan de Guadalupe (which rejected the coup after the Decena Trágica), the 1914 Aguascalientes Convention (which sought to unite rival revolutionary factions) and the 1917 Constitution.

The parade continued with military contingents marching through the Centro Histórico and along Paseo de la Reforma to the Monument to the Revolution while the Defense Ministry’s mariachi band entertained the dignitaries in the Zócalo.

Spectators lined the parade route, cheering on the participants throughout, while many lingered afterward in the shadow of the Monument to the Revolution where military vehicles were on display.

With reports from El Economista, La Razón, Milenio

World.title: SpaceX denies responsibility for latest space debris on a Mexico beach
World.content:
While Mexican authorities and environmentalists are engaged in clean-up efforts on Tamaulipas beaches, Elon Musk’s aerospace company SpaceX is denying that an explosion after a rocket launch last week is responsible for pieces of debris found along the shoreline.

Environmentalists claim to have found “thousands, possibly millions, of fragments of space debris” off the coast of Playa Bagdad and say they have evidence that it comes from the SpaceX launch last week. Mexico’s Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa) has been investigating SpaceX’s possible responsibility and according to various news reports has indicated it will take action.

In response, SpaceX issued a statement on social media saying its Mexican government contacts reported finding “very few” pieces of rocket debris on the coast. “Our partners on the ground informed us that they have found very little debris on their beach sweeps, and it is not clear that what little they have found came from SpaceX operations,” the statement said.

SpaceX asserted that most social media posts about widespread debris and damage are “fabrications or deliberately intended to deceive,” while insisting that any debris that might have come from its booster “poses no chemical, biological or toxicological risks.”

Activists from Conibio Global identified remnants of white plastic with gray tape, fragments of tape with black rubber, and pieces with blue glue, which presumably correspond to the internal lining of the booster. They also confirmed that these materials were found mixed with tourist waste.

On Nov. 13, SpaceX conducted a Starship launch with the goal of “catching” the launch vehicle and the Super Heavy booster upon their return. While the upper chamber of the rocket was captured the following day, the booster exploded in the Gulf of Mexico shortly after takeoff.

A similar incident occurred in October when suspected space debris was found on the same beach after a Sept. 28 launch by SpaceX. Both launches took place from SpaceX headquarters in Starbase, Texas, about 2 miles north of the Mexican border. Playa Bagdad is another mile further south.

Meanwhile, federal agencies have begun collecting the current debris, Profepa is carrying out an inspection and the Navy has been conducting maritime and land surveillance.

With reports from Wired, The Independent, LopezDoriga.com and El Financiero

World.title: Netanyahu Year-End Exit Odds Fall to 44.5%
World.content:
Polymarket traders give Netanyahu slightly less than an even chance of leaving office this year, but the price has swung about 14 points within a day on thin trading.

File photo: the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, in Jerusalem.

ISRAEL · POLITICS · PREDICTION MARKETS

Traders now price a 44.5% chance that Benjamin Netanyahu is out as Israel’s prime minister by 31 December, down 10 points in 24 hours. On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, a “Yes” share on that outcome cost about 44.5 cents at 10:31 a.m. Eastern Time on Saturday 21 November.

The drop undoes yesterday’s jump: the same price stood near 40.5% on Friday morning, rose to about 54.5%, and is back where it began. It matters to US readers because Israel, a major US security partner, still has no new government after its 27 October election.

Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief who leads the Yashar party, is trying to form one.

Key Facts Prediction markets Polymarket: 44.5% for Netanyahu out by 31 December 2026, down 10 points in 24 hours (10:31 a.m. ET, 21 November).

Trigger No single trigger was reported for the move.

Volume About US$27,400 traded on this row in 24 hours, so it is thinly traded.

Deadline Eisenkot, asked to form a government, has until 6 December, extendable to 20 December.

Seats Eisenkot’s bloc holds 48 seats, Netanyahu’s bloc 53, two Arab-led parties 19, in a 120-seat Knesset.

Polymarket traders give Netanyahu slightly less than an even chance of leaving office this year, but the price has swung about 14 points within a day on thin trading.

In plain English Polymarket is a platform where people buy “Yes” or “No” shares on future events. A price of 44.5 cents means traders collectively give the event about a 44.5% chance. Knesset is Israel’s 120-seat parliament. A caretaker prime minister keeps running the state after an election until a new government wins the Knesset’s approval. Mandate is the president’s formal task to one politician to build a governing majority within a set time. A minority government takes office with fewer than 61 votes in favour, relying on others to abstain. Likud is Netanyahu’s party; Yashar is Eisenkot’s. Shas and United Torah Judaism are the two ultra-Orthodox religious parties in Netanyahu’s bloc.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket’s market “Netanyahu out by…?” asks whether Netanyahu leaves the prime minister’s post by a series of dates. Its rules say the market resolves “Yes” if he “ceases to be Prime Minister of Israel for any period of time” before the date, and that an announcement of his “resignation/removal” resolves it “immediately”.

An announcement alone is therefore enough, whether or not he actually leaves. Traders price the three live date rows as follows.

By 31 December 2026: 44.5%, down 10 points in 24 hours and down about 2.5 points in a week; about US$27,400 traded in 24 hours.

44.5%, down 10 points in 24 hours and down about 2.5 points in a week; about US$27,400 traded in 24 hours. By 31 March 2027: 65.5%, down 5.5 points in 24 hours and up 3 points in a week; about US$4,000 traded in 24 hours.

65.5%, down 5.5 points in 24 hours and up 3 points in a week; about US$4,000 traded in 24 hours. By 30 June 2027: 68.5%, down 8 points in 24 hours and up 2.5 points in a week; about US$6,700 traded in 24 hours.

Across the whole event, about US$38,100 changed hands in 24 hours and about US$125.6 million since it opened, mostly in earlier date rows that have closed. Because 24-hour trading is below the US$50,000 level we use to call a market liquid, the market is thinly traded, and a few bets can move a price by many points.

Polymarket’s hourly price history for the 31 December row ran from a low of 40.5% (09:00 UTC on Friday 20 November) to a high of 54.5% (22:00 UTC the same day). The price was near 45% by 07:00 UTC on Saturday and 44.5% by 13:00 UTC.

Kalshi is the exchange regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). It has no contract on the timing of Netanyahu’s exit, but its market on Israel’s next prime minister shows Eisenkot at 69 cents, with about 143 contracts traded in 24 hours and about 26,000 in total, which is thin.

Each contract pays US$1 if the outcome occurs. These are bets, not polls.

A price cannot tell us whether a government will win a vote in the Knesset, only what a few traders are willing to pay today.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Netanyahu Email address Follow

Why the Odds Moved

No single trigger was reported for the move, and we do not claim one. We found no dated statement from a government body or named outlet that ties this fall to a specific event.

The background is a standoff. On Saturday 14 November Netanyahu renewed his appeal for a unity government, saying such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all”, Al Jazeera, a Qatar-based broadcaster, reported on 15 November.

Eisenkot called the appeal a “bluff” and said Yashar and Likud, Netanyahu’s party, were nonetheless talking about a shared government, the same report says. Netanyahu casts a unity government as essential to national security, Al Jazeera reported.

Eisenkot has meanwhile stepped up efforts to bring United Torah Judaism into his government, but talks remain far from agreement, mainly over the military conscription law and guarantees the ultra-Orthodox parties demand, the Jerusalem Post, an Israeli daily, reported on 15 November. These reports predate the price move and we cannot link them to it.

A thinly traded market can also move on a few large orders.

How the Clock Runs

Israel’s President Isaac Herzog gave Eisenkot until 6 December to form a government and can grant up to 14 more days, which would take the deadline to 20 December, Al Jazeera reported on 15 November. Both dates fall before the market’s 31 December cut-off.

In the 27 October election Eisenkot’s four-party bloc won 48 of 120 seats, Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc 53, and the Joint List and Ra’am, two Arab-led parties, a record 19, Al Jazeera reported. Eisenkot’s bloc and the Arab-led parties together hold 67, but Avigdor Lieberman, leader of Yisrael Beiteinu, and Naftali Bennett, leader of the Together party, both inside Eisenkot’s alliance, have rejected relying on them.

One option Al Jazeera describes is a minority government backed by Ra’am’s eight lawmakers, which would take office with 56 votes against 53 if the Joint List abstained. The other is a deal with Shas and United Torah Judaism, which would lift the bloc to 61 seats.

What It Means for US Readers

Israel’s next prime minister decides who speaks for a close US security partner on Iran, Gaza and defence cooperation. For now the story is about vote counting in the Knesset, not about a confirmed change in policy toward Washington.

Readers who follow event risk can treat the price as one live input among many. It is far thinner than a stock or bond market, and a 44.5% price is not a forecast.

More on this story: our reports on yesterday’s jump in exit odds, Eisenkot’s mandate and the Bennett and Netanyahu meeting.

What It Means for Latin America and Africa

We found no report on how a change of Israeli prime minister would affect ties with Latin American or African governments. Our earlier report on how the Israeli vote clouded Somaliland recognition covers one open case in Africa.

Follow the region on our Latin America odds page and the Africa odds page.

What Is Not Known

We do not know why traders sold this week’s jump, or whether Eisenkot can reach 61 seats without Arab-party support. We also do not know whether the president would grant the 14-day extension.

Nor do we know what happens if no government forms. More market stories are on our Prediction Markets hub.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does 44.5% mean here?

Polymarket traders price Netanyahu leaving office by 31 December 2026 at 44.5%, meaning a “Yes” share costs about 44.5 cents. It is a bet, not a forecast, and it peaked at 54.5% on Friday.

Why did the odds fall?

No single trigger was reported. Netanyahu appealed for a unity government on 14 November and Eisenkot called it a bluff, but we found no dated statement linking any event to this drop.

How thin is this market?

About US$38,100 traded on the whole event in 24 hours, below the US$50,000 level we use to call a market liquid. The 31 December row saw about US$27,400.

What settles the market?

Polymarket says it resolves “Yes” if Netanyahu ceases to be prime minister for any period before the date. An announced resignation or removal also counts at once, using official Israeli sources and credible reporting.

Is there a Kalshi market on this?

Kalshi lists no contract on the timing of Netanyahu’s exit. It does list who will be Israel’s next prime minister, where Eisenkot trades near 69%, on very thin volume.

Sources: Polymarket and Kalshi public market data (read 21 November 2026, 10:31 a.m. ET); Polymarket market rules for “Netanyahu out by…?”; Al Jazeera, 15 November 2026 (election seats, mandate deadline, Netanyahu and Eisenkot statements); Jerusalem Post, 15 November 2026 (talks with United Torah Judaism).

World.title: Latin America Defense Monitor — November 15–21, 2026
World.content:
The Latin America Defense Monitor: military moves, arms deals and security policy across Latin America and the Caribbean, in plain language

Weekly Edition · Saturday, 21 November 2026 · Issue #31

Latin America Defense Monitor — November 15–21, 2026. File photo: an MV-22B Osprey departs the flight deck of the USS Iwo Jima during a US Southern Command visit in the Caribbean Sea, 23 May 2026 (US Navy photo by Petty Officer 3rd Class Nathan Huang, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Executive Summary

The Big Picture: US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who heads the US defence department, signed a defence cooperation document in Caracas on Wednesday, 18 November, and then travelled on to Colombia and Ecuador. For US readers, the week was about signed agreements and equipment rather than strikes: a defence document in Venezuela, a transport aircraft for Colombia and security talks in Quito. At Miraflores, the presidential palace, Hegseth met Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s acting president, and signed the document with Defence Minister Gustavo González López, according to the US Department of War. The department’s account gives no text or terms, and we found no Venezuelan statement setting them out. In Colombia, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Saturday, 21 November, that a bombing in Meta department killed five members of a FARC dissident group, a preliminary figure, which he counts as the 11th bombing of his government. The FARC dissidents are fighters who rejected the 2016 peace deal with the former guerrilla army. On the day of Hegseth’s visit to Bogotá, 18 November, Colombia’s foreign minister was reported to say the government will ask Congress to approve joint military operations with US forces. Bottom Line Up Front: The open questions are what the Venezuelan document actually commits each side to, because no text has been published, and whether Colombia’s Congress will back joint operations. We found no new US boat strike and no court ruling on the strikes for 15–21 November, and no verified Mexico or Cuba defence decision.

Latin America Defense Monitor: Where Things Stand

Venezuela Medium Defence cooperation document signed with the US Secretary of War on 18 November; the text was not published in the accounts we read. US / SOUTHCOM Medium No boat strike found from US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), the US military’s command for the region, for 15–21 November; the last confirmed was on 27 October. No ruling found in the federal suit over the strikes. Colombia High Bombing announced on 21 November in Meta, five dead (preliminary); a US C-130 transport aircraft handed over on 18 November; Nancy Gómez, the wife of a mayor, and Army Sub-Lieutenant María Camila Pantoja, both kidnapped this month, not reported freed. Colombia’s National Liberation Army (ELN) guerrilla group holds Pantoja. Brazil Medium On 18 November a committee of the House of Representatives backed suggestions to shield about R$6.5 billion (about US$1.2 billion) of 2027 defence spending on fighter jets, transport aircraft, submarines and warships from cuts, as reported; they are not yet law. Argentina Low No verified procurement decision dated 15–21 November. Ecuador Medium President Daniel Noboa met Hegseth in Quito on 19 November on narco-terrorism and border security. Mexico Low No verified US military step or defence decision on cartels dated 15–21 November. Haiti High El Salvador says its troops will stay until four missing Salvadoran personnel are found; protesters in Haiti backed the troops on 17 November, as reported. The UN-authorised Gang Suppression Force is a separate multinational mission. Cuba Medium No new US military or Cuban defence announcement found for the week; Polymarket, a prediction market where traders bet real money, priced US military action by 31 December at 8.5%. C. America / Caribbean Medium Guatemala’s 30-day state of siege in Zacapa and Izabal departments, decreed on 14–15 November, was reported ratified by Congress on 17 November.

01 The Week’s Key Stories 15–21 November 2026

VENEZUELA Hegseth Signs a Defence Cooperation Document in Caracas On Wednesday, 18 November, Hegseth met Delcy Rodríguez at Miraflores palace and signed a defence cooperation document with Defence Minister Gustavo González López, according to the US Department of War’s account of the meeting. The department said it advances military cooperation and combined operations, and that Hegseth restated US support for President Donald Trump’s three-stage plan for Venezuela: stabilisation, economic recovery and reconciliation, and a democratic transition. We found no published text, no list of what joint operations or training it covers, and no statement from Venezuela’s defence ministry setting out the terms. Last week’s edition covered Venezuela’s Apure border operation. Why it matters for US readers: it is a signed military document between Caracas and Washington, months after the January capture of Nicolás Maduro, yet its content is unknown. See it is a signed military document between Caracas and Washington, months after the January capture of Nicolás Maduro, yet its content is unknown. See our report on the visit and our Venezuela coverage

COLOMBIA 11th Bombing Hits FARC Dissidents; a US C-130 Is Handed Over President Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Saturday, 21 November, a bombing in Mapiripán, Meta department, against the 44th Front of the FARC dissidents led by Iván Mordisco, a dissident commander, as reported. He put the toll at five dead, a preliminary figure, and said each attack by “narco-terrorists” will get a “more forceful” response. Reports say another bombing was announced on Thursday, 19 November, in Dagua, Valle del Cauca department, and we found no published result for it. Reports number the operations differently, so we use the president’s count of 11. On Wednesday, 18 November, Hegseth handed over a C-130H Hercules transport aircraft to Colombia’s air force at the CATAM air base in Bogotá, the first of up to three, as reported. CATAM is the Colombian military’s main air transport base. Colombia’s foreign minister, Omar Bula Escobar, was reported to say the government will ask Congress to approve joint operations with US forces, and we found no date for a vote. We found no new attack by the ELN, a guerrilla group, or by dissidents on troops dated 15–21 November. Nancy Gómez, wife of the mayor of Uribia, a town in La Guajira department, was reported still held as of 18 November, and we found no report of Sub-Lieutenant Pantoja’s release since an ELN proof-of-life video circulated on 13 November. File photo: US Army Brig. Gen. Peter Gilbert greets a Colombian Army soldier at the opening of the Southern Vanguard 27 exercise, Tolemaida, Colombia, 2 November 2026 (US Army photo by Staff Sgt. Peter Martinez, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons) Why it matters for US readers: Colombia is a US security partner, and this week it received US equipment while its government said it will seek approval for joint operations with US forces. See our Colombia is a US security partner, and this week it received US equipment while its government said it will seek approval for joint operations with US forces. See our report on drone attacks outpacing state defences and our Colombia coverage

ECUADOR Hegseth Meets Noboa in Quito On Thursday, 19 November, Hegseth met Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa in Quito, according to the US Department of War. The department said they discussed narco-terrorism, cooperation on border security and illegal mining. The Pentagon account lists Honduras as a further stop on the trip, and we found no detail of what was agreed there or on what date. Why it matters for US readers: the visit shows the US defence department dealing directly with Ecuador’s government on security. See our the visit shows the US defence department dealing directly with Ecuador’s government on security. See our Ecuador coverage

US MILITARY No New Boat Strike Found; the Court Challenge Is Still Open We found no boat-strike announcement from SOUTHCOM for 15–21 November. The last one we have confirmed was announced on 27 October, in the Eastern Pacific, and killed five people, according to the SOUTHCOM press release. A federal lawsuit over the strikes, Burnley v. United States, was filed on 27 January 2026 in the federal court in Boston by the American Civil Liberties Union and the Center for Constitutional Rights for families of two Trinidadian men killed in a strike in October 2025. We found no ruling or hearing in the case this week. Why it matters for US readers: whether the strikes are lawful remains an open court question even in weeks with no new strike.

BRAZIL House Committee Moves to Shield About US$1.2 Billion for Jets and Submarines On Wednesday, 18 November, the House of Representatives’ foreign affairs and defence committee approved suggestions that would protect about R$6.5 billion (about US$1.2 billion, at about R$5.6 per US$) of 2027 spending from budget cuts, as reported. The programmes named in reports include the Gripen fighter jet, the KC-390 transport aircraft made by Embraer, the Navy’s nuclear and conventional submarines (the PROSUB programme) and its Tamandaré-class frigates. These are committee suggestions to amend the 2027 budget guidelines law, not decisions, and we found no confirmed date for the final vote. We could not verify the current number of Gripens delivered, because sources conflict. Why it matters for US readers: if Congress adopts the proposals, Brazil’s fighter-jet and submarine programmes would be protected from budget cuts that could slow deliveries. See our if Congress adopts the proposals, Brazil’s fighter-jet and submarine programmes would be protected from budget cuts that could slow deliveries. See our Brazil coverage

HAITI Salvadoran Troops Stay for Now as the Missing-Airmen Dispute Continues On Monday, 16 November, El Salvador’s security minister, Gustavo Villatoro, said the Salvadoran troops will leave once four Salvadoran personnel missing in Haiti since about 18 October are found, as reported. Haitian minister Patrick Pélissier was reported to have met El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele the same day. On Tuesday, 17 November, protesters in Haiti marched in support of the Salvadoran deployment, as reported. The UN-authorised Gang Suppression Force, a multinational police and military mission, has just over 2,000 personnel against 5,500 authorised, according to a November report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, and its mandate runs to 31 March 2027. Most Salvadoran troops, reported at 2,000 to 2,500, are reported to operate outside that force. Why it matters for US readers: Haiti’s gang fight now depends on a bilateral Salvadoran deployment as much as on the UN-backed mission. See Haiti’s gang fight now depends on a bilateral Salvadoran deployment as much as on the UN-backed mission. See What Is Happening in Haiti? and our Haiti coverage

GUATEMALA Congress Backs a State of Siege in Zacapa and Izabal Guatemala’s Interior Ministry said on 15 November that Government Decree 8-2026 declares a 30-day state of siege in Zacapa and Izabal departments, with the Defence Ministry in charge of carrying it out. The decree restricts vehicle movement, public meetings and demonstrations, and gives the authorities extra powers. Congress was reported to ratify the decree on Tuesday, 17 November, with changes. We could not confirm the vote count, which differs between reports. Why it matters for US readers: this is a military-led security measure in two Guatemalan departments, and it shows how Central American governments are using emergency powers against armed groups. See our this is a military-led security measure in two Guatemalan departments, and it shows how Central American governments are using emergency powers against armed groups. See our Guatemala coverage

CUBA No New US Military Step Found; Market Price Is 8.5% We found no US military order, Pentagon statement or new Cuban defence announcement dated 15–21 November. The last items we covered were President Donald Trump’s radio remarks on 12 November that he would “certainly consider” military action, and new US sanctions on Cuba announced on 5 November. What Prediction Markets Say Polymarket, a prediction market where traders bet real money, priced “US military action against Cuba by December 31” at 8.5% as of 10:01 ET (15:01 UTC) on Saturday, 21 November, with about US$7.8 million traded across all dates of that market. The price is a bet, not a poll or an official forecast, and we show it next to the reporting, never instead of it. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them. Why it matters for US readers: a presidential remark is not an order, and the date to track is the market’s 31 December expiry. See our a presidential remark is not an order, and the date to track is the market’s 31 December expiry. See our Cuba coverage

02 What to Watch Next Next 7–30 days

Venezuela Whether Washington or Caracas publishes the text of the 18 November document; date not confirmed. Colombia Whether Congress takes up the government’s request on joint operations with US forces, and what the Dagua and Mapiripán operations are shown to have achieved; no date confirmed. The fates of Nancy Gómez and María Camila Pantoja remain open. Haiti Whether the four missing Salvadoran personnel are found and whether Salvadoran troops leave; the Gang Suppression Force mandate runs to 31 March 2027. Guatemala The state of siege runs 30 days from mid-November, so it would end around mid-December unless extended. Brazil The final vote on the 2027 budget guidelines law, where the committee’s suggestions must still be adopted; no date confirmed. Cuba The Polymarket contract on US military action against Cuba runs to 31 December; it stood at 8.5% on 21 November. US Military The next SOUTHCOM strike announcement or any ruling in Burnley v. United States; neither has a confirmed date. Next issue The next Defense Monitor appears on Saturday, 28 November 2026.

03 What Is Not Known as of 21 November

The content of the Venezuela–US defence document is not public in anything we found, so we cannot say whether it covers joint operations, troop access or training. The Colombian casualty figure for Mapiripán is the president’s preliminary count, which has not been confirmed by the Defence Ministry in anything we found, and the result of the Dagua operation is unreported. We do not know what was agreed in Honduras, or the dates of that stop. The Guatemalan Congress vote count differs between reports, and we found no official text of the ratification. We found no verified defence news dated 15–21 November for Argentina or Mexico, and nothing verified on a security link in Paraguay’s political crisis this week, so this edition leaves them out. Several official sites were not reachable from our servers, so some statements are given as reported and marked as such.

Background: What Is Happening in Haiti?.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Hegseth sign in Venezuela?

On 18 November, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Venezuelan Defence Minister Gustavo González López signed a defence cooperation document in Caracas, according to the US Department of War. No text has been published in the accounts we found.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said on 21 November that a bombing in Mapiripán killed five members of a FARC dissident group, a preliminary figure. He counts it as the 11th bombing of his government.

World.title: Gates Mine Visit Stirs Chile Copper Debate
World.content:
A reported private tour of a copper mine has become a test of how far Chile's government may go in letting private money into its state miner.

Haul trucks inside Codelco's Chuquicamata open pit near Calama, Chile, pictured in 2016. File photo, not from this month. Photo: Diego Delso / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

CHILE · COPPER

Two Chilean opposition lawmakers have asked Codelco, the state-owned copper miner, to explain a reported private visit by Bill Gates to its Chuquicamata mine in early November 2026. Deputies José Antonio Rivas and Valentina Cáceres announced their official letters on Friday 6 November, a day after Codelco said its own output figures had been inflated.

Ask. They want to know who arranged Gates’s visit, who attended, and whether investment came up.

The deputies’ letters take the reported tour by Gates, the Microsoft co-founder, as their starting point and ask who arranged it. We found no public confirmation from Codelco of the visit, which Chilean media reported citing unnamed sources close to the company.

The letters went to four bodies: Codelco, the Finance Ministry, the Mining Ministry and Cochilco. They ask Codelco who approved the tour, which executives attended, and whether any investment or technology cooperation came up, and they ask the Finance Ministry whether a formal plan for private capital exists.

The deputies also asked about contacts with KoBold Metals, an artificial-intelligence mineral explorer backed by Breakthrough Energy Ventures, the climate fund Gates founded. Nothing public shows that KoBold, Gates or his fund approached Codelco.

The visit landed in a country already arguing over its state miner. On Thursday 5 November, Codelco’s chairman Bernardo Fontaine told shareholders that production had been wrongly counted by more than 40,000 tonnes over 2024 and 2025, including 18,100 tonnes in 2025, with audits still unfinished.

Fontaine put the preliminary accounting effect of the inventory errors at US$120 million to US$140 million, and said the audits could change the figure. The affair has fed a wider debate on private capital in Codelco.

Codelco also said that the audit firm KPMG is reviewing 2024 and 2025 production across all its divisions, while the audit firm EY is running a forensic audit. Fontaine said both reviews are unfinished and that the figures may change.

Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz said in an interview published on 11 November that Chile may in the long term need to consider more private capital in Codelco itself. He called it a long-term idea, not part of immediate plans, and said state control would never be lost.

At the 5 November meeting, Economy and Mining Minister Daniel Mas announced a review of Codelco’s institutional set-up, including how Cochilco and Sernageomin, the national geology and mining service, relate to it. Quiroz has said the idea of private money is not privatisation.

Rivas said in the letters’ announcement that the irregularities “cannot become an excuse to weaken Chile’s heritage”. Cáceres said that lawmakers “will keep looking after our state company and overseeing it responsibly”.

Codelco is among the world’s largest copper miners, yet its divisions produced 1,334,400 tonnes in 2025, according to Cochilco data released in February 2026. BHP’s Escondida mine alone made 1,345,100 tonnes that year.

For US readers the stake is supply, because Chile mined 22.9% of the world’s copper in 2025 according to Cochilco. Fontaine told the 5 November meeting that Codelco’s output has fallen from about 1.6 million tonnes to about 1.2 million, and how fast that gap closes is an open question.

The government has not named the deposits or plants it might open to private firms. We found no public response from Codelco on the reported Gates visit, so the deputies’ questions remain open.

Did Bill Gates negotiate with Codelco?

No public document shows that he did, and Codelco has not commented. The deputies’ letters ask exactly that question.

Quiroz says state control will not be lost and calls private capital a long-term idea, not part of immediate plans. He says it is not privatisation.

World.content:
Banco do Brasil's chief is under pressure after a steep profit fall, but the government has confirmed no change. The reports leave open who would take over and when.

Está erguido na Praça dos Três Poderes, que tem este nome por também abrigar o Palácio do Planalto (sede do Poder Executivo) e o Palácio do Supremo Tribunal Federal (instância máxima do Poder Judiciário). Construído em terreno elevado, é visto de longe como culminância da avenida Eixo Monumental, que abriga a Esplanada dos Ministérios e atravessa a cidade de norte a sul. Foto: Pedro França/Agência Senado

BRAZIL · BANKING

Brazil’s government is reportedly weighing whether to replace Tarciana Medeiros, chief executive of state-controlled Banco do Brasil, according to Brazilian press reports in November 2026. We found no statement from the Finance Ministry, the presidential palace or the bank confirming or denying it.

The federal government is the controlling shareholder of Banco do Brasil, so the choice of its chief is a political decision as much as a corporate one. Medeiros became the bank’s first woman president in January 2023.

On Wednesday 11 November 2026 the bank reported adjusted net profit of R$1.3 billion, down from a year earlier, and cut its 2026 profit guidance to between R$9 billion and R$11 billion (about US$1.5 billion to US$1.9 billion at R$5.95 per dollar, the market close of 20 November). The same release raised its expected cost of bad loans for the year to between R$80 billion and R$83 billion (about US$13.4 billion to US$13.9 billion), as we reported in our earnings story.

Management blames mainly loans to medium and large farms, especially soy and corn producers. Loans to farmers more than 90 days overdue reached 6.92% in September, from 4.84% a year earlier, according to the bank’s results documents.

Farm groups reject that account. Farsul, the farmers’ federation of Rio Grande do Sul state, puts the bank’s rural arrears at about 7%, against 1.95% at the cooperative lender Sicredi and 2.5% at Banrisul, the state bank of Rio Grande do Sul, while Aprosoja Brasil, a soy growers’ association, rejects the bank’s account.

The bank has also asked the Central Bank and the Finance Ministry for looser provisioning rules on rural loans, according to the reports, and the ministry has not decided. Provisioning means setting money aside for expected losses, and Resolution 4.966 of the National Monetary Council, Brazil’s top financial rule-making body, has required banks to do so on expected losses since 1 January 2025.

We found no on-record comment from the government or the bank on the replacement reports. Any change would follow a quarter in which the bank cut its own profit forecast by about half.

For US investors the stake is practical, because the shares fell 8.35% on Thursday 12 November 2026 on B3, the São Paulo stock exchange. The bank’s American depositary receipt (ADR), BDORY, is a sponsored Level I programme, the lightest US disclosure tier, with BNY Mellon, a US custodian bank, as depositary, traded over the counter rather than on a US exchange.

The bank also cut its 2026 payout, the share of profit paid out as dividends, to 25% from 30%, and said it does not plan interim dividends in 2027. A leadership change would not alter that arithmetic, but it could change how the bank handles the farm loans behind it.

The Finance Ministry and the presidential palace have not confirmed any change, and no date has been announced. Any appointment would have to follow the bank’s own nomination and eligibility procedures, according to the reports.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Banco do Brasil replaced its chief executive?

No. Tarciana Medeiros remains in charge, and neither the Finance Ministry nor the presidential palace has confirmed that a change is planned.

Who would choose a new chief?

The federal government, as controlling shareholder, picks the chief, subject to the bank’s own nomination and eligibility procedures. Reports have floated Finance Minister Dario Durigan, but nothing is official.

What does this mean for holders of BDORY?

The ADR tracks the same shares as BBAS3 in São Paulo, so its price follows the same news. A change at the top would matter mainly for how the bank handles its rural loan losses.

World.title: Six Shot Dead in Worcester, South Africa
World.content:
Police are searching for six gunmen after a night attack on people gathered around a fire in a Western Cape township, and say the motive is still unknown.

File photo: Khayelitsha township on the Cape Flats, Cape Town. Photo: KennyOMG, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped).

South Africa Crime

Six gunmen shot dead six people and wounded three more in the early hours of Saturday 21 November 2026 in Zwelethemba (also spelled Zweletemba), a township of Worcester in South Africa’s Western Cape province. The South African Police Service (SAPS), the national police force, said no arrests had been made.

The victims were sitting around a fire in an informal settlement, a neighbourhood of shacks built without formal planning. The attack came a week after two teenage learners were shot dead in the same township, although police have not linked the cases.

Key Facts Who. Six gunmen with covered faces; six dead and three wounded; police name no suspects.

What. Mass shooting at an informal settlement; police opened six murder and three attempted murder cases.

Where. Zwelethemba township, Worcester, Western Cape province, South Africa.

As of. 21 November 2026, 14:30 GMT

Police are searching for six gunmen after a night attack on people gathered around a fire in a Western Cape township, and say the motive is still unknown.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Western Cape (South Africa) Email address Follow

SAPS spokesperson Brigadier Novela Potelwa said the shooting began at about 1.20am on Saturday. Six gunmen with their faces concealed entered a yard and opened fire.

Potelwa said preliminary information suggests the victims were sitting around a fire when the gunmen stormed the dwelling. Four men and two women died at the scene.

File photo: the Western Cape coast at Muizenberg, Cape Town, 2018 (Thomas.king364, CC BY 4.0).

Three other people were taken to a medical facility with serious gunshot wounds. The police statement gives no further word on their condition.

Police opened six cases of murder and three of attempted murder. Provincial detectives who handle serious violent crime are gathering evidence to establish a motive.

The identities of the dead have not been released, and police have named no suspects. They have not said whether the gunmen knew the victims or how they left the scene.

Lieutenant General Sizakhele Dyantyi, the Western Cape’s provincial police commissioner, said additional resources have been deployed. He said no resources will be spared in bringing the perpetrators to book.

Zwelethemba is a township, a type of urban neighbourhood created for black South Africans under apartheid, and it still houses many working families. Worcester is the main town of the Breede Valley municipality in the Cape Winelands, a wine region inland of Cape Town.

Police are also investigating the killing of two 18-year-old learners, as South Africans call school pupils, in Zwelethemba the previous week. No link between those deaths and Saturday’s shooting has been established, and police have not said what motivated either case.

Police figures released by the Western Cape Government for the first quarter of 2026/27 recorded 1,071 murders from April to June 2026, down 6.7% from 1,148 in the same months of 2025. That quarter ended months before this attack and says little about one township.

Premier Alan Winde, the head of the province’s government, and Anroux Marais, the provincial minister for police oversight and community safety, welcomed that drop on 31 August 2026. Nationally, murders fell 5.9% in the same quarter, police figures show.

Winde added that “far too many of our residents are still losing their lives at the hands of gangsters”. The same statement said the level of violence in the province “remains unacceptably high”.

The same statement said murders fell 17% in the six areas covered by the Law Enforcement Advancement Plan, a joint deployment of extra officers, with the largest drops in Gugulethu (33%) and Delft (24%). Both are Cape Town townships, far from Worcester.

Across the 91 days of the quarter that is roughly 12 murders a day, so six deaths in one attack equal about half of an average day’s toll for the whole province. That comparison says nothing yet about why this attack happened.

Police have not said whether the shooting was gang-related or whether it is connected to the earlier killings. Motive and the identity of the gunmen remain the central open questions.

Police have appealed to anyone with information to call the crime stop number 08600 10111 or to use the MySAPS app, the police reporting app. No dated next step has been announced, so the appeal stays open.

No. Police said on Saturday that no arrests had been made and that detectives are still working to establish a motive.

Police are investigating the deaths of two learners there the previous week, but they have not said the cases are connected. Investigators have so far given no motive for either.

World.title: Mashaba Says Rival Party Offered Him Money
World.content:
ActionSA’s leader makes a bribery claim against the DA while talks over who will run Johannesburg stay open.

File photo. Traffic at a central Johannesburg intersection, South Africa. Photo: Gsalamander, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

South Africa Politics

Herman Mashaba, leader of the South African party ActionSA, said on Saturday 21 November 2026 that the Democratic Alliance (DA), a rival party, offered him money behind closed doors for his 2029 election campaign. In an interview on Saturday, he called it bribery and said he is not for sale.

The claim lands in the middle of talks over who will run Johannesburg, South Africa’s biggest city. The DA has not answered it.

Key Facts Who. Herman Mashaba, leader of the party ActionSA

What. Says the Democratic Alliance offered him campaign money; the party has not replied

Where. Johannesburg, South Africa’s biggest city, where coalition talks decide the mayor

As of. 21 November 2026, 14:30 GMT

ActionSA’s leader makes a bribery claim against the DA while talks over who will run Johannesburg stay open.

In the interview Mashaba rejected criticism that he is prepared to take ActionSA’s votes to the African National Congress (ANC), the largest party nationally, led by President Cyril Ramaphosa. He said the DA forgets to mention that it “offered me money behind closed doors for 2029 election campaign”.

“Tell me if that is not bribery,” he said. “I am not for sale, I am not corrupt and no amount of money will make me lose my morals.”

The Hillbrow skyline with the Hillbrow Tower, Johannesburg (file photo).

Mashaba gave no detail in the interview on who made the offer, when it was made or how much was involved. On 16 November he had said that individuals and business groups offered him money for 2029 if ActionSA joined the DA, and the DA has not responded to Saturday’s claim.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “South Africa's first woman deputy president dies at 71” Get the brief

South Africa held local government elections on 4 November 2026. The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), the body that runs elections, declared results on 8 November that left 127 of 213 municipal councils with no party holding more than half the seats.

In such councils a mayor is chosen by deals between parties, which gives ActionSA a say in whether Johannesburg, South Africa’s biggest city, tips towards the DA or the ANC. On 7 November Mashaba wrote to Geordin Hill-Lewis, the DA leader, offering that he and Helen Zille, the DA’s mayoral candidate for Johannesburg, both withdraw from the race.

ActionSA chairperson Michael Beaumont confirmed the letter was authentic. Hill-Lewis responded in a radio interview on Wednesday 18 November.

He said the DA would not drop Zille, describing the objections to her as personal rather than political or technical. He added that “the final whistle has not yet blown” and that the DA was ready to go into opposition if needed.

Mashaba said the DA was given another chance in talks on Thursday 19 November, and a revised proposal was worked out with the DA’s coalition team led by Hill-Lewis. He said a letter reached him at 7pm on Friday 20 November, just before the deadline, and was “totally different” from what had been agreed.

In his account, the letter in effect still asked ActionSA to support Zille for mayor, which he called “the straw that broke the camel’s back for me”. He told Hill-Lewis to stop contacting him.

Mashaba said he will not work with Zille or with Cilliers Brink of the DA in Tshwane, the metropolitan area that includes Pretoria. He accuses Brink of making things hard for Dr Nasiphi Moya of ActionSA there.

He traces his break with Zille to his time as Johannesburg mayor, when he insisted that 30% of the renovated buildings in his A Re Sebetseng housing project be affordable housing. He said Zille wanted the properties sold to private owners.

Mashaba resigned as the DA’s mayor of Johannesburg on 21 October 2019, a day after Zille was re-elected chair of the DA’s Federal Council, a senior party body, he says. He now accuses the DA of disrespecting black voters and of political entitlement.

The DA’s Johannesburg mayoral campaign team, through Kyle Jacobs, Zille’s media liaison, declined to respond and said negotiations are handled by the party’s national leadership. DA national spokesperson Karabo Khakhau said the leadership will not communicate on negotiations until all is concluded, so the bribery claim stands unanswered.

Political analyst Sandile Mnguni said Mashaba appeared to be advancing what he believes are ActionSA’s best interests, but that his earlier refusal to work with the ANC set against his current position raises questions about political consistency. He added that it would be unfair to blame Mashaba alone without examining the conduct of the DA leadership.

On 18 November Beaumont described an ANC offer to ActionSA covering the Johannesburg and Tshwane mayoralties as attractive but in need of further negotiation. IEC chairperson Mosotho Moepya said on Friday 13 November 2026 that each council’s first meeting, where mayors are chosen, must be held within 14 days after councillors are declared elected, and we found no published date for Johannesburg’s.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Mashaba claiming?

He says the DA offered him money for his 2029 campaign, which he calls bribery. He gave no detail, and the DA has not responded.

Why does ActionSA matter for Johannesburg?

Johannesburg’s mayor is chosen by a vote of councillors, and ActionSA’s votes could tip it to the DA or the ANC. That makes Mashaba’s choice central to who runs the city.

Is the coalition question settled?

No. The talks between ActionSA and the ANC are unfinished, and the date of the first council meetings is not confirmed.

Sources Interview statements by Herman Mashaba (21 November 2026); DA statements of 21 November 2026 (Jacobs, Khakhau); Electoral Commission of South Africa declaration of the 2026 local government election results.; IEC statement on the gazetting of councillors (13 November 2026)

World.title: Ghana Party Chief Sues to Void Regional Vote
World.content:
Ghana’s ruling party faces a court test over whether the voter list for a regional election was altered by hand, as the losing candidate alleges.

Photo: Ijon / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Ghana Politics

A defeated candidate for the Central Region chairmanship of Ghana’s ruling National Democratic Congress (NDC) has asked the Accra High Court to cancel the vote that beat him. Richard Kofi Asiedu, the party’s outgoing regional chairman, filed the suit on Friday 20 November 2026 against the NDC, the winner Obeng Inkoom and the Electoral Commission.

The Electoral Commission is the state body that supervises elections in Ghana. The poll took place on Saturday 14 November 2026 at Dunkwa-on-Offin, a town in the Central Region, and the next general election is due in December 2028.

Key Facts Who. Richard Kofi Asiedu, outgoing Central Region chairman of Ghana’s ruling NDC, against winner Obeng Inkoom.

What. A suit to annul the chairmanship vote and order a new poll run by the Electoral Commission.

Where. Accra High Court, over a party election held at Dunkwa-on-Offin.

As of. 21 November 2026, 14:30 GMT

Ghana’s ruling party faces a court test over whether the voter list for a regional election was altered by hand, as the losing candidate alleges.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Accra High Court (Ghana) Email address Follow

Inkoom won with 372 votes against Asiedu’s 364 as cited in the suit, while a count of 367 circulated on 15 November, and a third candidate, Ibrahim Mohamed, had 16. Asiedu demanded a recount at the count, and by Sunday 15 November 2026 he had threatened legal action while police formed a guard around the ballot boxes.

On Monday 16 November 2026 Asiedu petitioned the NDC’s Functional Executive Committee, a senior party organ, for a fresh election. The suit says the committee neither acknowledged nor acted on the petition.

The stands of Black Star Square in Accra (file photo).

RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat this means, and what's next › RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. × Economy impact Key players Stability What's next Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The statement of claim alleges that the register used differed materially from the official album of qualified delegates supplied to candidates and agents. It says the party’s Director of Elections had directed that no supplementary register would be provided after 2 November 2026, yet nine names were added by hand to the Cohort 4 register, a delegate list for regional executives and special voters, with a printed total of 137.

The suit alleges that an Asiedu agent saw an Electoral Commission officer entering names in red ink on a separate sheet outside the approved register. It adds that some people voted in the names of others.

The suit also says the Cohort 1 total, a delegate list for constituency polling stations, was changed by hand from 223 to 224 to admit a coordinator of the party’s Zongo Caucus, a group for Zongo communities, historically migrant neighbourhoods. Asiedu says that person was not a qualified delegate.

Asiedu’s agents queried the figures at Cohort 2, another delegate list, and asked for a recount, the suit says. They walked out without signing the results when the presiding officer refused.

His lawyer, Martin Kpebu, relies on Article 55(5) of the 1992 Constitution, which deals with internal democracy in political parties. He also cites sections 17(1) and (2) of the Political Parties Act, 2000 (Act 574), Article 18(5) of the NDC Constitution and the party’s 2026 electoral guidelines.

Asiedu asks the court to declare the election null and void and to order a fresh poll supervised by the Electoral Commission. He also wants an order stopping the NDC from recognising Inkoom as chairman, preservation of all electoral materials, and costs.

Inkoom has said there was “no controversy” over his declaration, in his response when the complaints first surfaced. He has also pledged to unite the party.

The NDC has not publicly responded to the suit, and we found no response from the Electoral Commission. The record is silent on what the party itself wants from the case.

The party’s national chairman, Johnson Asiedu Nketia, had earlier urged police to arrest anyone buying votes in the regional polls, as set out in our vote-buying warning. Asiedu’s suit does not allege vote-buying, but it adds to the scrutiny of how the party runs its internal elections.

If the court annuls the result, the region would need a new chairman election under Electoral Commission supervision. If it dismisses the suit, the declared result stands and the complaints about the registers go untested in court.

Each defendant has eight days after being served to enter an appearance, and no hearing date is known. The court has not said whether it will grant any order.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the suit ask the court to do?

It asks the Accra High Court to void the Central Region chairmanship election and order a new one run by the Electoral Commission. It also seeks to stop the NDC from recognising the winner.

Has Obeng Inkoom lost the chairmanship?

No. He was declared the winner, and the suit asks the court to stop the party recognising him. He has said there was no controversy over the result.

Who will decide the case?

The Accra High Court will decide, once the defendants have responded. No hearing date has been announced.

He said the youths resisted and blocked the Gombe-Bauchi highway. Local officials, led by Bello Sulaiman, chairman of the Akko North council area, calmed the crowd.

Idris Lawanti alleges that the personnel returned later that night and started shooting indiscriminately. Another resident, El Lawanti, wrote in a public social media post that about 15 people were shot and some died.

El Lawanti said the dispute began from allegations that stolen military property was being kept in the community. He called on the federal government, Air Force authorities and Nigeria’s National Human Rights Commission, the official rights watchdog, for an independent investigation, treatment, accountability and compensation.

The state report names three dead. Yayaji Alhaji Abdul Kura died from gunshot injuries, according to the report.

Hamma Magaji, 35, was reportedly beaten to death. Inna Antu Umar Bello died from shock at the village.

Twelve injured people, aged 19 to 44, are being treated at Federal Teaching Hospital Gombe, a major public hospital. One of them, Sale Abubakar, 30, was moved to the operating theatre for emergency surgery.

The thirteenth casualty, Paul Simple, was taken to Cottage Hospital, Amada, a smaller local hospital, over an alleged beating. The state report lists the 13 injured as one group, with 12 of them at the teaching hospital.

Governor Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya condemned the incident and called for calm, in a statement issued by his spokesman Ismaila Uba Misilli. The statement says the governor ordered “a thorough, impartial and transparent investigation” into what took place.

He sent a delegation led by Prof. Ibrahim Abubakar Njodi, Secretary to the State Government, to the village. The governor promised support for the injured and the bereaved families.

We found no published statement from the Nigerian Air Force, the Nigerian Army or the Ministry of Defence. The residents’ version of events therefore stands unanswered.

Who fired, how many shots were fired and whether the dead were shot are not established. Some accounts place the incident on Saturday night, while the state report and most accounts say Friday night.

The state itself says its facts remain subject to verification, so the toll could change as officials finish their checks. Until the Air Force speaks, the public record rests on residents and a preliminary state report.

An independent inquiry, as El Lawanti requested, would be the route to settling who fired and why. No date has been confirmed for the investigation or its findings.

Who says the Air Force was involved?

Residents of Lawanti say so, and the state report records that account without confirming it. The Air Force has not yet responded.

Has anyone been blamed officially?

No. The Gombe State government says the circumstances are still subject to verification and has ordered an impartial investigation.

What happens next?

The state’s delegation is in the village and an investigation has been ordered. No date for findings has been confirmed.

World.title: A Slow Earthquake Equal to Magnitude 6.4 Happened Off Osa and Nobody Felt It
World.content:
A slow-motion earthquake with the energy of a magnitude 6.4 tremor took place off Costa Rica’s Osa Peninsula in Octobe and no one on land felt a thing. The Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (Ovsicori), part of the National University, detected the episode offshore of southern Osa, where the Cocos Plate meets the Panama Microplate. Its findings appear in a preliminary report updated on November 17.

In a slow earthquake, the strain stored between two plates escapes little by little across days or weeks rather than in one violent break. Because nothing shakes, only instruments that track ground position down to the millimeter can pick it up. Those instruments showed the observatory’s satellite positioning station in Puerto Jiménez sliding about 4.2 centimeters (1.7 inches) to the southwest over the month. Deeper down, Ovsicori’s model puts the largest slip between the two plates at roughly 13 centimeters (5.1 inches).

For comparison, the two plates normally close on each other at around 8 centimeters (3.1 inches) a year, as the Cocos Plate dives beneath the Panama Microplate. Ovsicori seismologist Cyril Müller stressed that the 6.4 figure measures the tectonic movement added up over the whole process and does not mean a quake of that size struck.

This is not the first such episode in the area. The observatory recorded slow slip in the same offshore area in 2018 and again in 2022, and both years brought a second episode, five months after the first in 2018 and two months after in 2022. The second 2022 episode covered more ground, spreading into a neighboring area to the northwest.

Since October’s slip sits in much the same place as the opening episodes of those earlier sequences, researchers consider a second episode possible in the coming months, though the report says the data cannot yet show whether, when or how far it would spread.

The report makes no forecast of a conventional earthquake and it neither claims the October episode will set one off nor estimates any rise in the odds. Studies published in 2023 and 2025 suggest slow slip can redistribute stress onto neighboring parts of a fault, a mechanism scientists are still working to understand.

The monitoring matters because parts of the plate boundary keep building up strain, among them the zone tied to the magnitude 7.4 Osa earthquake of 1983. Ovsicori will keep reviewing its station data for signs of a new episode or a spread to the northwest and will continue tracking ground deformation and seismic activity in the region.
