The finding comes in a year when more earthquakes have been felt. Ovsicori data show felt quakes averaged 12 a month from January through April and 25 a month from May through October. The observatory’s researchers said the year’s activity shows nothing anomalous compared with recent years.

Costa Rica sits on one of the most active plate boundaries in the Americas, and strong earthquakes can occur at any time. Emergency authorities recommend keeping water, food, a flashlight and important documents within reach and agreeing on a meeting point with the people you live with.

World.title: Three Salvadoran Soldiers Die in Haiti Explosives Accident
World.content:
Three Salvadoran soldiers have died after an accidental explosion at a military camp in Haiti, El Salvador’s Armed Forces said yesterday. They are the first confirmed deaths since President Nayib Bukele sent troops to the Caribbean nation a month ago. Two soldiers died at the scene while handling explosive material, the Armed Forces said in a statement and two others were wounded.

Hours later, the military reported that one of the wounded had died in a hospital in the Dominican Republic, where he had been flown for treatment. The fourth soldier is out of danger, the Armed Forces said. The military has not identified the dead. It has not said where in Haiti the blast happened, when it occurred or what type of explosives were involved.

Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé offered his condolences to the Salvadoran government. The United States Embassy in San Salvador also expressed its condolences on X to the soldiers’ families and to the Salvadoran people. Bukele ordered more than 2,000 troops into Haiti after four Salvadoran airmen went missing in a gang attack in Port-au-Prince on October 18. The four were serving with the Gang Suppression Force, a United Nations-backed international mission.

The new deployment operates separately from that force. What began as a search for the missing airmen has since widened into a broader offensive against the armed groups that control much of the Haitian capital. Salvadoran troops have destroyed facilities belonging to two gangs and helped drive armed groups out of a soccer stadium in Port-au-Prince. On Thursday, Bukele said his soldiers were teaching Haiti’s gangs a lesson.

The president has said he will withdraw the troops once the four airmen are rescued. However, El Salvador and Haiti have signed a cooperation agreement that could extend the Salvadoran military presence. Its terms have not been made public. Haitian authorities have welcomed the deployment. They have long asked for more outside help against the gangs.

Bukele built his regional profile on a hard-line crackdown that dismantled the gangs once dominant in El Salvador. The Haiti operation is the first time he has applied that approach outside his own country. The four airmen remain missing.

World.title: JetBlue Announces Daily Flights From Fort Lauderdale to Honduras Starting in 2027
World.content:
JetBlue Airways is expanding its Central American network with new daily nonstop flights between Fort Lauderdale and Tegucigalpa, Honduras, beginning February 25, 2027. The route gives South Florida travelers another direct connection to the region as the airline continues growing its international operations.

The airline announced the new service yesterday, confirming that tickets are already on sale. Flights will operate between Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) and Palmerola International Airport (XPL), located in Comayagua, which serves the Honduran capital of Tegucigalpa.

The new route will operate seven days a week, with Flight B6 457 departing Fort Lauderdale at 10:05 a.m. and arriving in Honduras at noon. The return flight, B6 458, will leave Palmerola at 1:05 p.m. and arrive in Fort Lauderdale at 4:35 p.m. All times are local.

JetBlue is introducing promotional one-way fares starting at $183 in its Main cabin and $262 for EvenMore seating. The introductory fares must be booked by November 21, 2026, for travel between March 2 and March 17, 2027, on Tuesdays and Wednesdays only. Prices are subject to availability, and additional baggage fees may apply.

Tegucigalpa will become JetBlue’s second destination in Honduras, joining San Pedro Sula, which the airline already serves from Fort Lauderdale. The addition gives travelers more options for reaching different parts of Honduras without connecting through another airport. The new service also fills a gap left by Spirit Airlines, which previously operated flights between Fort Lauderdale and Palmerola before ending operations on the route in May 2026.

Honduras is part of a broader expansion by JetBlue across Latin America and the Caribbean. The airline is also adding daily nonstop flights between Fort Lauderdale and Grand Cayman beginning February 23, 2027, two days before the Tegucigalpa service launches. Grand Cayman introductory fares start at $99 one way in Main and $144 in EvenMore, subject to promotional booking restrictions.

JetBlue has also announced temporary daily flights between Fort Lauderdale and Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, from January 29 through February 15, 2027, to serve travelers attending the country’s Carnival celebrations. The expansion follows the airline’s recent introduction of flights from Fort Lauderdale to Barranquilla and Cali, Colombia. By the end of February 2027, JetBlue expects to offer nonstop service to 20 international destinations from Fort Lauderdale.

During the busiest periods of the winter travel season, the airline expects to operate more than 150 daily departures from Fort Lauderdale, its largest schedule ever at the airport. The new Honduras and Grand Cayman routes will use Airbus A320 and A220 aircraft. Passengers will have access to JetBlue’s complimentary onboard entertainment, Wi-Fi, snacks and beverages, while EvenMore customers receive additional legroom and other benefits.

For travelers heading to Tegucigalpa, there is one important distinction: Palmerola International Airport is located outside the capital in Comayagua, meaning passengers must arrange ground transportation for the final portion of their journey. The flights are available for booking through JetBlue’s website and mobile application. The airline says the expansion is intended to strengthen Fort Lauderdale’s position as a gateway between the United States, Central America and the Caribbean.

The new routes remain subject to government operating approval.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Main Airport Faces Up to 21% Fewer Seats Through August 2027
World.content:
Travelers flying into San José’s Juan Santamaría International Airport could find up to 21% fewer airline seats from October 2026 through August 2027, tourism business leaders said this week. The projection stretches the squeeze on capacity well past the current high season.

Hans Pfister, president of the National Chamber of Ecotourism and Sustainable Tourism (Canaeco), said officials from the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) shared the figure with the sector during a recent meeting. Nationwide, seats on flights to Costa Rica are expected to fall by about 15% in the coming months, while the cut at Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia would be closer to 3%.

The ICT has not publicly confirmed the projection. It covers a longer period than the one outlined earlier this month, when estimates from two international consultancies pointed to a 20% drop in seats from the United States into San José between August 2026 and March 2027.

Arrival figures released this week show the slowdown is already under way. Air arrivals fell 1.9% in October compared with the same month last year, to 126,906, the third consecutive monthly decline, according to ICT data. Juan Santamaría received 90,728 arrivals in October, down 8% and its seventh straight month of declines. Liberia moved in the opposite direction, with 36,127 arrivals, up 17.4%.

Arrivals from the United States, which made up 51.3% of air arrivals in October, fell 3.6% to 65,071. Visitors from Canada rose 19%, from Mexico 22.9% and from Europe 3.9%. From January through October, air arrivals still totaled 2,254,412, up 5% from a year earlier.

Pfister attributed the cuts to higher fuel costs, which he said have pushed airlines to offer fewer seats and fly fuller planes to protect profitability. Shirley Calvo, executive director of the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur), pointed to recent changes by several US carriers.

Spirit Airlines stopped flying in May after its second bankruptcy filing, ending its service to San José from Orlando and Fort Lauderdale. JetBlue suspended its Orlando route in July, and American Airlines ended its Chicago connection. According to the tourism chambers, United has also withdrawn December flights, and Southwest has cut its planned growth for 2026 in half.

A report by the Center for Tourism Studies (CET), released October 26, found that seat supply grew just 0.7% from January through July. Growth slid from between 6.7% and 8.2% early in the year to a decline of 8.6% in July. At San José, seat supply swung from growth of 6.3% in March to a drop of 12.3% in July, according to the CET, while Liberia grew every month. The center linked the trend to higher aviation fuel prices tied to conflict in the Middle East.

The CET also cited four weaknesses in the competitiveness: high costs, the strong colón, road infrastructure and insecurity. Some new capacity is still arriving on US routes. JetBlue this week moved to daily flights from New York to both of the main airports, one of the few additions heading into the busiest months of the year.

For now, the figures point to a country whose air traffic is shifting steadily toward Guanacaste. How deep the cuts at San José run will become clearer in monthly arrival data as the high season continues into the spring.

World.title: Carlos Alcaraz Overcomes Injury Scare to Set Up Ben Shelton ATP Finals Semifinal
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz brushed aside concerns about his fitness Friday with a commanding 6-4, 6-1 victory over Italy’s Flavio Cobolli, completing an undefeated group stage at the ATP Finals and setting up a semifinal showdown against American Ben Shelton. The 23-year-old Spaniard needed just 65 minutes to defeat Cobolli at Turin’s Inalpi Arena, extending his winning streak to 12 matches and keeping alive his hopes of winning the prestigious season-ending championship for the first time.

Alcaraz entered Friday’s match under a cloud of uncertainty after experiencing discomfort in his left hamstring during Wednesday’s victory over Daniil Medvedev. The problem prompted medical examinations and the cancellation of a practice session Thursday. An MRI scan reportedly ruled out a muscle injury, but questions remained about whether Alcaraz could compete at full strength as the tournament approached its decisive stages.

Those concerns appeared to ease quickly against Cobolli. Playing with his left thigh strapped, Alcaraz broke the Italian’s serve in the opening game and controlled the match with aggressive baseline hitting. He produced 29 winners compared with just nine from Cobolli and never faced a break point.

Alcaraz converted four of his nine break-point opportunities, maintaining control throughout the second set as the Italian struggled to match his pace and precision. After the match, Alcaraz acknowledged that his biggest concern now involves recovering physically before Saturday’s semifinal.

“The challenge is no longer on the court, it is off the court,” Alcaraz said, emphasizing the importance of his recovery before facing Shelton. The victory completed a perfect 3-0 record in the Ivan Lendl Group, where Alcaraz also defeated Frances Tiafoe and Medvedev without dropping a set.

It also continued a remarkable late-season run for the Spaniard, who has claimed consecutive titles in Vienna and at the Paris Masters after missing more than four months earlier this year with a wrist injury. His next opponent presents a familiar challenge. Shelton secured his semifinal place Thursday after defeating Spain’s Rafael Jódar 7-6(8), 7-5. The American has emerged as one of the ATP Tour’s leading players this season, reaching the US Open final and establishing himself among the world’s top five.

Saturday’s meeting will renew a rivalry that has produced two significant encounters in recent months. Shelton defeated Alcaraz in a five-set US Open quarterfinal in September before the Spaniard responded with a straight-sets victory in the Paris Masters final earlier this month. The American will be looking to repeat his New York success, while Alcaraz hopes to continue his unbeaten run in Turin.

The ATP Finals represent one of the few major titles missing from Alcaraz’s growing collection. He reached the championship match in 2025 but lost to Jannik Sinner. With Sinner absent from this year’s tournament because of a knee injury, Alcaraz has another opportunity to capture the season-ending trophy.

Alexander Zverev, the world’s top-ranked player, has also advanced to the semifinals after winning all three of his group matches. For Alcaraz, however, the immediate priority remains his physical condition. His performance Friday suggested he can still produce exceptional tennis despite the discomfort in his leg, but Shelton is likely to provide a considerably tougher test.

The Alcaraz-Shelton semifinal is scheduled for Saturday, November 21, with the championship match set for Sunday in Turin.

World.title: Organized Crime Has Become Costa Rica’s Third Economy, Report Warns
World.content:
Organized crime has grown into a third economy in Costa Rica, operating alongside the domestic market and the export and free-trade-zone sector, according to the 2026 State of the Nation report released yesterday. The report, produced by the State of the Nation Program (PEN) of the National Council of Rectors (Conare), links the trend to economic exclusion, a lack of state investment in priority areas and the steady expansion of illicit activity.

Its authors describe the findings as exploratory but say the evidence is sufficient to show the scale of the challenge. The criminal economy described in the report spans drug sales, contract killings, electronic fraud, contraband, informal “gota a gota” lending and money laundering. Drug trafficking profits remain the main source of the money being laundered.

Criminal groups have also spread across the map. Authorities dismantled 20 criminal organizations operating in 17 cantons in 2020, and 48 operating in 37 cantons in 2025, a 2.4-fold increase. Five years ago those groups were concentrated in the Central Valley, San Carlos and the Caribbean. By 2025 they had expanded west and onto the Pacific coast.

Complaints about drug sales rose 18% in a single year, from 1,211 in 2024 to 1,427 in 2025. Increases were recorded in five of the seven provinces, with the largest growth in the three coastal provinces, which are exposed to maritime drug routes in both the Pacific and the Caribbean.

The report singles out real estate as an attractive channel for laundering. It points to high liquidity in tourist areas, the use of shell corporations and the absence of systematic data on property transaction prices. It also flags three broader financial vulnerabilities: informal currency exchange, unexplained cash movements and transactions with no supporting documentation.

According to the PEN, dirty money can distort market prices, weaken institutions, add economic volatility and discourage legitimate investment. The Moín container terminal on the Caribbean coast is described as a critical node because of rising cocaine seizures. The report cites a 2025 U.S. government report that identified Moín as a key export point for drugs bound for the Northern Hemisphere.

Other illicit markets are growing as well. Assaults and thefts targeting cargo vehicles rose 29% between 2016 and 2025, and 90% of those incidents occurred on routes linking the Caldera and Moín ports to the Central Valley. About half of the cigarettes sold come from the illegal trade, according to the report. Complaints of computer crimes rose roughly sixfold between 2019 and 2025, driven mainly by online scams.

The findings arrive as Costa Rica goes through the most violent period in its recorded history, measured by homicide rate, a trend that began in 2022. This week alone, the killing of journalist Camilo Rodríguez on Route 32 drew condemnation from the United Nations, the European Union and the United States.

The PEN notes that while Costa Rica tracks many types of crime, little information exists on how the criminal economy actually functions. It calls for systematic, more precise measurement of criminal activity and how it interacts with the legal economy. For now, the researchers say, the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. It is, however, enough to show that understanding and curbing the criminal economy has become one of the central challenges.

World.title: The Costa Rica I Remember and the Changes I Have Seen
World.content:
I like going to the weekly feria in Perez Zeledon. Unlike much of the Costa Rica I know, it is largely unchanged over the past thirty years. Same location, same set up, same rows and rows of vendors selling fresh fruits, veggies, and assorted other agriculture and artisanal products. I once had a booth there, selling my homemade breads and cookies. I can stand at the spot where I had a booth and look out and see the same scenes I saw thirty years ago. There is a comfort in that kind of familiarity.

As time passes, not everything stays the same. Change is inevitable. Things that once were fade into distant memory. While I can stand in that spot at the feria and remember being there thirty years prior, once I step outside, I am in a Costa Rica where much has changed. There have been major changes– in infrastructure, with new highways and bypasses, and in construction, with thousands of new houses, and a San Jose skyline that features dozens of high rises that have sprung up in that time span. But there are also smaller changes, more subtle, less noticeable at first, that have occurred. Here is my own list of 20 random changes I have seen in Costa Rica:

The disappearance of the Lada Niva. The Russian made 4×4, cheapest on the market, could be classified as a vanishing species. I personally can’t remember the last time I saw one on the road. The machete wielding landscapers have been replaced by gas powered weedwhackers. We traded the rhythmic whinging of the machete for the incessant drone of the machine. Whatever happened to the amateur blood pressure takers? They once roamed the cantinas and public areas, dressed in medical garb, blood pressure measurement devices in hand. For a small fee they would let you know how serious your hypertension, though the accuracy of their units was always in doubt. Informal, front of the house bars were once fairly common. Up front, a small bar with uncomfortable wood block chairs, with a door that separated the bar from the living area. It was always a bit odd when the door opened and you would see a family sitting around in their living room while at the bar, borrachos sang along with a ranchero tune. While on the topic of bars, many will remember the days of a free boca with every drink order. You could get a full meal with 3 or 4 beers. Some bars kept it basic with only ‘sustancia’, others offered small portions of meat, chicken or fish. Now virtually extinct. In a good change for taller people like myself, the 6-foot high doorways have been universally adjusted. I banged the top of my head more than once in older Tico houses and cantinas. Likewise, most buses have more legroom than previous, thanks to a new generation of larger Ticos. Speaking of which, large doesn’t always mean tall. My first years in Costa Rica, I marveled at the overall fitness of the country. Everybody looked like a soccer player or a cowboy. Today the country deals with the health issues brought on by poor diets and lack of exercise. Obesity rates are up everywhere in the world, so Costa Rica is hardly alone. I remember a time when people looked ahead as they walked down the street. They are still around but the number of distracted walkers is astronomical compared to the pre-cell phone epoch. For every person you saw back then who was reading a book or newspaper as they walked down the street, today there are ten staring into their phones. At least. Cooking con leña – The wood fired cooking of meat, The Cocina con Leña, was once as common as fried chicken, but is now more artisanal, offered up in higher-end restaurants. The masses eat it fried, skin and all. My barrio in San Isidro de el General has paved streets, I remember when it didn’t. But I’m not complaining. We still have one-lane bridges. Relics of simpler days. Medical care was once incredibly cheap. People come here because it still is a good deal. How’s this for a good deal?: In 1991 my son was born in a private clinic in San Jose, the doctor an accomplished Costa Rican who had worked in well known US hospitals. An anesthesiologist was called in as my son was delivered by caesarian. His mother spent four nights, and a 24-hour nurse on call. The total bill was $1,100. Here’s another: In 1992, I had emergency surgery to remove an ulcerating parasite from my intestines. I spent 10 nights in the hospital after surgery. Had daily doctor visits and nurses always around. The cost was $800. Adjusted for inflation, $2,700 and $2,000. Still astounding.

The rest of the list is what I call the Virtually Extinct list:

World.title: Dollar Hits Its Third Record Low in a Week in Costa Rica
World.content:
The U.S. dollar fell to a new all-time low against the Costa Rican colón yesterday, its third record in a week. The weighted average on Monex, the foreign exchange market run by the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR), closed at 444.45 colones. That was 0.40 below Wednesday’s record of 444.85, which in turn broke the previous low of 446.10 set on Nov. 13.

The dollar began 2026 at 497.07 colones and has since lost 52.62 colones, or 10.6% of its value. It now sits 36% below its all-time high of 696.76 colones, reached on June 21, 2022. For anyone paid in dollars and spending in colones, the decline is direct. At Thursday’s average, $2,000 converts to about 888,900 colones, compared with roughly 994,100 colones at the start of the year, a difference of about 105,000 colones.

The BCCR’s reference rates for today were 442.31 colones to buy and 446.48 to sell. Prices at bank windows vary by institution. The new low coincided with the release of the 2026 State of the Nation report, which divides the past decade of exchange-rate movement into four stages.

From 2016 to 2020, the rate was relatively stable with a slight tendency to depreciate, ranging between 535.47 and 628.85 colones. It stayed below 600 on 1,068 of 1,251 trading days. In 2021 and 2022, the pandemic and global shocks, including the shipping container crisis, drove a sharp depreciation of the colón. The dollar peaked at its record 696.76 in June 2022 before falling back below 600 by the end of that year.

Between 2023 and 2025, the colón appreciated and returned to pre-pandemic levels, with the rate ranging from 488.06 to 596.73. It dipped below 500 in only 33 of 751 sessions. In 2026, that appreciation accelerated. The rate has moved between 444.45 and 499.39 colones this year, setting several new lows in a data series that began on Dec. 6, 2007.

According to the report, an oversupply of dollars has been the main driver since 2023, and that pattern persisted into 2026. BCCR president Róger Madrigal has maintained that market forces determine the exchange rate. The Central Bank has shifted from supplying dollars to absorbing part of the surplus. It has said it will buy dollars when necessary to prevent abrupt movements that do not reflect economic fundamentals.

Seasonal factors are adding pressure. The high tourism season, along with companies converting dollars to pay year-end aguinaldo bonuses and taxes, typically increases the supply of dollars in November and December.The State of the Nation report notes that a low exchange rate creates clear winners and losers. Households and businesses that earn colones but carry dollar debts or costs need fewer colones to meet those obligations.

Those who earn in dollars but spend in colones must convert more dollars to cover the same expenses. Domestic producers face tougher competition from cheaper imports, which can squeeze margins and limit investment and hiring, and exporters have asked the BCCR for additional measures to counter the appreciation, mainly during 2026.

Projections from several institutions compiled in September placed the year-end rate between 440 and 465 colones. Analysts have said the dollar could keep falling through the end of the year, and the drop has already raised the cost of retiring in Costa Rica.

Today’s Monex session will show whether the dollar sets yet another record before the weekend.

World.title: World Fisheries Day highlights importance of sustainable Fishing and Fisherfolk livelihoods
World.content:
World Fisheries Day highlights importance of sustainable Fishing and Fisherfolk livelihoods

By Zoila Palma: World Fisheries Day is being observed with renewed calls for responsible fishing practices, sustainable management of aquatic resources and improved working conditions for people employed in the fisheries and aquaculture sectors.

The annual observance recognizes the contributions of fisherfolk, aquaculturists and fish workers to food security, nutrition, economic development and the livelihoods of communities worldwide.

The Organization of the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sector of the Central American Isthmus (OSPESCA) highlighted the important role fishing plays in generating economic opportunities, preserving cultural traditions and supporting thousands of families across the region. The organization reaffirmed its commitment to promoting sustainable fishing, the responsible use of fishery resources and the conservation of aquatic ecosystems for present and future generations.

This year’s theme, “Empowering People for Change: Advancing Decent Work in Fisheries and Aquaculture, Particularly for Youth and Women,” also draws attention to the need for safer working conditions, greater opportunities and equitable participation in the sector.

World.title: International News: Three Salvadoran soldiers killed in explosives accident during Haiti security operation
World.content:
International News: Three Salvadoran soldiers killed in explosives accident during Haiti security operation

By Zoila Palma: Three Salvadoran soldiers have been killed while working with explosives during a security operation in Haiti, El Salvador’s military confirmed on Friday.

The incident marks the first officially reported fatalities among Salvadoran troops deployed to the Caribbean nation as part of a major anti-gang mission launched approximately one month ago.

The military also reported that one soldier died while receiving treatment in neighbouring Dominican Republic, while another was injured and remains in stable condition, Reuters report.

Authorities have not disclosed where the explosion occurred or the type of explosives the soldiers were handling.

A Salvadoran government spokesperson said further details were not immediately available.

The deployment began last month when President Nayib Bukele sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti following the disappearance of four Salvadoran personnel attached to a United Nations-backed mission on October 18. Bukele has said the operation aims to locate the missing personnel, although a gang leader operating in the area has suggested they were killed.

Since the deployment, Bukele has released videos showing military strikes targeting suspected gang leaders and their residences around Port-au-Prince. The intervention has received support from thousands of Haitians who have demonstrated in favour of the operation.

However, security analysts have warned that military offensives without a long-term strategy to maintain control of recovered territory could expose civilians to further violence. Haiti has also faced criticism from human rights organizations over the use of explosive-equipped drones in densely populated communities.

World.title: Corozal Sustainable Future Initiative promotes Jaguar Conservation during Children’s Day celebration in Sarteneja
World.content:
Corozal Sustainable Future Initiative promotes Jaguar Conservation during Children’s Day celebration in Sarteneja

By Zoila Palma: The Corozal Sustainable Future Initiative (CSFI) joined students and staff of Sarteneja La Inmaculada R.C. School on Friday, November 20, for their Children’s Day celebration, bringing an educational touch of wildlife conservation to the festivities. The CSFI team hosted an interactive educational booth as part of activities marking Jaguar Month.

During the event, students and parents learned about jaguars, their importance to Belize’s ecosystems and the need to protect the country’s iconic wild cats. The team shared information about CSFI’s ongoing jaguar conservation efforts while encouraging children to develop a greater appreciation for wildlife and the environment.

CSFI said the children’s curiosity and enthusiasm made the experience rewarding, highlighting the importance of educating young people about conservation and promoting peaceful coexistence between communities and wildlife.

CSFI thanked Principal Nelson Garcia and the school for the invitation and opportunity to engage with students and parents, encouraging the next generation to become wildlife protectors.

World.title: GTA 6 breaks entertainment records with $3.8 Billion in first-day sales
World.content:
GTA 6 breaks entertainment records with $3.8 Billion in first-day sales

By Zoila Palma: Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) has made history after generating an estimated US$3.8 billion in retail sales during its first full day of release, setting a new record for the biggest entertainment launch across any medium, BBC reports.

Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of Rockstar Games, confirmed the figures on Friday, reporting that the highly anticipated video game had also secured 32.5 million pre-orders ahead of its worldwide launch on November 19.

The record-breaking performance surpasses the previous achievements of its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V, which generated US$1.15 billion in its first five days of sales following its release 13 years ago.

The launch also outperformed major entertainment releases, including this year’s highest-grossing film, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which earned approximately US$2.5 billion during its entire theatrical run. Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare reported significant increases in gaming activity, with PlayStation 5 downloads in the United Kingdom reaching 8.6 times normal levels around the launch.

The latest instalment in Rockstar’s popular crime-themed franchise follows two new characters, Lucia and her partner Jason, as they navigate a fictional state inspired by Florida called Leonida.

The game reportedly cost more than US$1 billion to develop, potentially making it the most expensive video game ever produced. Research firm Sensor Tower estimates that approximately three-quarters of its sales have come from PlayStation 5 users, with the remaining purchases made on Xbox. Analysts predict that the game’s popularity could significantly reduce the time players spend on other single-player titles.

Gaming industry analysts expect GTA 6 to generate more than US$3 billion in worldwide sales this year, with additional revenue anticipated through future releases and online multiplayer features.

World.title: Jet ski found in Belize, Two American men acquitted in Angie Peña disappearance case
World.content:
Jet ski found in Belize, Two American men acquitted in Angie Peña disappearance case

By Zoila Palma: A Honduran court has acquitted two United States citizens of human trafficking charges in connection with the 2022 disappearance of 22-year-old Angie Peña, whose case drew international attention after the Jet Ski she was riding was discovered in Belize.

The court ruled on Friday that there was insufficient evidence linking Harold Green and William James Murdock to Peña’s disappearance and alleged sexual exploitation.

However, both men were convicted of the lesser offence of criminal association, alongside fellow US citizen Gary Lee Johnston and Honduran national Gustavo Trejo, AP reports.

Peña disappeared on January 1, 2022, while vacationing with her family on the Honduran island of Roatán. She had reportedly gone for a Jet Ski ride and never returned.

Authorities initially investigated the disappearance as a possible accident, but the discovery of the Jet Ski in Belize, approximately 90 nautical miles (170 kilometres) away, prompted a broader investigation into possible human trafficking.

Honduran prosecutors alleged that the four men were part of a criminal network involved in sex trafficking, including the exploitation of minors, as well as other illegal activities.

The ruling has sparked criticism from advocates and representatives of Peña’s family, who say important questions about her disappearance remain unanswered.

Julissa Villanueva, a former Honduran Vice Minister of Security who has campaigned for justice in the case, described the decision as leaving a significant debt of justice unpaid.

Lawyers representing the family have also questioned the transparency of the investigation and trial, which was held behind closed doors and excluded the media and general public.

The family has reportedly received death threats, while the August killing of protected witness Dereck McNeil raised further concerns about the risks surrounding the case.

Kenia Paz, a lawyer with the Legal Team for Human Rights representing Peña’s family, said the ruling should prompt the Public Prosecutor’s Office to continue investigating because all possible lines of inquiry have not been exhausted.

World.title: International News: El Salvador’s Bukele registers for unprecedented 3rd Presidential Term
World.content:
International News: El Salvador’s Bukele registers for unprecedented 3rd Presidential Term

By Zoila Palma: El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele officially registered his candidacy on Thursday to seek an unprecedented third consecutive term in office ahead of the February 2027 elections.

Bukele, 45, is expected to secure another victory, despite growing criticism from opposition groups and human rights organizations over changes to the country’s constitution that removed presidential term limits.

He will run alongside Vice President Felix Ulloa, following his party’s nomination in July, Reuters report.

Supporters gathered outside the Supreme Electoral Tribunal as Bukele arrived to submit his candidacy documents, chanting “six more years” in support of his re-election bid. After completing the registration process, the president thanked the crowd and described the upcoming vote as a democratic election that would guarantee freedom of expression. Opinion polls indicate that Bukele enjoys between 55% and 70% support, placing him well ahead of his political opponents.

Bukele’s popularity has largely been driven by his aggressive crackdown on organized crime and gangs, although human rights organizations have raised concerns about mass arrests, due process violations and the impact of the state of emergency introduced in 2022.

World.title: International News: FBI most wanted cartel leader captured in dramatic Mexican military operation
World.content:
International News: FBI most wanted cartel leader captured in dramatic Mexican military operation

By Zoila Palma: Mexican military forces have captured alleged drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” during a major security operation in Sinaloa on Friday.

Meza-Flores, who was among the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, leads the Guasave-based Meza-Flores criminal organization, also known as Los Mazatlecos.

Mexico’s Defense Ministry confirmed that the operation was carried out with assistance from the United States and that the suspect was transported to Mexico City following his arrest, CNN reports.

According to the FBI, Meza-Flores is accused of overseeing the possession, distribution and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States. Authorities had offered a US$5 million reward for information leading to his capture. He was previously indicted in 2012 and 2019 on drug trafficking and firearm-related charges.

The arrest triggered violent confrontations between Mexican security forces and armed militants in Guasave.

Mexico’s Defense Ministry reported that military personnel came under attack with gunfire and explosives, while armed individuals established roadblocks in several nearby municipalities. Footage from the operation showed helicopters firing toward the ground as security forces moved to regain control of the area.

World.title: He swallowed all his ‘crack’ so police wouldn’t find it but still spent 2 months in prison and got fined $255
World.content:
He swallowed all his ‘crack’ so police wouldn’t find it but still spent 2 months in prison and got fined $255

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man who allegedly swallowed crack cocaine to prevent police from finding it has been fined $255 after spending more than two months behind bars because he was unable to post bail.

Dario Fabian Flowers, 44, appeared before a magistrate in Court #8 on Friday, November 20, where he changed his previous not guilty plea to guilty for obstructing a police officer in the execution of his duties.

The incident occurred on September 12, 2026, around 4:35 p.m., when a police sergeant was conducting a mobile patrol on Ebony Street and noticed Flowers behaving suspiciously while carrying a black schoolbag.

According to police, the officer stopped Flowers to conduct a search and noticed a small white substance believed to be crack cocaine. When instructed to remove the substance, Flowers allegedly refused and instead pushed it into his mouth.

The officer reportedly attempted to open Flowers’ mouth to recover the suspected drugs, but by the time he succeeded, the substance had dissolved. Police were therefore unable to recover the suspected cocaine and charged Flowers with obstruction instead.

Flowers, who had been unable to post bail since September, admitted in court that he had placed the crack cocaine in his mouth. The magistrate imposed a $250 fine plus $5 in court costs, giving him until January 29, 2027, to pay or face three months’ imprisonment.

Flowers was released after the hearing.

Flowers is no stranger to the Magistrate’s Court. In September, he was fined $460 after pleading guilty to possession of a crack pipe and 0.5 grams of crack cocaine in a separate incident on King Street.

World.title: Special Olympics officials request privacy for loved ones after Beach Games tragedy
World.content:
Onlookers at the Harmony Beach Park in Montego Bay, St James, after an athlete went missing in a swimming competition during the Special Olympics Caribbean Beach Games on Friday. (Photo: Collin Reid)

MONTEGO BAY, Jamaica — Special Olympics officials are requesting privacy for the friends and family of the Rwandan athlete who died during the Caribbean Beach Games at Harmony Beach Park on Friday.

The athlete went missing during swimming competition on Friday morning, and his body was later discovered in the water.

READ: Rwandan athlete at Special Olympics Beach Games believed to have drowned

“We are saddened to confirm that an individual involved in a water-related incident during the Beach Games event has died. The cause of death has not yet been determined.

“Our deepest condolences are with their family and friends, and we ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time,” said a statement from Special Olympics North America, which has oversight of the Caribbean programmes.

The 2026 Caribbean Beach Games — the first of its kind to be held in Jamaica — officially began with the opening ceremony on Thursday. The closing ceremony is set for this evening.

The Beach Games comprise delegations from 18 Special Olympics regional programmes, as well as the invited contingent from Rwanda. Athletes have been competing in swimming, football, volleyball, basketball, and bocce.

World.title: From House to court
World.content:
The war of words between the Government and Opposition triggered by the November 3, 2026 ruckus in Parliament has spiralled into a legal battle with House Speaker Juliet Holness taking her allegations against St Andrew South Western Member of Parliament (MP) Dr Angela Brown Burke to the Supreme Court.

In a claim filed on November 19, Holness is seeking damages for assault and battery, alleging that Brown Burke stepped towards her and made physical contact with the left side of her body as she was leaving the parliamentary chamber.

According to the particulars of claim, the incident occurred after the House had been adjourned and Holness was making her way out of the chamber. The Speaker alleges that Brown Burke pointed at her while shouting “Coward! Coward!”, before stepping towards her and lunging with her upper body, causing contact with the left side of her body.

Holness claims that the contact was intentional and occurred without her consent or lawful justification. She is seeking general and aggravated damages, interest, and legal costs.

Attorney-at-law Alexander Shaw, who represents Holness, confirmed that the court documents had been served on Brown Burke. He also disclosed that a police report concerning the incident was made on November 9.

“My client has placed her allegations before the court and will pursue the matter through the established legal process. Holding public office does not diminish a person’s right to personal safety or to seek redress through the courts,” Shaw said in a release on Friday.

The November 3 confrontation followed a tense sitting of the House during debate on a motion concerning Jamaica’s decision to abstain from a United Nations resolution calling for an end to the United States’ decades-old trade embargo against Cuba.

Opposition members objected to the way the debate was brought to a close, arguing that their participation had been curtailed. The disagreement continued after the sitting was adjourned, with a separate heated exchange involving Opposition MP Mikael Phillips and Government MP Desmond McKenzie.

It was during that disorder that the Speaker left the chamber.

Brown Burke has since denied physically assaulting or pushing Holness, although she has acknowledged using the word “Coward” during the exchange.

Brown Burke had also taken steps to challenge public statements alleging that she physically assaulted the Speaker.

On November 10, her attorneys at Chen Green & Company wrote to Holness, Senate President Tom Tavares-Finson, and Deputy Senate President Charles Sinclair demanding that they withdraw statements alleging that Brown Burke had pushed or physically assaulted the Speaker.

The attorneys said the statements had damaged their client’s reputation and demanded written withdrawals, apologies, and compensation. They gave the three parliamentarians 10 days to respond.

The People’s National Party subsequently indicated that Brown Burke could pursue claims in the Supreme Court if the matter was not resolved. However, as at November 20, there had been no public confirmation that she had filed a civil claim against the three.

The November incident was not the first major clash between the two parliamentarians. On April 28, Brown Burke was suspended for the remainder of a sitting after liftng the ceremonial mace during proceedings on the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) Bill.

The incident occurred during the Committee of the Whole House’s examination of the Bill. Brown Burke removed the mace from its designated position, prompting the chair, Holness, to name her. The House subsequently suspended Brown Burke for the remainder of that sitting.

That incident was later cited by the Government when it moved to suspend Brown Burke again following the November confrontation.

At last week’s sitting of Parliament, Leader of Government Business Floyd Green moved a motion under Standing Order 43(13), accusing Brown Burke of obstructing the Speaker’s path as she left the chamber, making physical contact with her, and shouting “Coward!”

The motion described the alleged conduct as a breach of the respect owed to the authority of the chair and the dignity of Parliament.

Green also relied on Brown Burke’s earlier suspension in April, arguing that the seriousness of the November incident, together with the previous disciplinary action, warranted a further suspension.

The motion proposed that Brown Burke be suspended from the service of the House until the conclusion of the sixth sitting following November 17. It also required her to leave Parliament immediately and barred her from attending House or committee meetings or entering the parliamentary precincts during the suspension.

World.title: Access fair brings vital services to Mandeville youth
World.content:
Minister of State in the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information Rhoda Moy Crawford (centre) listens as Keneive Hibbert (right) from the Child Diversion Division, Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs, highlights the various services offered by the ministry. Occasion was a tour of booths during the Youth Access Fair at Cecil Charlton Park in Mandeville, Manchester, on Thursday, November 19. Looking on is director of community engagement for the HEART/NSTA Trust Ronique Rhoden. Photo: JIS

Scores of young people benefited from employment and career support, and access to essential government services at a YOUth Access Fair on Thursday, November 19, 2026, at Cecil Charlton Park in Mandeville, Manchester.

The event was part of National Youth Month activities under the theme ‘YOUth WILL’.

It brought essential government services, career pathways, and training opportunities directly to young people in Mandeville and surrounding communities.

Attendees were able to apply for crucial services in one location, including Taxpayer Registration Number and National Insurance Scheme card.

Young people explored vocational training programmes offered by the HEART/NSTA Trust and had the opportunity to complete on-site assessments to gain certification as a customer service representative.

Representatives from the Ministry of Labour and Social Security and partner agencies provided job readiness resources, career guidance, and networking opportunities.

Minister of State in the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information Rhoda Moy Crawford said that this year’s Youth Month targets young people at all levels.

“There is something for every category, including youth who need help with writing résumés and job applications as well as three ‘Pon Di Corna’ activities in Portland, St Ann, and St Thomas for underserved and at-risk youth,” Crawford said.

She said that the activities also include a youth leaders’ summit, capacity-building workshops and the national youth parliament to help young leaders strengthen their skills.

“Student leaders have received several capacity-building workshops that strengthen young people who are already in leadership positions. The youth parliament will feature 70 youngsters from across the island representing the different constituencies, who will speak on topics relevant to youth. There was also a summit held in partnership with the Planning Institute of Jamaica for Corporate Area youth,” she said.

On Wednesday, November 25, a Youth Ignite Forum will be held in Westmoreland targeting 800 youngsters.

Director of Community Engagement at HEART/NSTA Trust, Ronique Rhoden, told JIS News that she was pleased with the turnout of young people for the YOUth Access Fair, including those accessing on-the-spot certification in customer service.

— JIS

World.title: Well done!
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (second right) greets a resident of the new Trelawny Adult Care Residential Facility, formerly the Trelawny Infirmary, in Falmouth, during the facility’s official opening on Thursday, November 19. Looking on are Minister of Local Government and Community Development Desmond McKenzie (right), Mayor of Falmouth Councillor C Junior Gager (third right), and other stakeholders.Photo: JIS

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Local Government and Community Development Minister Desmond McKenzie has praised Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager and his team for mobilising private sector support to help sustain critical services and rebuild Trelawny in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa.

Speaking during Thursday’s official opening of the Trelawny Adult Residential Care Facility (formerly infirmary) in Falmouth, McKenzie said Gager, who is chairman of the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC), had demonstrated strong leadership by proactively engaging corporate Jamaica to assist with recovery efforts.

He cited donations of seven air-conditioning units for the facility as an example of the mayor’s success.

Executive chairman of Sandals Resorts International Adam Stewart donated four units, while Roy Lafayette of Geddes Refrigeration contributed three, McKenzie disclosed, noting that the donations would ensure the facility is properly equipped to accommodate its residents.

The minister said the facility would also benefit from a solar system, adding that the private sector contributions reflected confidence in both central and local government. He urged other corporate entities to support initiatives aimed at improving the lives of vulnerable Jamaicans rather than simply criticising government efforts.

McKenzie also commended Gager for securing more than $10 million from Gore Homes towards construction of office spaces for the municipal corporation, which continues to operate amid the disruption caused by the October 28, 2025 hurricane.

The donation will fund the conversion of two containers into office spaces at the corporation’s Works Department site in Falmouth. The mayor’s parlour and administrative assistant’s office, the chief executive officer’s office and administrative assistant’s space, a meeting room and the revenue services department will be housed in the space.

“This is what good leadership, strong leadership, is all about,” McKenzie said, pointing to the initiative as an example of the efforts being made to restore municipal operations following the hurricane.

Delivering the keynote address during Thursday’s opening, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness said the facility, which can accommodate 60 residents, provides a temporary but improved home for the 54 residents displaced when Hurricane Melissa damaged the infirmary.

Residents were initially relocated to Hague Primary School before being moved to Elleston Wakefield Complex, where staff continued providing care amid the upheaval.

“Today, those residents finally have a fit-for-purpose facility to which they can return,” Holness said.

Gager described the reopening as a restoration of dignity, comfort and hope for some of Trelawny’s most vulnerable residents, noting that many had fallen on hard times due to circumstances beyond their control.

He thanked Holness and McKenzie for their leadership and support, and lauded donors, partners and staff — particularly the matron and care team — for helping bring the facility back into operation.

Gager also urged residents to protect the institution from vandalism, saying it must remain a place of compassion, dignity, and hope for years to come.

World.title: Majah Hype stars in award-winning HOMAGE
World.content:
Majah Hype

Majah Hype is bringing a different kind of performance to Jamaican cinema screens. Known internationally for his comedy and Caribbean characters, the entertainer takes a dramatic turn in

HOMAGE, the award-winning crime thriller opening through Palace Amusement on Wednesday, November 25.

Written by Jamaican screenwriter Dianne Diaz, and directed by actor and film-maker Miles Mussenden, HOMAGE follows a couple who try to help an old friend get back on his feet, only to discover that some debts should never be repaid.

Majah Hype plays Squeeze, whose return disrupts the lives of Marcus and Angie, portrayed by Mussenden and Nadirah Shakir. His performance earned him Best Actor at the Caribbean Film Awards, where HOMAGE also won Best Caribbean Film of the Year.

The production brings together Jamaican, Caribbean, and Diaspora talent, with a cast that includes Julie Mango, recording artiste Demarco, comedian and actor Negus Imara, and Reuben Shaw, who has family ties to Morgan Heritage. Their involvement, alongside Diaz’s screenplay, gives the film a strong Jamaican creative connection.

For audiences who know these personalities through comedy, music, and social media, HOMAGE offers an opportunity to see familiar faces in a tense story of friendship, loyalty, and the dangerous obligations of the past.

The Jamaican theatrical release follows HOMAGE’s selection at the American Black Film Festival, where it played to a sold-out screening in Miami Beach.

The film marks Mussenden’s feature directorial début. The British-born, Brooklyn-raised actor of Guyanese parentage is known for television roles in Marvel’s Cloak & Dagger, The Good Lord Bird, and Tulsa King.

Mussenden also has long-standing ties to Jamaica’s music industry, having produced recordings with his former Two Friends Records partner Mikey Bennett for artistes including Dennis Brown, Shabba Ranks, and Gregory Isaacs. HOMAGE extends those creative connections into film-making, bringing Caribbean and Diaspora artistes together for an independently produced thriller.

Opening just ahead of the US Thanksgiving holiday, HOMAGE gives Jamaican movie-goers the opportunity to experience the award-winning film on the big screen.

World.title: Proposed shared communities law could come with big bill for homeowners
World.content:
MONTAGUE... you’re forcing the people to go take on an accountant and run up expenses for a small scheme of 10 people.

SOME legislators reviewing a Bill to regulate shared communities have questioned whether its financial and administrative requirements could create more problems for homeowners than they solve.

The concerned legislators warned that proposed rules requiring professional accounting services and regular reporting may prove difficult for small communities to meet.

The concerns were raised during a meeting of the joint select committee reviewing the Registration (Shared Community) Act, 2026 on Thursday where members debated whether the proposed framework strikes the right balance between ensuring that common areas are properly maintained and protecting residents from additional financial pressure.

A major point of contention was clause 22(2) of the Bill, which requires community corporations to submit their annual financial statements to an accountant and engage an accountant to carry out specific checks on their accounts. Under clause 22 (3), the corporation would also be responsible for paying the associated costs.

Committee Chairman Robert Montague questioned whether the requirement was necessary for small developments, particularly those with only a handful of homes.

He argued that the cost of meeting the requirement could be disproportionate for smaller communities, which may have limited funds and rely on residents to manage their affairs.

“I’m a little uncomfortable right here…because you’re forcing the people to go take on an accountant and run up expenses for a small scheme of 10 people…This is making an industry out of a shared community, finding work for the accountant. So I’m going to ask that we relook again at this provision,” said Montague.

The Bill, as drafted, requires community corporations to submit their financial statements to an accountant within two months of the end of their financial year and to engage an accountant to undertake verification procedures approved by the corporation at a general meeting. The community corporation would be responsible for the resulting expenses.

The proposed requirements are intended to strengthen oversight of money collected from homeowners, particularly contributions towards maintaining shared facilities such as roads, drains, recreational areas, and other common property.

However, Government Senator Sherene Golding Campbell questioned whether the requirements took sufficient account of the circumstances of ordinary Jamaicans who purchase homes in these developments, many of whom may not have the resources or experience to manage the administrative demands.

“These people bought a house, some of them family and friends support putting a deposit together to finally have their own little place…Not everybody goes to the bank and ‘say, well, boy, draw out my $10 million and put it on the deposit’. That’s not the reality of the majority of Jamaica,” Golding Campbell said.

She questioned what would happen when communities could not afford to meet the requirements, particularly given the existing difficulties with compliance among strata corporations.

Mercede Scott, a senior inspector at the Real Estate Board, told the committee that fewer than half of the strata communities under the existing regulatory system comply with similar financial reporting requirements.

Scott explained that the Commission of Strata Corporations monitors the bodies, reviews annual returns, and issues notices where it identifies breaches. It also provides assistance through workshops and meetings, with cases referred to its legal department for enforcement when communities fail to comply.

Golding Campbell said the figures raised questions about whether the proposed legislation would be practical to enforce, especially if the number of shared communities eventually exceeds the number of strata developments.

She warned that requirements which communities cannot afford to meet could place unnecessary stress on homeowners, even where there was no evidence that their funds were being mismanaged.

The concerns were echoed by Opposition Member of Parliament for St Andrew East Central Dennis Gordon, who questioned whether the proposed law had sufficient measures to ensure compliance without imposing additional costs on residents.

He also raised the possibility of incorporating the proposed framework into existing strata legislation rather than creating a separate law.

Meanwhile, permanent secretary in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development Arlene Williams said the comparison with strata communities needed to be considered more broadly.

She argued that the proposed law could be strengthened through adequate penalties to encourage compliance, while the reasons for low compliance under the existing system should also be examined.

Not all committee members shared the concerns about the proposed requirements.

Member of Parliament for St Andrew North Western Duane Smith argued that the problems affecting shared communities required rules that could be enforced, pointing to situations in which some residents failed to contribute towards the upkeep of facilities while others carried the cost.

Government Senator Rose Bennett-Cooper also defended the Bill’s intention, saying it was designed to provide relief to residents who were shouldering maintenance expenses on behalf of their neighbours.

She said the legislation was not intended to punish homeowners, but to ensure that everyone who benefited from shared facilities contributed towards their upkeep.

The proposed law is intended to address problems involving the management and maintenance of common areas and the responsibilities of homeowners who share those facilities. It is separate from the existing legislation governing strata developments.

World.title: MBJ Foundation gives boost to Anchovy High
World.content:
Students who benefited from MBJ Foundation Scholarship grants, during an awards ceremony on Wednesday.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — For months, Hurricane Melissa-inflicted damage to Anchovy High School in St James forced students and staff to operate under tents. Then a $24-million donation from MBJ Foundation helped fund rehabilitation of their auditorium which was completed earlier this year.

The support rebuilt more than the physical structure.

“When Melissa struck us and we looked at the damage, it was not just the roof that was lost, it was not just the teaching and learning resources, books and computers, and many other things that were lost; we were shaken, our spirit was shaken,” Acting Principal Lorraine Dennis-Rowe told the audience gathered, on Wednesday, for an award ceremony to hand over funds raised from a recent walk/run.

Dennis-Rowe said after the Category 5 storm, the school experienced “a little dark moment” but a visit from the MBJ team helped turn things around.

“We were using tents for a while after Melissa, and because of the rebuilding of the auditorium we were able to come out of a hot tent [and go] back in the auditorium with fans that were installed from this contribution,” she said gratefully.

“The contribution is not just a contribution, but it’s an indication to us as a school family that MBJ has made a declaration that you care not just for the Anchovy High School, but for our nation’s children,” added Dennis-Rowe.

Her comments came after she accepted a ceremonial plaque from MBJ Airports Limited Chief Executive Officer Shane Munroe.

“On behalf of the board and staff, students, parents of the Anchovy High School family, we want to express profound thanks to the MBJ team and sponsors for such support,” said the acting principal.

Munroe said a random visit to the institution prompted the decision to help.

“We decided to just drive to the school — and this was just after the hurricane. To see the damage there was heartbreaking,” he recalled. Anchovy High School operates two campuses, one in Montpelier and its main campus in Anchovy. The Montpelier campus sustained major damage, forcing classes from that location to be relocated to the Anchovy campus. In total, there are 1,700 students enrolled and many regularly use the auditorium which is now fully operational. “We knew we had to make an impact at that institution and we decided that’s where we wanted to contribute to that school,” MBJ’s Munroe explained. The work was done out in collaboration with National Education Trust (NET), a registered charitable organisation and an agency of the Ministry of Education. “NET organised the entire procurement and rebuilding process and we funnelled funds through them. They have been our partner in this, we consider them to be our friends,” said Munroe. While the announcement of the support for Anchovy High was a major highlight of the awards ceremony, the main focus was presentation of grants totalling $20 million to 200 students at the secondary and tertiary levels. The funds were raised through the MBJ Foundation’s Charity Run/Walk held earlier this year. “We don’t see it, though, as just simply 200 grants or 200 scholarships, we see this as investing in 200 futures,” Munroe stated. “Among the students receiving grants today are future teachers, engineers, doctors, nurses, business leaders — maybe the next prime minister of Jamaica — and this is why education means so much to us,” added Munroe.

World.title: READY FOR THE WORLD
World.content:
An architectural design of the National Stadium redevelopment project unveiled by the Sports Ministry in 2025. The venue will host games at the FIFA Women’s World Cup in 2031..

IN two days, Jamaica will enter a new chapter in its football history when it becomes the first Caribbean country to host a senior FIFA World Cup, officially being named a co-host of the 2031 Women’s World Cup.

The Jamaica Observer first reported on Friday evening that the island will be formally confirmed alongside the USA, Mexico and Costa Rica as hosts of the expanded 48-team tournament with FIFA President Gianni Infantino set to make the announcement at FIFA’s Extraordinary Congress in Zurich, Switzerland on Monday.

A FIFA source with knowledge of the matter told the Observer that the announcement is a mere formality and that Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts, who arrived in the Swiss City on Friday, is expected to be notified during the congress.

The announcement will bring an end to a 13-month wait for the JFF and the Government after Jamaica joined the hosting bid in October last year.

The award of hosting rights was initially expected to be confirmed at the FIFA Congress in Vancouver, Canada in April this year but FIFA postponed the decision, reportedly because US President Donald Trump had yet to sign off on the guarantees required by the body.

The delay created an anxious wait for Jamaicans, particularly those at the JFF. A FIFA delegation visited the island in February to assess Jamaica’s hosting capabilities, including an inspection of the National Stadium, which is set to undergo major upgrades ahead of the tournament.

In July, the Observer reported that FIFA had concerns around the country’s infrastructure after its visit, with FIFA consultant and Women’s Football Division advisor Jose Andres Portabella saying “there’s a lot of work to be done”.

However, some of the anxiety was eased in August after Sports Minister Olivia Grange and Ricketts signed the guarantee agreements needed by FIFA.

A further boost came in September with the visit of Infantino, who travelled to Kingston for the Reggae Boyz’s Concacaf Nations League match against El Salvador at the National Stadium.

The Observer understands Infantino expressed confidence to Grange and Ricketts, who were also in attendance, that Jamaica was in pole position to host the 2031 showpiece.

With the announcement now days away, Ricketts speaking with the Observer late Friday evening in Zurich says that the JFF has made every effort to ensure Jamaica secured hosting rights.

“The directors would have given me personally every ounce of support that I would have needed in this regard and we really worked assiduously to ensure that we get over the line,” he said. “We would have had a number of meetings, we would have had several discussions, we would have put plans in place and we would have put a task force in place, headed of course by Omar McFarlane, who was selected by the JFF to be the liaison person between the organisers and of course the Jamaica Football Federation. Omar is actually here with me.

“We have a first meeting [this] morning at 8:45 am then of course we meet again on Sunday and the grand finale will be Monday when the announcement will be formalised, so we are just super excited.”

Hosting rights would also be significant for the Reggae Girlz, who would automatically qualify for the World Cup and could make it four consecutive World Cup appearances if they beat Costa Rica in their Concacaf W Championship quarter-final on Friday.

During the guarantee agreement signing in August, Grange said that Jamaica will host five group-stage matches and a round of 32.

This means the Reggae Girlz could play all their group games on home soil. It would be similar to last summer’s men’s World Cup when co-hosts Mexico and Canada played all three of their three group games in their respective home countries.

While that arrangement is yet to be confirmed, Ricketts is hoping the Reggae Girlz will enjoy the same advantage.

“I don’t think it’s something that we can demand, but certainly we can have a discussion on it and we will have a discussion because certainly I will raise it with the competition department at FIFA and see how best they could accommodate that,” he said.

“The precedence has been set, so I don’t think it’s far-fetched and I don’t think it will be an unreasonable ask. So, this is something that we will definitely be hoping for so that our Girlz will play in front of Jamaican fans.”

The hosting rights announcement will place the National Stadium upgrade timeline under renewed scrutiny. Construction, which was initially expected to begin earlier this year, is now scheduled to start in July or August 2027 after Minister Grange’s announcement in March. However, no new completion date was given, leaving uncertainty over whether the original 2029 target remains achievable.

World.title: Russian ship damaged by drone attack in Gulf of Finland, Helsinki and Moscow say
World.content:
Ilja Iljin of the Finnish coast guard told broadcaster Yle that the ship was known to have links with the Russian armed forces, but that it could not be confirmed whether military equipment was on board. Russian state-owned news agency Tass said the vessel was transporting “paints and coatings,” citing a single unnamed source.

Iljin also said the drones were Ukrainian.

The ship, which Estonian border authorities identified as Sparta II, was heading to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad which borders Lithuania and Poland. The Kaliningrad Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh, said in a statement that Russia’s early assessment was that two drones were involved.

“War is spilling over into our neighboring regions,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement on X.

Orpo added: “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

The Finnish Border Guard is leading a maritime rescue operation and preparing for possible environmental consequences in Finnish waters, according to Yle.

World.title: Russian threats ‘less and less hybrid,’ Von der Leyen says after assassination plot in Denmark
World.content:
Officials said at a press conference that a Russian intelligence service had hired two members of the Copenhagen-based gang Loyal to Familia to carry out the attack, but that police managed to stop them before it took place. The concert was then cancelled.

The suspects deny the allegations.

The Danish government reacted on Friday by expelling the Russian defense attaché, giving him seven days to leave the country.

“Moscow will respond accordingly,” Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told state-owned news agency Tass.

“The accusations against Russia are again not supported by any evidence, except for the unsubstantiated and unverifiable ‘conclusions’ and ‘data’ of Danish intelligence services,” the Russian embassy in Denmark said in a statement.

Von der Leyen said in her statement that the EU has “the tools to act” against cases like this. She said actions could range from “rapid response teams” to sanctions. She added that an upcoming European Security Strategy, which she announced in her State of the EU speech in September, could reinforce the bloc’s “preparedness and deterrence.”

It is the second time Kyivstoner has been targeted in an attempted murder plot this year. On Aug. 7, a Russian man was detained in Poland for planning an attack against the musician, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Russia’s FSB security service accused the rapper in July of helping to plan drone attacks on a defense facility in the Moscow region, an allegation he denied on social media.

World.title: Costa cuts proposed EU budget by €44B
World.content:
"This proposal is fit for tackling the challenges we are facing in our societies, and gives the European Union the necessary capacity to act," Costa said on Saturday morning.

Costa, who is guiding discussions over the 2028-2034 budget which needs to be agreed by all EU governments, suggested the reductions, which are based on current prices, from the previous proposal presented by Ireland, in its role holding the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, last month.

Overall, the cuts amount to a reduction in size of the budget by €204 billion, or 10.2%, from the European Commission’s original proposal in July last year.

In another major development, Costa suggested introducing a new tax on large digital companies such as Google and Meta to help finance the budget over the coming years.

In recent years, Brussels held back from levying this tax for fear retaliation from Washington, but the Republicans' bruising defeat in the midterm elections earlier this month created an opening.

These ideas set the scene for fraught discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during a summit next week. Even then the agreed budget will have to be approved by the European Parliament.

World.title: UK will take its time setting out Brexit options, says minister
World.content:
Andy Burnham pledged in September to set out “options” to fix the U.K. relationship with the bloc — which he said could include rejoining its single market, customs union, or even the EU itself.

But speaking in Brussels on Friday, the prime minister suggested the process could take longer and signaled the start of an “informal brainstorming process” with the European Union to conclude at the next U.K.-EU summit near the end of 2027.

It comes after rumbles of Cabinet discontent over the policy shift and speculation the prime minister may be taking a more cautious approach to avoid spooking his own government allies.

Defending the length of the process, Falconer said there was “a lot of variation” in the different relationships Britain could have with the EU and detail to work through.

“People say, ‘Oh, the options are obvious’ … but I think most people would struggle to describe the precise difference between the different arrangements,” he said.

Burnham has said he will be led by the public on the issue and told reporters in Brussels on Friday that he would “not be running ahead of public opinion on the issue.”

World.title: The biggest winners and losers of the EU-UK summit deals
World.content:
British renewable energy producers have double reason to celebrate. The decision to link the U.K. and EU emissions trading schemes from 2028 means clean energy exported to the continent will no longer be subject to the EU’s carbon border tax — making British clean energy exports more competitive.

Perhaps even more significant is a plan for the U.K. to join the EU internal electricity market, which they hope to finalize next year. If that comes off, it will make it much easier for British electricity generators to sell power to EU customers.

“That would be a major prize for consumers and the renewable energy industry,” RenewableUK chief executive Tara Singh said in a statement Friday, adding it would allow “electricity to be traded more efficiently across our interconnectors and enabling Britain and Europe to make better use of the cheapest clean power available at any given time.” EU renewables groups have made the same point.

The tech industry



The plan to launch an EU-U.K. Digital Partnership early next year is a win for the tech industry on both sides of the channel.



The statement’s wording is loose and doesn’t provide a ton of detail for industry types to sink their teeth into, but it spans a wide range of potential areas that “could cover” secure connectivity, quantum, online safety, as well as AI and its safety — areas that have seen considerable divergence since Brexit.



The statement also includes digital wallets and credentials, which are of interest to U.K. businesses, especially since Andy Burnham ditched the British government’s plans for digital ID.



Of the more political parts of the agreement, the youth visas scheme element is a big win for smaller U.K. tech companies who want to welcome keen young Europeans and entrepreneurs to the British tech scene.

The City

While there was nothing of great direct benefit to the City of London in today’s deal, the mood music matters for the U.K.’s financial services industry.

World.title: Andy Burnham discovers nothing in Brussels is ever easy
World.content:
A joint statement by the Council and the European Commission, circulated by EU diplomats, said three long-planned deals on carbon emissions trading, food standards and a youth experience scheme would not be formally adopted until both sides had concluded talks on a pact “providing for equal treatment on tuition fees.”

This derailed Downing Street’s media strategy on summit day after months of pitch-rolling.

Negotiators had spent months tying together deals to align food standards and emissions trading, and finalized a cap on the youth experience scheme — allowing 100,000 EU citizens under 32 each year to move to the U.K. for up to three years, and vice versa.

They also agreed, as expected, to delay the resolution of two issues by six months — Britain would work on a pledge to cut university tuition fees for EU students, in exchange for assurances that its industries would be protected from the EU’s Made in Europe scheme.

David Henig, the U.K. government’s former assistant director on trade policy, said that different things could be true at the same time — that the three deals announced Friday were contingent on a tuition fees breakthrough, but also that “in reality, there will be a deal on tuition fees” no matter what.

Henig, who now leads the U.K. Trade Policy Project at European Centre for International Political Economy, said the situation was “entirely normal” in the trade world but that handling of the communications had still been a “complete mess.”

World.title: France and Germany complete political deal for ECB leadership
World.content:
The new set-up paves the way for Spain’s former central bank governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to become ECB President once Christine Lagarde steps down on Feb. 7.

The Netherlands had hoped to secure the top job. But having Dutch and German monetary hawks in what are typically the ECB’s two most influential posts would have been unacceptable to the dovish south, analysts said.

If approved, Boone will step into a pivotal position at the Bank if strains in French and other European debt markets continue to worsen — a clear risk in the European Commission’s new forecasts that show many eurozone members’ budget deficits widening next year.

In an October interview with POLITICO, former ECB Chief Economist Peter Praet said the markets role matters most when market tensions increase pressure on the ECB to intervene in bond markets.

“I think this would be a very strong board, combining deep economic expertise, extensive policymaking experience and strong international networks,” EFG Chief Economist Stefan Gerlach said. “These are all important qualities, particularly at a time when the ECB faces considerable economic and political uncertainty.”

Fewer politicians

A board stacked with economic expertise would mark a break from the previous lineup, when former politicians, Lagarde and Luis de Guindos, held both the presidency and vice-presidency.

World.title: Latvian leader calls for closure of EU borders to all Russians
World.content:
Latvia was among the 11 countries that signed a Swedish-led letter in June urging Brussels to restrict visas for Russians. Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner suggested to POLITICO in October that the European Commission could present a proposal next year.
