World.title: Kazakhstan’s Processed Agricultural Exports Rise 35% to $3.4 Billion
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s exports of processed agricultural products reached $3.4 billion in January-September 2026, up from $2.5 billion in the same period last year, Agriculture Minister Aidarbek Saparov said.

The increase amounted to 35%, while processed products’ share of the country’s total agricultural exports rose from 51.3% to 53.3%, reported the ministry’s press service.

Saparov said expanding the production and export of finished agricultural goods was a key government priority, as it would allow Kazakhstan to generate greater economic returns from its agricultural resources.

“Kazakhstan must earn not only from grain sales, but also from finished products. This represents a completely different level of economic returns from agriculture,” he said.

Kazakhstan produces between 18 million and 20 million tons of wheat and 1 million to 1.2 million tons of corn annually. This year’s corn harvest reached 1.7 million tons, according to the minister.

Expanding deep grain processing

More than 5 million tons of grain are currently processed in Kazakhstan each year, including nearly 510,000 tons through deep-processing technologies. In 2025, the country produced 145,100 tons of starch products, an increase of 21.8% from the previous year. Bioethanol production reached 21,000 tons, more than doubling year on year.

The Agriculture Ministry plans to launch six major facilities for deep processing of wheat and corn by 2029. Together, the enterprises are expected to have an annual processing capacity of 5.8 million tons of raw materials.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Pure Technics Receives San Marino Approval to Maintain Foreign-Registered Aircraft
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan-based aviation maintenance company Pure Technics has received a CAR-145 maintenance organization certificate from the Aviation Authority of San Marino, expanding its ability to service aircraft registered in the country, the company reported on Nov. 18.

The certificate took effect on Oct. 30 and covers maintenance work at Pure Technics’ facilities in Astana and Atyrau, according to the official San Marino Aircraft Registry.

The approval authorizes the company to maintain Embraer EMB-135BJ aircraft and Leonardo AW109, AW139 and AW169 helicopters. It also allows Pure Technics to issue certificates of release to service following maintenance, within the scope of its approved activities.

The certification follows the implementation of the company’s development strategy and expands the range of maintenance services it can offer to operators of foreign-registered aircraft in the region.

“Obtaining the CAR-145 certificate is one of the results of the consistent implementation of our service center’s development strategy. Our team completed the necessary preparations and successfully passed the audit at our production facilities,” said Pure Technics Executive Director Dmitry Sokolov.

He added that the approval gives current and prospective customers in the region greater flexibility in choosing maintenance locations and planning their work.

San Marino has been a member of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) since 1988. Its aviation authority oversees civil aviation matters, including aircraft registration, operations and continuing airworthiness.

Aircraft registered in San Marino carry the national registration prefix T7. The expansion of its network of approved maintenance organizations allows operators to access technical services in different regions. Pure Technics’ inclusion in this network increases the availability of maintenance support in Central Asia.

About Pure Technics

Pure Technics provides line and scheduled maintenance for aircraft and helicopters, as well as continuing airworthiness support. Its services include maintenance planning, budgeting and the development of technical support programs.

The company supports aircraft including the Pilatus PC-12 and PC-24, Beechcraft King Air 300 series and Embraer 145/135, including Legacy 600/650 models. Its helicopter portfolio includes the Leonardo AW109, AW139 and AW169, as well as Airbus Helicopters EC-145 and H-145 models.

Pure Technics holds maintenance organization certificates issued by Kazakhstan’s Aviation Administration and the State Agency of Civil Aviation of the Kyrgyz Republic, in addition to its new San Marino approval. Its production facilities are located at Astana and Atyrau international airports.

The company also maintains partnerships with aircraft manufacturers Embraer, Leonardo Helicopters and Textron, as well as engine manufacturers Rolls-Royce and Pratt & Whitney.

World.title: Neighbors mourn the dead and collect belongings from the ruins of their homes. Explosion in Tbilisi
World.content:
Explosion in Fonichala

Six people were killed in a gas explosion in a residential building in Ponichala, a district in Tbilisi. Two of the victims were young children who died alongside their mothers.

One of the five people injured in the explosion remains in critical condition. Two minors are also still receiving hospital treatment.

The destruction left 28 families homeless. They are currently staying in hotels.

Photographs of the six victims at a small park next to the building. Neighbours have set up an impromptu memorial here.

What is happening near the site of the explosion

In Lower Ponichala, where a gas explosion on the morning of November 19 caused two stairwells of a residential building to collapse, the area remains cordoned off with yellow tape. Rescue workers are still at the scene.

Trucks loaded with construction debris stand in the courtyard. Rescue teams are clearing the collapsed building of concrete rubble.

A makeshift memorial has been set up in a small park near the building. It is covered with photographs of the victims, flowers, candles and colourful stuffed toys. Little girls are tying black ribbons around the memorial.

The small park next to the building where the explosion occurred. Photo: Interpressnews

It has been raining in Tbilisi for several days. To protect the photographs, flowers and candles from the rain, the memorial has been covered with a tarpaulin.

Relatives of the victims, neighbours and acquaintances keep coming to the park. No one seems able to talk about what happened. People are still struggling to hold back their tears.

The victims’ classmates and friends also come to pay their respects, bringing dozens of large stuffed toys.

With the help of rescue workers, survivors are returning to their damaged apartments to retrieve whatever personal belongings remain intact. They carry them out in plastic bags.

“There was a terrible noise and everything shook – we thought it was an earthquake.” What happened in Ponichala

At around 9 a.m. on November 19, a powerful explosion rocked Lower Ponichala, at 16 Rustavi Highway. People were getting ready to leave for school and work. Some were already out on the street.

The explosion was caused by a build-up of natural gas on the fifth floor of a five-storey residential building. The blast wave destroyed part of the building, brought down the floor slabs and turned two stairwells into a pile of concrete within seconds.

People jumped from windows in an attempt to escape.

The blast wave threw a young man out of the fifth-floor apartment where the explosion occurred. He was the owner of the apartment. He is now in hospital with severe burns.

“There was a terrible noise and everything shook. At first, we thought it was an earthquake,” survivors who narrowly escaped the building recall.

Seven people were trapped under the rubble.

Neighbours say that in the first minutes after the explosion, they could hear several people screaming for help from beneath the debris. They were trapped under enormous concrete slabs, and it was impossible to reach them.

Of the seven people trapped, only one — three-year-old Taiya — was rescued alive. The other six were found dead. The rescue operation ended around midnight.

November 22 was declared a national day of mourning in Georgia.

Survivors: children remain in hospital, 31-year-old man in critical condition

Five people were taken to hospital following the explosion. Four were admitted in the morning, immediately after the incident. The fifth, a three-year-old girl, was brought to hospital later.

Three of the five injured people remain in hospital. They include two minors — 11-year-old Andria and three-year-old Taiya.

As of November 20, both children’s conditions were stable and satisfactory. According to doctors, a psychologist is also working with them. The three-year-old girl is expected to be discharged before the 11-year-old boy.

The third patient, a 31-year-old man, remains in critical condition.

The other two injured people sustained minor injuries and have already been discharged from hospital.

Three-year-old Taiya – eight hours under the rubble

Footage of the rescue of three-year-old Taiya.

Three-year-old Taiya was the only person rescued alive from the devastating collapse. She spent eight hours trapped beneath the rubble.

Firefighter and rescue worker Gaga Gigashvili describes the operation to save her:

“There were what amounted to three floors of debris on top of her – concrete slabs, blocks and wooden materials. When we reached her, only one leg was visible. When we touched it, she moved her leg slightly. Then we managed to reach her hand. She was holding a toy, as well as a hair clip, which she had kept clenched in her fist for all eight hours. When we opened her hand and took the clip, we held her hand and asked her to squeeze ours if she could hear us. When she squeezed our hand, we realised she was conscious and responding to us.”

The footage of the girl’s rescue is deeply moving. She is wearing a blue sweater covered in dirt and white tights. Her face is also smeared with soil and concrete dust. Rescuers carry her out of the rubble in their arms.

“Bless you, my dear,” one of the rescuers can be heard saying. It is Gaga Gigashvili. His face is contorted with emotion and exhaustion.

Gaga hands the little girl to another rescuer, who holds her close and runs towards the ambulance.

A huge crowd has gathered outside the building. People greet Taiya’s emergence with applause and tears. Her rescue gives those gathered hope that the other six people might also be found alive.

By this point, it is already known that Taiya’s mother and her seven-year-old sister are among those trapped beneath the rubble.

11-year-old Andria sustained serious injuries

Eleven-year-old Andria remains in hospital. He was admitted together with his mother, a 38-year-old woman.

According to Gia Bibilashvili, a doctor at Ingorokva Clinic, the boy was brought to hospital with more serious injuries than his mother.

Andria sustained focal brain injuries, several areas of bruising, a lung contusion, skull bone injuries, damage to his outer ear, and multiple injuries to his skin and soft tissues. He also required plastic surgery to repair the damage to his ear.

His condition is now relatively stable. Doctors plan to transfer him from intensive care to a regular hospital ward soon.

Andria’s mother suffered a concussion. She was discharged from hospital shortly afterwards.

31-year-old Ilia Isaev – the man whose apartment was the site of the explosion

The most seriously injured of all the survivors is 31-year-old Ilia Isaev. He was admitted to hospital with burns covering 87% of his body. According to doctors at the burns centre, his respiratory tract was also damaged.

Ilia was initially conscious. Before being taken to hospital, he managed to describe how the explosion happened.

He did not live in the apartment permanently. He had returned to Tbilisi from Batumi just one day before the incident. According to his account, he had tried to switch on the gas heater during the night but was unable to do so.

In the morning, he tried again. A powerful explosion followed. The blast wave threw Ilia out of the apartment.

He is now in hospital in extremely serious condition and is on a ventilator. Doctors continue to describe his condition as critical.

Who were the victims of the Ponichala explosion?

Six people died in the explosion: two young mothers and their young daughters, a 54-year-old woman and a 28-year-old man.

Nino Chelidze and her seven-year-old daughter Nutsa

Nino and seven-year-old Nutsa

Nino Chelidze was the mother of three-year-old Taiya. She was raising five children and worked at a clothing store.

At the time of the explosion, Nino was at home with two of her children — three-year-old Taiya and seven-year-old Nutsa. Her husband had taken their other three children to school shortly before the blast.

Nino’s body was found shortly after rescuers managed to pull Taiya out of the rubble. Nutsa was found much later, after hours of searching.

“Nino and her husband were raising five wonderful children. They were very happy – cheerful, good people. And suddenly, everything came crashing down on them. I have no words. When Taiya was found, I truly hoped the others would also be found alive, but unfortunately, that did not happen,” a family friend, still shaken by the tragedy, says.

Veriko Vanishvili and first-grader Ariana

Veriko Vanishvili and Ariana

Veriko Vanishvili lived on the second floor of the apartment building in Fonichala with her six-year-old daughter, Ariana Ristich. Both mother and daughter were at home that morning.

Veriko worked as the head of marketing at Grand Bellagio casino.

“Her smile, sincerity and dedication to her work will remain with our team forever,” the casino wrote in a Facebook post.

Ariana is remembered by staff at Tbilisi Kindergarten No. 58 and by her classmates.

“You will forever remain a tremendous pain, an irreplaceable loss, an emptiness and an unhealed wound for us, our bright, lively, warm and sweet girl,” kindergarten staff wrote.

“Ariana, you were and will always remain a little part of our school. It is difficult to come to terms with the fact that your childhood smile will no longer light up the classroom,” the administration of Helios private school wrote.

Lali Shishmanashvili — “the mother of the twins”

Lali Shishmanashvili

Lali Shishmanashvili, 54, lived on the first floor. Her twin daughters were also at home when the explosion occurred.

According to neighbours, when the building began to collapse, Lali managed to shout to her daughters to jump out of the window. This helped save their lives.

“The mother managed to shout: ‘Jump!’” one neighbour recalls. The neighbours called Lali “the mother of the twins”.

According to the neighbour, Lali was calling for help and pleading to be rescued. She said she was afraid of the dark.

“Her bedroom door was blocked by concrete slabs, and a slab had also collapsed inside the room. There was nothing anyone could do to help her. I kept telling her: ‘The rescuers are already here. They will get you out soon,’” the neighbour recalls.

Lali was a philologist and also tutored students at home.

“She was a mother who lived for her children. She did everything she could to give them a good life,” recalls a friend of Lali. She spent the entire night outside the building, hoping her friend would be rescued.

Jaba Sakevarashvili — a 28-year-old courier

Jaba Sakevarashvili

Another victim of the Fonichala explosion was 28-year-old Jaba Sakevarashvili. He worked as a courier for Georgian Post.

His colleagues remember him as a responsible, hardworking employee who was dedicated to his job.

According to someone close to Jaba, the young man had only recently moved into the apartment.

28 families left homeless, while 62 remain in the same building

The building where the explosion occurred is a multi-apartment residential block with six entrances. According to Tbilisi City Hall, 90 families lived in the building. All residents were evacuated immediately after the explosion.

Initially, Tbilisi City Hall said it was ready to accommodate all evacuated residents in hotels. On the same day, a municipal service inspected the building. Following the inspection, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said that only two entrances were affected – the one where the explosion occurred and the adjacent one. The remaining four entrances were considered safe for residents to return to.

The 28 families who lived in the two collapsed entrances – a total of 143 people – are currently staying in hotels.

According to the mayor, the municipality will offer these families a housing replacement programme. Until new apartments are built for them, they will be accommodated in rented housing, with the rent covered by the city.

Remains of family photo albums near the collapsed building. Photo: Georgian Public Broadcaster.



Late in the evening on November 20, the ruling Georgian Dream party released a condolence letter from Bidzina and Eka Ivanishvili. The letter stated that the Ivanishvilis would purchase apartments for the 28 families left homeless.

The announcement followed an earlier statement by the Tbilisi mayor. It is not yet known where the Ivanishvilis will purchase the apartments, when the families will receive their new homes, or how the assistance will be distributed. It has also not been clarified how this initiative will be coordinated with the housing replacement programme proposed by the municipality.

According to Tbilisi City Hall, residents of the building’s four surviving entrances will also be offered the opportunity to participate in the housing replacement programme. These are the 62 families who are still living in the building.

Could the tragedy have been prevented? The investigation must establish the facts

Giorgi Lefsveridze, deputy technical director of the gas distribution company Tbilisi Energy, said that the apartment where the explosion occurred was listed in the company’s database as disconnected from the gas supply.

According to him, no gas consumption had been recorded at the address from December 2025 until the day of the explosion, and the subscriber had received zero-balance bills every month. The company also said it had received no reports of a smell of gas from this address over the previous two years.

Lefsveridze said that scheduled inspections of the building had been carried out in January 2025 and January 2026. However, in January 2026, company employees were unable to enter the apartment where the explosion later occurred. With the help of neighbours, they contacted the owner, who said he was outside Tbilisi and would allow the inspection once he returned.

The investigation must establish what exactly caused the explosion and who bears responsibility for what happened.

A criminal investigation has been launched under Article 240 of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which concerns violations of safety regulations during construction work.

In parallel, the Energy Ombudsman’s Office has also launched its own examination of the incident. On the day of the tragedy, the office requested relevant information from Tbilisi Energy.

One-off incident or systemic problem? Tbilisi has seen similar tragedies before

The explosion in Ponichala is not the first incident of its kind. Gas explosions have occurred periodically in Tbilisi for years. Some have claimed lives, while others have caused such extensive damage that dozens of families have been temporarily left homeless.

In 2019, the organisation FactCheck published statistics based on data from the gas distribution company KazTransGaz.

“According to KazTransGaz data, between 2016 and the first quarter of 2019, 101 people died and another 285 were poisoned in Tbilisi as a result of explosions caused by natural gas leaks and gas-related intoxication.”

Every such tragedy reignites the debate over responsibility: who is accountable for these incidents? Who should inspect the structural integrity of residential buildings and ensure that gas distribution networks are functioning properly and safely?

Now, new questions have emerged: what happens when gas company employees cannot gain access to an apartment? Does zero gas consumption mean that an apartment is safe? What mechanisms are in place when a property owner is away for an extended period and a technical inspection cannot be carried out?

Engineer and professor Temur Mikiashvili, speaking to Netgazeti, says that the absence of gas consumption does not guarantee safety. According to him, a meter may fail to register a small leak, while gas can gradually accumulate inside an unoccupied apartment.

He also points to the deterioration of plastic pipes and rubber hoses connected to gas appliances, which can cause leaks that go unnoticed.

According to the expert, gas detectors are an important preventive measure. These devices sound an alarm or send a notification when they detect a leak. Some models can also automatically shut off the gas supply.

Another problem in Tbilisi: ageing residential buildings

Faulty gas systems are not the only problem facing Tbilisi. The residential building in Fonichala collapsed so rapidly that the tragedy has once again raised questions about the lifespan and structural safety of residential buildings.

Tbilisi has numerous old and deteriorating apartment blocks. Many buildings constructed decades ago no longer meet modern safety standards.

Tbilisi City Hall has a dedicated programme and budget for addressing the problem of unsafe residential buildings.

According to data published by corruption researcher Irakli Abesadze, two main municipal budget programmes are being implemented in this area:

Reinforcement of unsafe buildings – between 2018 and 2025, during Kakha Kaladze’s tenure as mayor, a total of GEL 87,742,800 was spent on the programme. A total of 269 buildings were fully or partially reinforced.



– between 2018 and 2025, during Kakha Kaladze’s tenure as mayor, a total of GEL 87,742,800 was spent on the programme. A total of 269 buildings were fully or partially reinforced. Replacement of unsafe buildings – launched in 2022, the programme received a total of GEL 19,081,700 in funding between 2022 and 2025.

Abesadze compares the funding allocated to these programmes with sums allegedly misappropriated through suspected corruption schemes.

According to him, the GEL 41,105,298 allegedly embezzled from the Tbilisi metro carriage modernisation project alone would have been enough to increase funding for the building reinforcement programme by 50%.

Abesadze estimates that this additional funding could have enabled the reinforcement of around 100 more buildings. The same amount, he says, would also have made it possible to triple the budget of the unsafe building replacement programme.

Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association: The state’s responsibility does not end with launching an investigation

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) also points to the scale and systemic nature of the problems. According to the organisation, the state’s obligations do not end with launching an investigation. It is necessary to establish whether inspection requirements under the gas distribution network regulations are being properly enforced and what measures are taken when access to a consumer’s apartment cannot be secured.

GYLA refers to the regulations approved by Resolution No. 80 of the Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission (GNERC), dated December 31, 2021. Under these rules, the system operator is required to regularly inspect the gas supply system within a consumer’s property. If violations are identified, the consumer must be notified in writing and appropriate measures must be taken.

This issue is particularly important in older residential buildings, where infrastructure installed decades ago, modified pipes, outdated heating appliances and inadequate ventilation systems remain in use.

World.title: Georgian Orthodox Church delegation arrives in Moscow for Patriarch Kirill’s anniversary celebrations
World.content:
A delegation from the Georgian Orthodox Church has arrived in Moscow to attend events marking the 80th birthday of Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and All Rus’.

The delegation includes a chorepiscopus of the Georgian Patriarchate, three members of the Holy Synod and a protopresbyter. Catholicos-Patriarch Shio III did not travel to Moscow for the celebrations.

The Georgian Patriarchate delegation arrived in Moscow on 19 November. It includes Metropolitan Theodor Chuadze of Akhaltsikhe and Tao-Klarjeti, Metropolitan Gerasim Sharashenidze of Zugdidi and Tsaishi, Metropolitan Andria Gvazava of Gori and Ateni, Bishop Vakhtang Liparteliani of Nikortsminda and Protopresbyter Giorgi Zviadadze.

The delegation is accompanied by Archpriest Vladimir Alexandrov, the Moscow Patriarchate’s representative in Georgia.

According to the Moscow Patriarchate’s Department for External Church Relations, representatives of the Russian Orthodox Church greeted the Georgian clergy at Moscow’s Vnukovo airport.

Who is Patriarch Kirill?

Kirill has led the Russian Orthodox Church since 2009. He supports Russian President Vladimir Putin and has publicly backed Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.

In September 2022, just days after Russia announced a partial mobilisation, Kirill said during a sermon that the sacrifice of those killed while performing their military duty “washes away all sins”. His remarks sparked widespread criticism.

Ukraine, the UK, Canada, Lithuania and the Czech Republic have imposed sanctions on Kirill over his support for the war.

Patriarch Kirill turned 80 on 20 November. The main anniversary celebrations took place at Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. Heads and representatives of local Orthodox churches attended a solemn liturgy.

Those who travelled to Moscow included Patriarch John X of Antioch, Patriarch Theophilos III of Jerusalem, Patriarch Porfirije of Serbia and Metropolitan Rastislav of the Czech Lands and Slovakia. Delegations from the Bulgarian, Albanian and Macedonian Orthodox churches also took part in the events.

Background

Georgia and Russia severed diplomatic relations after the August 2008 war. However, ties between their Orthodox churches have continued.

Official contacts between the two patriarchates have intensified in recent months. On 30 September 2026, Shio III received a Moscow Patriarchate delegation in Tbilisi. It was the first official meeting between the leaders of the two churches since Shio III’s enthronement.

The Russian delegation was led by Metropolitan Anthony of Volokolamsk, chairman of the Moscow Patriarchate’s Department for External Church Relations.

According to Archpriest Andria Jagmaidze, head of the Georgian Patriarchate’s public relations service, the meeting addressed the situation in occupied Abkhazia and the Tskhinval region (South Ossetia).

He said the Georgian Church could not hold religious services in these territories, while displaced people could not visit their ancestors’ graves.

Jagmaidze also said the two sides discussed restoring one of the Georgian churches located in Russia.

World.title: Turkey establishes ‘Abkhazia Friendship Group’ to end its isolation
World.content:
The founding meeting of the Abkhazia Friendship Group took place in Ankara, the capital of Turkey. Its founders – Turkish politicians and activists from the Abkhaz diaspora – have made ending the isolation of Abkhazia their main goal.

More than 20 members of the Turkish parliament attended the founding meeting, most of them representing opposition parties.

The event also brought together activists involved in the initiative to end Abkhazia’s isolation and an Abkhaz delegation comprising members of the Abkhaz parliament and representatives of official bodies.

The initiative to end Abkhazia’s isolation aims to secure Turkish recognition of Abkhaz documents and establish maritime and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia. These issues have entered Turkey’s public and political debate thanks to the End Abkhazia’s Isolation campaign, launched in late June 2026 by representatives of Turkey’s sizeable Abkhaz diaspora. Estimates suggest that between 500,000 and 700,000 Abkhaz people live in Turkey.

Calls for action have since featured in public statements by representatives of several political groups, civil society organisations and Caucasian associations, known as derneks, in Turkey.

On 5 August, opposition MPs made a joint statement on the Abkhaz issue for the first time in the history of the Turkish parliament.

A permanent group will now be established within parliament. It will serve as the main advisory body for Turkish MPs on humanitarian issues. For Abkhazia, this presents an unprecedented opportunity to break the deadlock over external mobility and strengthen ties with the diaspora.

Against this backdrop, 13 Georgian civil society organisations in Turkey issued a joint statement opposing the creation of the Abkhazia Friendship Group. They point out that Turkey’s official policy supports Georgia’s “territorial integrity” and argue that ending Abkhazia’s isolation would not contribute to regional stability.

The End Abkhazia’s Isolation campaign responded with another public statement. It stressed that the movement has no ethnic focus and is a civil society human rights initiative aimed at ending the isolation of all Abkhaz residents, regardless of their ethnicity:

“We are not raising international political issues such as territorial integrity. We are defending the most basic human rights: the right to life, education, healthcare, freedom of movement, family unity and respect for family life,” the statement said.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: From drones to paragliders: Azerbaijan’s border service reports drug smuggling by air from Iran
World.content:
Azerbaijan: Drug smuggling by paraglider

Azerbaijan’s State Border Service has reported another attempt to smuggle drugs from Iran into Azerbaijan using a powered paraglider.

According to the agency, the incident took place in an area patrolled by the Geytepe border detachment. Officers found 21kg and 210g of drugs on board the powered paraglider, including 19kg and 270g of cannabis and 1kg and 940g of opium. They also found 4,000 tablets of Methadone M-40, a drug containing psychotropic substances.

The State Border Service says it detained the Iranian national piloting the paraglider for illegally crossing the border. The agency has not disclosed his name or details of the further investigation.

In its statement, the service noted that attempts to smuggle drugs using aircraft continued “despite repeated warnings”. It said it would continue to “neutralise” aircraft and other technical equipment used for smuggling.

In March this year, we reported on operations by the Interior Ministry and the State Border Service to combat drug trafficking in 2024–2025.

How has aerial drug smuggling across the Iranian border changed in 2026, and why does the use of paragliders mark a new stage?

What has happened this year?

This year, Azerbaijan’s State Border Service has reported the following cases of aerial drug smuggling across the border with Iran:

24 February: According to the State Border Service, border guards heard the sound of a drone near the border. They later found more than 10kg of drugs, apparently dropped by a drone that had flown in from Iran.

According to the State Border Service, border guards heard the sound of a drone near the border. They later found more than 10kg of drugs, apparently dropped by a drone that had flown in from Iran. June: The agency reported foiling an attempt to smuggle 11.5kg of cannabis by drone across a section of the border patrolled by the Lankaran border detachment.

The agency reported foiling an attempt to smuggle 11.5kg of cannabis by drone across a section of the border patrolled by the Lankaran border detachment. 6 September: According to the State Border Service, border guards recorded two cases of aerial smuggling in a single night in an area patrolled by the Horadiz border detachment. At 01:30, smugglers used a drone to transport 21kg and 700g of drugs and 1,000 tablets. At 04:10, they delivered 17kg and 78g of drugs and 6,680 tablets by paraglider.

According to the State Border Service, border guards recorded two cases of aerial smuggling in a single night in an area patrolled by the Horadiz border detachment. At 01:30, smugglers used a drone to transport 21kg and 700g of drugs and 1,000 tablets. At 04:10, they delivered 17kg and 78g of drugs and 6,680 tablets by paraglider. 11 September: The agency reported finding 65kg and 500g of drugs dropped from a paraglider that had flown in from Iran. The incident took place at 03:11 in an area patrolled by the Horadiz border detachment. This was the largest consignment of drugs that the State Border Service reported smugglers had attempted to transport by air this year.

The agency reported finding 65kg and 500g of drugs dropped from a paraglider that had flown in from Iran. The incident took place at 03:11 in an area patrolled by the Horadiz border detachment. This was the largest consignment of drugs that the State Border Service reported smugglers had attempted to transport by air this year. Early November: The State Border Service reported seizing a total of 22.9kg of drugs transported by drones across sections of the border patrolled by the Horadiz and Geytepe border detachments.

The State Border Service reported seizing a total of 22.9kg of drugs transported by drones across sections of the border patrolled by the Horadiz and Geytepe border detachments. 16 November: According to the agency, border guards detained a paraglider pilot and seized the aircraft in an area patrolled by the Geytepe border detachment.

This list is not exhaustive. The State Border Service does not publish separate annual statistics on aerial drug smuggling. All the figures above come from the agency’s official statements. The service has also not disclosed the names of those detained or said whether prosecutors have brought their cases to court.

Drone or paraglider: what is the difference?

A drone is an unmanned aircraft that operators can control remotely, including from the other side of a border. However, its payload capacity is limited. According to the State Border Service, this year the consignments of drugs apparently transported by drones ranged from 10kg to 22kg.

Unlike a drone, a paraglider carries a pilot. A powered paraglider, also known as a paramotor trike or paratrike, consists of a small motorised cart and a parachute wing. According to the State Border Service, smugglers dropped more than 65kg of drugs from a paraglider on 11 September. That is roughly three times the largest consignment that smugglers reportedly tried to transport by drone, according to the agency’s statements.

Flights with a pilot involve additional risks. In two statements in September, the State Border Service reported only that smugglers had dropped cargo from the air. It gave no details about the paraglider or its pilot. The agency said that “operational and investigative measures are continuing”. However, on 16 November, it reported that border guards had managed to stop the aircraft inside Azerbaijan and detain its pilot.

Flights take place at night

In all the cases where the State Border Service specified the exact time, the flights took place at night, between 01:00 and 04:30. Most incidents occurred along sections of the border patrolled by the Horadiz and Geytepe border detachments. Horadiz is in the Fuzuli district, while Geytepe is in the Jalilabad district. Both districts border Iran.

According to the State Border Service, most of the seized drugs consisted of cannabis. The substances also included opium and methadone tablets.

Border security and Washington

The State Border Service’s regular reports of operations along the border with Iran also carry foreign policy significance. In 1992, the US Congress passed Section 907 of the Freedom Support Act, which prohibits the US government from providing direct assistance to the Azerbaijani government. Since 2002, the US president has had the authority to waive this restriction each year.

To do so, the president must formally certify to Congress that the assistance helps the United States combat terrorism, “is important to ensure the security of Azerbaijan’s borders” and does not undermine efforts to achieve peace with Armenia. This wording has appeared in presidential memorandums since 2003, including a memorandum issued by the Trump administration in August 2025. In June this year, Ilham Aliyev also thanked US President Donald Trump for a commemorative copy of the memorandum extending the waiver.

The US State Department reports to Congress every year on assistance provided under this mechanism. According to a 2022 report by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO), US agencies provided Azerbaijan with around $808 million between 2002 and 2020. Of this amount, $164 million, or 20%, went towards security assistance granted under an exemption from the restrictions imposed by Section 907.

For Baku, therefore, border security is not just a domestic issue. It is also one of the official conditions governing its cooperation with Washington. The anti-smuggling operations along the Iranian border reported by the State Border Service fall within this area of cooperation.

What does Iran say?

Iranian officials have not yet commented on these incidents. Azerbaijan’s State Border Service has also not said who organised the flights from Iranian territory or which group the detained pilot was linked to.

Relations between the two countries have been tense this year. In March, Azerbaijan accused Iran of carrying out drone attacks on Nakhchivan, but Tehran rejected the allegations.

The State Border Service says it continues to identify and detain those involved in the smuggling operations. It remains unclear when prosecutors will bring the case against the Iranian pilot detained on 16 November to court.

Azerbaijan: Drug smuggling by paraglider

World.title: Georgian and Russian representatives meet in Minsk: Reaction in Tbilisi
World.content:
Georgian and Russian representatives meet in Minsk

On 19 November, Georgian Prime Minister’s Special Representative for Relations with Russia and First Deputy Foreign Minister Giorgi Zurabashvili met Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin in Minsk.

In official statements issued following the meeting, the Russian side described it as part of the “resumed direct dialogue” between Russia and Georgia.

The Georgian government, meanwhile, said in a brief statement that the two sides had “reached a number of agreements”.

This was the first meeting of its kind since Giorgi Zurabashvili’s appointment as special representative. It drew strong criticism in Tbilisi, with former diplomats and experts viewing it as the restoration of direct dialogue with Russia.

What the official statements say

The Russian Foreign Ministry published a brief statement on its website, consisting of just a few paragraphs. The opening paragraph said that the “meeting took place as part of the resumed direct dialogue between Russia and Georgia”.

According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, the two sides discussed trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian cooperation, as well as regional security issues.

Moscow said the two sides had reached “a number of practical agreements” and agreed to maintain contact. However, the ministry did not specify what exactly these agreements concerned.

The Georgian government’s statement was published slightly later. Its content was almost identical to that of the Russian Foreign Ministry.

According to official Tbilisi, Zurabashvili and Galuzin discussed trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian relations, as well as existing challenges in these areas.

“The need to continue dialogue in order to achieve concrete results was emphasised,” the statement said.

The talks also touched on regional security:

“Particular attention was paid to the importance of the Geneva International Discussions as the main format for resolving outstanding issues between Russia and Georgia, as well as for discussing security and humanitarian matters.”

The statements issued by both countries noted that the heads of the delegations had thanked the Belarusian side for its assistance in organising the Russian-Georgian meeting.

The two sides also agreed to maintain contacts with a view to further developing relations between Russia and Georgia.

What is new about the meeting: Format, venue and expanded mandate

Zurabashvili-Galuzin meeting. Photo: Russian Foreign Ministry

On 21 October 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Giorgi Zurabashvili as his special representative for relations with Russia. Zurabashvili also retained his position as first deputy foreign minister.

At the time of his appointment, Kobakhidze said the special representative’s responsibilities would include not only trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian issues, as before, but also the peaceful resolution of the conflict with Russia.

Since 2012, talks with Russia on trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian issues had been held in the so-called Karasin–Abashidze format. Georgia was represented by the prime minister’s special representative, Zurab Abashidze, while Russia was represented by Deputy Foreign Minister Grigory Karasin. The meetings were held mainly in Prague.

In parallel with this format, the Geneva International Discussions were established after the 2008 war as the only international negotiating format in which Georgia and Russia participate alongside representatives of the EU, UN, OSCE and US.

The Geneva Discussions address security and humanitarian issues, including the situation in Georgia’s occupied territories.

“Agreeing to move meetings from Prague to Minsk is a diplomatic mistake”: Reactions from Tbilisi

Russia had been calling for the Geneva talks to be moved to Minsk for many years. The new format of dialogue with Russia, the venue of the meeting and the possible expansion of Zurabashvili’s mandate have therefore drawn particular criticism in Tbilisi.

Former Georgian ambassador to Russia Valeri Chechelashvili said that agreeing to move the meetings from Prague to Minsk was a diplomatic mistake:

“Mikhail Galuzin is a very experienced diplomat with very clear positions on Abkhazia and Tskhinvali. He says they are Russia’s allies, that Russia must take care of them, and so on. Giorgi Zurabashvili has been entrusted with a difficult task!”

According to Chechelashvili, it is unclear who decided to expand the negotiating mandate and how that decision was made. The former diplomat believes the public should be given more information about such changes:

“The meetings in the Karasin-Abashidze format have exhausted their mandate, as Irakli Kobakhidze told us. But the mandate of the current meetings has been expanded: it covers not only trade, transport and cultural relations, but is also supposed to contribute to conflict resolution. This is somewhat surprising, because a mandate cannot be changed unilaterally. So someone, somewhere, has been negotiating with the Russians, and we know nothing about it.”

Security expert Giorgi Shaishmelashvili believes the new format could be a step towards restoring institutional diplomatic relations with Russia:

“The ruling Georgian Dream party has prepared everything needed to move to a new stage in relations with Russia, which will ultimately mean the restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia. What difference does it make whether you go to Minsk or Moscow?”

Political analyst Vakhtang Dzabiradze believes the meeting in Minsk could be an interim stage and does not rule out Giorgi Zurabashvili travelling to Moscow in the future:

“Minsk is a temporary venue for the meetings. Eventually, they will move to Moscow if things continue this way and Georgian Dream does not change its political course. Today, the authorities’ talk about the Geneva format is purely a propaganda manoeuvre. They want Georgian society to talk less about the fact that the country’s political direction has changed. Today, even geographically, it is clear that the foreign policy orientation has shifted northwards.”

Dzabiradze also believes that the Geneva International Discussions format has effectively already been abolished.

The Georgian Diplomatic Society also believes that the meeting is another clear indication of a change in Georgia’s foreign policy course:

“Expanding the mandate of the Georgian prime minister’s special representative to include the peaceful resolution of the Russian-Georgian conflict, and appointing the incumbent first deputy foreign minister to this position, can be regarded as a form of restoration of diplomatic relations. This contradicts Georgia’s previously stated approach and, at the same time, jeopardises the international format of the Geneva talks.”

According to the diplomats, Georgian Dream’s dialogue with Russia serves to normalise relations on Russia’s terms rather than achieve the de-occupation of Georgia’s occupied territories.

World.title: ‘What special status does the Russian language have?’: Russian-language education debated again in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Russian-language education in Azerbaijan

A lawmaker from the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Hikmat Babaoglu (Mammadov), has proposed reviewing state funding for Russian-language school education. He made the proposal on 16 November during a plenary session of the Milli Majlis, Azerbaijan’s parliament, as lawmakers discussed the 2027 state budget.

According to Babaoglu, 157,000 pupils study in Russian-language classes, compared with 1.57 million in Azerbaijani-language classes. The state spends 2,000 manats (around $1,177) a year on each pupil.

The MP stressed that “national identity and national ideology are shaped through education”. He also questioned whether Azerbaijan had any state-funded schools that taught in English or Chinese:

“Why is that? It is something worth thinking about.”

He said a similar situation existed in higher education.

Over the past two years, the future of Russian-language education in Azerbaijan has repeatedly come under discussion. This time, however, a lawmaker from the ruling party raised the issue from the parliamentary podium and backed his argument with budget figures. This raises a question:

Is this a debate about education spending, or does it reflect relations between Baku and Moscow?

What do the figures tell us?

According to the figures cited by the MP, around 9% of all schoolchildren in Azerbaijan study in Russian-language classes. Based on his estimate of annual spending per pupil, the state spends approximately 314 million manats a year on Russian-language education.

Elshan Azim, head of School No. 35 in the Kalbajar district, cited the same figure. He said that the government allocates 314 million manats a year to Russian-language education, while schools for internally displaced people receive 188 million manats (around $184.7 million). Comparing the two amounts, he stressed:

“For 30 years, these schools have played an important role in preserving the folklore, music, national values and spiritual heritage of their regions.”

Azim argues that if the authorities close schools to save public money, they should assess Russian-language schools by the same criteria.

In recent years, authorities have closed hundreds of small schools in rural areas or merged them with other educational institutions because they had too few pupils. Judging by the headteacher’s remarks, the future of schools for internally displaced people is also under discussion.

The Ministry of Education has not yet commented on the MP’s remarks.

What has the ministry said previously?

In July 2025, rumours spread widely that the authorities might close Russian-language classes. Messages in parents’ WhatsApp groups claimed that schools teaching in Russian would switch to Azerbaijani within three years. The Ministry of Education denied these reports. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova also dismissed them as “fake news” and said Moscow remained in constant contact with Baku on the issue.

In June 2026, Education Minister Emin Amrullayev said that closing Russian-language classes had “never been on the agenda”. He said it was “technically impossible” to shut them down “as early as tomorrow”, adding that parents themselves chose the language of instruction. However, he did not rule out restructuring for “objective reasons”, such as a decline in pupil numbers or a shortage of teachers.

Babaoglu’s proposal, however, concerns a different issue. The MP is not calling for Russian-language classes to close. Instead, he is questioning whether the state should continue to fund them.

Against the backdrop of improving relations with Moscow

The MP’s remarks come amid a period of improving relations between Baku and Moscow. In December 2024, an AZAL passenger plane crashed, killing 38 people. In April 2026, the two sides acknowledged in a joint statement that Russian air defence systems had unintentionally shot down the aircraft.

In September, Azerbaijan placed three Russian propagandists – Semyon Uralov, Ivan Knyazev and Alexey Chadayev – on its wanted list over public calls for a violent change of government. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador over the matter. Moscow dismissed their remarks as “personal opinions”.

Babaoglu did not mention Russia in his speech. He justified his proposal by referring to the need to preserve “national identity” and concerns over public spending. Moscow has not yet responded to his remarks.

The draft 2027 state budget contains no separate proposal to change the funding arrangements for Russian-language education. The government has also not responded to the issue raised by the MP.

Russian-language education in Azerbaijan

World.title: ‘Your own husband could be human trafficker’: tackling human trafficking in Armenia
World.content:
Every life matters: how people and animals save each other in Armenia

Over the past four years, Armenia has recorded 109 cases of human trafficking. Reports by international organisations show that Armenia is making efforts to prevent human trafficking. However, the government has scaled back its anti-trafficking efforts in the legal sphere.

We tell personal stories, present figures and facts about the scale of human trafficking in Armenia, and examine programmes that support victims.

Married to the enemy?

“My husband would drive me to different addresses in his car. He would wait in the car until I finished work and came out. He would take all the money from me right there in the car, then drive me to the next address,” Anna (not her real name, at her request) recalls.

Anna describes providing sexual services as her work. She says her husband had never been particularly keen on working. After they married, he decided to use his wife’s previous experience in the sex trade to support the family. The situation did not change even after they had a child.

Family life became hell not only for Anna but also for their child.

“I worked day and night. I had no right to complain or refuse. And it wasn’t just sexual exploitation. I also faced physical, psychological and economic abuse. I lived in constant fear and anxiety. He could beat me or insult me in front of other people, then show me affection, try to win me over and say that we were a family. But the very next day, he would take me to other men again. Sometimes I wouldn’t see my child for several days. Different women I didn’t know would look after them,” Anna says.

Years of exploitation, extreme physical and mental exhaustion, beatings and emotional suffering – but above all, anxiety about her child – drove Anna to flee her husband and report him to the police.

Anna says she found the decision difficult:

“The police force is made up mostly of men. I found it difficult to tell them all the details of what had happened to me – the abuse and the sexual services I had to provide. It felt as though I was going through it all over again. I was overwhelmed by shame, but I knew I had no other choice.”

The police offered to take her to a shelter for victims of human trafficking. Anna agreed, and she still lives there.

Shelter residents and those who do not “save” them

The NGO Sexual Violence Crisis Centre provides victims of human trafficking with shelter and support in dealing with the problems they face. In 2025, the government fully covered the shelter’s operating costs. It also signed its first three-year contract with the centre, allowing it to continue its work on a full scale.

Over the years, social worker Mané Chobanyan has witnessed many tragic stories while working with victims:

“The hardest part of social work is accepting that you are not a saviour. One of its principles is that you must not make decisions on behalf of the people you support. As a professional, I can only guide them and show them the options available. I can never influence their decisions. Of course, this can be very difficult at times. You can never be sure that months or even a year of work will not go to waste – that someone leaving the shelter will not return to the same path, trust an abuser or trafficker again, and end up in the same situation.”

Even so, she has no regrets about the effort she puts into helping these people change their lives.

Mané says an atmosphere of fear and intimidation sometimes forces people to remain in situations where traffickers exploit them. This happens most often to victims of labour exploitation. Given their vulnerable position, the prospect of losing their jobs frightens them more than anything else.

“When we work with people who have experienced sexual exploitation, we mainly try to show them that they can change their circumstances and find another job. In cases of labour exploitation, our priority is to inform people about their rights,” she explains.

With financial support from the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, the Sexual Violence Crisis Centre provides more than just shelter. It also offers psychological and medical care, legal advice and other assistance. Mané says many shelter residents have told her that they would have tried to escape their situations sooner if they had known about the support programmes available.

Anyone who finds themselves in a situation that resembles human trafficking or exploitation can contact the NGO Sexual Violence Crisis Centre for help on +374 77 991280.

US State Department and GRETA say government efforts remain insufficient

The US State Department publishes an annual report on human trafficking worldwide. The Council of Europe’s Group of Experts on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings (GRETA) also publishes a report every four years.

Both reports say that the Armenian government does not fully meet the minimum standards for combating human trafficking, although it has made considerable efforts in this area.

The US State Department welcomed the government’s decision to draw up a new national action plan for 2026–2028, although the authorities have yet to adopt it. However, the report considers the country’s efforts in the legal sphere insufficient.

Articles 188 and 189 of Armenia’s Criminal Code criminalise both sexual and labour trafficking. They provide for prison sentences of five to eight years if the victim is an adult, and seven to 10 years if the victim is a child. However, the US State Department cites statistics that point to shortcomings in the enforcement of these penalties:

“In 2025, law enforcement authorities investigated 29 human trafficking cases: 15 involving sex trafficking, 13 involving labour trafficking, and one in which the type of trafficking remained unspecified. The authorities continued investigating 11 cases from previous years. Prosecutors brought charges against eight suspected traffickers: seven for sex trafficking and one for labour trafficking. In 2025, a court convicted two people of sex trafficking. One person convicted of human trafficking received a 16-year prison sentence, while the other died before the court issued its verdict.”

Reviewing the previous four years, GRETA notes that 90 people received official victim status between 2022 and 2025.

Twenty-two of them were children. Women accounted for most identified victims, except in 2025. Armenian citizens made up 84% of all victims. Most experienced trafficking within Armenia, while a smaller proportion faced exploitation in Russia.

“According to official police statistics, the number of criminal cases opened in connection with human trafficking offences increased during the reporting period: eight in 2022, 19 in 2023, 36 in 2024 and 27 in 2025. Most investigations concerned labour exploitation. Several cases involved the sexual exploitation of children, forced begging or domestic servitude. Between 2022 and 2025, courts issued a total of 11 convictions in human trafficking cases: six for labour exploitation and five for sexual exploitation,” the Council of Europe report says.

As in previous years, GRETA again points out that Armenia still fails to ensure victims of human trafficking receive compensation. To date, no victim has received compensation through criminal proceedings. The government provides one-off financial assistance to no more than seven victims a year.

The government’s efforts – sufficient and insufficient

In 2024, Armenia identified 25 victims of human trafficking. In 2025, that figure rose to 59. Of these, 16 experienced sexual exploitation and 43 forced labour. Eighteen were women, 27 were men, seven were boys and seven were girls. For the first time in four years, the government identified 14 foreign nationals among the victims.

In the first nine months of 2026, authorities recognised 19 people as victims of human trafficking. Fifteen were women and four were men. Three victims were children, one of whom had mental health problems. Two children experienced sexual exploitation, while traffickers subjected the third to labour exploitation. Among adult victims, nine cases involved sexual exploitation and the rest involved labour exploitation. The foreign victims came from Russia, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

“Armenia plans and implements strategic programmes and provides services to combat human trafficking, prioritising the safety and protection of victims. In other words, access to these services does not depend on or remain limited by the progress of law enforcement investigations. This means the state supports both victims and potential victims according to their needs,” says Armine Alaverdyan, head of the Gender Policy Department at the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs.

In 2026, as in the previous year, the government allocated around 32 million drams ($88,000) from the state budget to combat human trafficking.

The funding covers the following services for victims and potential victims of human trafficking:

accommodation;

material assistance, including clothing, food and essential items;

issuing or restoring necessary documents;

medical assistance and services;

psychological support;

counselling;

legal assistance;

care, including in specialised institutions;

interpretation services;

access to basic education;

access to secondary or primary vocational education;

employment assistance;

arrangements for safe return;

one-off financial assistance of 250,000 drams ($694).

According to Armine Alaverdyan, as the number of human trafficking cases rises, so does the need for additional shelter places.

People can stay in the shelter for up to a year, but staff can extend their stay if necessary.

“The state provides support with considerable flexibility. We once had a case in which a person repeatedly broke the shelter’s rules, eventually left, but then asked to return a week later. Naturally, we let them back in. Sometimes, after receiving an initial consultation, a person decides not to accept other forms of support. In cases of sexual exploitation, medical services naturally become more important. This year, only one person received the one-off financial assistance.”

He was rescued

S., a foreign national, came to Armenia on the recommendation of friends. He quickly found a job, unaware of what awaited him in the months ahead.

According to Mané Chobanyan, a social worker at the Sexual Violence Crisis Centre, what happened to S. was like something out of a horror film.

“He did not speak a single word of Armenian. He found himself in a foreign country where people took away all his documents, restricted his freedom of movement, forced him to work and then refused to pay him for his labour. When S. arrived at the shelter, it became clear that our priority was to provide him with a safe environment and help him reclaim his labour rights.”

S. spent more than a year at the shelter. During that time, he taught himself to read and write in Armenian and introduced other residents to his country’s cuisine. Mané says that, despite everything he had been through, S. never lost his faith in people or his will to live. Today, with the help of the shelter staff, he has found a job in administration.

The crisis centre’s social worker says his story is not just one of personal triumph, but also “an example of targeted and effective support that can change a person’s life.”

Combating human trafficking in Armenia: personal stories

World.title: Sanctioned Russian online retailer Wildberries expands operations in Georgia
World.content:
Illustration: Centre for Economic Policy Research (EPRC)



Amid sanctions imposed on its founder, Russia’s largest online marketplace, Wildberries, is expanding its operations in Georgia. The company has acquired more than 19 hectares of land, leased a large warehouse and is preparing to launch a taxi service.

As the Centre for Economic Policy Research (EPRC) found, Russian online marketplace Wildberries, which began operating in Georgia in October 2024, is no longer focusing solely on expanding its network of parcel collection points.

The company’s Georgian operator plans to expand its logistics infrastructure and enter new sectors.

________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

The authors of the EPRC study argue that this expansion should not be viewed solely as business development. They focus on the company’s links to Russia, the possible impact of sanctions, its role in Georgia’s logistics network, and the political and business connections of the local operator’s owners.

________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

From a single collection point to logistics infrastructure

Wildberries’ Georgian operator, Transcom Group LLC, was registered on 26 July 2022. The platform launched sales in Georgia on 22 October 2024 under a franchise model.

Initially, the platform offered consumers around eight million products. Customers could collect their orders from a single collection point in Tbilisi.

The network later expanded, and Georgian entrepreneurs also gained the opportunity to sell their products through the platform.

A parcel collection point and a warehouse serve different purposes. A warehouse receives, stores, sorts and distributes goods, while a collection point hands over parcels that are already ready for customers.

According to the EPRC study, Wildberries’ operations in Georgia also aim to establish warehouses.

19.25 hectares near the highway

According to Georgia’s Public Registry, in January 2026, Transcom Group acquired four plots of land from the state through privatisation. All four are located close to the Tbilisi-Red Bridge international highway.

The plots cover a total area of 192,521 square metres, or 19.25 hectares. The site lies near the road leading to the Azerbaijani border and customs facilities, making it an attractive location for logistics operations.

The EPRC believes that the concentration of the plots in one area, combined with the company’s existing warehouse operations, suggests that the land could be intended for a warehouse or a larger logistics complex.

However, no public documents currently confirm this. It remains unclear what project the company plans to develop on the land, how large the buildings will be or when construction might begin.

Existing warehouse

In addition to acquiring the plots of land mentioned above, Transcom Group already leases warehouse premises in the village of Gamardjveba, seven kilometres from Tbilisi.

According to the study, the company announced a tender on 28 October to improve mobile phone reception at the warehouse. The technical specifications describe a facility covering around 13,000 square metres.

The lease record gives the building’s area as 12,816.8 square metres. The agreement runs until 19 June 2028.

The study also mentions a second lease agreement that Transcom Group signed in another area near Tbilisi in May 2025. It runs for two years.

The EPRC believes that if the company also develops the planned logistics complex near the highway, it will have much greater capacity to receive, store and distribute goods outside Russia.

Taxi service on the way

Another important finding of the EPRC study concerns the possible launch of a WB Taxi service in Tbilisi.

On 16 and 21 October 2026, Transcom Group announced tenders for branding taxi vehicles. One of them covered the production and application of special vehicle wraps for around 150 cars in Tbilisi.

These documents point to preparations for the launch of the service. However, public records do not yet confirm whether the company has signed the relevant contracts, how many cars it has branded or whether it has started carrying passengers.

By early November, WB Taxi was operating in several cities in Belarus, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. In Armenia, the company launched an early-access service in September.

If the company launches the service in Georgia, the Wildberries group will enter the passenger transport market in addition to online retail and logistics.

In this context, the EPRC highlights concerns about personal data protection. Taxi apps process passengers’ addresses, travel routes, journey times and payment information.

Analysis of this data could reveal where people live and work, their regular routes and other personal details.

The study also cites a 2024 case in which Georgia’s Personal Data Protection Service found that the local operator of the Yandex taxi service had illegally transferred users’ personal data to Russia. The company received a fine of 4,000 lari [around $1,480].

The EPRC says that if WB Taxi launches in Georgia, it will be important to establish who operates the service, where it stores users’ data and on what legal basis it may transfer that data to another country.

What links Wildberries to Georgia’s government?

One important part of the study examines the owners of the company’s local operator and their business connections.

According to records from Georgia’s Public Registry examined by the EPRC, Lasha Megrelidze initially owned Transcom Group. In 2023, he became deputy chairman and an independent member of the supervisory board of Cartu Bank. Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party, established the bank. He initially owned it himself, then transferred ownership to his son. The bank eventually passed to the Cartu charitable foundation, which Ivanishvili himself had established.

Since 2024, Sergi Tvalchrelidze has served as Transcom Group’s director and sole owner. A Public Registry extract dated 11 June 2026 also lists him as the company’s only owner and director. According to the study, Tvalchrelidze personally donated 30,000 lari [around $11,100] to Georgian Dream in 2025.

The EPRC also examines Tvalchrelidze’s business ties with Giorgi Barvenashvili, a Georgian Dream MP. According to a registry extract from March 2025, Tvalchrelidze served as director and owned a 33% stake in Nama Consulting, while Barvenashvili held 34%. Nama Consulting and Transcom Group share the same registered address.

Public records confirm that people involved in bringing Wildberries to the Georgian market and managing its operations have links to Cartu Bank and to business and political circles close to Georgian Dream.

The study’s authors say these connections deserve scrutiny, particularly as the Russian company expands its operations in Georgia and its founder faces EU sanctions.

Who owns Wildberries, and why has she been sanctioned?

On 16 November, the European Union added Tatyana Kim, the founder and head of Wildberries, to its sanctions list. The decision forms part of a new package of sanctions against Russia, aimed at restricting the funding of its war against Ukraine.

The sanctions freeze Kim’s assets in the EU, ban her from entering or transiting through EU territory, and prohibit people and entities under EU jurisdiction from providing her with funds or economic resources.

The Council of the European Union considers Wildberries one of Russia’s largest taxpayers. The company’s tax payments therefore go into the Russian state budget and increase the government’s capacity to finance military spending.

The EU also links the company to Russia’s military supply network. According to Brussels, the platform connects sellers and buyers, making it easier to purchase equipment that could serve military purposes, as well as dual-use goods.

The EPRC study cites a journalistic investigation that found Wildberries had listed products that Russian armed forces could use. The Russian outlet Meduza found listings for goods linked to military needs, including body armour, drone components, batteries and night-vision devices.

Wildberries founder Tatyana Kim says other global online marketplaces also sell such products. The Kremlin, meanwhile, has denied that the company’s warehouses serve military purposes.

Wildberries says the group has no assets or operations in the EU, so sanctions against Kim will not affect its business.

What risks does Wildberries’ expansion pose for Georgia?

The EPRC study identifies several potential risks associated with Wildberries’ expanding operations in Georgia.

The first concerns sanctions. The sanctions against Tatyana Kim could affect the company’s international financial transactions, banking services and relationships with business partners.

This risk also concerns Georgian companies that work with the platform or use its infrastructure.

The second concerns logistics infrastructure. The land purchases and warehouse operations indicate that the company is building capacity for larger-scale operations in Georgia.

However, the infrastructure’s ultimate purpose and the routes goods will take remain unclear.

The third issue is users’ personal data.

If the Wildberries group also launches a taxi service in Georgia, it will gain access to a much wider range of personal information – not only users’ purchases and addresses, but also data about their everyday movements.

Finally, the business and political connections of the company’s local owners are significant. This is particularly important when the company acquires state-owned land and develops infrastructure that could have regional implications.

The EPRC study does not claim that Wildberries’ existing infrastructure in Georgia already supports Russian military supplies, or that it will necessarily take over the functions of warehouses damaged in Russia.

However, the study argues that the scale of the company’s expansion, the sanctions against its owner and the connections of its Georgian operator raise questions that require public and transparent answers.

Wildberries expands its operations in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan, Nepal discuss prospects for cultural cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 21. Azerbaijan’s Minister of Culture Adil Karimli met with Nepal’s Minister of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Khadak Raj Paudel in New Delhi on November 21.

According to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Culture, the meeting was held on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Forum on Inter-civilizational Dialogue.

The parties discussed prospects for strengthening cultural ties between Azerbaijan and Nepal.

They also explored opportunities to establish a legal framework for cooperation in the cultural sector and exchanged views on other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Azerbaijan to host European U20 Basketball Championship for first time
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 21. Azerbaijan will host the European U20 Basketball Championship for the first time in its history.

The decision was made on November 20 at a meeting of the FIBA Europe Board of Directors held in Hamburg, Germany.

Under the decision, Division B matches of the European U20 Championship will be held in Baku from July 9 to 18, 2027.

The meeting also determined the host cities for other European youth basketball championships scheduled for 2027.

Hosting the prestigious tournament for the first time is expected to contribute to the development of basketball in Azerbaijan and provide the country with further experience in organizing and hosting international sporting events.

World.title: Turkmenistan exchange sees $1.7 million deal for Turkmennebit polypropylene
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 21. One transaction worth 6 million manat ($1.7 million) was concluded during the November 14 trading session of the State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET) on the domestic market.

According to a press release published by SCRMET, local entrepreneurs reached an agreement with the Turkmennebit State Concern to purchase polypropylene grade TPP D 30 S.

Established in 1994, SCRMET is Turkmenistan's main organized commodity marketplace and one of the key institutions facilitating the country's foreign trade. It brings together domestic producers, exporters and foreign buyers through regular trading sessions, offering a range of export-oriented goods.

Its trading portfolio includes petrochemicals, polymers, textiles, cotton products, construction materials, machinery and chemical goods, among other commodities.

In addition to organizing trading sessions and registering export-import contracts, SCRMET publishes official quotations based on transactions conducted on its platform. These quotations provide information on traded commodities, their values, and the markets involved, serving as an indicator of the composition and direction of exchange-based trade.

They also provide an overview of the value and sectoral composition of goods offered to international buyers during each trading session, reflecting changes in the country's export offering and highlighting the industries that dominate Turkmenistan's exchange-based trade.

World.title: Azerbaijan and India discuss expanding cultural cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 21. Azerbaijan’s Minister of Culture Adil Karimli met with India’s Minister of Culture and Tourism Gajendra Singh Shekhawat in New Delhi on November 21.

According to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Culture, the meeting was held on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Forum on Inter-civilizational Dialogue.

Karimli expressed his gratitude for the organization of the forum and the hospitality extended to the Azerbaijani delegation.

The discussions focused on the current state of cultural relations between Azerbaijan and India, as well as prospects for their further development.

The sides also explored opportunities to organize cultural days, joint exhibitions and festivals, and expand cooperation in the museum, library, and other cultural sectors.

World.title: Pezeshkian calls Iran's economic challenges a silent war
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 21. Iran is currently facing a silent economic war that is more complex than conventional warfare involving missile strikes and destruction, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said.

According to the Iranian president’s official information portal, he made the remarks on Saturday, November 21, at the annual capital market conference in Tehran.

"At present, Iran is waging a silent war. This war is more complex than one in which missiles are launched and destruction is inflicted," Pezeshkian noted.

He stressed that despite the challenges facing the country, economic activity continues, ensuring production and meeting domestic market needs. According to the president, maintaining economic stability has required considerable effort and hard work.

Pezeshkian also identified ensuring an uninterrupted energy supply to the manufacturing sector as one of the country's key priorities. He said measures were being taken to guarantee that industrial facilities receive electricity, gas, and other essential energy resources throughout the winter, while mitigating the effects of the current energy shortage and the possible tightening of restrictions in the coming months.

The president emphasized that if energy consumption restrictions become necessary, industrial enterprises and the manufacturing sector should be the last to face shutdowns. He called on citizens and non-industrial consumers to reduce their energy consumption during such periods to ensure the uninterrupted operation of factories.

"Limiting electricity consumption under difficult circumstances should not lead to a halt in production or the loss of jobs," he said.

Furthermore, Pezeshkian stressed the need to review the performance of loss-making state-owned companies. He noted that the reasons behind persistent financial losses must be identified, adding that some of Iran's economic problems stem from inefficient management.

He also described the payment of annual bonuses to executives of consistently unprofitable state-owned companies as unacceptable.

The Iranian president highlighted the need to reassess the future of state-owned enterprises, banks, ministries, and other institutions. According to him, management reforms should be introduced to improve their efficiency, while institutions that lack economic justification should be reconsidered.

It should be noted that Iran has faced numerous sanctions across various sectors since 2018. This year, amid the conflict between Iran and the United States, restrictions were also imposed on the country's maritime and air transport sectors.
