World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva takes part in opening ceremony of "Baku Corner" and Azerbaijani culinary zone at Hanoi College of Commerce and Tourism (PHOTO)
World.content:
HANOI, Vietnam, November 21. On November 21, a Baku corner and an Azerbaijani culinary zone were opened at the Hanoi College of Commerce and Tourism. The project was implemented as part of ongoing, purposeful cooperation with the college's Azerbaijani partners.

Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation Leyla Aliyeva attended the opening ceremony.

The Baku corner features depictions of the Palace of the Shirvanshahs, a model of the Maiden Tower, as well as images of Icherisheher, the Heydar Aliyev Center, the Flame Towers, and Baku Bay. Meanwhile, the culinary zone will serve to promote Azerbaijani cuisine, and training sessions on Azerbaijani cuisine will be organized there for the college's students.

Speaking at the event, college rector Trinh Thi Thu Ha noted that the foundation of friendship between the two peoples was laid by the visits of Vietnamese President Ho Chi Minh to Baku and National Leader of the Azerbaijani people Heydar Aliyev to Vietnam. Since gaining independence, relations between the two countries have developed in all spheres, reaching the level of a strategic partnership. She also noted that the Hanoi College of Commerce and Tourism implements various projects to contribute to friendship between the peoples.

The rector fondly recalled Leyla Aliyeva's meeting last April with the college staff and Vietnamese alumni who had studied in Azerbaijan, as well as the Heydar Aliyev Foundation's support for the educational institution.

Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation Leyla Aliyeva expressed her gratitude to the college's leadership for the attention shown to Azerbaijani culture. She expressed confidence that the opening of the Baku corner and the Azerbaijani culinary zone at the educational institution would help the college's students and Hanoi residents get to know Azerbaijan more closely. Leyla Aliyeva stated that holding such an event during the days of the Azerbaijani President's official visit to Vietnam carried special symbolic meaning. She also highlighted that the educational and socially oriented projects of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation extend to Vietnam.

At the event, artists performed songs dedicated to Azerbaijan-Vietnam friendship, excerpts from the musical comedy "Arshin Mal Alan" in Vietnamese, and the newly composed song "Azerbaijan-Vietnam."

World.title: Princess Catherine reflects on cancer journey in new documentary
World.content:
The Princess of Wales will share her experience with cancer and recovery in a new documentary to be broadcast internationally in the coming weeks, her office has said.

Described as a "deeply personal" documentary, Heal will broadcast on the BBC on November 29 before airing internationally. In Australia it will broadcast on Channel 9 on December 1.

"Cancer does change you," Princess Catherine says in the documentary.

" It changes your body, it changes you physically, but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you. "

Catherine, wife of heir-to-the-throne Prince William, announced in March 2024 that she was receiving treatment for cancer after tests following major abdominal surgery found the disease. She has not disclosed the type of cancer.

After undergoing chemotherapy she revealed she was in remission in January 2025.

Loading Instagram content

The documentary "follows the princess on a personal journey through some of Britain's most spectacular landscapes" as she takes part in one of the UK's best-known endurance events, the Three Peaks Challenge, Kensington Palace said in a statement.

Participants in the challenge, which 44-year-old Catherine completed in June, climb the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.

"Set against the backdrop of the challenge itself, the princess reflects on her own experience alongside individuals navigating their own health journeys," the statement read.

"Together they explore the profound impact serious illness can have on the whole person and the people, places and experiences that can help us heal."

Catherine's father-in-law, King Charles III, was also diagnosed with cancer, which was revealed by Buckingham Palace on February 5, 2024.

Charles, 78, has returned to public duties but is still being treated for an undisclosed cancer.

All funds generated by the documentary's distribution will go to Britain's Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Mexico's military captures drug kingpin on FBI's most wanted list
World.content:
Mexico's military says it has captured the leader of a drug trafficking group among the 10 most wanted fugitives sought by US law enforcement.

Fausto Isidro Meza — whose alias is "Chapo Isidro" — and two other leaders of his gang were captured during a special forces raid on Friday night, local time, in Sinaloa state, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat announced on X.

Giving his name as Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, the FBI listed him as one of their 10 most wanted fugitives and the alleged leader of the Beltran Leyva gang, which is allied with one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.

Fausto Isidro Meza faces faces criminal charges in both Mexico and the United States. (Supplied: US Department of State)

The FBI had offered a $US5 million ($7.55 million) reward for information leading to his arrest.

The US intelligence organisation's bulletin says his group is responsible for importing "large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States".

US charges Sinaloa governor over alleged cartel ties The indictment is a significant escalation of US anti-cartel action that is likely to increase tensions between the United States and Mexico.

He was captured alongside his number two in the group and another man identified as a financial operator.

The Mexican government said in an early Saturday report that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how the two countries coordinated.

Videos and photos from the city of Guasave, Sinaloa — where Meza Flores was captured — show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as burnt cars.

Mexican authorities said they used "stealth and surprise" to capture him.

They said after being attacked with guns and explosives from likely cartel operatives, the officials entered a home and arrested him.

They later evacuated Meza Flores and others detained in the clash in a Mexican Air Force plane to Mexico City.

He faces criminal charges in both Mexico and the United States.

AFP/AP

World.title: Australia win thriller to snap England's T20I streak
World.content:
Inexperienced Australia have pulled off a record MCG run chase to beat world number one England in the first of five T20 Internationals on home soil.

In front of 39,289 fans on Saturday night, Australia snapped England's seven-match T20 winning run by chasing down 188.

Young all-rounder Nikhil Chaudhary announced himself on the international stage, blasting a brilliant 66 off 38 balls and taking a handy 2-21 with the ball.

He set up Australia's chase before Jack Edwards (25 off 11 deliveries) landed the plane, hitting a four on the second-last ball to give his team a three-wicket win.

Debutant Sam Harper (32 off 15) and captain Mitch Marsh (37 off 15) were other key contributors with the bat.

England continued to take wickets to take the game into the last over. (AAP: James Ross)

Missing a raft of their T20 regulars, Australia were uncharacteristically poor in the field early as England posted 9-187.

The hosts dropped five catches in the first seven overs.

While scooping up easy chances from openers Phil Salt (0) and Aneurin Donald (10 off 7), England captain Harry Brook was afforded lives on two by Jake-Fraser McGurk and three by Adam Zampa.

Left-arm quick Ben Dwarshuis (1-23 off two overs) put down a tough caught-and-bowled chance from Tom Banton on three, before Tim David dropped him again on 11 at long on.

Debutant Sam Harper was a busy body with both the gloves and bat. (AAP: James Ross)

Brook and Banton punished the Australians for their mistakes, pushing the run rate past 12 an over.

In his Australia debut, hometown hero Harper also put down a flying edge from Donald.

But the 29-year-old Victorian made up for it by pouching a fine edge to remove Brook for 65 off 28 while keeping to the stumps to Chaudhary.

Soon after, fellow debutant Lachlan Shaw put on his Superman cape with a diving catch to send Banton back to the sheds for 39 off 22.

Zampa then trapped Will Jacks in front cheaply for three and the runs started to dry up for England.

Shaw showed more poise in the outfield to claim the wicket of all-rounder Sam Curran (21 off 20), as did Joel Davies running around in the deep to remove Jordan Cox (27 off 20).

Jamie Overton and Liam Dawson (17 off 14) both fell in the last over as Australia fought back to restrict England well below 200.

AAP

World.title: Top End shaken as major quake hits East Timor
World.content:
The Top End has been shaken by an earthquake that rocked homes in the Northern Territory capital and surrounds and rattled a few nerves.

Darwin is regularly shaken by quakes occurring in and around the islands of Indonesia and East Timor to the north but the one that struck around 7:15pm on Saturday was stronger than usual.

The US Geological Survey on its website said the 6.8-magnitude quake had an epicentre 103 kilometres north-east of Lospalos in East Timor at a depth of 143km.

Geoscience Australia also reported the quake at 6.8-magnitude and said on its website that it had received over 1,600 reports from people who felt the tremor.

Many Top End residents took to social media to describe the shaking.

Shania Rose said everything was shaking, including cupboard doors, and that her dog was "freaking out".

Cami Vilanova, in the Darwin suburb of Bayview, said the quake was the strongest she had felt in the city.

"We could hear the walls and ceiling moving," she said.

People reported the quake well inland in Katherine, about 320km south-east of the NT capital.

Susan Bligh of Eva Valley, about 110km south of Darwin, said she was sitting on her couch when it "started jumping around".

"When I put my feet down on the floor, even the concrete floor felt as though it was moving. The ceiling fans were swinging around," she said.

Darwin felt a lighter shaking just days ago from a 6.6-magnitude quake in the Banda Sea about 700km north of Darwin.

AAP

World.title: World record-breaking Australian swimmer Jon Henricks dies aged 91
World.content:
Jon Henricks, a record-breaking Australian swimmer who won two gold medals at the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, has died aged 91.

Henricks, who first came to prominence in distance events, will be remembered as one of Australia's greatest sprint swimmers.

At the 1956 Olympics, he won gold in the 100 metres freestyle and with Australia's 4x200 metres freestyle relay team, following three gold medals at the 1954 Commonwealth Games in Vancouver.

Ian Chesterman is the head of the Australian Olympics Committee (AOC). (Supplied)

Henricks' death came on the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, the Australian Olympic Committee (AOC) said.

Ian Chesterman, president of the AOC, paid tribute to the swimming star in a statement.

"Jon Henricks was a giant of the Melbourne 1956 Games and part of a remarkable generation of Australian Olympians alongside Murray Rose, John Devitt, longtime friend Dawn Fraser and many others," he said.

"In front of a home crowd, he won Australia's first swimming gold medal, then anchored the 4x200m relay team to a world record.

"That week helped establish Australia's reputation as a swimming nation, and it still inspires our athletes today.

"While he made his life in the United States, he remained a proud Australian Olympian. On behalf of the Australian Olympic family, I extend our deepest condolences to Jon's family, friends and the Australian swimming community."

Emerging as a teen sensation in the early 1950s, Sydneysider Henricks held multiple world records and, with greater luck, could have won more Olympic medals.

It was not until months after the 1952 Helsinki Games that he realised he was a sprinter, and at the 1960 Games in Rome — where he was the favourite — Henricks was struck down by a gastrointestinal bug and missed the finals.

Henricks was also involved in some of the sport's most enduring innovations.

Henricks worked with coach Harry Gallagher. (Getty Images: Hulton Archive)

Thanks to the proto-sports science of Sydney University physiology professor Frank Cotton, working under the supervision of Henricks's coach Harry Gallagher, Henricks was the first prominent swimmer to use "tapering off" training before major events.

At the urging of his father, Clyde, he was also reputedly the first swimmer to shave his body to reduce drag.

Henricks was named the world's (amateur) athlete of the year for 1954 by the Helms Athletic Foundation, and his victory in the 100 metres final in Melbourne put him at the centre of an iconic Australian sporting moment, with his countrymen John Devitt and Gary Chapman taking silver and bronze in a clean sweep.

"After I touched the wall, I looked for the timekeepers," Henricks told The Age in 1999.

"They were all smiling at me, and I knew. As I scanned the lanes, I could see Gary Chapman and John Devitt being congratulated. We had made history.

" Everyone knew that this was something special. "

'One of the greatest swims of all time'

Born John Malcolm Henricks on June 6, 1935, 'Jon' Henricks was the son of Bessie Patersen and Malcolm 'Clyde' Henricks, a company director in Sydney.

By the age of 11, Henricks was winning Cub Scout races at the Balmain baths.

He came to wider attention during his time as a student at Fort Street Boys' High School in the Sydney suburb of Petersham.

John Malcolm Henricks was the son of Bessie Patersen and Malcolm 'Clyde' Henricks, a company director in Sydney. (Supplied: International Swimming Hall of Fame)

There, Henricks dominated the field in inter-school competitions and, while still a schoolboy, became a national champion and holder of the Australian record for the 110-yard and 220-yard freestyle events.

In 1952, Henricks was a medal-winner in three freestyle events at the national championships — bronze in the 1500 yards, silver in the 800 yards and gold in the 400 yards. But an ear infection prevented his selection for the 1952 Helsinki Olympics.

Later that year, "by accident" but with the endorsement of Cotton, Henricks realised he was more suited to sprinting events and convinced Gallagher to allow him to focus solely on them.

At the New South Wales state titles in January 1953, the 17-year-old announced himself as a sensation when he shaved 1.2 seconds off the national record for the 110 yards freestyle.

TV memories of the 1956 Olympics Watching the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Games was many Australians' first experience of television.

That swim would have won him silver in Helsinki, and was described by race announcer Sid Grange as "one of the greatest swims of all time".

The next morning, an article in Sydney's Sunday Herald was even less subtle, dubbing Henricks "the best sprint swimmer Australia has ever produced".

Within a month, he had added the national 55-yard freestyle record to his collection, and even his school swimming carnivals received breathless media coverage.

Due to parental pressure to focus on obtaining his leaving certificate and becoming a doctor, in 1953, Henricks declined US college scholarship offers, including from Harvard.

Regardless, his subsequent selection in Australian squads for the Japanese Nationals of 1953 and the 1954 Commonwealth Games in Vancouver meant his studies were put on hold for the better part of two years.

In Japan, Henricks was disappointed with his times yet still claimed gold medals, but his increasing travel commitments had an unforgiving press claiming that he was "gadding about".

Henricks trained alongside Dawn Fraser in Gallagher's squad. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

In reality, training alongside Dawn Fraser in Gallagher's squad, there was no respite from the hard work.

In Vancouver, Henricks removed any doubts about his focus with gold medals in three freestyle events — the 110 yards, the 3x110 yard relay and the 4x220 yard relay.

The press now lauded him as "the fastest swimmer the world has ever seen" and a "human torpedo".

'The look that every son yearns for'

Henricks's death comes on the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Olympics, says the AOC. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

At the Melbourne Games, Henricks's performance in his pet event, the 100 metres freestyle, fulfilled half a decade of promise and belied the pressure that came with his raging favouritism for the gold.

At just 21, Henricks was also the senior member of the 4x200 metre freestyle team that included teenagers Devitt, Kevin O'Halloran and Murray Rose.

In winning gold, they chopped 0.9 of a second off the world record, never surrendering O'Halloran's healthy lead in the first leg.

But that arrival at the summit of the sport was a bittersweet moment for Henricks.

"That [Olympic gold] had been the focus of my life up until that point," he later admitted.

"And I thought, 'Gosh darn it, what am I going to do now?' It's a feeling that comes over you that you just don't know. It's not sadness … impending doom I guess … my life's over.

"It really impacted me."

Indeed, Henricks's immediate reward for his Olympic feats was to complete the national service he had deferred to compete in the Games.

In 1958, he finally accepted a college offer in the US, becoming a member of the University of Southern California (USC) team alongside his countryman Murray Rose.

The team became a "machine", winning four consecutive national collegiate titles.

An article in Sydney's Sunday Herald dubbed Henricks "the best sprint swimmer Australia has ever produced". (Supplied: Sport Australia Hall of Fame)

At USC, Henricks also met his future wife Bonnie Wilkie, sister of his teammate Mike Wilkie.

Though it would eventually pale into insignificance, Henricks's Olympic title defence of 1960 in Rome was ill-starred.

Three days before the 100 metres final, he contracted an especially bad case of what the press dubbed "Rome belly" — sensing immediately he would be weakened too badly to repeat his 1956 heroics.

Summoning himself from his sick bed, Henricks won his first heat, and at the 35-yard mark of his semi-final had raised hopes of a miracle.

But with his tearful fiancée Wilkie urging him on, Henricks faded badly to finish with the 12th-best time and miss the final.

"I was so weak I just could not do it," Henricks told the waiting press pack.

" When I saw the times go up on the board, I felt like crying for having let the team and my coach, Harry Gallagher, down so badly. "

In reality, the question about the Henricks-Gallagher alliance that would linger in the following decades was whether the let-down went the other way.

By the 1970s, Gallagher's Cerutty-inspired methods of training his swimmers to exhaustion were suspected to have ruined more careers than they had advanced.

Soon after Rome, Henricks married Wilkie, and they made a life together in Chicago, then Santa Barbara, California. Until 2018, they also maintained a home in the Sydney suburb of Mosman.

Inducted into the International Swimming Hall of Fame in 1973 and the Sports Australia Hall of Fame in 1986, Henricks was awarded the Australian Sports Medal in 2000.

Henricks was inducted into the International Swimming Hall of Fame in 1973. (Supplied: International Swimming Hall of Fame)

In the 2018 Australia Day honours list, he was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia (OAM) for service to swimming at the elite level and his work as a mentor.

Three decades after his 100 metres triumph in Melbourne, the aftermath of his most famous race remained clear in Henricks's mind.

"I searched the crowd frantically for my parents," Henricks recalled.

"In the pandemonium that was going on, there was no way I could pick them out. It would have to wait till much later for me to see that look of pride in my father's face. The look that every son yearns for.

World.title: Lehmann denies knowledge of sandpaper plot despite Bancroft statement
World.content:
Former Australian cricket coach Darren Lehmann has once again denied knowledge of a plan to use sandpaper in the Cape Town Test against South Africa in 2018, revealing the fallout left him in a "dark place".

Speaking on ABC Radio before Australia's T20 against England at the MCG, Lehmann apologised for his role in the team's culture at the time, admitting that the team's attempts to find reverse swing during the tour "went too far".

Lehmann said he had not signed a Non Disclosure Agreement with Cricket Australia and therefore was permitted to talk about the subject freely.

Cummins to retain captaincy with CA board's 'unanimous' support Cricket Australia's board throws its support behind embattled skipper Pat Cummins as the sandpaper furore continues.

"I haven't changed my views from what happened in 2018," he said.

"It was a dark time, and we got a lot of things wrong, but my version still stays the same. It was just a bad time. We all made mistakes."

Lehmann said he could not remember being a part of a conversation where David Warner raised the prospect of using sandpaper on the ball, as Cameron Bancroft detailed in his statement earlier this week.

"I can't remember being present in that conversation," he said.

"But again, it is eight and a half years ago; you'll have to ask those people. That's the issue, I have my version, and that's where I stand."

Darren Lehmann said he felt 'empathy' towards Cameron Bancroft after his statement. (Reuters)

Bancroft's statement mentioned Lehmann speaking to squad member Peter Handscomb via a walkie talkie asking him to tell Bancroft to remove the sandpaper from the field.

However, Lehmann stated that he only knew sandpaper was on the field after seeing vision of Bancroft hiding it on the TV screen.

Lehmann denied intentionally not asking about how the players were tampering with the ball during the 2018 tour.

"With reverse swing, you throw it into the dirt, you rough up one side of the ball, you might pick at it; that's been happening for 100 years, "he said.

"For me, I didn't know, but you're always ball tampering to try and get the reverse swing happening, but you never go to that extent.

"In 2018, it went too far, and I'm [responsible] for that as the coach."

Lehmann hit back at suggestions he did not pay a price for his involvement in the saga as he detailed the mental toll it took at the time.

"People said I didn't lose anything. I actually lost the best job in the world, and I'm sorry for that, and I'm sorry for what happened. That's all I can say to the general public," he said.

"I went to a really dark place. I went to as dark a place as you can think about.

"It took me probably three to four years to actually get back to some sort of normality.

Lehmann described the job of being Australia's coach as 'the best job in the world'. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

"I'm not going back to that dark place. I'm trying to move forward. I'm not going back.

"There's things I remember and not remember. It is eight and a half years ago, it was a traumatic time.

"I don't want to go back to that dark place, and I hope no one does. I feel for everyone and their families."

When asked what he felt towards Bancroft in particular after his statement, Lehmann said "empathy", adding that he felt empathy for all the players and staff involved.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

He also took aim at reporters doorstopping the individuals involved and the general media coverage of the sandpaper saga.

"Some of the things that have been said are just outright hurtful to a lot of people. That's what I care about," he said.

"There's a lot of people being hurt at the moment and I think people have forgotten about that aspect.

"Yes, we made mistakes, we apologise as best we can and you try and move on.

"I'm not going back to that place … but it feels like everyone is pushing everyone to these bad places."

Lehmann denied knowledge of a specific conversation Khawaja detailed in his book in which he claimed a coach told the players to get the ball moving by any means possible.

Lehmann says he trusts Australian bowlers' accounts of the events in 2018 despite having no evidence to back them up. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"I don't understand that statement as such, because at the end of the day, I didn't get that statement," he said.

"I didn't get that question posed to me, so I can't comment for anyone else."

However, Lehmann admitted the environment surrounding the team at the time was centred around winning at all costs.

"You're always trying to get the ball moving anywhere, in any Test match, whether it's normal or reverse," he said.

"It was an ugly series, that's what I do know. A lot of people suffered and paid the price.

" I just remember how volatile that series was … and we certainly could've handled it better. "

Lehmann also could not recall whether there were any meetings where an individual stood up and voiced their concerns against the use of sandpaper.

"Everyone talks about meetings at the moment; there [were] a whole heap of different meetings," he said.

"There are conversations going on and some people are privy to them and some people are not. I'm not privy to every conversation or meeting.

"So a lot of different conversations happen all the time, different meetings, not altogether, that's how it is."

Lehmann said he had no evidence to back up the fierce denials from Australia's bowling quartet at the time — Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon — but said: "I trust the bowlers. Everyone is entitled to their own opinion."

Lehmann confirmed that he would attend Cricket Australia's independent forum for those involved on the 2018 South Africa tour to tell their version of events.

Australian captain Pat Cummins has also stated his intention to attend the forum, as have Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

World.title: Eyre Peninsula residents worried about further blackouts
World.content:
Eyre Peninsula residents say they are counting on temporary fixes to the power grid to carry them through the next few weeks.

About 24,000 properties were without power on Thursday during a mass blackout.

The region is now temporarily being serviced by the mothballed Port Lincoln power station and reconfigured power lines.

An intense storm damaged three transmission towers, which operator ElectraNet said crippled the "radial line" powering much of the peninsula, including Port Lincoln.

Storm clouds above grain fields on the Eyre Peninsula where wild weather lashed the region on Thursday afternoon (Supplied: Benjamin Wandel)

The company is investigating whether any structural defects were to blame but said that it is unlikely.

'Can't be without power'

Port Lincoln mayor Diana Mislov acknowledged the severe weather was "an unexpected event" but wanted assurances that the construction requirements were met.

"I think the whole line needs to be looked at and more work undertaken to ensure that this doesn't happen again," Ms Mislov said.

Port Lincoln's Mayor Diana Mislov said she was putting her faith in the people operating the regional city's mothballed power station. (Robert Lang)

"I understand the cost-benefit analysis that needs to happen with some of this decision-making, but we can't afford to allow our communities to be without power."

The nearby power plant, which is privately owned and will shut down permanently in 2028, will be used for several days, according to ElectraNet.

Ms Mislov wanted to see the plant maintained long-term as a back-up option.

"The fact we were able to fire up the power station … and get it back into action for our communities is incredibly important," she said.

She also urged people who had lost power to switch off their solar panels, in line with SA Police's instructions, to avoid overloading the grid.

Multi-day blackout 'wouldn't be good'

On Friday, Premier Peter Malinauskas also warned that predicted storm events and hot weather on Sunday could further strain the grid.

The Bureau of Meteorology is predicting early thunderstorms and temperatures to reach around 30 on the Lower Eyre Peninsula.

Restaurant owner Craig McCathie, of the Fresh Fish Place, said he was concerned about more blackouts over the next few weeks while repairs are underway.

The venue's back-up generator kicked in, but Mr McCathie said a blackout running into several days – such as in 2016 – "wouldn't be a good scenario" if the town's reserves run out.

"It does cause a bit of a stress because of what's happened in the past," he said.

Fresh Fish Place owner Craig McCathie said businesses and industry in the region are dependent on reliable power. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

"We keep enough [fuel] for about 20 hours, but when the town is down, the diesel pumps are down too, so we haven't got a back-up plan for when we run out of our storage."

There is still no timeline for when the damaged towers will be permanently replaced, but temporary structures are expected to go up within days, which will bolster energy reliability.

Speaking to 891 Adelaide, ElectraNet's Alex Trento said the company was confident its designs were structurally sound.

"Depending on the investigation, that'll determine whether we go down the path of looking at a different design," Mr Trento said.

"But at this point in time we're of the strong view that the design is adequate, tested to the requirements of the Australian standards ... and constructed by very competent contractors, with ElectraNet personnel overseeing [them]".

World.title: Aussie bowlers no longer in control of public perception of legacies
World.content:
Three days ago — an eon in the context of Australian cricket's most embarrassing and avoidable omnishambles — former Australian wicketkeeper Ian Healy offered a reasonable take on Australia's famed bowling group.

"I would say it taints their personal legacies … I don't think it's going to taint their performance legacies," Healy said. "Personally now, they're not as credible as they once were, unless they change something drastically in the next few days."

Healy's personal stake in this is self-evident: his niece is married to Mitchell Starc. And in a fast-evolving crisis, his qualifiers were understandable, although we will get to Josh Hazlewood's version of drastic intervention later.

Cummins to retain captaincy with CA board's 'unanimous' support Cricket Australia's board throws its support behind embattled skipper Pat Cummins as the sandpaper furore continues.

Healy was right to differentiate between the professional and personal: one need not disparage all the hard work, all the joy, all the winning they have given Australians, by admitting that Australia's bowlers have, in recent times, irreparably damaged their own and Australia's credibility.

The bowlers also surely must concede that the precise and absolute truth of what happened in 2018 no longer matters to most fans. In fact, their carefully-worded prevarications and collective obsession with semantic distinctions project an air of guilt almost comically out of proportion with the original offence.

No matter what they saw or heard, barely anyone believes what they are saying about it.

Even if players have publicly approved of Cricket Australia's "truth forum", the rest of us surely agree it is as likely to establish an agreed and convincing set of facts as it is to locate Jimmy Hoffa.

So, to extend Healy's thought, what is their legacy, exactly?

They can hardly blame us for pondering it now in unflattering light. Because the obsession with the "legacy" of Australia's bowlers predates Usman Khawaja's book.

In the past 12 months, the idea has been fairly rammed down our throats as justification for keeping the gang together for a marathon 12 months of Test engagements against South Africa, New Zealand, India and England. The last hurrah for a golden generation, they said.

The legacy of Australia's veteran group of bowlers remains up in the air amid the recent sandpaper furore. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

It could be argued that the very concept was rendered pointless weeks ago, before Sandpapergate's flare-up, on Australia's disastrous recent tour of South Africa.

It is one of the ironies of the present crisis engulfing the bowlers: it has precluded lengthier analysis of their deep and abject failure in the most recent Cape Town Test.

All the noise coming from within the team, of course, suggested this was a mere setback: South Africa are world champions for a reason, ya know? Geez, I guess we shouldn't have bowled first. Oh well, onward and upward, eh?

Actually, it was proof not just of muddled selection priorities and dwindling returns from old stagers, but a deeper crisis of philosophy and proof that the bowlers, in particular, were not operating in a meritocracy.

Having played out of his skin in the second Test, Scott Boland was dropped for Nathan Lyon, who was in turn out-bowled by Simon Harmer, an off-spinner most Australians had previously thought of as a glorified clubbie.

Nathan Lyon was brutally out-bowled by South Africa's Simon Harner in Australia's most recent Test performance. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

And Harmer didn't merely take wickets. He publicly called out and dismantled the Australian captain in a manner that should have caused far more alarm than whatever Cummins did or didn't see as a 24-year-old.

To delve into another modern-day obsession — being "aura" — the loss went far deeper than a 2-1 scoreline. Before its present distraction, Australian cricket pretended otherwise, but symbolic damage was done on a scale we will see more clearly in a few years.

Which brings us to Josh Hazlewood. On a very simple level, his claim yesterday that he would "review" his place in the Australian team if Cummins lost the captaincy was an impassioned if artless expression of loyalty and solidarity with the skipper in times of disloyalty.

More so, it smacked of the cart being placed a hell of a long way in front of the horse. It was an expression of entitlement that brought to mind another unflattering scene from a year ago, of an "absolutely filthy" Nathan Lyon sulking away to a sideline TV reporter after being omitted from last December's pink-ball Test. There have been others.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

For a long time now — long before Sandpapergate reared up again — there has been an inescapable sense that Australia's senior players see themselves not as members of a team chosen by an independent selection panel, nor as merely a self-selecting elite within that team, but as the self-appointed bosses of Australian Test cricket.

It is hard to escape the feeling that it is this self-absorbed culture of entitlement and the desire to control its own narrative — much more so than anything that happened in 2018 — that now defines what the public thinks of Australia's bowlers.

And yes, it is true that those who've thrown their weight around like this are, by most definitions, indisputably Australia's best. And it is also true that they have sometimes needed to exercise their collective power for the benefit of others, too, as in their pay negotiations.

But what is the average fan — who, by the time the Perth Test rolls around in nine days, will have been subjected to weeks of a melodrama which is only a paternity test and a few exploding boats away from a Home and Away plot — to make of a 35-year-old multi-millionaire threatening to take his ball and go home if his mate's not in charge?

Australia's bowling 'cartel' has always been inseparable, particularly in the years following the infamous 2018 South Africa tour. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

"The cartel". It has always had a faintly sinister ring to it, don't you think? Some of the behaviour is, frankly, gangsterism, albeit in the territory mined by Martin Scorsese and David Chase — the petty spats over matters of honour and respect, the fragile egos and wounded pride.

In this light, we now see Cameron Bancroft as the hapless 'Spider', egged on and then assassinated. Perhaps we suddenly respect Steve Smith a little more for silently doing all that time for crimes he didn't commit.

Which leaves us with how Australia proceeds in the short-term. Cricket Australia, more to blame for the mess than any player, confirmed on Saturday that Cummins would be retained as captain. It was the most predictable and probably the most sensible course of action based on a sober appraisal of all relevant facts, but it did also have the unfortunate effect of validating Hazlewood's veiled threat.

Even granting the need to extinguish a tabloid bin-fire, and acknowledging the overwhelming good Cummins has done for Australian cricket, there is an irony in this: backing him in as leader guarantees him a higher work and stress load than he would ideally be shouldering at this point of his career. In an ideal world, free of this scandal, honest conversations about succession planning would already be happening.

Hazlewood's defence of Cummins came after Mitchell Starc had also previously whacked down claims of knowing about the plot to ball tamper in 2018. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Hazlewood's interjection and the self-conferred gravitas of his Test spot, meanwhile, sit somewhat at odds with the prevailing views of his contemporaries. Only a week ago, players' union boss Paul Marsh admitted there was "decreasing" support among players for the idea of Test cricket as the pinnacle of the sport.

Fans, by extension, are now buffeted by administrators who care too little about Test cricket and a few players who care too much.

In the time since Sandpapergate, Cricket Australia has had six chairmen, four CEOs, three men's head coaches and capped 21 new Test players. That a few mainstays attained an over-mighty status is perhaps natural enough, but it is surely time that senior players are reminded that Test selection is not their birthright.

Australia's next 15 Tests would have been brutally difficult in any context. Against such a draining and unpleasant backdrop, the degree of difficulty for an aging and now embittered group of old hands has only increased.

And that really is the stuff of "legacy" — not just everything in totality, but the aftertaste left by the final few bites.

World.title: Trailer for HEAL from the Princess of Wales
World.content:
Trailer for HEAL from the Princess of Wales

In a new documentary, the Princess of Wales explores life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness.

World.title: Princess of Wales opens up about cancer treatment in new documentary
World.content:
WorldEuropeCatherine, Princess of Wales Princess of Wales opens up about cancer treatment in new documentary David Crowe November 22, 2026 — 3:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. London: The Princess of Wales has spoken about the “greater beauty” she has found in life after being diagnosed with cancer and undergoing treatment, leading to an emotional moment with her family when she climbed Britain’s highest mountains. The princess speaks with fellow cancer patients in a new documentary that follows her through her treatment and recovery, with proceeds from the film going to a specialist cancer charity. “Cancer does change you. It changes your body. It changes you physically,” she says in the documentary, called Heal. Loading “But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”



Catherine, 44, revealed in March 2024 that she had been diagnosed with cancer after undergoing abdominal surgery two months earlier. She kept the details of the cancer private but said she was receiving chemotherapy, and in January 2025 she announced that she was in remission. The film includes footage not seen before of Catherine hiking to the top of three mountains – Ben Nevis in Scotland, Scafell Pike in England and Snowdon in Wales – to complete the “three peaks” challenge within 24 hours. It also captures the moment when William and their three children – George, Charlotte and Louis – hugged her upon her descent from Snowdon. “It’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone,” she says in the documentary.



“Things can renew and grow. Often, it is through pain that we realise there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.” The film includes reflections from other cancer patients who speak about the challenges of their treatment. The Princess of Wales on her completion of The National Three Peaks Challenge on June 28, 2026. Kensington Palace Catherine hiked the three mountains on her own in June with support from Mountain Rescue volunteers, saying she wanted to raise awareness of the impact of serious illness and the importance of holistic healthcare. The walking distance ranges from 37 to 44 kilometres, depending on the route. The hike raised money for the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, a specialist care centre in London that will also receive the proceeds from the new documentary.



Some scenes from the mountain challenge have already been released to the public, including Catherine’s statement before she began the trek. “I’m so grateful to be here, to be strong enough to walk these hills,” she said at the time. Social media posts also showed her meeting fellow climbers on the summit of Mount Snowdon and crossing paths with an 11-year-old paraplegic boy, Ted Haslem, and his family on the climb up Ben Nevis. Haslem was doing the three peaks challenge in a wheelchair with support from his father, Pete, and a team of volunteers. Catherine had the father and son, and their family and friends, to afternoon tea at Windsor Castle in September. In one scene during the hike, Catherine tells her brother, James Middleton, that she did not mark the end of her treatment at Royal Marsden by ringing a bell at the centre, something many patients do.



“Maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” her brother says, referring to her three peaks challenge. The latest sign of her recovery came last week when she travelled to India with the Prince of Wales to speak at the Earthshot Prize, their initiative to support environmental projects. This was her first overseas visit since the cancer diagnosis. Prince William, Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales smile as they attend The Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony at the Jio World Convention Centre on November 17, 2026 in Mumbai, India. Getty Images The 30-minute documentary premieres on the BBC next week before airing elsewhere. It will air on the Nine Network in Australia on December 1 at 7.30pm AEDT. (This masthead is owned by Nine Entertainment, which also owns the Nine Network). The film was produced by Will Warr and directed by Benji Jackson, with original music composed by Erland Cooper. World.title: ‘Galactic emissary sovereign citizen’ loses appeal over gun licence cancellation
World.content:
NationalWAWA courts ‘Galactic emissary sovereign citizen’ loses appeal over gun licence cancellation Hannah Murphy November 22, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A woman who claimed she was acting as a galactic emissary when she sent the WA police commissioner and Governor two “deranged, irrational” affidavits claiming she had a right to ignore the state’s laws has lost her fight to keep her firearm licence, with a tribunal declaring she is not a fit and proper person. May-Ring Chen, 69, appeared in the State Administrative Tribunal back in May, challenging a decision by WA’s Commissioner of Police to cancel her firearm licence after she was raided during an operation to seize weapons from those who had expressed views in line with “sovereign citizen” ideologies, following the Dezi Freeman shooting. The decision was handed down this week. WAtoday Police cancelled her licence after finding she was not deemed a “fit and proper” person to own a firearm under the Firearms Act 2024 . “We are of the opinion that the applicant is not a fit and proper person to hold the firearm authority because she genuinely believes, amongst other things, she has acted on the belief that she is not bound by the authority of the Parliament, laws, government, courts and officers of Western Australia,” the judgment found.



It comes seven months after Chen made her case in the tribunal, with State Solicitor’s Office lawyer Nick John highlighting the letters she had sent to both the Governor and Police Commissioner as signs she did not subscribe to the law. The affidavits purported to be from “Yuna”, who Chen claimed was her “soul name”, and said her “purpose” was Galactic Emissary, and she lived on the planet known as Earth. The tribunal heard the documents set out a number of assertions, including “truth is sovereign”, “he who leaves the battlefield first loses”, and purported that “the malicious designs of men must be thwarted”. However, Chen repeatedly denied the documents existed, even as they were shown to the courtroom. She claimed she had rescinded them, and as a result they did not exist and she could not comment on their contents.



The tribunal said it was unable to accept her contention. Related Article Updated

Guns Two Perth gun club members had their weapons seized by police. The club had no idea why “The applicant has not taken us to, nor are we aware of any rule… which gives the applicant the right to ‘rescind’ a document which contains relevant and probative evidence,” the judgment said. At the hearing, John said at the time of writing the letters, Chen had meant “every word”. “The applicant is entirely entitled to her beliefs, she can believe in galactic consciousness, she can believe all governments are corporations, that affidavits cease to exist … but they are dangerous beliefs,” he said.



Chen disagreed, and again argued she was not a sovereign citizen. “She is an honest person who rejects violence. She upholds natural laws, the common law and God’s law. She has no criminal or traffic history. She is not a sovereign citizen,” her evidence said. However, the tribunal ultimately agreed with the Commissioner of Police’s position. “On at least three occasions the applicant has sent pseudo law manifestos to government officials … these documents make it clear that the applicant does not consider herself bound by laws passed by the parliament and perceives some pseudo-legal effect in proactively announcing as such,” the judgment said. “While the applicant has not yet engaged in violent conduct, she does hold ideas which are capable of leading to violence.”



It is the second instance of WA’s courts backing up the Commissioner’s decision to seize weapons from sovereign citizens, after 44 had their licences cancelled in Operation Ascendant. WA officers executed 70 searches at different addresses across suburban Perth and regional towns. Police said they had seized 135 firearms and cancelled or suspended 44 firearm licences. Officers also inspected 26 firearm storage units. A number have since taken their fight to the State Administrative Tribunal or the WA Supreme Court.

World.title: WA burger joint ranked 10th best in the world on global list
World.content:
NationalWABurgers WA burger joint ranked 10th best in the world on global list Michael Philipps November 22, 2026 — 2:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A WA business has been hailed for serving up one of the top-10 best burgers in the world, according to a recent article by an online comparison website. A Perth burger joint has been named in the top-10 in the world according to an online site. RoyAl’s In an article released this month ranking the top 50 burgers in the world, Enjoy Travel placed WA’s own RoyAl’s Chicken and Burgers at number 10 in the world. The well-known Perth eatery, run by Alasdair and Ken Craigie, has locations in Victoria Park and Wembley, and was one of only two Australian offerings to make the top 10. “RoyAl’s has built a cult following in Perth for two reasons: chicken and burgers, and both are done exceptionally well,” the article read.



“The burgers are big, juicy and bursting with flavour, while the succulent and crispy fried chicken can be paired with the burgers – either as a topping for the brave, or to enjoy as a side for the hungry. “It’s a truly relaxed Australian burger joint, and a great example of how good Aussie burgers aren’t just restricted to Sydney and Melbourne.” Brothers Ken and Alasdair Craigie run the two RoyAl’s restaurants. RoyAl’s Ken Craigie, who runs the Wembley establishment while brother Alasdair manages the Victoria Park business, said there was a significant customer focus for the staff at their restaurants. “Al and I have always preached something we call ‘customer awesomeness’,” he said.



“We tell our staff, you can make all the mistakes and we won’t be mad as long as you make customers leave here thinking ‘that was awesome’. “That means food, service, music, cleanliness ... everything has to be geared toward making our customers feel awesome. “You do that, and this place can be a lot of fun to work.” Ken Craigie said the efforts of the staff was a major factor behind the success of the business and may have helped their high ranking. “I think that’s why we have such a great team of staff that have helped us achieve this ranking,” he said.



“I can only assume whoever it was at Enjoy Travel got to experience that. “We’ve had an overwhelming amount of support from the community, that’s who we thank the most. Plus their support has drowned out the few sulking trolls who are synonymous with Perth’s burger scene.” Ken Craigie said being ranked so high had been a major highlight in what had been a tough year for the local food and hospitality scene. “We couldn’t be happier, especially after the toughest year we’ve ever had as small business owners,” he said. “People often mistake our two stores for a franchise, but we’re definitely not, and we’re sharing all the same pains every business owner is going through at the moment.



“This ranking gave us a much-needed lift.” Enjoy Travel is an English-based comparison and booking platform for car hire, airport parking, airport lounges and hotels. The company brings together options from different suppliers to allow consumers to see what’s available and compare prices. According to the list, the only other Australian restaurant to be ranked in the top 10 was Sydney-based Eat at ROBs (Rozelle’s Original Burgers), which came in at number five on the list. Across the ditch, New Zealand’s Fergburger came in at ninth place, while the number-one burger went to Hamburger America based in New York.

World.title: Federal inquiry targets online clinics peddling ‘wonder-drug’ peptides
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHealthcare Federal inquiry targets online clinics peddling ‘wonder-drug’ peptides Rob Harris November 21, 2026 — 10:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Australia’s booming online medicines industry faces a sweeping federal parliamentary investigation amid warnings that a new generation of digital health businesses is making it dangerously easy to obtain unapproved drugs. Health Minister Mark Butler has ordered an inquiry into the prescribing and sale of peptides, turning the spotlight on telehealth operators, online dispensaries and social media platforms fuelling demand for products promising dramatic physical transformations. Health Minister Mark Butler has ordered an inquiry into the prescribing and sale of peptides. Alex Ellinghausen The investigation will examine whether Australia’s medical safeguards have kept pace with a business model that allows consumers to seek treatment, obtain prescriptions and have drugs delivered to their doors without ever setting foot inside a doctor’s surgery. At the centre of the government’s concerns is a growing market for peptides, substances increasingly promoted for weight loss, muscle growth, recovery and anti-ageing, despite warnings that many products have never been assessed by Australian regulators for safety or effectiveness.



It marks a significant escalation in scrutiny of the digital healthcare economy, where the boundaries between medical advice, pharmaceutical sales and consumer marketing have become increasingly blurred. Related Article Medicine They promise glowing skin, a ripped body and better sex. Peptides are having a moment – but are they safe? The Therapeutic Goods Administration has reported a rise in the importation, compounding, supply and advertising of unapproved peptide products, driven in part by online prescribing services and social media promotion. The Australian Medical Association has also cited a sharp increase in cases of people obtaining peptides from the grey market – often encountering them on social media – who experience serious side effects, hospitalisation and, in some cases, permanent health problems. “I know peptides are often marketed on social media as wonder-drugs, but the reality is that they can pose serious health risks to Australian consumers,” Butler said. “I am extremely concerned about escalating reports by the TGA of unapproved peptides being prescribed and delivered via telehealth and one-stop-shop style dispensaries.”



While peptides are used in legitimate, approved medicines, regulators are concerned about the proliferation of unapproved preparations being sold to consumers seeking rapid results. The inquiry will examine the commercial incentives underpinning the industry’s growth, including vertically integrated healthcare businesses that control multiple stages of a patient’s treatment, from consultation and prescribing to dispensing. Health authorities have warned against using unregulated injectables being hyped by social media influencers. 60 Minutes Such models can improve access to healthcare, particularly for Australians who struggle to see a doctor in person, but also raise questions about whether businesses that profit from selling treatments can provide independent clinical advice. The inquiry was requested in a letter to Labor MP and doctor Mike Freelander, chairman of the House of Representatives health committee, on Friday.



Its terms of reference go beyond the safety of individual drugs to examine whether Australia’s regulatory and enforcement systems are equipped to oversee new models of online healthcare. Related Article Updated

Weight loss What to know about the new GLP-1 pills now on sale The committee will investigate prescribing patterns, the use of medicines outside their approved indications, consumer demand and the responsibilities of digital platforms in promoting peptide products. Special Envoy for Men’s Health, Labor MP Dan Repacholi, said social media was full of people promising bigger muscles, faster recovery and a better body. “But just because someone with a six-pack is promoting something online doesn’t mean it’s safe,” he said. “I’m particularly concerned about young blokes being influenced by what they see online and turning to unapproved products without understanding the risks.”



The move also reflects growing alarm within Australian sport about the availability of substances that can pose both health and anti-doping risks. The inquiry is expected to begin consultation hearings this month and deliver its final report by mid-2027, potentially laying the groundwork for tighter controls on prescribing, advertising and the online supply of unapproved medicines. World.title: ‘I didn’t know’: Lehmann adamant he didn’t know about sandpaper plot, reveals how he sank to a ‘dark place’
World.content:
SportCricketBall tampering ‘I didn’t know’: Lehmann adamant he didn’t know about sandpaper plot, reveals how he sank to a ‘dark place’ Scott Spits and Russell Bennett November 21, 2026 — 9:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Former Australian cricket coach Darren Lehmann is adamant he had no knowledge that sandpaper was being used on the field in the infamous 2018 Test tour of South Africa. As the ball-tampering saga took another twist on Saturday when the Cricket Australia board expressed its unanimous support for Test captain Pat Cummins, Lehmann opened up on ABC radio about the heavy toll the scandal has taken on him and others in cricket. “No. I didn’t know sandpaper was being used”: Darren Lehmann. AP Photo/Asanka Brendon Ratnayake Lehmann has previously denied prior knowledge of Cameron Bancroft using sandpaper on the ball during the infamous series, but the West Australian batter drew him into the conspiracy in an extraordinary 4500-word personal account on Wednesday evening in which Bancroft said “we all knew” about the team’s under-handed tactics. On Wednesday, Lehmann had been unable to answer questions put to him about Bancroft’s claims during commentary on ABC radio for the third one-day international between Australia and England in Hobart and was excused from commentary duties.



Asked again on Saturday about the extent of his knowledge of the team’s practices eight years ago and whether he was aware of the use of sandpaper on the field, Lehmann replied: “No. I didn’t know sandpaper was being used. “I was coach at the time, I’ve got to take that responsibility. It was the best job in the world. “I’m sorry for what happened. It’s my fault it went too far. At the end of the day, the biggest thing with ball tampering is ... it was a bad time. We all made mistakes. Loading “One of the things I will say is – and this is no excuse – do you know what’s not happening any more? Reverse swing. It’s amazing. It’s out of the game.”



Bancroft claimed that Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present for a conversation at Port Elizabeth (now Gqeberha), the site of the second Test, in which David Warner proposed deploying sandpaper to rough up one side of the ball and get it reverse swinging. “I recall people in the room agreeing with the proposal,” Bancroft said. “Saker and Lehmann were certainly present, although I cannot speak for every word shared. “Captain Steve Smith came into the conversation and, as I remember it, made it clear that he wanted no part in it, before distancing himself.” Cameron Bancroft is questioned by umpires Richard Illingworth and Nigel Llong during the third Test match in Cape Town in 2018. AFP But Lehmann stressed he had no recollection about Warner’s proposal.





“In my opinion, if he [Lehmann] didn’t know, he wouldn’t have said that,” Bancroft claimed. “Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I’d been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants,” he wrote. “He [Handscomb] said to me: ‘I think it’s time I take that off you now’. World.title: Princess of Wales opens up about cancer treatment in new documentary
World.content:
WorldEuropeCatherine, Princess of Wales Princess of Wales opens up about cancer treatment in new documentary David Crowe November 22, 2026 — 3:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. London: The Princess of Wales has spoken about the “greater beauty” she has found in life after being diagnosed with cancer and undergoing treatment, leading to an emotional moment with her family when she climbed Britain’s highest mountains. The princess speaks with fellow cancer patients in a new documentary that follows her through her treatment and recovery, with proceeds from the film going to a specialist cancer charity. “Cancer does change you. It changes your body. It changes you physically,” she says in the documentary, called Heal. Loading “But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”



Catherine, 44, revealed in March 2024 that she had been diagnosed with cancer after undergoing abdominal surgery two months earlier. She kept the details of the cancer private but said she was receiving chemotherapy, and in January 2025 she announced that she was in remission. The film includes footage not seen before of Catherine hiking to the top of three mountains – Ben Nevis in Scotland, Scafell Pike in England and Snowdon in Wales – to complete the “three peaks” challenge within 24 hours. It also captures the moment when William and their three children – George, Charlotte and Louis – hugged her upon her descent from Snowdon. “It’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone,” she says in the documentary.



“Things can renew and grow. Often, it is through pain that we realise there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.” The film includes reflections from other cancer patients who speak about the challenges of their treatment. The Princess of Wales on her completion of The National Three Peaks Challenge on June 28, 2026. Kensington Palace Catherine hiked the three mountains on her own in June with support from Mountain Rescue volunteers, saying she wanted to raise awareness of the impact of serious illness and the importance of holistic healthcare. The walking distance ranges from 37 to 44 kilometres, depending on the route. The hike raised money for the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, a specialist care centre in London that will also receive the proceeds from the new documentary.



Some scenes from the mountain challenge have already been released to the public, including Catherine’s statement before she began the trek. “I’m so grateful to be here, to be strong enough to walk these hills,” she said at the time. Social media posts also showed her meeting fellow climbers on the summit of Mount Snowdon and crossing paths with an 11-year-old paraplegic boy, Ted Haslem, and his family on the climb up Ben Nevis. Haslem was doing the three peaks challenge in a wheelchair with support from his father, Pete, and a team of volunteers. Catherine had the father and son, and their family and friends, to afternoon tea at Windsor Castle in September. In one scene during the hike, Catherine tells her brother, James Middleton, that she did not mark the end of her treatment at Royal Marsden by ringing a bell at the centre, something many patients do.



“Maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” her brother says, referring to her three peaks challenge. The latest sign of her recovery came last week when she travelled to India with the Prince of Wales to speak at the Earthshot Prize, their initiative to support environmental projects. This was her first overseas visit since the cancer diagnosis. Prince William, Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales smile as they attend The Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony at the Jio World Convention Centre on November 17, 2026 in Mumbai, India. Getty Images The 30-minute documentary premieres on the BBC next week before airing elsewhere. It will air on the Nine Network in Australia on December 1 at 7.30pm AEDT. (This masthead is owned by Nine Entertainment, which also owns the Nine Network). The film was produced by Will Warr and directed by Benji Jackson, with original music composed by Erland Cooper. World.content:
NationalWAWA courts ‘Galactic emissary sovereign citizen’ loses appeal over gun licence cancellation Hannah Murphy November 22, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A woman who claimed she was acting as a galactic emissary when she sent the WA police commissioner and Governor two “deranged, irrational” affidavits claiming she had a right to ignore the state’s laws has lost her fight to keep her firearm licence, with a tribunal declaring she is not a fit and proper person. May-Ring Chen, 69, appeared in the State Administrative Tribunal back in May, challenging a decision by WA’s Commissioner of Police to cancel her firearm licence after she was raided during an operation to seize weapons from those who had expressed views in line with “sovereign citizen” ideologies, following the Dezi Freeman shooting. The decision was handed down this week. WAtoday Police cancelled her licence after finding she was not deemed a “fit and proper” person to own a firearm under the Firearms Act 2024 . “We are of the opinion that the applicant is not a fit and proper person to hold the firearm authority because she genuinely believes, amongst other things, she has acted on the belief that she is not bound by the authority of the Parliament, laws, government, courts and officers of Western Australia,” the judgment found.



It comes seven months after Chen made her case in the tribunal, with State Solicitor’s Office lawyer Nick John highlighting the letters she had sent to both the Governor and Police Commissioner as signs she did not subscribe to the law. The affidavits purported to be from “Yuna”, who Chen claimed was her “soul name”, and said her “purpose” was Galactic Emissary, and she lived on the planet known as Earth. The tribunal heard the documents set out a number of assertions, including “truth is sovereign”, “he who leaves the battlefield first loses”, and purported that “the malicious designs of men must be thwarted”. However, Chen repeatedly denied the documents existed, even as they were shown to the courtroom. She claimed she had rescinded them, and as a result they did not exist and she could not comment on their contents.



The tribunal said it was unable to accept her contention. Related Article Updated

Guns Two Perth gun club members had their weapons seized by police. The club had no idea why “The applicant has not taken us to, nor are we aware of any rule… which gives the applicant the right to ‘rescind’ a document which contains relevant and probative evidence,” the judgment said. At the hearing, John said at the time of writing the letters, Chen had meant “every word”. “The applicant is entirely entitled to her beliefs, she can believe in galactic consciousness, she can believe all governments are corporations, that affidavits cease to exist … but they are dangerous beliefs,” he said.



Chen disagreed, and again argued she was not a sovereign citizen. “She is an honest person who rejects violence. She upholds natural laws, the common law and God’s law. She has no criminal or traffic history. She is not a sovereign citizen,” her evidence said. However, the tribunal ultimately agreed with the Commissioner of Police’s position. “On at least three occasions the applicant has sent pseudo law manifestos to government officials … these documents make it clear that the applicant does not consider herself bound by laws passed by the parliament and perceives some pseudo-legal effect in proactively announcing as such,” the judgment said. “While the applicant has not yet engaged in violent conduct, she does hold ideas which are capable of leading to violence.”



It is the second instance of WA’s courts backing up the Commissioner’s decision to seize weapons from sovereign citizens, after 44 had their licences cancelled in Operation Ascendant. WA officers executed 70 searches at different addresses across suburban Perth and regional towns. Police said they had seized 135 firearms and cancelled or suspended 44 firearm licences. Officers also inspected 26 firearm storage units. A number have since taken their fight to the State Administrative Tribunal or the WA Supreme Court.

A WA business has been hailed for serving up one of the top-10 best burgers in the world, according to a recent article by an online comparison website. A Perth burger joint has been named in the top-10 in the world according to an online site. RoyAl’s In an article released this month ranking the top 50 burgers in the world, Enjoy Travel placed WA’s own RoyAl’s Chicken and Burgers at number 10 in the world. The well-known Perth eatery, run by Alasdair and Ken Craigie, has locations in Victoria Park and Wembley, and was one of only two Australian offerings to make the top 10. “RoyAl’s has built a cult following in Perth for two reasons: chicken and burgers, and both are done exceptionally well,” the article read.



“The burgers are big, juicy and bursting with flavour, while the succulent and crispy fried chicken can be paired with the burgers – either as a topping for the brave, or to enjoy as a side for the hungry. “It’s a truly relaxed Australian burger joint, and a great example of how good Aussie burgers aren’t just restricted to Sydney and Melbourne.” Brothers Ken and Alasdair Craigie run the two RoyAl’s restaurants. RoyAl’s Ken Craigie, who runs the Wembley establishment while brother Alasdair manages the Victoria Park business, said there was a significant customer focus for the staff at their restaurants. “Al and I have always preached something we call ‘customer awesomeness’,” he said.



“We tell our staff, you can make all the mistakes and we won’t be mad as long as you make customers leave here thinking ‘that was awesome’. “That means food, service, music, cleanliness ... everything has to be geared toward making our customers feel awesome. “You do that, and this place can be a lot of fun to work.” Ken Craigie said the efforts of the staff was a major factor behind the success of the business and may have helped their high ranking. “I think that’s why we have such a great team of staff that have helped us achieve this ranking,” he said.



“I can only assume whoever it was at Enjoy Travel got to experience that. “We’ve had an overwhelming amount of support from the community, that’s who we thank the most. Plus their support has drowned out the few sulking trolls who are synonymous with Perth’s burger scene.” Ken Craigie said being ranked so high had been a major highlight in what had been a tough year for the local food and hospitality scene. “We couldn’t be happier, especially after the toughest year we’ve ever had as small business owners,” he said. “People often mistake our two stores for a franchise, but we’re definitely not, and we’re sharing all the same pains every business owner is going through at the moment.



“This ranking gave us a much-needed lift.” Enjoy Travel is an English-based comparison and booking platform for car hire, airport parking, airport lounges and hotels. The company brings together options from different suppliers to allow consumers to see what’s available and compare prices. According to the list, the only other Australian restaurant to be ranked in the top 10 was Sydney-based Eat at ROBs (Rozelle’s Original Burgers), which came in at number five on the list. Across the ditch, New Zealand’s Fergburger came in at ninth place, while the number-one burger went to Hamburger America based in New York.

Australia’s booming online medicines industry faces a sweeping federal parliamentary investigation amid warnings that a new generation of digital health businesses is making it dangerously easy to obtain unapproved drugs. Health Minister Mark Butler has ordered an inquiry into the prescribing and sale of peptides, turning the spotlight on telehealth operators, online dispensaries and social media platforms fuelling demand for products promising dramatic physical transformations. Health Minister Mark Butler has ordered an inquiry into the prescribing and sale of peptides. Alex Ellinghausen The investigation will examine whether Australia’s medical safeguards have kept pace with a business model that allows consumers to seek treatment, obtain prescriptions and have drugs delivered to their doors without ever setting foot inside a doctor’s surgery. At the centre of the government’s concerns is a growing market for peptides, substances increasingly promoted for weight loss, muscle growth, recovery and anti-ageing, despite warnings that many products have never been assessed by Australian regulators for safety or effectiveness.



It marks a significant escalation in scrutiny of the digital healthcare economy, where the boundaries between medical advice, pharmaceutical sales and consumer marketing have become increasingly blurred. Related Article Medicine They promise glowing skin, a ripped body and better sex. Peptides are having a moment – but are they safe? The Therapeutic Goods Administration has reported a rise in the importation, compounding, supply and advertising of unapproved peptide products, driven in part by online prescribing services and social media promotion. The Australian Medical Association has also cited a sharp increase in cases of people obtaining peptides from the grey market – often encountering them on social media – who experience serious side effects, hospitalisation and, in some cases, permanent health problems. “I know peptides are often marketed on social media as wonder-drugs, but the reality is that they can pose serious health risks to Australian consumers,” Butler said. “I am extremely concerned about escalating reports by the TGA of unapproved peptides being prescribed and delivered via telehealth and one-stop-shop style dispensaries.”



While peptides are used in legitimate, approved medicines, regulators are concerned about the proliferation of unapproved preparations being sold to consumers seeking rapid results. The inquiry will examine the commercial incentives underpinning the industry’s growth, including vertically integrated healthcare businesses that control multiple stages of a patient’s treatment, from consultation and prescribing to dispensing. Health authorities have warned against using unregulated injectables being hyped by social media influencers. 60 Minutes Such models can improve access to healthcare, particularly for Australians who struggle to see a doctor in person, but also raise questions about whether businesses that profit from selling treatments can provide independent clinical advice. The inquiry was requested in a letter to Labor MP and doctor Mike Freelander, chairman of the House of Representatives health committee, on Friday.



Its terms of reference go beyond the safety of individual drugs to examine whether Australia’s regulatory and enforcement systems are equipped to oversee new models of online healthcare. Related Article Updated

Weight loss What to know about the new GLP-1 pills now on sale The committee will investigate prescribing patterns, the use of medicines outside their approved indications, consumer demand and the responsibilities of digital platforms in promoting peptide products. Special Envoy for Men’s Health, Labor MP Dan Repacholi, said social media was full of people promising bigger muscles, faster recovery and a better body. “But just because someone with a six-pack is promoting something online doesn’t mean it’s safe,” he said. “I’m particularly concerned about young blokes being influenced by what they see online and turning to unapproved products without understanding the risks.”



The move also reflects growing alarm within Australian sport about the availability of substances that can pose both health and anti-doping risks. The inquiry is expected to begin consultation hearings this month and deliver its final report by mid-2027, potentially laying the groundwork for tighter controls on prescribing, advertising and the online supply of unapproved medicines.
