World.title: Half of Kiwi adults are skipping the dentist
World.content:
The latest health survey shows half of adults aren't going to the dentist when they should.

An advocate for free dental care says the lack of access to dentists is a public health crisis, and New Zealand risks billions in lost productivity and quality of life.

Dental for All campaigner Hana Pilkinton-Ching said the survey showed 52 percent of New Zealanders aren't attending check-ups.

"Around the half of the population either never goes to the dentist, or only goes when there's problems, which shows that there's a really large part of the population which isn't getting the preventative care they need," she said.

"That lack of access to care directly impacts the rest of people's health and wellbeing, and does add more strain to the health system."

The NZ Health Survey also showed that 42.6 percent of adults reported an unmet need for dental care due to its cost.

Pilkinton-Ching said that statistic had persisted over several years.

"Sadly it's already been this way for many years, more than four in 10 adults not accessing dental care due to cost for more than five years now," she said.

"Which should be taken seriously by the Government and seen as a crisis in access to oral healthcare."

She noted 75.3 percent of adults had reported their oral health was "good, very good or excellent", but this was down from 79.6 percent in 2020/21.

Ignoring the issue carried an economic cost, she said.

World.title: Southland storm review has 'done nothing to restore public trust' - farmer
World.content:
A Southland Federated Farmers board member says he has no confidence the local Emergency Management response has improved on the response to a storm seen last year.

In October 2025, a destructive storm with winds up to 180km/h caused widespread damage and power cuts.

A review of Emergency Management Southland's response found a number of problems, including poor communication and stretched staffing.

Southland Federated Farmers executive member Chris Dillon says Emergency Management ignored people with local knowledge and failed to take timely action.

"What they've done in the review is got one of their bureaucratic mates to do the review and to make sure that they covered their own arses.

"They haven't addressed any of the main shortcomings in the whole event and that's why they've done nothing to restore public trust."

Formal emergency procedures were largely followed, the review found.

But it also found that people in governance roles during the emergency were not getting the right information at the right time, or in the right format to do their jobs effectively.

The review made several recommendations, including:

increasing the pool of trained, competent staff genuinely available to work in the Emergency Coordination Centre

updating plans and policies to reflect the Emergency Management Act 2026

introducing an operational system providing real-time information, coordination and record-keeping that approved councils and agencies could access.

World.title: Caution urged as more travel booking sites hacked
World.content:
The Travel Agents' Association is urging travellers to be vigilant after an influx of scams using data from the likes of Expedia and Booking.com.

Travel booking companies Bookit, Booking.com and most recently Expedia have each confirmed data breaches in recent months.

Travel Agents' Association chief executive Julie White said that data had allowed scammers to make convincing phishing attempts.

"The thing is, they're so sophisticated. Most will actually know your name, the dates you're travelling," she said.

"What's common is 'please update your card details, we've had an error in the system.' You should not be asked that."

University of Auckland Professor of Commercial Law Alex Sims said scammers were also using AI to generate websites that looked very similar to legitimate providers.

"There's websites with AI now that look really convincing, and people are booking directly, thinking they're booking with a legitimate accommodation provider," she said.

"Yes, you know it's a real hotel, but you don't realise you're actually dealing with a fake website."

Julie White said travellers should consider booking with local providers or travel agents to make sure they would be protected by New Zealand's consumer rights laws.

"There's very little recourse if travellers have booked with an offshore third party. New Zealand law does not cross over into other jurisdictions," she said.

World.title: Roos head to fourth straight final after booking decider against Melbourne
World.content:
Back in the AFLW grand final for the first time in four years, Melbourne are determined to embrace every bit of the lead-in to a blockbuster decider against two-time defending premiers North Melbourne.

After North beat a gritty Sydney by 32 points to reach a fourth straight decider, Melbourne overcame a stern challenge from Carlton to prevail 10.15 (75) to 6.9 (45) in front of 8,037 fans at Ikon Park on Saturday.

The preliminary final victory under first-year coach Tom Wilson sets up arguably the most hotly-anticipated grand final in years, next Friday night at the same venue.

The Demons and Kangaroos have never faced off in a decider but North only beat Melbourne, then playing under 2022 premiership coach Mick Stinear, by 10 points in last year's preliminary final.

North beat Melbourne by 31 in round seven but Melbourne will feel primed to deny Darren Crocker's Kangaroos an unprecedented three-peat after a high-pressure win in hot conditions.

"I couldn't be more positive and optimistic about what this week looks like," Wilson said.

"We're just going to enjoy every second of it because we worked extremely hard to get here and I don't want the girls to let that go by.

"I want them to sit in it and enjoy what comes with the week because they deserve to."

Midfield double act Olivia Purcell (31 disposals) and Tyla Hanks (20) were particularly influential.

"I'm extremely biased, but they're superstars in my eyes," Wilson said.

Defender Maeve Chaplin (27 disposals, 15 intercepts) was exceptional, skipper Kate Hore (20 disposals) and Megan Fitzsimon kicked two goals apiece while Tayla Harris (nine marks) made her presence felt.

"Really proud of the playing group. The way they went about it today was really professional," Wilson said.

"Difficult conditions, quite hot and Carlton threw a few punches.

"So for us to be able to absorb their throws … just really pleased for the girls and the playing group for the work that they've done."

Carlton skipper Abbie McKay (27 disposals) fought hard with support from Irish livewire Erone Fitzpatrick (two goals), Claudia Whitfort (17 disposals) and Lila Keck (two goals).

Down back, Harriet Cordner and the retiring Gab Pound never gave up as Mathew Buck's Blues suffered a second straight preliminary final exit.

"Disappointed as a group, of course," Buck said.

"But when we get time to reflect post this, it'll be a chance to reflect back on the whole season and be proud of another prelim that we've made it to.

"To fall short is disappointing, and we've got lots of stuff we still need to improve on, but achievement of itself to make it."

Melbourne led by six at quarter-time, then at the start of the second quarter, Carlton jagged two quick goals and took a seven-point lead.

But Melbourne wrested the contest back their way, peppering the goal until Shelley Heath-Barker drilled a terrific finish to restore the Demons' lead.

They wouldn't lose it again.

The Demons led by eight at half-time then seized control with a four-goal third quarter, with Maggie Mahony toe-poking home just before the siren to deliver a 26-point lead at the final change.

Poppy Scholz gave the Blues a lifeline at the start of the final quarter but the Demons romped to victory.

Buck conceded the Blues, who are set to again target GWS defender Cambridge McCormick, were currently five or six goals off the competition's best — North and Melbourne.

"We look forward to hitting the draft again this year and our trade period as well," Buck said.

"Any way we can do it (improve), we'll look to achieve it."

Roos survive Swans scare

North Melbourne is within touching distance of an AFLW premiership "three-peat" after fighting out a 32-point victory over a Chloe Molloy-inspired Sydney in their preliminary final.

Ash Riddell and veteran Emma Kearney were centre stage as the Kangaroos kicked six goals clear in the first half before holding off a brave Swans challenge in the 13.5 (83) to 8.3 (51) triumph at Princes Park on Saturday.

Darren Crocker's all-conquering side is into a fourth consecutive grand final, with the chance to complete the first flag hat-trick in the history of the women's competition.

But there is some concern over ruck Kim Rennie, who spent some time on the turf in the final quarter and eventually hobbled off with what appeared to be a right knee injury.

Riddell (29 disposals) and Eilish Sheerin (22) were outstanding, while superstar Jasmine Garner finished with three goals from 18 disposals despite attention from Swans tagger Tanya Kennedy.

Tahlia Randall and Blaithin Bogue kicked two each for the Kangaroos.

Kearney (15 disposals) was dependable as always on managed minutes in her return from a hamstring injury, and got under her opponents' skin in trademark fashion.

Molloy (three goals) did her best to lift Sydney, sparking a second-quarter fightback, but North had a greater number of contributors across the ground.

Laura Gardner (25 disposals), Zippy Fish (18) and Cynthia Hamilton (two goals) also fought hard for the gallant Swans.

A global Ticketmaster outage caused long queues for frustrated fans outside the ground, but those lucky enough to get in early witnessed a slice of history.

Hamilton opened the scoring for Sydney with the fastest AFLW goal, finishing well on the run just 21 seconds into the contest.

But Garner responded within a minute, and the opening term belonged to North, who led 4.2 to 2.1 at the first break.

Garner added her second early in the second quarter and it opened the floodgates, with the Kangaroos piling on another four consecutive goals.

Molloy breathed life back into the contest with three of Sydney's four goals in a nine-minute burst before half-time.

The Swans' superstar caught both Riddell and Kearney holding the ball, and kicked team-lifting goals against the tide.

The North duo demonstrably disputed the decisions with umpires but were not penalised further for dissent.

Kearney also sparked a melee when she riled her opponents by sarcastically joining in the Swans' celebrations.

Molloy's third major cut what was a 36-point margin back to 18 by half-time, with North leading 9.2 to 6.2 at the main break.

It was one goal apiece in a tight third quarter and the Swans got within a couple of kicks when Maddie Quinn (two goals) kicked the first major of the final term.

But North held firm and Garner kicked the sealer when she snapped her third major with less than four minutes left on the clock.

AAP

World.title: Khawaja and Warner taken off commentary as CA backs Cummins' captaincy
World.content:
Usman Khawaja and David Warner have been removed from Fox Cricket's commentary team as another day of developments in the sandpaper saga saw Cricket Australia back captain Pat Cummins.

Khawaja and Warner will miss Australia's T20 series against England but are expected to return for next month's Test series against New Zealand.

"In light of recent events both Usman and Davey will be rested from our broadcasts over the next few weeks," Fox Sports managing director Steve Crawley said.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

"While we always support all members of our commentary team and welcome a diversity of views which is a feature of our summer of cricket, we also understand the pressure they are under to respond to each and every new comment.

"We think it is increasingly difficult to focus on the game while the situation continues to unfold and think it is unfair on both commentators to put them in that position.

"Our focus remains on providing our viewers with the best broadcast of Australia's summer of cricket. We will continue to monitor the situation.''

Fox's decision to sideline Khawaja and Warner comes as Cricket Australia threw its support behind embattled Test and one-day captain Pat Cummins on Saturday afternoon.

Cummins was unanimously backed by the CA board to continue as captain after meeting with CA chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg on Friday in Sydney, with Cummins saying the meeting "meant a lot" amid the ongoing speculation

Pat Cummins will remain the captain of Australia's men's cricket team amid ongoing speculation. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

His captaincy had been questioned following claims by former Test batters Usman Khawaja and Cameron Bancroft that knowledge of the sandpaper plot during the 2018 South Africa tour was widely known.

"Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly," Cummins said in a statement on Saturday.

"David and Todd have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this, and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.

"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations, but that is what's needed.

"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."

Cummins has come under fire for his denials made in a 68-minute press conference on November 13. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cummins encountered several reporters at his house this week after Bancroft broke his silence on the sandpaper saga with a 4,500-word statement.

In the statement, Bancroft said he was left feeling "angry, betrayed and alone" by Cummins's lengthy press conference where he denied any knowledge of sandpaper being brought onto the field.

Among the issues discussed in the meeting between Cummins, Boon and Greenberg were Cummins's welfare and the support required for the upcoming home Test series against New Zealand.

"We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn," Boon said in the same CA statement.

Cricket Australia chair David Boon (pictured) says CA "unequivocally" rejects suggestions Cummins's integrity has been compromised. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke )

"That's what the independent forum we announced this week is about, and the board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there. We will be publishing the terms of reference in due course.

"We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.

"We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised."

Cummins has been Australia's Test captain since 2021 and is also the captain of the one-day team, having led Australia to the 2023 50-over World Cup title.

World.title: Hazlewood backs Cummins as sandpaper saga continues
World.content:
Josh Hazlewood has thrown his support behind Pat Cummins to remain Australian men's captain following the resurfacing of the ball-tampering scandal.

Speculation about Cummins's future in the role has intensified since Cameron Bancroft alleged the entire Australian cricket team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot.

Cummins has maintained he and the Australian bowling unit did not know sandpaper was being used on the field during the infamous Test series in South Africa.

He was not Australia's captain at the time.

Cummins spoke at length in a media conference last week and released a statement via his management following Bancroft's allegation on Wednesday night.

Several former international Test players, including retired Australian fast bowler Mitchell Johnson, have publicly questioned whether Cummins could continue as captain.

Speaking to News Corp, Hazlewood, who played alongside Cummins in Cape Town, said he had no knowledge of ball-tampering being used in the series against the Proteas.

Hazlewood said he supported Cummins remaining Australia's captain.

"It feels like it's been a bit of a pile-on the last few days from different people," Hazlewood said.

"I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain.

"To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that [sandpaper] is never going to happen again — I think is just a remarkable job."

Hazlewood said Cummins was an outstanding captain.

"He's a great leader," Hazlewood said.

"If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you'd hear the same response.

"I think if we turned up for the first Test [against New Zealand] and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."

Pat Cummins has maintained his stance on the ball-tampering allegations. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Hazlewood said he might reconsider his position in the Australian squad if Cummins was removed as captain.

Last week, Cummins held a 70-minute media conference in response to Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering allegations, which were published in his memoir, Sabr.

"When he [Khawaja] says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins told reporters in Sydney.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

"But Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper.

"That's complete and utter nonsense."

World.title: The key takeaways from 2026 AFL Draft
World.content:
The AFL Draft occupies a unique space for footy fans: one of hope and ambition.

It's when the stars of tomorrow take their first steps in the professional footballing landscape, even if exactly who they are is unclear.

All 18 clubs have stocked up for the future, with each looking at how their future can be set up (and be Tasmania Devils-proofed) for the next decade.

The surest bet of this year's crop is second-generation Port Adelaide player Dougie Cochrane.

The youngster joins his brother at the club he loves most. Despite playing no junior football this year, Cochrane's potential is almost limitless: tall, agile, smart and skilful.

To some draft watchers, his potential is reminiscent of names like Adam Goodes, Matthew Pavlich or Anthony Koutoufides.

But Cochrane is far from the only prize from this year's crop.

This year's draft is considered to be particularly deep, with names such as Cody Walker, Ethan Drever, Harry Van Hattum, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody set to dominate footballing discourse over coming years.

The home state of football

Ask a football fan where the home of football is, and you'll get a different answer based on your location.

The passion for the game spreads throughout the nation, with several places holding strong claims to being the spiritual home of the sport.

While the draft attracted nominees from right across this country, it was one state in particular that continued to be tapped as the source of the league's future talent.

Victorians again dominated the draft with 13 of the top 20 picks and 58 per cent of all new draftees.

While not quite as dominant as Victoria's 2024 draft showing, it represents a shift back from some stronger years for other states in recent years, such as Queensland's big haul last year.

The strong draft year for Victoria comes off the back of yet another Under 18 National Championships victory for Vic Metro.

Despite this, the first two Victorian players chosen, Walker and Drever, come from the Vic Country zone.

It's also worth noting the top 10 was spread much further, with five states represented and only four Victorians among their ranks.

An absence in the middle

The draft is often topped by those who dominate traffic in the middle.

But just seven midfielders were taken in the first 20 picks, the equal lowest since 2023.

Across the whole draft, only 25 midfielders were tabbed.

Draft watchers have a couple of different theories on why this might be the case.

The simplest one is that each crop has a different shape, with some stronger in some parts and weaker in others.

Another theory is that because this year's draft was considered to be particularly deep and even, clubs focused on drafting for need more than pure talent.

One further theory posits that clubs are looking to target players who can perform in a defined role rather than those who need to be moulded.

Success stories such as Nick Watson have provided a pathway for young talents looking to maximise their chances of making a quick impact at AFL level.

There's only a small number of dedicated midfield roles in any best 23, so drafting for difference-makers elsewhere may have come back into vogue.

This year's average draftee also stood about 2 centimetres taller than their counterpart last year, an indication of where the strength of this year's crop lay.

North Melbourne had the tallest group of draftees at 194cm on average, while the Bulldogs and Cats had the shortest at around 182cm.

First Nations representation

Earlier this year, the AFL acknowledged the declining numbers of First Nations players in the AFL, saying there was plenty of work ahead to address the fall.

In recent seasons the number of First Nations players at the top level has dropped almost 30 per cent from 87 in 2019 to 62 this year.

But there are signs that the short-term prospects might be shifting even before new AFL-led measures take full effect.

This year's draft saw a number of records achieved for First Nations players.

For the first time two of the first three selections involved First Nations players (Cochrane and Walker).

Five of the first 14 picks involved Indigenous players.

By the end of the National Draft seven First Nations players were selected by clubs.

If each club uses their new dedicated list spot, this would mean 25 additional First Nations players will be on AFL lists this year compared with last season.

But, as Dillon noted in May, recruitment was not the only issue.

"It's not only just about identifying [talent]," Dillon said.

"It's then that the players are on a list. How can we make sure that the Indigenous player stays on the list as long as any other player?"

Time will tell if the tide has really turned.

Bidding wars

The talk of night one of the draft was the selection of Brisbane Academy player Caylen Murray by Sydney, with the Swans pouncing on a series of moves by the Lions that left him ripe to be poached.

The Lions have been aggressive in maximising the value of their picks under the various iterations of the draft points bidding systems.

But Sydney has perhaps had more experience testing other clubs' willingness to match.

Later in the draft, Geelong embarked on the longest streak of bids yet seen, racking up five in quick succession, eventually hitting on Adelaide's unwillingness to match for Anthony Long.

The Cats forced several clubs to draft players they may have been hoping to slide onto the rookie list.

Murray is the first top-10 bid to go unmatched, but there has been an uptick in clubs letting tied players go in recent years.

A third of the successful (unmatched) bids since 2015 came in the last two drafts. While many of these draftees were fringe prospects, the higher points value has now forced clubs to prioritise more strictly.

Last year, Sydney's Lachlan Carmichael (pick 21) and Brisbane's Tyan Prindable (pick 32) both went unmatched due to a focus on another prospect.

Previously, Sydney's refusal to match the Bulldogs' bid for Josh Dunkley in 2015 was famous as a rare occurrence.

The bidding wars have also created opportunities for arbitrage against other clubs' very short-term needs. Many trades saw future draft picks swapped for small changes of draft position.

Of particular note is that Brisbane (2027), Port Adelaide (2027) and Sydney (2028) added to an extensive slew of extra first- and second-round picks in a specific upcoming draft.

With the next two drafts set to be dominated by the Tasmania Devils, this year's draft might be the last chance some clubs have to tap into the best young talent pool for a while.

World.title: Canberra United star on 'reclaiming the narrative' as she marks 200 games
World.content:
If there ever were a mountain top to reach in Australian women's domestic football, there is no doubt Michelle Heyman would stand at the top, alone with all the accolades one could dream of.

Today, the 38-year-old will add yet another accomplishment to her already glittering resume, becoming just the first A-League Women's player to reach 200 games for a single club, Canberra United.

It is a point Heyman herself did not think she would ever reach.

"It's a really proud moment," she said.

"I've been thinking about it a lot lately. Did I think this day was ever going to come? Definitely not."

Michelle Heyman will play her 200th game for Canberra United this weekend. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Along with the goals, the national team call-ups and Olympics, in 2019 her football journey was put on hold, and she was forced to find her love of the game — and herself —again.

"I had to leave Canberra … play in Adelaide and have a year away, which was a terrible season for myself," Heyman said.

"I just wasn't feeling good. I didn't like who I was as a person. I wasn't getting the best out of my football, so I thought, 'This is it, this is time.'

" For me, having that time away from football, at the time I didn't think it was going to be so important, but it actually changed the way I viewed the game. "

After rejoining the competition in the 2020/21 season, Heyman returned as if she never left — winning that season's Julie Dolan medal, the highest individual honour in the league.

Michelle Heyman has been part of the competition since its inception. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

The return to the league was not just about proving something to herself; for the star striker, it was also about "reclaiming the narrative".

"The last five, six years have been probably the most important journey that I've ever had within football," Heyman said.

"I think that amount of time is probably better than the first 10 years that I had playing the game.

" So, for me, I was lucky enough to get a second chance. "

Having been a part of the competition since its inception, the 38-year-old has seen and done it all: a two-time premiership winner, multiple Julie Dolan medals and golden boots, and watching the league expand from 10 games to 20.

Michelle Heyman started playing at Canberra United in 2010. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

But the one thing she says has not changed is the league's professional status.

"I'm not going to lie, I don't think a lot of things have changed; we just play more games. I still think we still have the exact same problems as we did back then," Heyman said.

"People might judge me for saying that, but I still think we've got a long way to go to make it a more professional league.

" You look over what's happening in England, in America, and I'm like, 'Why are we so far behind?' So if we can copy them, I think we can improve and make it an incredible league. "

Though her time in the league will eventually come — now being closer to the end of her chapter as a footballer than the start — her legacy will forever remain solidified not only at Canberra United but in A-League Women.

Michelle Heyman has not decided when she will retire, but says it will be on her terms. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

That legacy is something her coach Antoni Jagarinec believes cannot be overstated.

"You talk about people being part of the furniture, and I've heard that a lot this week," Jagarinec said.

" She's not [part of the furniture]. She's the whole house. "

While Heyman has not set a date for when her time in football will end, she said she "won't be around in five years' time, that's for sure".

But one thing is certain — she will do it the way she has always done it: on her terms.

"I don't want them to tell me that I need to retire because it's their opinions on me. I want to do it because I want to do it," Heyman said.

World.title: Alcaraz wears elastic band on injured thigh to beat Cobolli at ATP Finals
World.content:
Seven-time major singles champion Carlos Alcaraz has eased concerns about a hamstring injury by cruising past Italian fifth seed Flavio Cobolli 6-4, 6-1 at the ATP Finals in Turin.

Wearing an elastic black band on his injured left thigh and a strip of tape on his right knee, Alcaraz completed an unbeaten group-stage campaign ahead of the semifinals.

The Spaniard had already booked his place in the last four ‌after victories over American seventh seed Frances Tiafoe and Daniil Medvedev.

But his fitness came under scrutiny after he left the court with heavy strapping on his left leg following his win over Medvedev, who was the 2020 ATP Finals champion.

Any doubts were quickly ‌dispelled as Alcaraz broke the already-eliminated Cobolli in the opening game and surged into a 2-0 lead.

The 23-year-old ⁠delivered an efficient display, keeping rallies short and dictating play without putting unnecessary strain ‌on his body.

Carlos Alcaraz's left thigh was heavily bandaged during his match against Flavio Cobolli. (Reuters: Guglielmo Mangiapane)

He carried that momentum into the second set, breaking for a 2-0 ‌lead and again to move 4-1 ahead before closing out a 65-minute victory.

Alcaraz finished with 29 winners to Cobolli's nine.

"It was a difficult match to see how I was going to feel on court and playing against Flavio is not easy," Alcaraz said.

"He is a great player and person off the court.

"I tried to play as ‌aggressively as I can, hit the ball as hard as I can.

"The way I felt on court today was incredible. I am getting more confident after every match and hopefully I can keep it going."

Alcaraz had already secured a place in the semifinals against Ben Shelton at the elite eight-player event.

The semifinal will be a re-match of the US Open quarterfinal between Shelton and Alcaraz.

While Shelton won that five-set clash in New York, Alcaraz recently got revenge in the Paris Masters final.

In the other semifinal, top-ranked Alexander Zverev will face either Medvedev or Tiafoe.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Sidelined Swans star on making first prelim in a 'really tough year'
World.content:
Right after Sydney upset Geelong in the AFLW semifinals last weekend, a photo was taken that perfectly encapsulated the moment for the Swans.

In it, injured star Ally Morphett is crying while holding a beaming Lexi Hamilton.

"I mean, [at] first glance, I hated the photo," Morphett laughed to ABC Sport. "I thought I looked absolutely terrible. But there's so much meaning and emotion behind it.

"I just care so much about the girls … I was so proud of them once they won because it was just an unbelievable game. I think it was one of the best games of the year."

Sydney booked its first preliminary final in the AFLW competition with an upset win over Geelong. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

With the victory, the Swans booked a spot in their first preliminary women's final in head coach Colin O'Riordan's first year at the helm.

Some AFLW pundits had questioned whether the Swans could go deep in finals without Morphett, who did her ACL in round 8.

"It's very bittersweet to be watching on the sidelines because all you want to do is be out there," Morphett said, adding it had been "probably the most emotional year of my life".

"But I was just so incredibly happy for all the girls. I think the difference in the way we play this year compared to previous years is we do it for each other, rather than worrying about how you personally play."

Chloe Molloy was the leading AFLW goal kicker for the 2026 season. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

The success has come while the club was repeatedly in headlines due to male players under a police investigation for allegations of a sexual assault and breaching club standards. The investigation is over and players will not be charged.

The saga has added extra emotional weight, Morphett said, but strengthened their bonds internally in the AFLW program.

"It's been a really tough year. Not just for our program, but also women amongst the whole organisation," Morphett said.

"When you go through adversity like that, it brings you closer together compared to other teams who don't really go through something like that and as significant as that.

"But I think vulnerability is such a massive strength, especially around strong women and so many of us, and that happening has brought us so much closer.

Ally Morphett says this year has made the Sydney Swans AFLW side even closer. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

"It's just brought so much care amongst the group between Colin, all the staff and the players. And all together as a whole program, we just care so much about everyone.

"It's been a massive [emotional] roller coaster. As for the football side of things and how we're performing, our connection has gone onto the field and the way that we go about it."

With the rehab group not travelling to Melbourne, Morphett will now have the tough task of watching her side face North Melbourne from home.

When the pair faced each other in round eight this year, the two-time reigning premiers in the Kangaroos won by 51 points.

Morphett knows it will be a huge challenge for the Swans, but also knows finals footy is a different game.

Sydney went down by 51 points when they played North Melbourne earlier this year. (Getty: Robert Cianflone/AFL Photos)

"Yes they're nervous, but I think everyone's more geed up than nervous. It makes us hungry, the fact that they're going for a three-peat, and we want to be the ones to stop them," she said.

"If we played how we did last weekend against the Cats, I think that it is very achievable.

"Finals footy is very much grit and desire, and we aren't the number one pressure team in the comp for no reason. So I think … Bloods [Swans] footy is finals footy, really. So I'm really excited to watch it."

World.title: Tim Tszyu hunting 'legacy-defining' win on Gold Coast
World.content:
Tim Tszyu knows all about the highs boxing can deliver.

He knows a fair bit about the lows, too.

Three years ago, Tszyu, the WBO junior middleweight world title holder, was eyeing up unification and US domination.

Three defeats in four fights later, his career was on the trash heap.

"You learn more about your character," Tszyu told ABC Sport from his Rockdale gym.

"You realise life isn't just going to go on an upward scale. It goes up and down. You've got to ride through the waves.

"One thing I learned was don't get too high from your wins, don't get too low from your losses, maintain a stable way of living and keep approaching every day with the foundation of something to work towards.

"That's how it's always been for me."

Tim Tszyu is headlining the event, with Jermell Charlo lower on the card. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Three wins later, including against American legend Errol Spence Jr, the 32-year-old is fighting for another world title, this time at the 160-pound-limit against WBA middleweight champion Erislandy Lara.

Not everyone is happy about Tszyu's return to the top.

"We all know he don't deserve a world title fight," American fighter Jermell Charlo told media on Wednesday via Zoom link from the United States.

"You didn't work your way up [at middleweight] for real. He fought a 147-pounder [welterweight] that just happened to overlap 154 [junior middleweight].

"Errol Spence wasn't the Errol Spence we all know, right?

"He can't beat Lara. Styles make fights, and this is just stylistically a bad fight for Tim.

"Lara's going to destroy Tszyu."

Tim Tszyu is leaving no stone unturned in his bid for glory. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Charlo, a former unified champion in Tszyu's former weight division, light middleweight, may have a vested interest in shooting down Tszyu's chances.

Tszyu was supposed to face Charlo in January 2023, but the bout collapsed after Charlo broke his hand in sparring.

Despite Tszyu still being keen, Charlo wanted to hunt bigger fish and stepped up two weight divisions to take on Canelo Álvarez in a big-money blockbuster.

The WBO were not amused, stripping Charlo of his title the second he stepped into the ring, elevating Tszyu.

Tszyu has rebuilt his reputation since, while Charlo has stagnated.

Tim Tszyu knows the threat Erislandy Lara poses. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Charlo has not fought since losing to Canelo, returning as the third-billed fight on December's spectacular Gold Coast card.

"Don't forget that, Charlo," Tszyu said, mockingly.

"You're on my undercard."

Tszyu's resurrection into a world title challenger has been nothing short of remarkable.

And although Lara will pose an enormous test of Tszyu's resilience, "He's going to present a lot of challenges," Tszyu noted, with the Australian backing himself to claim victory.

A big part of Tszyu's recovery has been his partnership with former three-weight world champion Jeff Fenech.

"He just came on board at a time where I really needed it," Tszyu said.

Tim Tszyu has been training with Jeff Fenech and Billy Hussein. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Despite that, Fenech has been dealing with several health challenges of late, including a third heart operation in October.

"I wouldn't say it impacted my training camp. I was more impacted personally because I felt like a lot was missing from Jeff," Tszyu said.

"But then when Billy [Hussein] came on board, we just started flowing with things, and we've just been working ever since."

Fenech is one of just two Australian male fighters to win championships in different weight classes (IBF bantamweight, WBC super-bantamweight and WBC featherweight), the other being Liam Paro (IBF super lightweight and welterweight titles).

"Playing it safe all the time is not the way I do things," Tszyu said.

"You got to chase the hard stuff. The tricky stuff. The legacy-defining type stuff."

Tech.title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.

The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.

All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.

You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder.

Thanks. Great to be here.

I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos.

I know.

It’s like a normal thing that happened.

It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.

[Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.

Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.

Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”

What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?

I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.

But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.

I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.

So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.

Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?

Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.

Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that.

Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year.

I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs.

Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work?

They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry.

But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today.

I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really. It’s the founders and this special trust, which we can get to in a second, that have the power.

But either way, they were all saying it doesn’t matter if shareholders have a say here really in voting. It’s about the fact that no matter who has a say, Anthropic is going to be under so much pressure to make money and to buy compute and catch up with OpenAI in that way, that this is going to be a huge reckoning for them. We’re probably going to see a lot of things fall by the wayside, maybe even some expensive safety efforts.

I want to come to the governance structure angle here. We live in a time of Nvidia scandals. Corporate governance is all the rage now. It’s the hottest topic in American business, but let’s come to that in one minute.

I just want to stay on “can you sell a token for a dollar more than it cost you to make it” for one more turn. It’s just the dumbest way of thinking about this. Anthropic rents capacity from big cloud providers, from hyperscalers. They run the GPUs in them. They pay for power, they pay for the GPUs. There’s some input cost and then they have to sell the token for more than all those input costs.

That is the dumbest way of thinking about their business. I promise you that they think about it in a more sophisticated way than that, but that is how I think about it. I was just at the Microsoft Ignite conference this week and I saw Satya Nadella and he was very clear to me and others that they’re going to try to bring the price of tokens down, that their whole system is designed to make all the AI vendors fungible underneath Copilot and they’ll pick the best model for the task and make sure you get the cheapest one for whatever it is you’re trying to do.

That seems totally at odds with what Anthropic needs to do, which is get more and more margin for every single token they sell so they can keep renting capacity from data centers or buy more chips than OpenAI or whatever it is they need to do. How are they structured to solve that problem? Is it just more people using AI or is it more expensive tokens?

I think it’s a little of both, and it’s interesting because Anthropic has been kind of sneakily trying to do this. We wrote a piece in the past year about how there was a big outcry, particularly focused on Anthropic, for passing on costs to consumers. Individuals who were customers of Anthropic were really mad because they felt like the prices were going up for the same stuff or for worse quality and that costs were just getting passed on to them.

This became a thing across the industry, a big outcry, but Anthropic bore the brunt of it. Anthropic had to have a public statement. They’re like, “Look, we’re going to work on this.” And they did roll it back a little, but I mean, they’ve got to keep doing it in some way.

The other thing they’re focused on is hoping that their models are going to be good enough that people just form an attachment — not emotionally, well maybe — but form an attachment to them and they can moat people in. They’re all about the moat these days: “We’ve got to build a moat.” OpenAI is about this, too. They want so much of your everyday life and business to be married to Anthropic’s tools that it’d be really hard to port it all over and you won’t want to and you’ll just keep paying. So that’s what they’re going for.

They’re also, of course, hoping that enterprise and government contracts are going to really make up a bunch of this, in which case you don’t have to worry quite as much about nickel-and-diming because they’ve got a lot of money. But I think that’s the interesting part here. When it comes to people that do care about the price a lot, they’re just trying to moat them in and hope for the best.

What’s interesting there is that consumers are sensitive to price in one way. I think Anthropic’s big business customers, which is where they’ve been historically focused, are sensitive to price in different ways.

If you’re paying Anthropic a lot of money, you might want to be able to switch providers quickly and you might demand data sovereignty and all this stuff that big enterprises are thinking about. Anthropic either has to deliver that, which would kill their moat for their big enterprise customers, or say, “We’re so good, you can’t have that.” I’m not sure that they can say the second one yet.

That’s why they’re marketing this safe, trustworthy AI line so deeply, because it’s the only thing they’ve really got going for them here. When you have an enterprise customer, most of the time you do have to give them data sovereignty. You can’t trade on their data. There’s a lot of stuff that Anthropic could be doing to make more money that they can’t do when someone is paying that much.

I think that’s really why they’re driving home this point of being the safe, trustworthy alternative because that’s the only thing that’s really going to get people to stick around, particularly if they also drive home the cybersecurity tools in an age when everything’s getting hacked all the time.

The other interesting thing is even not with huge enterprises, but with small to medium-sized businesses, I’ve been chatting with a bunch of them and they’ve all been creating their own internal tools to kind of track which tasks they need specifically to use an expensive Anthropic model for and which ones they can port over to maybe an open-source model or a really cheap model.

So a lot of companies like law firms — and people in a lot of different industries that have small to medium-sized businesses — are literally creating their own internal benchmarks about, “Okay, let’s save money as much as we can to just only put 10 percent of our tasks toward the expensive Anthropic model, and then this 40 percent can go to an open-source model and this 50 percent can go to a mid-tier, cheaper model.”

So that’s what’s really interesting to me. People are trying to figure this out on their own and not even sharing those benchmarks publicly because it’s their own way of budgeting.

I actually heard Nadella this week say every company will have its own set of evaluations and they will test the models against them and always use the most efficient one and this will become one of the major things that every company does.

The flip side to that is I’ve heard Anthropic executives say, “Well, you will always want the frontier model because your competitor will always be using the frontier model and if you use a cheaper one, you’ll be left behind.” And that has always seemed somewhere between naive and idealistic to me because I think a lot of companies do cheap things knowing that their competitors will also do cheap things.

I agree completely. Everyone’s being cheap.

Yeah, I think if you can get away with good enough, you’re going to find out exactly where good enough is and you will not assume that your competitor is going to eke out a 5 percent advantage by using a more expensive model. Somewhere on the margin is where all of the costs should be and the market will figure it out.

Exactly.

It just feels like the basics of the business, maybe on IPO day, the pressure isn’t on that, everyone’s just very happy and rich. The next quarter’s earnings are going to be where we start to see this shakeout. Can it keep growing the way it’s growing at the margins it needs to build everything, especially when its own suppliers are now major shareholders?

Totally. And we saw one quarter where they experienced huge growth and then the next quarter wasn’t that much. So yeah, I mean they’re going to have a lot to reckon with.

Let’s talk about the governance issues. Because of Nvidia, corporate governance is the hottest topic in American business. Like you said, OpenAI and Anthropic have some of the most complicated governance structures in history.

If you think that Anthropic’s future is to sell the best intelligence — the most capable, the most cutting-edge frontier, close-to-AGI intelligence possible — you would probably not do a bunch of safety work. You would probably not kill your margins on a bunch of researchers who are telling you to stop or slow down or not release the best model.

Anthropic is deeply committed to doing that. You and I have had conversations before about whether that can withstand the pressures of capitalism and growth. That was hard when they weren’t a public company, but now they are. Talk about Anthropic’s structure and how they’re trying to codify their commitment to safety.

Yeah, that’s a really great question. I just published a piece about this. It’s so interesting to me that Anthropic, despite seeing all the roller-coaster drama that OpenAI went through around the Sam Altman ouster and all of the restructurings that that company has gone through, Anthropic has a similarly unusual structure. And in a way it’s helpful because they’re not beholden, as we said, to shareholder pressure besides if shareholders start selling off their stock or don’t buy more.

But the two kinds of groups of people that have power over what happens at Anthropic are the founders and this group called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). Anthropic likes to market this as being like, “Oh, don’t worry about that the founders are doing what’s best for humanity but with no checks. We’ve got this trust above us that can appoint or remove us anytime.” As we’ll see in the movie Artificial, Sam Altman famously says, “Oh, well, the board can fire me whenever.” He says that a million times.

Now, Anthropic is implying the same thing: “Oh, we have this trust above us. They can remove or appoint the majority of board members,” even though it’s actually not all of them, but we’ll get to that in a minute. So this trust is a group of right now four people and none of them have a lot of AI experience. It’s [former Federal Reserve Chairman] Ben Bernanke, a foreign policy analyst named Richard Fontaine, an experimental physicist named Christopher Stubbs, and a former GiveWell executive named Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT.

I spoke to a couple of former Anthropic employees that left not too long ago and one of them said that this trust is kind of handpicked to not rock the boat at Anthropic. The founders appointed them. They’re not going to be appointing someone that’s going to probably disagree with them a lot.

Ironically, the trust doesn’t have the authority to step in on everyday decisions at Anthropic, unlike even the OpenAI nonprofit board that existed. They could say, “Oh look, don’t release this model. It’s too dangerous.” The trust doesn’t have any of those powers. All it can do is appoint or remove certain board members. Even then, they have to give 30 days’ notice to a small committee of the board, which includes Daniela Amodei, the chair of that little committee who is also a founder of Anthropic.

To oversimplify things, out of these seven board seats, the trust gets to pick three, the founders get to pick three, and then the kind of tie-breaking seat, the seventh one, the trust technically appoints, but they have to basically get founder approval to do it. So it’s one of these things that’s so complex, but when you really look at the nitty-gritty of it, the founders have pretty unchecked control here. I think that’s something that’s getting lost in the narrative of, “Oh, this trust is above us. Don’t worry.” Okay, well, they don’t really have much power to check you.

The founder control structure is the wildest thing I have ever read about in years of doing the show and thinking about business. Anthropic has seven founders. They have been issued a single share of stock that holds 50.1 percent of the voting power of the company. That is issued to a company called Founder LLC, and they’re the seven co-owners of Founder LLC.

How on earth does that work? Do they just all get together and then decide how to vote the one share of stock?

Yeah, it’s really interesting and that’s why I was kind of oversimplifying it a minute ago with who gets to choose this tie-breaking seat because it’s technically Founder LLC. It’s just a total mess. But when you really look at the simplified version, it’s that yes, through all of these weird structures and things they’ve done, they basically have pretty unchecked power and that’s the way they want it.

When I was talking to a former employee who recently left, they said it’s not necessarily that the founders have a financial interest in making the most money. In their eyes, it’s more that they have an interest in unchecked control. I think that’s a really important point here.

Some dissenters within the ranks of Anthropic think it’s not about them wanting to get rich, but rather it’s about them wanting that total control, which does track with a lot of their public statements. They say, “You can’t do safety from second place.” They’re all in on speeding up this race, but the problem is when you speed up the AI race, you’re speeding it up for everyone involved.

The safety piece is the really interesting portion of this to me because it’s the thing you would spend money on, absent some huge litigation drama or liability concern, that no other company would spend money on.

So let’s say it’s proven in court that model companies are liable for what people’s agents do. I think then all the model companies would build safety systems. They would have some big incentive to make sure their models are safe. That has not yet happened. We don’t know. There’s a big debate about safety and where the regulation will come from and what will create the incentives.

In the meantime, you’ve got seven founders holding a single share of stock who right now appear to be aligned on investing in safety in various ways inside of Anthropic. What happens if they start to disagree?

Yeah, that’s a great question. I think that the other interesting question here is what happens when you can explain away anything in the name of safety if you’re thinking it’s “for the greater good,” which as we know is a common villain trope in every movie. But it’s also one of Anthropic’s main things on its website. They’re like, “We want to do this for the greater good, for the global good.”

If you’re saying, “Hey, we have to win this race at all costs because we’re the only good guys and anyone else who wins it is going to do worse than us,” are you really the good guy at that point? And can’t you just explain away any single decision, even dropping some safety measures, as saying, “Oh, it’s slowing us down too much. We’re going to lose. We’ve got to win at all costs”? So you drop this or drop that. And then you look in the mirror at the end of the race and you say, “Oh, actually, we’re the exact same as the other company we’re trying to be different from.” I think that’s increasingly happening.

So I mean, right now they’ve said, “Look, we’re really committed to this.” You do have to remember that these people are almost religiously dedicated to this idea of safe AI. A lot of them think that AI systems are potentially conscious. I mean, this is by Anthropic founders’ own statements.

So I think that it’s not like they’re just secretly only trying to make money and just talking about safety and they don’t mean it. I think it’s more something a little more dangerous in that they want complete control because they believe that they have the right plan for AI safety and they will do it better than anyone else.

But as we know, absolute power corrupts absolutely. So a lot of Anthropic employees that I was talking to, former ones, were saying, “Yeah, it does not make sense that this industry is so unregulated. There’s no external regulation. Even if these seven people think they have the best idea for AI safety, okay, then prove it to someone else — that you shouldn’t be the only ones deciding this. Because you’re not elected.” So that’s the consensus among some.

They have a morally binding handshake agreement to allow external auditors, Hayden. It’s going to be fine.

Oh, yeah, with employee-level access.

Also, it’s called “Super Intelligence” now. It’s going to be totally fine. They all went to the White House and they looked deeply into each other’s eyes and said it was going to be fine.

Obviously Anthropic came up with this structure well before the events with Nvidia and Jensen Huang, but I can’t help but put them together in my head. They are happening at the same time. And Nvidia has a very traditional corporate governance structure.

Jensen owned 3 percent of the company, but he had a board of directors. The board of directors determined that he had violated the company’s code of conduct in some way. He resigned. It’s very obvious that he was thoroughly encouraged to resign, but that’s just normal corporate governance. That’s what you learn about in school. A company has a board of directors. Their number one job is to hire and fire the CEO.

That’s very different in Silicon Valley, right? Founder control of companies is a big story everywhere. Mark Zuckerberg famously has control over Meta, even though Meta shareholders repeatedly vote to remove him, which is one of the underemphasized stories in all of American business. Sergey Brin and Larry Page control Google.

Is this more in the, “We need to insulate our founders from the demands of the market and boards of directors” in classic Silicon Valley style? Or is it, “We need to insulate our founders and Dario from the demands of the market so we can stay focused on AGI and safety”? Because it feels like a combination of both.

It’s definitely a combination. I mean, they say it’s the latter. I think in a lot of ways it’s like the former. It’s totally a combination. I’d say it’s about 50/50. I mean, they want control so that they can focus on what they think is best and not lose control to someone that they don’t think knows best. But ironically, as we know, no one group of people should be in control of what is best here. So at least that’s what a lot of my sources say.

So I think that, yeah, I mean, it’s just a combination. Elon Musk famously won’t run a company that he doesn’t have voting control over. So I think it’s just a new Valley thing and it’s pervading here for a couple of different reasons.

There are seven of them. What seven different people do over the course of the next five to 10 years is as unpredictable as anything. What happens if one of them does something illegal or lies to the board or smuggles chips to China or anything? Is there some way to remove one of these founders from this LLC?

Yeah. I mean, allegedly the trust has the power to remove. They haven’t said whether they have the power to remove all of the board or just some, but in some way when you’re looking at the fine print of the S-1, basically if the trust gives 30 days’ notice to essentially Daniela Amodei and her other two people on this subcommittee, then they can suggest removal of a board member. Again, they can waive that 30-day notice if they deem it correct, if Daniela does.

But yeah, there’s a lot of fine print here. Essentially, yes, you can remove someone and there is stuff about that in the S-1 saying if they’ve done something illegal, if they’ve done something really bad, they can be removed, but it’s definitely not easy. It also depends on who it is, I think.

It’s interesting. I keep coming back to this because it is so complicated, it’s so unusual, and it is right next to the Nvidia situation where he materially misrepresented his relationship to the shareholders by having his PR people issue statements saying it was all normal. He had to admit that it wasn’t all normal and he was in fact involved in extramarital affairs and the board fired him.

I felt a little bad for that PR guy who had to put his name on all those statements that ended up being a lie.

I feel nothing. As the audience may know, as Hayden is well aware, we make all the PR people put their names on everything just in case something like this happens. That’s just a little bit of Verge trivia.

Anyhow, right, I mean, that’s just normal governance. Here you have a company where the only check might be the market itself, right?

Yep.

If they can’t sell tokens for more than what they make them for, they’re going to have to report that in the financials and the market might say this company is failing and pull all the money back. That is a very different kind of pressure.

If the only meaningful way that Dario might lose his job is if the company goes bankrupt and then the swirl of things is he’s got to buy chips before OpenAI can buy the chips, he’s got to increase the number of verticals that Anthropic competes in within the enterprise, and he also idealistically has to train the next model and the next model with RSI to get to AGI, it feels like actually the pressure is to go as fast as possible. If I just added that up, I would say I would not slow down ever.

Yeah. That’s why I say you can kind of explain away anything if you’re trying to be first, which they are. And they’ve been very public about that. Regarding the money thing, Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Law School, told me this week that the trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power and that you either trust that they’re going to balance the interest of society appropriately or you don’t.

But either way, the real constraint on whatever impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money. That’s the thing, Anthropic needs money. In a livestream recently, Dario told the CEO of JPMorgan Chase that compute is the “deepest business dilemma” that the company faces. Essentially if you buy too much, you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers.

Even more importantly, you can’t do the R&D. You can’t come up with new models. So they’re extremely compute-constrained, even maybe more so than OpenAI because OpenAI was made fun of for a long time for losing a ton of money, but they were investing a lot in compute. Anthropic did not do that as much, and now they’re having to pay the piper.

So it’s an interesting turnaround here. Hopefully for them and their interests, I guess, if they can get the compute they need. But as we know, the supply is a lot lower than the demand. So it’s just going to be interesting to see what they will do to make money and therefore money to buy compute.

It’s funny. A couple of weeks ago I told our colleague, Liz Lopatto, that the Anthropic IPO would be one of the biggest stories of the year. She was laughing at me today, because she says it’s not even the biggest story of the week because of Jensen Huang and Nvidia.

My argument — take it or leave it, and you can judge whether I’m correct — is that they are the same story. That if Nvidia’s financing architecture fails or wobbles because Jensen isn’t there to bully everyone into believing in it, then maybe you do have a glut of chips sitting in data centers without the appropriate permitting or power to light them up and the market for chips will change dramatically.

Maybe a company like CoreWeave does get way more wobbly or some of the already wobbly neoclouds start to get wobbly and the price of compute falls and lets Anthropic compete differently. Maybe a bunch of chips that were allocated to China on the gray market come flooding back to the United States.

That apparently will happen.

Right? So there’s a lot of ways the Nvidia story affects Anthropic’s financials. Has the company said anything about that yet? Is the market reacting to that in any way?

Not yet. They’ve just talked about how important compute is and that it’s going to be a really big issue for them. And Anthropic’s IPO, it has a lot of ties to Nvidia and there’s a lot of complexities here because Nvidia had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement on top of a $10 billion funding promise it made last year.

So they are in bed together, and that’s going to be interesting to see, too. The new CEO of Nvidia has made a lot of claims about diverting chips that were potentially going to China and bringing them back so they’re not doing that anymore.

Now we’re going to see if there’s more supply or not. Also, Jensen personally made some of these deals, especially with large financial institutions to fund the AI infrastructure buildout last August. So he’s wheeling and dealing a lot. And so it’s going to remain to be seen whether the new chief executive has that kind of power to wheel and deal and pressure people into doing stuff like this or not.

This is my last question. Obviously everyone’s just celebrating today. We are probably throwing the most cold water on this by noting that the structure of Anthropic is very odd. What should people be looking for? What are the signs that you’re looking for now that Anthropic is a stock that’s trading? What’s the relationship in your mind between the value of Anthropic stock on any given day and the broader AI story?

I think that stock is a little bit like benchmarks in the AI industry in that sometimes it doesn’t mean what you think it means and also it never means everything. So you always take it with a grain of salt. It’s all vibes based. It’s all hype. So people get scared, they sell, and people hear one good thing or a rumor and they buy. So I think it’s important to look at it and see what’s driving that fear or hype that day or that week. But it’s also really important to see what the company says in these reports and earnings calls.

That’s what I think is the most interesting. Not really the numbers all the time, but instead, what they try to sneak into these reports by saying, “Oh, we sidelined this team,” or, “We discontinued this safety initiative all in the name of being first.”

That’s the type of thing that I think we’re going to see a lot of and that’s what I want to watch for. Because the company that made its bed on safe AI is increasingly looking the same as OpenAI and is going to have a lot of swept-under-the-rug type of updates like that, if my sources are right.

You heard it here first. Former CNBC reporter Hayden Field says, look past the day-to-day swings into the fundamentals of the company. That’s good. Also, the stock market is only vibes. That’s the other thing I heard you say.

Yep. I mean, it’s controversial, but after being a financial reporter, yeah, I mean, there’s a lot of vibes there. It’s a lot of vibes.

Oh, I agree. I think sometimes the only thing they ask me to go on CNBC to say is this is just vibes, and then they usher me off the air very quickly.

Hayden, this is great. We’re obviously going to be talking about this story many times with you in the year to come. Hopefully we can do another straightforward business story and not just a soap opera one.

I’ll be here for both. We’ve got to do them both.

Amazing. Thank you so much, Hayden.

Thanks.
